en: The Fourth Quarter.
(Topic 1) It has been stated that the Vedic corpus exists for the sake of ritual action; therefore, everything [in it] must be for that purpose. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.1)

In this context, regarding all words such as *udbhid*, *soma*, and so forth—which are accepted either as injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or as names (*nāmadheya*)—and which are nominally inflected (*subanta*) and distinct from the word denoting the fruit, there arises a doubt as to whether they possess authority (*prāmāṇya*) or lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
Since no mode of authoritative validity is possible, they lack authority.

To explain: in cases such as "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" and "One should sacrifice with *soma*," these words like *udbhid* cannot function as *arthavādas* (eulogies), because no cognition of praise arises from them.
Furthermore, it is not so because there is no established status as a *mantra*;

for when these are uttered at the time of performance, since there is an absence of any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) indicating that the meaning they convey is an auxiliary to the sacrifice (*yāgāṅga*), it is untenable that they serve to remind one of the matters inherent in the performance.
Nor can they be included within the category of injunctions (*vidhi*).

Because, in the absence of words denoting desire (*kāma*) and so forth, there is no expression of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*); because, once the instrument (*karaṇa*) has been established by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) contained within a single word, it is impossible for these [other words] to establish that same instrument; and because established entities such as *soma* and the like cannot constitute the objective realization (*bhāvanā*) or the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) without an intervening operation.

If, however, [the word] were a name (*nāmadheya*), then precisely because it is non-different [from the sacrifice], the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) consisting of the assistance to the instrument and so forth would be untenable.
Nor should it be argued: "Even if connection with the *bhāvanā* is impossible in any way, let there be a connection with the sacrifice as its instrument";
for there can be no mutual connection between *kārakas* (factors of action).

Therefore, since it is impossible for [the sentence] to be connected with an action in any way, and since neither an injunction (*vidhi*) nor a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is expressed due to its not being a verb, and because no other mode [of meaning] can be defined, the conclusion reached was that it lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*). To this, [the reply is]: since it is impossible for that which has been taught by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) to lack authority, and since even though no other mode is possible, its inclusion within an injunction is clear, it must be so in that very case.

Thus it is established that its authoritative status is secured by avoiding all inconsistencies, whether as an injunction of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or as a name (*nāmadheya*), according to the method to be explained hereafter. // 1 // 17 //
Thus concludes the section on the authoritative validity of terms such as *udbhid*.
(B2) [An Examination of how the entire subject matter of this chapter constitutes a supplement to the first sūtra.
Here, the author of the Bhāṣya, having cited the example "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," asks: Are words such as *udbhid* injunctions regarding accessories (*guṇavidhi*)?

Having raised the doubt as to whether these are names of actions, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was established by the initial sūtra: "It has been stated that the Vedic corpus has a purpose; therefore, everything [in it] must be for that purpose. Then, by the subsequent sūtra: "Or rather, it should be a name, because what occurs in the restatement is not an injunction of something new" (Jaimini 1.4.2), the conclusion (*siddhānta*) was established that they are names.

Therefore, even though this investigation lacks utility for the means of knowing Dharma (*dharmapramāṇa*), its utility is established in both ways—either as a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*) or as a name (*nāmadheya*)—simply by virtue of the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*), just like an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Consequently, there is no risk of futility (*ānarthakya*). Since the authority of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) and of logical capacity (*sāmarthya*) has not yet been stated here in the form of an explanation of the sentence-meaning, [the discussion] will be undertaken in the second [book].

It is improper [to claim] that the examination of the meaning of sentences (*vākyārtha*) is incomplete because it would result in a lack of logical connection (*asaṅgati*) with the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*);
therefore, by the word *jijñāsā* (desire to know) in the aphorism "Then, therefore, the desire to know Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*), the meanings of all twelve definitions are generally proposed.
For this very reason, in the commentary on this [sūtra], the author of the Bhāṣya asks: "What is Dharma? and so forth.
"What are its characteristics?
What are its means of accomplishment?"—
thus has it been introduced.

In this regard, concerning the question "of what character [is it]?", by attaching the word *dharma* [to the suffix] *thamuñ*, which by its very nature signifies "of what measure," there is made an incidental determination of the mode [of proof], for the purpose of establishing the validity of the mode (*prakāra*) conveyed by the suffix *thamuñ*.
This serves as a preliminary promise of the subject matter of the first chapter, which consists in the investigation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding *dharma*.
However, it is not the direct subject matter of the chapter.

Even there, in the second sutra, by means of the word *codanā*— which denotes an impelling statement consisting of an injunctional prescription (*vidhyuddeśa*) through the etymological derivation "that by which one is impelled" (*codyate 'nena*)— the author first asserts the authority of those parts of the Veda that consist of injunctions,
and that very point is established at length by the first quarter of the verse.

Then, once the meaning promised in the second sūtra has been established, the author again considers the authority of the *arthavādas* and *mantras*— which were promised in the first sūtra as being distinct types of evidence for *dharma* and as specific components of the Veda, similar to *codanā*. Thus, when the authority of the threefold Veda has been considered in that same manner, and since there is an absence of any *smṛti* rooted in mere names [of deities], [the discussion proceeds].

The authority of that other means of knowledge in the form of Dharma— consisting of Smṛti which subsists upon the three Vedas— which was promised in the first Sūtra, was examined in the middle of the third Pāda, prior to the inquiry into names. Following that, there is now the examination of the status as a "name" of those very names, which constitute another means of knowledge for Dharma as promised in the first Sūtra.

Having established that [the Veda] is included within the injunctive portion (vidhyuddeśa) because it lacks the opposition of the three types of praise and so forth previously set forth, its authority alone is now demonstrated here.

Thus, since the entire chapter is indeed a supplement to the first sūtra, the author of the Vārttika intends that the investigation of authority and non-authority is necessarily appropriate in the first chapter; keeping this intention in mind, he begins the analysis of the topical section (adhikaraṇa).
"Here."

(The justification is as follows: one sūtra functions by focusing on the manner in which the authority of the name is established, while another sūtra proceeds for the purpose of determining that [name] through a "cleaning of the granary" (*koṣṭhaśodhanikā*); this is the method of interpretation.

Although, according to the principle stated in the *Arthavādādhikaraṇa*, once the general utility is established, a specific investigation conducted as a "cleaning of the granary" would not be irrelevant; yet...

Nevertheless, since this [third] sūtra cannot be a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)— because it lacks the character of being a statement of a quality-injunction (*guṇavidhi*) that contradicts the status of the name of the sūtra,

and because it would be inappropriate to produce an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādaka*) within the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)— the unity of the topic (*ekādhikaraṇya*) is not tenable. The point is that,

by establishing two separate prima facie arguments for these two sūtras, it is proper that there be a division of topics (*adhikaraṇabheda*), as the intent is to present two distinct final conclusions for these two sūtras.

In this first section (*adhikaraṇa*), having accepted that this inquiry— concerning the nature and object of validity (*prāmāṇya*) established by the consensus of ritualists— is settled even without deliberation regarding both positions, it is investigated whether the name [of a sacrifice] is a mode of the validity of *dharma* or not.
This is because, in the phrase "of what characteristic" (*kathaṃlakṣaṇaḥ*), the suffix *thamuñ* expresses a mode (*prakāra*), and since a mode also functions as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, the refutation of the view of the author of the Nyāyasudhā— who argues that there is no inconsistency because [the term] is used in its three-quarter sense— should be sought in the Kaustubha itself.
(The analysis of the subject matter of this section, including the refutation of other views:

The phrase "other than the word denoting the fruit" (*phalapadātirikta*) is stated to indicate that [the passage] is not a subject for inquiry, because neither of the two possible modes—being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) nor being a name (*nāmadheya*)—is possible in the case of a word expressing a fruit.
Furthermore, the term "fruit-word" (*phalapada*) is also an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for words denoting a cause (*nimitta*), an object of refinement (*saṃskārya*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the *udbhid*, *soma*, etc.," it was stated that words for place and time—such as "on level ground at full moon"—are not examples here because, even if they were injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*), the possibility of them being names (*nāmadheya*) is untenable.
That is incorrect;
for the examples here consist precisely of those words distinct from mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and injunctions, by way of being either injunctions of qualities or names.

It has been indicated that by accepting their inclusion within injunctions (*vidhi*), the establishment of their authority (*prāmāṇya*) is possible even in these cases; furthermore, since it will be established in subsequent sections that they are names (*nāmadheya*), and since their status as injunctions is established by implication through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) when other grounds for them are absent, it is justified that they fall within the scope of injunctions.

(An exposition on the commencement of the topical section [adhikaraṇa] for the purpose of determining the mode of authority even for terms such as *udbhid* and *soma*, despite their being included within the injunction to study [the Veda]):

Although, in this topical section, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on futility does not arise—since, by the force of the injunction to study, their purposefulness is established just like that of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—nor is there here a challenge [to the Veda's authority] through the impossibility of an alternative application, as occurs in the case of *arthavādas* and mantras where no other function is possible due to the absence of a means; nevertheless, [the discussion proceeds].
Since the authority of words such as *udbhid* is established even by their being injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*),

and since the specific nature of the door [of interpretation]— namely, their status as names (*nāmadheya*)— will be demonstrated through the refutation of the suspicion that they are injunctions of qualities within those very four specific sub-sections (*adhikaraṇa*),
it is not possible here to compose this first section in the manner of the specific sub-section on explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Nevertheless, even for words such as *udbhid* and others whose purposes are established by that injunction, their status as valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is established by first inferring a purpose—since the specific modes mentioned previously (namely, the manifestation of praise for the subject of the injunction) are impossible—and then determining whether they fall within the scope of the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) through one of two specific doors: being a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*) or being a name (*nāmadheya*).

It is precisely for this reason that the author of the Vārttika desists once the inclusion within the injunctive statement has been proven; with this in mind, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) beginning with the word "prakāra" (mode).
(The meaning of the section and the distinction between the subjects of the first and second chapters:

Here, it should be understood that although there is no immediate connection due to its belonging to a different section, there is no defect in the fact that the determination of the authority of words constitutes the subject matter of this section.

Thus, having resolved the objection by including [the term] within the injunction (*vidhi-uddeśa*), the intention is that in the subsequent sections (*adhikaraṇas*), its inclusion therein is established as being a name (*nāmadheya*) through the removal of the suspicion that it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*); therefore, everything is faultless. This is the sense.
(The uselessness of terms such as *udbhid* and *soma* as mere eulogies:

Since it must be established that [these terms] do not fall within the scope of the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), he first refutes their status as *arthavāda* (explanatory passages) in order to dismiss the notion that they might be perceived as eulogies based on the connection with the quality of being the "agent of breaking open" (*udbhedana*). He does so by stating: "Because of the cognition of praise...
It is not the case that something becomes an *arthavāda* merely by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with an injunction.
Otherwise, terms such as "desiring prosperity" (*bhūtikāma*) and so forth would also fall under that [category],
but rather they function as supplements to an injunction (*vidhiśeṣatvena*); for this [text] is not itself a supplement to an injunction.
The cognition of praise, consisting in the mention of a relationship between a quality and its possessor, does not arise from a single word contained within the injunctive portion [of the Veda].

Even if it were to arise, since the nominative case would prevail—as in the case of "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest"—the status of the instrumental case used [in the passage] as an instrument would be untenable; thus, the meaning is that it cannot be an *arthavāda* (explanatory eulogy).

He states that there is no inclusion among the mantras because of the impossibility of its being a primary mantra— due to the absence of the defining characteristic of a primary mantra consisting in being the object of the consensus of those proficient in such [texts] as "mantra," or the absence of the pervasive definition consisting in being distinct from being a prescription or a supplement to one—
by saying: "due to the absence of the established status of being a mantra."

He states that even for these [formulas], although they lack the status of being primary mantras (*mukhyamantra*)—as is the case with *ūha*, *pravara*, and *nāmadheya* formulas—they can nonetheless possess the status of secondary mantras (*gauṇamantra*), because they perform the function of a primary mantra by serving as reminders of the matters to be performed;
thus he says: "of these... (*eteṣām*).
(An argument establishing that [the mantra] is useless both as a mantra and as part of an injunctive statement:
First of all, it is not possible for it to serve as a reminder of a matter to be performed by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with a Brāhmaṇa passage;

for a Brāhmaṇa sentence such as "One desiring cattle should sacrifice" is injunctive in nature and is not to be employed at the time of the ritual action, and therefore it is illogical for this [mantra], which has entered into a single syntactical unit with that [Brāhmaṇa], to be so employed.
Nor can it be [the case] by way of being separate;
for since this object of denotation, such as the spade and so forth, is not enjoined as an instrument (*karana*) in the ritual action, it is incapable of being manifested.

Furthermore, it cannot be justified as a mere reminder (*smāraka*) through the assumption of an injunction regarding a substance based on the wording of the mantra—just as in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja*—in order to fulfill its status as an auxiliary (*anga*) to the sacrifice understood from proximity (*sannidhi*).

The point is that since it is impossible for a substance (*dravya*) to be syntactically connected either to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) or to the sacrifice (*yāga*), it is untenable to postulate an injunction for it; furthermore, because the expectancy [for a means] regarding the production of the sacrifice is satisfied by the very substance implied by the sense of the context, it is not proper to connect it by postulating another expectancy for the *bhāvanā* on the strength of that [substance]. He rejects its inclusion within another part of the Veda in the form of an injunctive statement with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
(The justification for the seen purpose of the injunction to study in the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa]). This concludes the prima facie view of the section with its clear wording.
Nor does this result in the subversion of the seen purpose of the injunction to study as established in the prima facie view; [for that purpose remains intact].
Even in the case of recitation (*pārāyaṇa*), there is a refutation of its having a visible purpose consisting in the utility of practice and swiftness;

for since it is established that even in recitation it serves a visible purpose in the form of utility and swiftness of practice, the words such as *udbhid* are not authoritative [as names of sacrifices]. This is the meaning.
(The Siddhānta by way of inclusion within the injunction):

Even though the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) pertaining to study has been established, he states the Siddhānta—beginning with the words "adhyayana"—to show that there is indeed authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*) so as not to undermine the previously proven fact that study aims at the knowledge of a purposeful meaning.
In this context, the phrase "even though other modes are impossible" means "even though other alternative modes are impossible."
Thus ends the first section concerning the authoritative validity of terms such as "udbhid" and others.
— — — — — (B1) (Section 2) Or rather, it is a name.

Henceforth, this section begins for the purpose of clearing the "storehouse" [of doubt], as to where there is the status of being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhitva*) and where there is the status of being a name (*nāmadheyatva*).

Thus, in this context, regarding words such as *udbhid* and others which function equally with respect to both a quality and an action, when considering whether they serve to provide a quality to be enjoined or are names, since it is well-known— based on the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "the root *bhid* means 'to split'"— that they denote tools such as spades capable of splitting, they would [initially] be considered names.
Furthermore, because [the alternative] would result in redundancy, it is more logical that this is indeed an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*).
In that regard, there is one position: that the very action, qualified by the accessory, is enjoined with reference to the fruit.
There is another position: that, by way of restating the previously mentioned Soma sacrifice, only the accessory is enjoined.

Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (vinigamanāviraha); for it is precisely the specific proximity of the *itikartavyatā* (the procedure) that serves as the regulator of the injunction regarding the ritual act (*karmavidhi*).
And thus, the word denoting the fruit is not rendered purposeless.

By the statement, “The Jyotiṣṭoma [is enjoined] for all [desires],” it is understood that it serves the purpose of all fruits; therefore, the word *yajati* functions as an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) for the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā) of a sacrifice that brings about the fruit of cattle.

For this very reason, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the mention of a qualified object. Nor is there any predominance of the Soma [enjoined] in the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).
Because a spade or similar tool, which is enjoined with reference to a specific application for one desiring cattle, sets aside the soma and other items that are enjoined in a general sense.

In reality, however, the third position is that it is precisely the quality of the spade and so forth, as dependent upon the Soma sacrifice under discussion, that is enjoined for the sake of the result. And since it is optional (kāmya), it follows that there is a sublation of the obligatory (nitya) Soma sacrifice. To this we reply: this is not an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi), because of the resulting complexity (gaurava).
For instance, in all cases, the first mode of injunction consists in enjoining a productive activity (bhāvanā) where the root-meaning itself is the instrument—as in, "One should offer the Agnihotra."
Another type of injunction has a different object (*uddeśya*): for example, "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
This is weaker because it depends on another word expressing the object of the injunction.

The third type is an injunction of a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) that has the meaning of a verbal root as its object and a different instrument (*karaṇa*); for example, "One should offer [the oblation] with curd."

In this case, because the status of being the object of injunction (*vidheyatā*) does not reside in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and because it resides instead in the meaning of another word, it is even weaker than that.

Having accepted that the verbal root serves merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), the fourth type of injunction is one where a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is enjoined with one thing as its objective (*uddeśya*) while having another as its instrument (*karaṇa*)—as in: "One desiring sensory power should sacrifice with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*).
In this instance, because the meaning of the verbal root is not connected even as the objective, it is even weaker than that.

The fifth [type of injunction] arises from the prescription of a *bhāvanā* (productive operation) wherein the object of the verbal root is qualified by a quality—as in "One should sacrifice with *soma*.
Because it involves the additional conceptualization of an injunction for the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-vidhi*), it is weaker than even that [fourth type].
The sixth, mentioned previously, is that which is directed toward another [object]—as in "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya."
However, [the opponent] is entirely weak.
Thus, if a sacrifice distinguished by the quality of *udbhid* were enjoined with reference to the fruit, there would be excessive complexity due to resorting to the sixth type of injunction;
furthermore, because the quality would not be syntactically connected to the sacrifice, there would be the fault of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (implication of the sense "possessing that").
For when the bhāvanā is already occupied by having the meaning of the verbal root— expressed in the same word— as its instrument, it is not possible for a quality (guṇa) to serve as the instrument.

Therefore, since that quality must necessarily connect with the sacrifice, and because a sacrifice is itself a factor of action (kāraka), and since it is impossible for factors of action to be related to one another, the ancient teachers maintain that a possessive indication (matvarthalakṣaṇā)— as in "by means of a sacrifice characterized by the udbhid" or "with soma"— is indispensable, just as in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with soma."

In reality, however, even in the case of the example, it will be explained in various places that *soma* is construed with the *bhāvanā* precisely as an instrument (*karaṇa*), and this is logical; for even when a *bhāvanā* is already occupied by one instrument, the construction of another instrument—though defined by a different [action]—as a mode (*prakāra*) within that *bhāvanā* is possible.
Indeed, the status of being the instrument of the sacrifice (*yāga*) is not defined by the *bhāvanā*.
Rather, it is defined by heaven;
and therefore, just as when something is defined by another, its status as an instrument (karaṇatva) is connected to the productive urge (bhāvanā) as a qualifier (prakāratayā).

In the same way, the status of *soma* as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) relative to the sacrifice is also established in both cases; and since the respective status of being the qualifier (*nirūpakatva*) is obtainable through a subsequent understanding (*pārṣṭhika-bodha*), there is no contradiction whatsoever. Thus, although there is no possessive indication (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*) even in this view, nevertheless, [the fault] arises from the injunction of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-vidhi*).
The burden of enjoining a *bhāvanā* qualified by both a quality (*guṇa*) and a sacrifice (*yāga*) cannot be set aside.

And just as it has been stated in the *Kaustubha* regarding "assumption" (*kalpanā*) and so forth— that even when the initial connection with the *bhāvanā* is accepted, at the time of the second cognition, the assumption of the possessive sense (*matvartha*) arises— so too, accepting inferior modes of injunction for the second and third [cases] is a defect.

And it was accepted as such [a name] only in the case of *dadhi* (curd), *soma*, and so forth, because of their extreme conventional usage (*atyanta-rūḍhatva*) there, which precludes them from being names [in other contexts]. However, in the present case, since the word can function as a name for the ritual action (*karman*) as well— by the same etymological derivation (*yoga*) through which it applies to a spade (*khanitra*), namely the analysis "that by which the fruit is *udbhidyate* (pierced/produced)"— there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in accepting the second type of injunction (*vidhi*).
Furthermore, the root *bhid* does not have "rending" as its only power, because it is listed in the Dhātupāṭha simply as *bhid*;
for it is established among grammarians that the phrase "rending" is merely an indicator of one possible meaning (*śakyārtha*) of the root.
Therefore, because the term is employed even in the sense of "producing" as it is in the sense of "tearing apart," its function is identical in both cases. Nor is the name meaningless,
for it serves a purpose in contexts such as the initial mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
In some cases there is the connection with a result—as in "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa";
and in some cases there is the connection with an accessory—as in "Having completed the Paurṇamāsī, he subsequently offers the Vaimṛdha.
And in the present case, the very purpose is the establishment of difference by means of the name.

Otherwise, since the connection between a quality and a fruit would apply to the very action under discussion, there could be no status as a distinct action. Nor does the assumption of a conventional (rūḍhi) meaning for the word in a new action follow from the fact that the etymological (yoga) sense of "producing the manifestation of a fruit" is over-extensive— leading to the undesirable consequence that words like *soma* would also have such a conventional meaning— because it is already established that in all cases of both etymological and conventional usage, the cause is simply prior usage, and such a cause is not assumed here.
The purpose is clear. // 2 // 18 //

Thus ends the second section concerning the name *udbhid*. (B2) [The Determination of the Basis for the Discussion of the *udbhid* Sentence Itself: Although its authority has been stated without specifying the particular means [of its application], it does not become firm without such specification; for this purpose, he indicates another section with the words "henceforth."

In that regard, although words such as *citrā* could serve as examples even among those devoid of other scriptural texts that clarify their meaning, it is difficult to establish them as names (*nāmadheya*) because that would require overcoming worldly convention and depending on auxiliary factors such as syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, setting those aside, since the application of the word is based on the connection of its constituent parts (*avayava-artha-yoga*),
and because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) supported merely by the contingency of implying a possessive sense (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*), [the discussion] begins first with...
He shows that these serve as examples because they are easy to examine, stating: "In that regard, here... (tadiha).
Because it is well known as being a statement.

Now, one might object: "Since it lacks conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) as a collective form like the word *vrīhi* (rice), how can it denote a spade? To dispel this doubt, it is stated that "the root *bhid* means 'cleaving' (*vidāraṇa*)," and so forth.
(An exposition that the word *udbhid* denotes only a digging instrument and not an action):
Thus, with the prefix *ut* signifying upwardness, the root *bhid* signifying cleaving, and the suffix *kvip* denoting the agent, [the term applies] to an agent capable of performing that [action].

In the case of the verbal root *khan* with the suffix *kvip* (*khān*), it is appropriate that its well-known conventional meaning as "a spade capable of digging upward" is understood through the form of the whole by means of the well-known meaning of its parts.

However, in the case of the object (the fruit), since it lacks the status of being the agent of upward splitting, one might attempt to justify it through etymological derivation (*yoga*) as "that which somehow splits forth or manifests the result. But in doing so, because this would necessitate a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding manifestation, there would be the undesirable consequence of overriding the well-known conventional meaning of the parts as understood from common usage and grammar.

The meaning is that, in order to avoid that [objection], one would have to resort to the assumption of a conventional meaning (rūḍhi), as in the case of words like *paṅkaja*; rather than that, it is more appropriate to accept the meanings understood from the individual parts of the word by means of their already established etymological powers (*avayavaśakti*).

(Refutation of accepting the status of a name even on the basis of the connection with the commonality of action): Granted that, for the sake of maintaining grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), some kind of occurrence of the mere etymological meaning of the parts might be possible in the case of a sacrifice;
nevertheless, he states the refutation against accepting it as a name on that basis: "If it were a name... (*nāmadheyatve*).

The meaning is as follows: since the determination of the specific [sacrifice] is established by the force of the injunction itself, even the name—being the genus *yāgatva* (sacrificeness) which consists of the general form of individuals delimited by that genus—cannot effect the determination of the specific; therefore, if it were intended for the determination of a specific individual, it would be redundant.

However, under the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), it possesses purposefulness because it provides the substance required by the sacrificial productive operation (*yāgabhāvanā*), and it achieves the state of inducing a specific activity in the person.

(Justification of the view that it is an injunction of a quality [guṇavidhi], by refuting the definition of "object" [artha] as established in the Siddhānta): As for the position here in the Siddhānta—that although all kārakas are connected with the productive operation (bhāvanā), because the productive operation is already occupied by the sacrifice as its instrument (karaṇa) expressed within the same word, a quality cannot be connected as an instrument; and because the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), being itself a kāraka, cannot also be connected therein—

If that [direct denotation] were impossible, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position would result in a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the possessive sense (*matvartha*) in the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), which is subordinate to the predominant suffix.

That is not tenable; for just as the sacrifice is connected to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) as its instrument by virtue of being defined in relation to heaven, so too the substance (*guṇa*, e.g., *soma*) can be logically connected to the *bhāvanā* as an instrument through a distinct operation.

Consequently, even though the sacrifice serves as the instrument of the *bhāvanā* by way of producing the fruit, substances such as *soma* function as separate instruments, just as vessels and the like serve as separate loci (*adhikaraṇa*).

Since there is no obstacle to the connection with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) by way of the accomplishment of the sacrifice (*yāga*), and in order to maintain that very connection with the *bhāvanā* first apprehended, a subsequent connection with the sacrifice is postulated for the sacrifice itself—just as in the case of the "red one-year-old cow" (*aruṇaikahāyanī*).

Thus, intending that there is no resulting recourse to possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), he establishes the first position, namely the view of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), with the words: "And in that case... (*tatra ca*).
(Refutation of the implication of possessive sense even in the case of subsequent cognition:

Nor does it follow that at the very time of subsequent syntactic connection (*pārṣṭhikānvaya*), there would be the undesirable consequence of employing a possessive sense (*matvartha*) that was not heard [in the text]; for at that stage, the connection of the accessory with the sacrifice is logically established precisely through its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*), which is explicitly stated.
For at that time, the sacrifice does not possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*),

such that there would be no syntactic connection due to a lack of expectancy; rather, it possesses the status of an object (*karmatva*) by virtue of having the nature of an end (*sādhyatva*) implied by the sense of the context.
Therefore, the meaning is that even in this view, there is no possibility whatsoever of the fault of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication of possessive meaning).
(Regarding the view that these are injunctions of accessories according to the *jyotiṣṭoma* context in the *Tāṇḍya* recension:
Therefore, although there is no indication by possessive implication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) in a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*),

nevertheless, because these sentences are recited immediately after the *jyotiṣṭoma* in the *Tāṇḍya* recension, they function solely as restatements (*anuvāda*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice under discussion.
Intending that this will be an injunction of an accessory (guṇavidhāna), just as in the case of "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), he states another alternative: "Or rather... (*athavā*).

(Regarding the refutation of the objection that there would be a necessity for possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) even under the view that this is an injunction of a quality, in accordance with the Vārttika beginning with "vidhāna eva" [Vārttika 1.4.2]):

Although, because the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the original injunction, and since here too it is an instrument, there would be the contingency of possessive indication when connecting the quality by way of restating what is already established; nevertheless, since that which has not been accomplished cannot function as an instrument, its status as the goal (*sādhya*) is understood through logical implication (*arthākṣepa*). Thus, by adopting that state [of being the goal], there is no inconsistency in the connection of the quality with the sacrifice as the instrument.

As for the Vārttika which states: "Whether in an injunction (*vidhāna*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*), the sacrifice (*yāga*) is intended as the instrument (*karaṇa*); in its proximity, that which ends in the third case does not lose its status as denoting that [instrument]," this—by virtue of the second half of that verse—refers to cases such as "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa on level ground," where there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a name ending in the third case.

In this context, it is intended to mean that there is a restatement (anuvāda) precisely of the status as an instrument (karaṇatva) understood from the originative injunction (utpattivākya), and not of the status as an end to be accomplished (sādhyatva) which is merely implied by the sense.

Nor should it be argued: "Even if [the *jyotiṣṭoma* sentence] were an originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), since terms such as *jyotiṣṭoma* function as qualifiers (*upapada*), this very case could serve as an example for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

Furthermore, in that case, because of the requirement of the word denoting the fruit (*phalapada*), the sacrifice must be the instrument (*karaṇa*); consequently, the connection of the quality would be untenable, resulting in the necessity of assuming a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). This objection cannot be maintained.

Where the secondary meaning (*upapada*) is conventionally established in its quality (*guṇa*), and its application to the action (*karman*) is impossible even through etymological derivation (*yoga*),

there— in the case of "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*)— since the assumption of a previously unknown power (*śaktyantara*) is more cumbersome than accepting possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), and since there is no obstacle to that very [sentence] being an originative injunction of the rite (*karmotpattividhi*), the meaning is that an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is appropriate here for the rite enjoined by that [originative injunction].
(Refuting the status of the *udbhid* sentence as an originative injunction and establishing its status as an injunction of a subsidiary quality:
"The procedure."

Since an injunction regarding a quality (guṇavidhi) is impossible in the absence of an injunction regarding an action (karmavidhi), and since some injunction of an action must necessarily be accepted, it follows that—given the proximity of the Jyotiṣṭoma sentence and the fact that many subsidiary procedures such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā are prescribed therein, and because those constitute an indicative mark of what is to be performed—the status of being the injunction of that very action belongs to it alone, according to the principle: "By virtue of its abundance, [the injunction belongs] to that which is mentioned in both texts. This is the meaning.
In various places it will be explained that, according to the Bhāṣya, the Vārttika, and other texts, even *soma* is construed solely as the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

In the seventh and ninth chapters, the Bhāṣyakāra refutes the connection of the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) with the root-meaning by means of the expression "one should sacrifice thus" (*yajetaittham*), establishing instead the connection with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) as "one should act thus" (*itthaṃ kuryāt*).

Even in the case of "One should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), according to the method explained in the *Tadbhūta-adhikaraṇa*, the root-meaning and its factors (*kārakas*)— being first connected to the *bhāvanā* without being mutually related to one another, like the red color (*aruṇā*) and the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*)— subsequently provide mutual assistance.
And so, the author of the Vārttika will state in the seventh and ninth [books] that there is no injunction of the meaning of the verbal root as qualified by *soma*, and so forth;

likewise, in the section on the Āghāra and Agnihotra, because the reasoning is equal to that of the *soma* sacrifice, it is established in the eleventh section for the purpose of demonstrating that the mantra of threshing—which is connected to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—is not repeated at every striking.
Likewise, in the seventh [book]: "After the connection with the productive operation, the connection with the two factors [the means and the result] follows as a matter of course."

The meaning is that, subsequently, in the *Śāstradīpikā*, it will be stated with the words "Whence [is there]... and so forth, that the application of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) is suspected during the interval between ritual acts.

Thus, having demonstrated through the refutation of the views of the predecessors that the objection regarding the non-occurrence of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) applies to the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he now says "And as... in order to refute what was stated—that even at the time of the subsequent cognition, there is no occurrence of that [indication].
(An examination of the necessity of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* [indication of possession] in the statement "one should sacrifice with soma" at the time of determining the sequence of subsequent relations.

This is the meaning: although all *kārakas* are first connected with the *bhāvanā* (productive operation), nevertheless, because a connection with a productive operation that lacks an object is impossible, there arises a requirement for an activity residing in the *soma* and so forth. Prior to this, however, there exists a requirement for the defining correlates (*nirūpaka*) pertaining to the fruit being the object and the sacrifice being the instrument.

Since both the sacrifice and the fruit are understood through the hearing of the same word, when the subsequent relationship between the fruit and the sacrifice arises, the sacrifice— already understood as an instrument— is perceived as the object (*karman*). Since it must be connected with other factors such as the spade as an instrument,

and since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible between two things with different referents, it is necessary to assume an unexpressed possessive suffix (*matvartha*) in order to allow for a connection by way of a general relation.

Furthermore, since it is logically impossible for a sacrifice that has not yet been accomplished to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*), once its status as the object (*karman*) is understood, at the time when other factors such as the spade (*khanitra*) are connected to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), they must be construed through their very nature as instrumental causes (*kāraṇatva*) and so forth, as heard in the text, precisely at the time of the injunction of the qualification. Therefore, at the time of this subsequent connection (*pārṣṭhikānvaya*), one must accept the form "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somavatā yajeta*); thus, the indication of the meaning of the suffix (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is unavoidable.
(Justification for the scriptural application of Soma in the view that there is no indication of possessive meaning):

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of Soma’s application being based on syntactical connection (*vākyīya-viniyoga*) in our view; for even if that consequence were to arise, it would only occur if one accepted the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) at the very outset, at the time of connecting [Soma] with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), in order to effect that connection.

Because, from the very outset, the connection of the factors of action (*kāraka*) with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is directly expressed by the Vedic word (*śrauta*), even without resorting to secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and disregarding their mutual relationship;

and because, subsequently, at the time of the secondary connection between the fruit and the sacrifice, it would be impossible for all the factors of action to be connected with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) through secondary indication based on possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
(The manner of establishing *matvarthalakṣaṇā* according to the view that it is a qualified injunction, as found in the *Kaustubha*:

Nor should it be argued: "At the time of the connection with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), the instrumental character of *soma* and other factors is already understood; how then can there be a cognition of their relation to the sacrifice when they are not yet presented for connection with the sacrifice?"—for there is no such inconsistency, since they are presented in the general form of a relationship characterized by possession (*matvartha*).

Alternatively, since the presence [of the meaning] is established by forming a single composite sentence such as "by means of a sacrifice characterized by Soma," so too in the case of the single sentence concerning the red [cow], one should see the formation of a sentence with an elided possessive suffix (*matup*)— namely, "that which is red is the one-year-old [cow]. Thus, the meaning is that it has been stated in the *Kaustubha* that, under the view of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the occurrence of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is unavoidable.

[This is] by way of the etymological derivation: "the determination of the meaning of the word *udbhid*—which is unknown and doubtful—is achieved through its grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj*," which establishes its status as a name (*nāman*).

The meaning is that [the word *yāga*] is so called because the fruit (*phala*) is "broken forth" (*udbhidyate*) or produced (*utpādyate*) by means of it; or else, according to the etymological derivation, it is that which "breaks forth" the fruit.

Otherwise, since the grammatical rule prescribes the suffix *kvip* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), demonstrating an etymology in the sense of the object (*karman*) would result in an inconsistency.
This is the point: "A word whose connection is unknown or doubtful [is explained] through well-known [synonyms], provided there is no separate hearing [of the word]."

In accordance with the method stated in the Vārttika—“That which is determined [by convention] is established as such, and it is not removed from its own meaning”—words such as *udbhid* lack a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) toward objects like a spade; furthermore, because they lack usage in common worldly parlance even through the connection of their constituent parts (unlike words such as *pācaka*), their meaning is unknown.
As for the passage: “The strength of the gods was indeed enveloped by darkness; there was a covering, and within that was another substance belonging to the cow... [and so forth].

In the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), "The gods were unable to split [it]; they said to Bṛhaspati, 'Release these [cows]'; he, by means of *udbhid* itself, caused the strength to be displaced," one understands that splitting—which is synonymous with the displacement of strength consisting of a hole filled with cattle—is the *pravṛttinimitta* (the basis for the application of the term).

However, because that passage lacks independence as a statement of its own meaning (*svārthaparatva*), there is no authority for such a meaning, and thus it is not useful [for establishing the definition].

Likewise, even in the absence of usage like that of the word "pika" and others, since application is possible in a sacrifice simply through the connection with the meaning of its constituent parts—as in the case of the word "khanitra" (a spade)—there remains ambiguity, as in the case of words such as "akṣa.
Therefore, it must be determined by its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the well-known root *yaj* ("to sacrifice").
"Even in the case of production" means that when a previously non-existent entity is produced by someone, it is used [linguistically] as "this was brought forth by this. This is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "at the time of the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth": the meaning is that [the name] is purposeful because it serves as a concise designation required by the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) at the time of execution.
The word "yathā" (as) means as follows:

if the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* were not a name (*nāmadheya*), then because there would be no distinction from the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), the auxiliary rites such as the *prayājas* would be included by virtue of being common to all six sacrifices, resulting in the undesirable consequence that all of them would be connected to the fruit.

However, when it is a name, the connection to the fruit is established for those six alone; thus, the purpose—namely, the connection to the fruit—will be explained in the fourth [book]. This is the meaning.
Regarding the word "yathā" (as):

in the case of the sentence concerning the Vaimṛdha offering, if the name "Paurṇamāsī" were absent, it would follow that the Vaimṛdha would be a subsidiary of the New Moon sacrifice (Amāvāsyā) due to the context (prakaraṇa); however, since the name exists, the context is set aside by the direct statement (vākya), and thus that consequence does not arise. Therefore, the purpose is the attachment of a subordinate quality (guṇopabandha). This is the meaning.

The phrase "the establishment of difference alone" (*bhedasiddhir eva*) contains the particle *eva* (alone), which indicates that even if other purposes—such as the connection with qualities (*guṇa*) or results (*phala*)—are impossible, a second purpose is obtained as an invariable concomitant: namely, that the establishment of difference occurs through the mental visualization (*ullekha*) within the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*). This is the meaning indicated.
The meaning is that, for this reason, there is no exclusion of the purpose consisting in the manifestation of conceptual construction.
(The suspicion of over-extension regarding the etymological meaning [of "soma"] as consisting in the act of breaking open;
the refutations thereof as stated by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, the *Bhāṣya*, and the *Prakāśa*.
[The phrase] "also of the words 'soma' and so forth" [is used].

By this [argument], that which was stated here by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* and others— namely, that having postulated for the word *udbhid* a *yogarūḍhi* (etymological-conventional) relationship like that of words such as *paṅkaja*, the very nature of a distinct sacrifice (*vijātīyayāgatva*) understood through the force of the injunction (*vidhisāmarthya*) is itself the delimitor of the conventional meaning (*rūḍhyavacchedaka*), just as "lotus-ness" (*padmatva*) is the delimitor of the conventional meaning of *paṅkaja*— is refuted; for even if one were to assume "lotus-ness" to be the delimitor of the conventional meaning because it is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is not established by the force of the injunction.

It has been indicated that the assumption of a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is to be disregarded, because such an assumption is untenable due to the impossibility of it serving as a delimiter [of the primary sense], and because assuming a conventional meaning would lead to the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) even for words like *soma*, which would result in the necessity of resorting to possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, although another alternative view was stated in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*)—namely, that in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the basis for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*) is simply the agency of piercing inherent in the object itself, by virtue of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice); [this view is also rejected].

That too is untenable; for since the word *yajati* denotes a sacrifice of a different class (*vijātīya-yāga*), if the capacity to manifest that specific [result] were the basis for the application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) of the term, it would follow that a different basis for application must be postulated for other sacrifices denoted by the word *udbhid*. Consequently, it would entail the postulation of a separate, distinct partial power (*avayava-śakti*) for that purpose.

By this, the argument of the author of the *Prakāśa*—that there is no over-extension because the word is etymological (*yaugika*) based on its being the basis for application as the "manifestor of the specific result of cattle produced by this sacrifice," due to semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) and syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*)—is also refuted.

That too is incorrect, because it would entail the assumption of distinct grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in different sacrifices, since a single uniform ground for application is impossible for the general category of "action" (*karman*). Therefore, he avoids this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in another way, stating: "For in all cases... (*sarvatra hi*).

(An exposition of the intended view regarding the avoidance of the aforementioned over-extension by means of the absence of prior usage in other senses): This is the meaning— since there is no experience of determining the word "jar" as having a power directed toward a jar, when there arises a requirement for a restrictive factor, the role of linguistic usage in the form of the employment of the word "jar" as a cooperative cause is established in the world.

In the present context, because the usage of the past [of the word *udbhid*] serves as a cooperative cause for determining its denotative power (*śakti*) toward the object [of the sacrifice], the determination of that power occurs only where such usage exists; since such usage is absent in other cases like the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, they do not come to mind.

Thus, since the matter is resolved through etymological derivation (*yoga*) alone, there is no need to postulate a separate category called "etymological-conventional" (*yogarūḍhi*). This is the meaning.
(Justification for the non-cognition of other meanings even if yogarūḍhi is not accepted): This should be understood in the same way regarding words such as *paṅkaja* ("lotus") and others.

Alternatively, even though the state of being the agent of arising from mud (*paṅkajanikartṛtva*) is understood through the power of the word's components (*avayavaśakti*), there exists [a requirement] for the cognition of the absence of such prior usage with respect to that kind of verbal cognition.

Alternatively, because it is postulated that a cognition having "the state of being previously employed" as its qualifier and "having *padma* as its qualificandum" acts as an inhibitor, there is no possibility of a cognition having anything other than *padma* as its qualificandum.

For even by one who maintains that the word has a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in *padma*, it must necessarily be admitted that the aforementioned apprehension (of the word's usage) is the generator of that power; and once that is admitted, it must be stated that such an apprehension acts as an inhibitor toward the aforementioned verbal cognition.
Therefore, it must be stated that the status of being an impediment belongs only to a planet whose aspect has been released; this is what is indicated by the word "everywhere" (sarvatra).
(Regarding the postulation of the ancient usage as a cooperative cause for the knowledge of word-meaning power,
and the demonstration of the inconsistency in the method used by the authors of the *Tantraratna* to establish *yogarūḍhi*):

And thus, since the ancient usage functions as a cooperative cause for the knowledge of word-meaning power, in a case where that cooperative cause is entirely absent, [the word cannot be established as having that meaning].

In that regard, since the absence of cognition of other [meanings] follows precisely from the absence of the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śakti*), it remains established that this is so. As for what was stated in the *Tantraratna* on the sixth [chapter], concerning the coreferential [expressions]: "But he who, by asserting that there is no usage simply because there has been no usage, does not accept conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in the case of lotuses and the like—he must be told: 'Granted, let the non-usage of subsequent speakers follow from the non-usage of preceding ones;'"
Cognition, which cannot be obtained through any other means, leads one to postulate a specific capacity [in the word].
How indeed could there be a cognition of a lotus from the word *paṅkaja* (mud-born) if it were devoid of such capacity?
If one were to say that this is due to its connection with the action of being produced in the mud as conveyed by the word itself, [the response would be as follows:]
One should reply to him: "Because it is inconclusive.
Indeed, the production of a lotus from mud is not an absolute rule, since that [production] would otherwise establish it [as a necessary cause].
Therefore, it must be the expressive power of the word itself that is postulated.

If one were to say: "It is true that the cognition of the lotus arises from the word alone; however, it is only by virtue of usage that the word conveys it, so the expressive power need not be postulated," [the response follows].

One might reply to him: "How could one who lacks [inherent] capacity cause comprehension through mere usage alone? For in that case, there would be an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*): namely, that it could be asserted that all words such as "cow" and so forth cause comprehension of their own meanings through mere usage alone, even without [inherent] capacity.
Thus it was stated for the purpose of establishing conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
It should also be noted that this [objection] does not apply to our position, because we do not admit that [a word] is expressive merely by virtue of usage in the absence of its [inherent] capacity.
(An examination of an alternative position: the acceptance of conventional indication [nirūḍhalakṣaṇā] in the word *paṅkaja*).

Even if it were argued that the cognition of a lotus qualified by the mode of being the agent of arising from mud is established by experience through the word *paṅkaja*, there would still be no fault; for on this view, such a cognition is accounted for by conventional indication alone, and thus there is no need for a separate conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) to accommodate it.

And thus, because the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the two words *yajati* and *udbhid* are distinct, there is the possibility of semantic coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—characterized by the occurrence of two words in a single referent—just as in the case of "blue lotus," provided that their grounds for application are different. (Regarding the resolution of the doubt concerning the pointlessness of the name if one were to accept that the delimitor of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word *udbhid* is simply the capacity to bring about the result of splitting [the earth]). Furthermore, since the property of being the producer of the result—which serves as the delimitor of the denotatum of the word *udbhid*—is already understood from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) co-occurring with the word *paśukāma* (desiring cattle), in the sense that "one should effect cattle by means of a sacrifice which is the cause of producing cattle," [the word *udbhid* would be redundant].
Since the fact that [the act] is the cause for the manifestation of the result— though already understood from the word "desiring cattle" (paśukāma)— is restated by means of the name (nāmadheya),
it has already been stated that this result consists of the mental visualization of the exclusion of others and so forth.

Therefore, just as the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the fact that Agni is the deity— already established by another sentence— is not contradicted when it serves the purpose of determining the *saṃkalpa* (intentional resolve) and so forth through the word "Agnihotra," likewise, the restatement of the status of being the cause of the fruit as understood from the phrase "desiring cattle" (*paśukāma*) within its own sentence is also not untenable.
(An exposition of the proponents of parsimony regarding the connection as a name, preceded by the demonstration that the relationship between a name and its bearer is not something to be enjoined.

For this very reason—the objection that "if it were a name, there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because the relationship between the name and its bearer would also have to be enjoined"—is refuted;

for since a name is not something to be performed, and since [the meaning] is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the well-known etymological derivation of its parts, the relationship with it is not something to be enjoined, and thus the objection does not arise.

Therefore, even when there is an injunction of a sacrifice qualified by the meaning of the name, because the meaning of the name is already known through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), no separate injunctive rule for the qualifier need be postulated in that respect; thus, even though it is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there is simplicity (*lāghava*) in the final view (*siddhānta*).

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, there is complexity (*gaurava*) because one must postulate separate injunctive rules for the qualifiers consisting of the accessories, as well as for the gender and number inherent in them.

Furthermore, in the Siddhānta, there is the distinction that there is parsimony (lāghava) because [the number and so forth] are merely restated (anuvādaka) as being conveyed by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), rather than being something to be enjoined (vidheya).

By this, it is shown that the Vārttikakāra’s attempt to establish the view that [the word ‘paśu’] is etymological (yaugika) is merely a bold assertion (prauḍhavāda); for the injunction would be established by the mere statement "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" (paśukāmo yajeta), and thus the name-injunction (nāmadheya-vidhi) "one should effect cattle through the splitting of animals" (paśūdbhedahetunā paśūn bhāvayet) would result in pointlessness.
What was stated by the author of the Nyāyasudhā—that has been refuted.
(An exposition on the inclusion of the name within the injunctive statement by way of delimiting the meaning of the verbal root, even though the name itself is not directly enjoined:

Therefore, since the meaning of the name here functions to delimit the meaning of the verbal root, its inclusion within the injunctive statement is justified—whether it be by being enjoined through a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) as an essential nature, like the concomitance [of the deities] in the case of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices, or like rice, redness, and so forth, which are understood from other means of knowledge. Thus, there is no deficiency whatsoever.

Although the designation "determinative" (paricchedaka) is observed elsewhere only in the sense of making known a specific form that was previously unknown— and since in this case that function is accomplished by the injunction itself, aided by other means of knowledge such as synonyms and so forth, there is no need for the name to act as a determinative— nevertheless, it should be understood that even when the specific object is already known, the name is conventionally treated as determinative precisely because it satisfies the desire to know what that specific object is.

(On the determination of the authority of names as indicators of difference and so forth, even though the referent of the name is established by other means of knowledge: Nor should it be argued— “In this way, since the referent of a name is merely restated because it is already established by other means of knowledge, and thus lacks the capacity to convey an unapprehended object, how can its authority be possible?”— for even while restating its own referent, its authority is established by its capacity to indicate an unapprehended difference and so forth, just as in the case of two sentences containing the term ‘vidvat’ (‘one who knows’).

Even in cases where there is no name, a distinction [between rites] is established solely through repetition (*abhyāsa*)—in the form of the restatement of an injunction that has no other purpose—as in "He offers the *samidh* oblation; he offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation," and so forth. Although such cases lack a specific indicator of distinction, the comprehension of a particular, determined form depends upon the name;
therefore, it is logical that names possess authority regarding dharma insofar as they establish a previously unknown unity of meaning.

(An exposition of Somanātha’s intention: that the term *udbhid* does not apply to the action by virtue of its causing the splitting of animals, but rather, as a name, it relies upon a derivation for the purpose of establishing its status as a name.

As for what [was said]—Somanātha, relying on another position mentioned in the Vārttika, raised the objection that since the quality of being the means for splitting animals is established from the verbal suffix itself (just as in the case of the word *paśukāma*), the name would be redundant; he then considered whether the word *udbhid* [denotes] the sacrifice by way of being the instrument for splitting animals.
If it were to merely inform [one of the name], it would be redundant;
rather, by way of being a designation (*saṃjñā*), it establishes the sacrifice through its specific naming.
And thus, although the specific nature of the action is already established by the verbal root itself as co-occurring with the injunction (*vidhi*), what kind of specific action is this?

In response to this expectation, since neither a substance nor a deity is mentioned in this sentence, it is impossible to convey a specific sacrifice by means of indicating a substance, deity, or the like;
therefore, because the word *udbhid* is intended to convey that specific sacrifice—namely, "this is the sacrifice named *udbhid*"—the word *udbhid* is not redundant.

Although the word *udbhid* is not denotative [of the sacrifice] itself, it functions as a qualifier by distinguishing its own referent from others based solely on the fact that it is directly heard in the text (*pratyakṣa-śrutatva*).
The rule that "only that which is presented by a word can be the object of the comprehension of syntactic connection" applies to cases other than those involving technical (saṃjñā) terms.

Alternatively, according to the view of the Grammarians (*śābdika*) that technical terms have their own form as the ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), it is possible for the word *udbhid* itself to convey its own form; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Nor should it be argued: "In this way, since the quality of being the cause of the splitting of cattle would not be an object of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, the recourse to a [derivative] etymological derivation (*yoga*) for that purpose is useless. This is because... [the argument continues].
A word possesses the status of a technical name (saṃjñā) only in that specific sense for which its derivation from constituent parts or other such factors is possible, and not elsewhere.
For this very reason, only such words are intended to have the status of a technical name.
Consequently, words such as *soma* do not function as names in the sentence "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*).

Consequently, since the recourse to the etymological derivation (*yoga*) of words such as *udbhid* for the sake of establishing their status as names (*saṃjñātva*) would otherwise be purposeless, there is no room for such futility.
Alternatively, the word *udbhid* denotes the ritual action by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), in the form of being that which is denoted by the word *udbhid*.
Furthermore, that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) operates by means of a connection (*yoga*) when its own primary denotation is applicable, and not otherwise; for this reason, recourse is taken to *yoga*.

Moreover, because it is established by usage (*nirūḍhatva*), indication is superior to the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*); thus, the fault mentioned regarding the position that [the word] is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) does not apply.
Or, let it be that [a term] is a name (*saṃjñā*) even without a connection based on its etymological parts.

Nevertheless, it has been stated that the recourse to etymological derivation (*yoga*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the equality of the derivation in both cases—effectively serving, as it were, merely to exclude the possibility that the word *udbhid* is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
(Refutation of the previous view that no defect arises when the meaning of yoga is prioritized):

Regarding the first position, since it is already established that the mental presentation of word-meanings (*padārthopasthiti*) produced by words is the cause for the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthabodha*), there is no evidence for abandoning this here; otherwise, one would be forced to deny the *adhyāhāra* (supplying of missing words) of the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) in the Viśvajit injunction, as well as the *ūha* (modification) consisting of the insertion of the word "Sūrya" in the *agnimantra*.

Regarding the second position, according to the statement of the Grammarians (*śābdika*): since words such as *ḍittha* and *aśvakarṇa*—where the meaning of the constituent parts is possible—are treated as names (*saṃjñā*) because they refer to those specific things and do not apply elsewhere, and since the status of being a name is observed in words like *ḍittha* even without a description of a sacrifice (*yāga*), the restrictive rule that "the status of being a name applies only where the connection with the meaning of the constituent parts is possible" is not a necessary determinant; consequently, resorting to the etymological sense (*yoga*) in the present case would result in futility. Regarding the third [position], by virtue of being denoted by the word *udbhid*...

If one resorts to indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the form [of the word], then even for that which is assisted by the etymological meaning (*yogārtha*), it is possible to establish its status as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) by resorting to indication of the possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

Since in the Veda—such as in the passage "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*)—every instance of indication is accepted as being merely conventional (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), it is also improper to claim that the indication of being denotable by the word *udbhid* is superior to the indication of the possessive sense because it is more conventional; thus, this [argument] was disregarded by the venerable teachers as being untenable.

(Regarding the refutation of the view that "the verbal cognition here is simply 'by means of the sacrifice named Udbhid,' while the cognition of the name occurs through secondary indication [lakṣaṇā]"):
By this [it is shown that]— since it is possible for the name to have an additional meaning, it is not proper to describe its purpose as being merely for delimitation (pariccheda).
However, since it is understood that [the result follows] from the sacrifice known by the name *udbhid*, it is proper to accept that the word *udbhid* conveys the sacrifice as qualified by its name.

Nor should it be argued: "In that case, it would follow that for them the very form of the word *udbhid* is the denoted object"; for, just as the logic proving that words such as *go* (cow) denote the genus (*jāti*)—because they generate a cognition qualified by that genus—it is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) that these words, which generate a cognition qualified by a name, must likewise be admitted to denote the name itself.

If it were suspected that there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) even for the named object (*saṃjñin*), on the grounds that— since denotation of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is impossible through identity (*tādātmya*) or other relations with the universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) expressed by words,

and since names (*saṃjñā-śabda*) lack a relation when they denote merely the word itself, a lakṣaṇā for the named object is untenable— one must therefore assume such a power for the named object in order to account for its cognition.
In that case, let there be *lakṣaṇā* (indication) with respect to the nominal suffix (*saṃjñāṃśa*).
Nor should it be argued: "If *lakṣaṇā* is equally present in the Siddhānta as well, for what reason is *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication of possessive meaning) abandoned?
For that [possessive indication] is to be rejected because it entails the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in the injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
The claim made by some—that it is logical for the word *udbhid* to function as a delimiting factor solely by generating a cognition characterized by the mode of being named "udbhid"—is refuted;

for such a cognition cannot arise unless the status of being a name (*saṃjñātva*) is already understood, and that understanding cannot be established by any other means of knowledge prior to the sentence concerning the *udbhid*. Therefore, this very sentence must imply its status as a name by producing a cognition of the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the name and the root *yaji* (to sacrifice), in the form: "by means of the sacrifice [named] *udbhid*."

For it is irrational to accept a figurative (lākṣaṇika) understanding of "by that which is named *udbhid*" at the conclusion of the sentence, when the subsequent cognition has already been established by that very first-born [cognition].
Furthermore, it is untenable to refer to the status of being named *udbhid*—which is established only in dependence upon this sentence—as if it were already established within this very sentence.

Moreover, if it is argued that because there is no relation between the word and its meaning, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the named object is impossible, then it would be equally difficult to establish a relation between the word and the named object itself.
Therefore, there is no impossibility regarding the definition of the word [as denoting the individual].

Consequently, since there is no disparity between the logic applied to universals (jāti) and this case, it would follow that the primary expressive power (śakti) resides only in the name (saṃjñā), while the secondary indicative function (lakṣaṇā) resides only in the named object (sañjñin).
For this very reason, even the common saying that "proper names are denotative" becomes consistent.

And likewise, in the case of "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*), since figurative grammatical coreferentiality (*lākṣaṇika-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) can be established, why should one resort to the cumbersome assumption of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*)?
If, however, even in the case of a name (*saṃjñin*), one were to accept a specific denotative power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) so that the coreferentiality is primary (*mukhya*),
this is not possible in the case of the *soma* sentence.

If it were argued that this is because words such as *soma* possess conventional meanings (*rūḍha*), then, rather than accepting their status as names (*nāmadheya*)—which would entail the conceptual complexity of postulating a specific, unique power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*)—it is more appropriate to rely on their status as names precisely by virtue of their etymological derivation (*yaugika*).

For the common usage "this is the one named *udbhid*" is established even by that much; furthermore, the avoidance of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is established through the method previously mentioned, and thus there is no purpose in accepting conventional meaning.
(Regarding the refutation of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*’s position that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *udbhid* by virtue of conventional meaning alone:

As for what was stated— that although the etymological derivation (*yoga*) accepted by the author of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra* to ensure semantic correctness might produce a corresponding cognition in other sentences, in this case it is by convention alone [that the meaning is determined]— because prior to this injunction, the specific nature of the sacrifice as being "the cause of the manifestation of the fruit" is not known, a cognition characterized by the mode "being the cause of the manifestation of the fruit" is impossible.

Nor should it be argued that the application of the word *udbhid* is based on the general capacity to produce a result— understood through the force of the universal rule (*vyāpti*) that "Vedic ritual is the means to its fruit"—
because the quality of being "Vedic" (consisting in being enjoined by the Veda) is not established prior to this point.
Nor is it correct to say that even the connection with a result in general is obtainable from the first cognition produced by the sentence concerning the *udbhid*.
Since the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) would lack authority if it were not dependent on the words *udbhid* and *paśukāma*,

it has been stated that here the word *udbhid* does not stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaji* through etymological derivation (*yoga*), but rather through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) alone.

That too is not correct; for if a *yoga* (etymological derivation) is accepted, since that [meaning] is established by the very power of the admitted parts [of the word], there is no evidence for postulating a *rūḍhi* (conventional meaning).
