Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating a *rūḍhi* even for words such as *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling), due to the fear of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication of possession). Furthermore, because of the fear of *matvarthalakṣaṇā*, if one were to postulate a *rūḍhi* for words like *soma*, they would consequently result in being mere names (*nāmadheya*). And it has been stated in the *Śāstradīpikā*, in the refutation of the Guru’s view in the second section (*adhikaraṇa*) and following: "It is better to accept *matvarthalakṣaṇā* than to postulate an unestablished meaning."

Otherwise, even in the case of "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*), the word *soma* would have to be considered a proper name (*nāmadheya*). For this very reason, where the conventional meaning (*yogārtha*) is not established by experience—

as is the case with words such as *go* (cow) or *dadhi* (curd), where there is no cognition of "going" (*gamana*) and so forth, but rather of the genus "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth— one must accept that the etymological derivation (*yoga*) serves merely to explain the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the term.
Even if one accepts conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), where that [usage] itself is possible, to abandon its meaning and postulate an additional conventional usage is entirely without proof.

(An exposition of the application of the word *udbhid* by taking into account the knowledge of its capacity to bring about the manifestation of a future fruit, followed by a conclusion that a noun determines the meaning of a verbal root solely by generating a cognition characterized by the capacity to bring about the manifestation of a fruit.
Nor is it the case that prior to this [application], there is an impossibility of cognizing the capacity to bring about the manifestation of a fruit;

for even from the term *agnihotra*, there would be no cognition of its being dedicated to Agni (*agnidaivatyatva*)—given that the very nature of the ritual action (*karmasvarūpa*) is unknown prior to the statement "one performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*), and given the absence of the attainment of the mantra-text whose status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is already established.
Because the impossibility of cognizing that [future state] is equal [in both cases],

and for this reason, just as the word *agnihotra* is established as a name by taking its future causal basis (*pravṛttinimitta*), so too is it appropriate here. Alternatively, since in the world it is established that only a general action (*karmasāmānya*) produces a fruit, [the designation is possible] even through a pervasion grasped by that general action.

It has already been stated previously that it is logical for the meaning of a name to serve as the delimitor of the root-meaning precisely by virtue of generating the cognition that brings about the manifestation of the result; this is the summary.
The purpose of the title has already been indicated by the very statement of the purpose of the name.
Thus ends the second section [of the first chapter], concerning the fact that words such as *udbhid* are names of sacrifices based on their etymological derivation.
(B1) (Section 3) "In which there is the teaching of a quality, there is a connection with the primary [act]. (Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.3)

In this context, regarding those words that are conventionally established as qualities— such as in the injunctions "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," "the Ājya-stotras are fifteenfold," "the Pṛṣṭha-stotras are seventeenfold," and "the Bahiṣpavamāna is threefold"— there arises an inquiry as to whether the words *citrā*, *ājya*, *pṛṣṭha*, and *bahiṣpavamāna* function as injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or as names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*).

Since these terms—like *dadhi* and others—are established as conventional names (*rūḍha*), it is impossible for them to be names of rituals; therefore, they must indeed be injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*).

In that regard, first, in the word *citrayā*, the quality of variegation (*citratva*) is enjoined by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and the quality of femininity (*strītva*) is enjoined by the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*).

Because the two things enjoined are understood to be mutually concomitant, and because the capacity of the thing enjoined leads to the understanding that a sacrifice involving an animal substance (*prāṇidravyaka-yāga*) is the object of reference (*uddeśya*).

Even regarding the archetypal sacrifices prescribed by the sentence, "Curd, honey, ghee, milk, parched grain, water, and rice— these mixed together constitute the Prājāpatya," although it is impossible for those sacrifices to be the objects of reference, [the rule] is enjoined either with reference to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, which is the archetype of all, or with reference to all animal sacrifices.

Nor does there arise a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) from the injunction of multiple qualities, because— as in the case of "the cow is the sacrificial fee" (*dhenurdakṣiṇā*)— there is no syntactical split since a single factor (*kāraka*) qualified by both [attributes] is being enjoined. Likewise, by the word *ājya* (clarified butter), ghee is meant, and by the word *pṛṣṭha*, a part of the body.

And that [number], being qualified by a specific count, is enjoined in due order as an auxiliary to the hymns prescribed by the sentences "They praise with *ājya*s" and "They praise with *pṛṣṭha*s," on the basis of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
In the same way, the substance consisting of three *iḍā* portions denoted by the word *trivṛt*, qualified by the act of purifying, is likewise enjoined by that very sentence.
In all cases, the subservience of the substances to the hymn is achieved solely by their placement near the hymn for the sake of an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

In the case of the originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*), however, words such as *ājya* (clarified butter) are restatements (*anuvāda*) because they have already been obtained from the subsidiary injunctions (*guṇavākya*);

it is only the *stotra* (laudatory hymn) that is enjoined. This being the prima facie view—(B2) [now begins] the section concerning whether words such as *citrā* are names of sacrifices (*yāganāmadheya*).
He provides an example whose subject matter is distinct from the subject matter of the preceding section: "In this case," [and] "only a quality."
(Discrimination of the subject matter of this section from the subject matter of those previously excluded by their emergence, renown, and designation:
In the term *guṇa* (quality), there is also an indication of both genus (*jāti*) and connection with action (*kriyāyoga*).

By this, there is an inclusion of the word *ājya*, which denotes the genus "clarified butter" (*ghṛta-jāti*); the word *pṛṣṭha*, which denotes a part of the body; and words such as *bahiṣpavamāna*, whose basis is their connection with the action of purifying (*pavana-kriyāyoga*).

By the use of the particle *eva*, it is indicated that even among derivative (*yaugika*) words whose application is possible with respect to the object (*karman*), they do not serve as examples [for this context], thereby stating that the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) does not apply here.

Although the word *pavamāna* is a derivative term denoting the agent of the action of purifying (*pavana-kriyā-kartṛ*), and thus would not properly be cited here as it falls within the scope of the previous section;
nevertheless, according to the principle that "in all cases, substances alone are denoted by derivative words," [it refers] to the agent of the action of purifying.

Because the word is established through etymological derivation (*yoga*) as referring to a substance (*dravya*), and because it is impossible for a hymn (*stotra*) to be the agent of the action of purifying (*pavana-kriyā-kartṛtva*), it does not function equally in both senses—as in the case of the word *udbhid*.

Consequently, since its status as a name (*nāmatva*) is untenable, it does not fall within the scope of the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*); thus, its suitability as an illustrative example is established.

Although, by the principles of "being mentioned as such" (*tatprakhya*) and "designation thereof" (*tadvyapadeśa*), words denoting genus (*jāti*) and so forth are indeed the primary examples; [this case is nevertheless valid].

Nevertheless, it should also be understood that when those two principles do not apply, and when they are being considered as examples here, even words such as *dadhi* (curd) and *soma*, which are not the domain of those principles, would undesirably become examples; therefore, to exclude them, it must be known that only those words are examples here for which, upon their inclusion in a sentence alongside words denoting a genus (*jāti*) or a quality (*guṇa*), the resulting syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) cannot be avoided except by treating them as names (*nāmadheya*).

For this very reason, although there is a possibility of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the sentence "for one desiring sensory power, [he should offer] with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya*), it is not cited as an example because that split can be avoided even without [the term 'curd'] being a name (*nāmadheya*).

Thus, the sense is that the examples here are words occurring within a sentence for which the principles of *tatprakhya* (being known from elsewhere) and *tadvyapadeśa* (designation by that) do not apply; these are words whose status as names is established only through their conventional usage (*nirūḍha*) in reference to a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, and which serve to avoid a syntactical split that would otherwise arise merely from their being names.
He shows those very same words as occurring within a sentence: "by means of the variegated [sacrifice]," and so forth.

(An examination of the grounds for citing [the examples] from the subsidiary injunctions, setting aside the words *ājya* and others occurring in the originative injunctions such as "They praise with *ājyas*"):

Although it is possible for these very words occurring in the originative injunctions—such as "They praise with *ājyas*" (*ājyaiḥ stuvate*) and "They praise with *ṣaṣṭhas*" (*ṣaṣṭhaiḥ stuvate*)—to be the subject of this inquiry;

furthermore, since they are denoted by words ending in the third case in grammatical apposition with "praise" (*stotra*) and so forth, there is even an additional possibility that they fall within the category of names (*nāmadheya*).

Nevertheless, the fact that those [other passages] do not serve as examples will be shown very shortly by the author himself under the guise of removing an objection; therefore, setting them aside, he has demonstrated that only those passages occurring within the descriptions of qualities (guṇavākya) serve as examples, in accordance with the portion of the sūtra beginning with "yasmin guṇopadeśaḥ."

(The connection of the *citrā* section as a counter-example to the *udbhid* section) Without explicitly stating the immediate connection in the form of a counter-example— since the opponent’s objection arises by overturning the logic of the preceding section, namely that the status of certain words as names is determined through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) when their meanings are otherwise doubtful due to being unestablished anywhere— the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
"As in the case of curd and so forth."

(Ascertainment of the meaning of words such as *citra*): The word *citra* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of a quality (*guṇa*) delimited by the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) of "variegation" (*citratva*), which is a subordinate genus (*avāntarajāti*) pervaded by color-ness (*rūpatva*). The word *ājya* [is conventionally established] in the sense of the genus of clarified butter (*ghṛtajāti*).
The word *pṛṣṭha* refers to a class of bodily parts;
the word *pavamāna*, according to the method previously stated, is established by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) as denoting a substance—this is the meaning.
(An exposition on the determination that the object of the sacrifice consists of a living being as a substance, by virtue of the force of enjoining both "variegatedness" and "femininity")—
namely, "in accordance with the force of what is to be enjoined."

Just as in the statement, "For whom both fires should go out, for him there is the re-establishment [of the fires] as an expiation," although by the principle of the section on the ruin of the oblation (*havir-ārti-adhikaraṇa*) the qualification "both" (*ubhayatva*) is not intended to be significant— such that the expiation would apply even when only one of the two fires goes out— nevertheless, because the re-establishment (*ādheya*) being prescribed has the inherent capacity to produce two fires, only the going out of both fires constitutes the occasion (*nimitta*), and not the going out of either one alone.
Its attainment will be established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the sixth [book];

by that same reasoning, since the two prescribed qualities—variegatedness (*citratva*) and femininity (*strītva*)—are perceived to reside in the substance (the animal), just like the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) and so forth, it is impossible for the instrumentality delimited by the prescribed variegatedness and femininity to be applied primarily to non-living things. Therefore, in accordance with the capacity of what is prescribed...

Since even here it is understood that only an animal substance is the object of the injunction, the prescription of the instrumentality qualified by "variegatedness" (*citratva*) and "femininity" (*strītva*) is made precisely with reference to that [animal].

For this very reason, the following view is also refuted: that when "variegatedness" is prescribed in the context of the primary sacrifice involving curd and other substances, it applies to those substances—such as curd—by virtue of the principle of "uselessness [of the main act] leading to its subsidiaries" (*ānarthakyatadaṅganyāya*), and thus the sacrifice is performed with curd and other substances of variegated colors within the primary sacrifice itself.
And because the syntactical connection with the term "desiring cattle" (paśukāma) is untenable.
(Refutation of the view that there is a single sacrifice in the passage concerning curds, honey, and so forth:
"Of the sacrifices... [and so on].

By means of the plural number and in accordance with the natural tenor of the *vārttika* on the section concerning the first quarter of the eighth book (*adhikaraṇa*), the position of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* regarding a single sacrifice (*ekayāga*) which was stated in the section on number (*saṅkhyādhikaraṇa*) has been refuted. The detailed demonstration and refutation of that position should be consulted in the *Kaustubha*.
Therefore, it is indicated that the position of multiple conjunctions (*anekayogapakṣa*) stated in the *Vārttika* on the twelfth topic (*adhikaraṇa*) is indeed superior.

And thus, the singular number found in the Siddhānta-vārttika passage, “The sacrifice under discussion is enjoined as the fruit,” as well as the singular number in the *Śāstradīpikā*, “The sacrifice under discussion is enjoined as the fruit,” are both intended with reference to the commonality of the nature of being a sacrifice (*yāgatva-sāmānya*). Furthermore, [this avoids] the objection that “the context would be sublated for the Prājāpatya sacrifice.”
The sense is that it must be explained.

(An exposition, following the view of the ancients, establishing the inclusion of variegatedness (*citratva*) and feminity (*strītva*) in the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, preceded by a demonstration that masculinity and the quality of being black-spotted (*kṛṣṇasāraṅga*) are not restricted therein:

Although the animal sacrifice is intended as the objective, nevertheless, in order to dispel the doubt as to why it is not enjoined universally across both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*) for all sacrifices involving living beings as the substance, it is stated: "belonging to every archetype."

The meaning is that although the *sautya* sacrifice has the *ekādaśinī* as its archetype, and the *ekādaśinī* sacrifices have animal groups (*paśugaṇa*) as their archetypes, the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice— by virtue of the eighth-lecture rule, "And [the details] of the *daikṣa* [apply] to the others"— is understood to be the archetype for all animal sacrifices; therefore, by the third-lecture rule, "Or rather, [they apply] to the archetype because they are not separately stated," these details find their place there alone and not in other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

Nor should it be argued that because the context is already occupied by other qualities such as masculinity (*puṃstva*) and being a black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāraṅga*), there is no possibility for the qualities of variegated color (*citratva*) and femininity (*strītva*)—which are taught as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*)—to find a place in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.

This is because, in the original injunction (*utpattivākya*), the word "animal" (*paśu*) is applied to females as well; thus, masculinity is not intended to be significant. Furthermore, even though the masculine gender is heard in the mantra "of the goat's omentum" (*chāgasya vapāyāḥ*), it is untenable to assume an injunction [for the animal] based on that gender when it is overridden by the femininity directly enjoined by the unattached rule. Moreover, [the masculine form] may be explained as a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Because it is possible to avoid [the contradiction],

and because even the injunction regarding the black-spotted [animal] and others is consistent— since it can be understood as serving the purpose of restricting the form of the black-spotted animal and so forth, which are already included in the subject matter by virtue of being the substratum for variegation—
it is therefore logical that those two [mantras] be inserted in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.

Having thus established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—according to the method of the ancients—that [the rule] applies only to the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, he now states another position independently: "in all animal sacrifices" (*sarvapaśuyāga*).
(An exposition on the connection of variegatedness (*citrātva*) and femaleness (*strītva*) with all animals, preceded by an examination of the absence of tautology and other such defects):

This is the intended meaning—just as, for instance, in the case of the seventeen syllables beginning with "āśrāvaya," which are designated as Prajāpati, there is a direct injunction by means of the rule, "This indeed is the seventeen-fold Prajāpati who is attached to the sacrifice," with reference to the sacrifice in its entirety; so too [is it here].
Even so, there is no application [of the rule] to the archetype (*prakṛti*) alone;

for since the operation of the direct injunction (*upadeśa*) occurs prior to the extension (*atideśa*), there is no possibility of conceiving an extension [at that stage], and thus there is no tautology (*dviruktatva*). For this very reason, in the case of the *parṇatā* (leaf-nature) and others, when there is an injunction with reference to the *juhū* ladle, an expectation of extension arises for the sake of obtaining it; because there is no operation prior to that [extension], there is a disparity in the time of attainment, and thus the charge of tautology is justified.
This is an inconsistency.

Likewise here as well, since there is no tautology in enjoining "variegatedness" (*citratva*) and "femininity" (*strītva*) by directly referring only to the sacrifice (*yāga*), that injunction is not improper as it applies generally to all sacrifices involving living beings as the substance, by virtue of referring only to the sacrifice itself.

For this very reason, because the animal is prescribed for all animal sacrifices (*paśuyāga*), there is no need for an extension (*atideśa*) here even for the purpose of establishing a connection through the medium of the form of the animal.

(An examination, preceded by a refutation of the method stated in the *Kaustubha*, regarding the fact that the qualities of variegatedness (*citratva*) and feminity (*strītva*) have as their scope animals other than the *vāyavya* [sacrificial animal]):

This being the case, in instances such as "a white [animal] for Vāyu" (*vāyavyaṃ śvetam*), where there is an extension (*atideśa*) even to the animal, it is impossible to enjoin these [qualities] in a manner common to those cases because of the consequence of redundancy (*dviruktatva*).
However, in cases such as "he dedicates the *savanīya* animal to Agni" (*āgneyaṃ savanīyaṃ paśum upākaroti*), apart from the connection between the substance and the deity...
Since the sacrifice itself cannot be established [without materials], the necessity of an instruction regarding the substance (*dravya*) follows;

because there is no disparity in the time of its acquisition, this injunction is not untenable as it applies equally to such modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*). As stated by the venerable author in the *Kaustubha*, this is likewise the case in the sentence concerning the Vāyavya sacrifice, since the establishment of the sacrifice is equally impossible without the connection between the substance and the deity.

Since the sacrifice must be conceived through its connection with the generality of "white substance," it is necessary to state that the white [substance] alone is first connected as the substance; therefore, even before the operation of the extended application (*atideśa*), the qualities of variegatedness and femininity can be logically connected by the primary injunction (*upadeśa*) as qualifiers of that [substance]. Thus, because the extended application of the "animal" (*paśu*) is postulated precisely due to the specific expectancy—namely, "What is that variegated and feminine white substance?"—it is the same [in both cases].
One must consider how this could possibly be logical.

Therefore, the resolution should be stated as follows: because the white color and the masculine gender are enjoined in the originative injunction of the Vāyavya passage by the term "white" (*śvetam*), it is impossible for the qualities of variegated color and femininity to be introduced there.
(The restriction of the application of "manifoldness" and "femininity" to all modified animal sacrifices that are not overridden by a contrary injunction.

Thus, even if it is impossible for such a contrary factor to apply to a specific modification where it exists, the second position is summarized as follows: the injunction [of the quality] is made with reference to the class of sacrifices in general that have animals as their substance, provided there is no such contrary factor in that modification. And it is not the case that—just as the application of the *saptadaśya* (seventeen-foldness) taught in an independent context (*anārabhyādhīta*) is impossible in all modifications due to being blocked by the *pañcadaśya* (fifteen-foldness) obtained through the extension of established auxiliaries (*klṛptopakāra*)—so too here, [the application would be blocked] by the obstruction of the *kṛṣṇasāraṅga* (black-spotted antelope) which has established auxiliaries.
How are these two to be applied?

This must be explained: because there is no contradiction according to the method previously stated, and because—just as a *śarādi* (the *śaramayī barhiḥ* rule) not studied within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) can override what is extended by *atideśa* due to its established benefit—the same logic applies here: that which is studied outside of a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*) can override what is extended by *atideśa* on the basis of the principle of "prevention of meaninglessness" (*ānarthakya-pratihatanyāya*).

Otherwise, because the immediate timing (sadyaḥ-kālatva) understood from the sentence "ya iṣṭyā" would be obstructed by the three-day timing of the archetypal rite (prakṛta), it would not be possible for it to apply to the modified rites (vikṛti).
Therefore, it is logical that its prescription applies even to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti).

(An objection regarding the injunction of variegatedness and femaleness in the sacrifice of a ewe, the refutation thereof according to Somanātha, and the demonstration that there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) even if those two qualities were enjoined in all animal sacrifices:

Now, an objection is raised: if both qualities are enjoined by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the sacrifice, there arises the fault of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), characterized by the repetition of the injunctive force (*vidhi*).

Therefore, since the female gender is already established in the ewe-sacrifice (*meṣīyāga*), there is no possibility of its application there through the mere injunction of a specific quality (*citratvamātra*). Consequently, it follows that the injunction must apply only to the modifications (*vikṛti*) of that sacrifice; thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it applies to the *agnīṣomīya* or to all animal sacrifices is not tenable. As for the argument that because the female gender is obtained here, the injunction applies to the modification in the form of the ewe-sacrifice—

Alternatively, Somanāthadīkṣita’s argument— that because the sentence "Three red-spotted ones for Aditi" prescribes a modified sacrifice (vikṛti), there is a lack of a determining factor (vinigamanāviraha) for the injunction of femininity due to the attainment of variegatedness—

is incorrect; for in the sacrifice to Aditi, the impossibility of introducing [femininity] is itself the regulating factor, since it is already barred by the masculinity prescribed by the original injunction (utpattiśiṣṭa-puṃstva).

Therefore, how is it that in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—or indeed in all animal sacrifices—there is no syntactical split (*avākyabheda*), given that there is no possibility of a repetition of the injunction (*vidhyāvṛtti*) when a single act qualified by both variegatedness (*citratva*) and femininity (*strītvā*) is enjoined as the instrument (*karaṇatva*) through a single word?

Even though the status of the factor (*kāraka*) is already established from the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) itself, making an injunction of something already qualified by it impossible, and thus leaving the problem of syntactical split unchanged if one were to enjoin both [qualities] by way of restating that [instrumentality];

nevertheless, although that [instrumentality] is established as residing in a substance (*dravya*), the injunction is still valid because the instrumentality residing in variegatedness and femininity has not yet been established.

This is because it is necessary to distinguish between the various instrumentality (*karaṇatā*) of substances, qualities, and so forth—which, depending on the difference in their operations, consist either in specific relations of essential nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*) or in distinct categories of entities (*padārtha*) such as "power" (*śakti*).

Therefore, the point is that even when there are multiple instances of instrumentality, there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), since they are all simultaneously presented by means of a single instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*).

(Refutation of Somanātha’s view that the archetype prescribes only female gender, and the establishment of the ancient view) As for Somanātha’s argument here— that because variegatedness (*citratva*) is already obtained in the archetype by way of being black-spotted (*kṛṣṇasāraṅga*) and so forth, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) can be avoided even by prescribing only female gender— that is [refuted] on the grounds that, in the absence of an injunction for variegatedness, the injunctions for being black-spotted and so forth would result in unintended *apūrva*-injunctions; therefore, in comparison to that, by the aforementioned method...

Since it is more appropriate to accept the injunction of variegatedness (*citratva*) itself— thereby avoiding a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*)— and to admit that the injunction regarding the black-spotted antelope (*kṛṣṇasāraṅga*) functions as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) required by that [injunction],
it is improper to suggest that the split in the sentence can be avoided by arguing for the attainment of variegatedness from that [black-spotted antelope];
therefore, that solution favored by the ancients, which accepts an injunction of a qualified factor (*viśiṣṭakāraka*), is the correct one.

(Conclusion on the Citrā-word’s status as denoting a quality, following the Eastern view, by demonstrating that even the connection with the fruit is understood [from the context], thereby removing the suspicion of syntactical split [vākya-bheda]:

Nor should it be argued: "In this way, because the connection with the fruit is also enjoined for the sacrifice, the occurrence of two sets of contradictory triplets or a syntactical split is difficult to avoid. This must not be said; for the word *paśukāma* (desiring cattle) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the desire to obtain cattle which serves as the means, and since it is not itself something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), those faults do not apply.

In this regard, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position should be observed in the Kaustubha as being formulated in an alternative manner: namely, that the injunction of *citratva* (variegatedness) applies either to the sacrifice of the ewe (*meṣīyāga*) or to the sacrifice of parched grains (*dhānāyāga*) which is under discussion.

Having thus established that the term *citrapada* has the purpose of enjoining a quality (*guṇavidhiparatva*), he establishes that the terms *ājya* and so forth also have that same purpose, beginning with the word "evam" (thus).
(An exposition of the performance of the sentence-meanings in accordance with the prima facie view regarding the *ājya* and *pṛṣṭha* verses:

This is the meaning— by means of the superimposition (*adhyāhāra*) of the verb root *as* (to be) in its first-person plural form, which is authorized by the grammatical rule stating, "The verb *as*, when followed by forms of the present tense (*bhavantī*), may remain unexpressed even if it is not actually employed," in relation to the sentences concerning the *ājya* and *pṛṣṭha* verses.

And since [the number] has not been previously established, by means of an injunction (*vidhi*), the existence of clarified butter (*ājya*) qualified by the number fifteen is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the hymns (*stotra*) due to the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Although, according to the principle that "a person is enjoined by an injunction toward his own activity," the injunction implies a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) consisting of human activity, and since such an operation cannot exist without being delimited, it requires a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*); yet, because existence resides in the object to be accomplished (*prayojya*) and thus lacks the nature of human activity, it is unfit to serve as a delimiting factor.

Nevertheless, by virtue of the subsidiarity to the *stotra* (hymn) understood from the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), it is established that [the substance] must reside in the same location as the primary act; and since this [subsidiarity] is accomplished by placing [the substance] in proximity, it is postulated that the verbal root-meaning of "placing" (*sthāpana*) itself serves as the delimiting factor for that [subsidiarity]. Consequently, in this case—as in the injunction "having placed the fire, he praises"—the fact that the *ājya* and other substances assist the *stotra* through the medium of their existence brought about by placement is not contradicted by the mode of being a *pṛṣṭha* (a specific type of chant).

Furthermore, because clarified butter (*ājya*) and other substances are *saṃsiddhika* (inherently existing) entities, it is impossible for them to be connected with a number in their own form; therefore, by implication, there must be a distinction between as many mantras as that number. Consequently, the performance consists of placing fifteen portions of ghee within the fifteen mantras at the time of performing the *stotra*. Likewise, having accomplished the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* by placing seventeen animals facing away, one should perform the recitation.
(An exposition on the contradiction with the rule for the suffix *ḍa* in the injunction regarding the *pañcadaśa* [fifteen-fold] *ājya-stoma*:

Nor can it be maintained that, according to the grammatical rule "the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed for *stoma* in the sense of *pañcadaśa* and so forth," words such as *pañcadaśa* ending in the suffix *ḍa* denote the number of hymns (*stuti*) produced by the number of verses (*ṛc*) in the *stotra*;
for even if the verses themselves were included therein, there would be no purpose served, and it is therefore logical that the number be enjoined as residing in the *ājya* chants and so forth.

If, however, it were suspected that the number would become unintended (avivakṣā) when enjoining a substance qualified by a number— following the logic of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section concerning the singularity of the animal (*paśvekatvādhikaraṇa*)—

then, according to the method stated in the *Kaustubha*, let there be an injunction, with reference to the *stotra*, of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of establishing [the Soma] as qualified by both the number and the substance.
Thus [it is said].

(An establishment of the fact that the terms *trivṛt* and *bahiṣpavamāna* denote substances qualified by the action of purifying, preceded by a refutation of their referring to triplicity or Vāyu, etc.
Here, the authors of the *Prakāśa* maintain that the word *pavamāna*, being etymological (*yaugika*) and requiring a qualificand, is connected with *soma* alone as the qualificand due to the context;
whereas the word *trivṛt*, because of the sequential recitation of three *ṛk*-verses, denotes a group of nine *stotrīyā* verses, as established in the *Trivṛccarvaśvavāla* section.

Even though it has been established [elsewhere], because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *pavamāna*, and because in expressions such as "the threefold rope" (*trivṛdrajjus*) it is used even for a triad of qualities while abandoning the sense of a group of nine *stotrīyā* verses, it is understood here—through its connection with its constituent parts—that it refers to a triad of qualities.

And this triad of qualities, by virtue of the context, is in relation to the quantity of Soma measured in ten handfuls; thus, it refers specifically to the Soma substance itself, which possesses the number three and is characterized by the *pavamāna* rite outside the *sadas*.
It was stated previously that "the procedure is as before," and in order to refute that, it was stated that "it consists of three *biṇḍī* substances.

This is its meaning: since it is possible for the word to denote the creeper known by the synonym *tribiṇḍī* through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there is no evidence for accepting its etymological meaning.
For this very reason, the meaning of the constituent parts is accepted only where conventional usage is sublated.

In cases such as "the threefold rope" (*trivṛdrajjū*), although the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "rope" is established through etymological derivation (*yoga*) alone and thus does not require the assumption of a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*); nevertheless, here, rather than adopting a dependent meaning, the adoption of an independent meaning is explicitly stated. Furthermore, when the word *pavamāna* requires a substantive (*viśeṣya*), it is improper to assume a substantive from the context (*prakaraṇa*) when a substantive already present within its own sentence can be obtained.

By this, the alternative view presented by Somanātha—which accepts that the words *trivṛt* and *pavamāna* refer respectively to triplicity and air, and thus concludes that according to the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), air should be produced outside the *sadas* by means of a fan or similar device—is also refuted. Therefore, it is more reasonable to follow the method stated by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*: that the three *bhindipāla* vessels themselves, characterized by the act of purifying (*pavana*), are what are enjoined.
He demonstrates the parsimony even in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words: "But it is merely praise" (stotramātram tu).
(Conclusion of the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] based on the meaningfulness of terms such as *ājya* in passages like "They praise with the *ājyas*"):

The meaning is that the term *ājya*, because it indicates a mutual relationship between the *ājya* substances and the mantras through their connection to a single hymn (*stotra*), is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the instrumentality residing in the mantras as indicated by their own connection [to the *ājyas*].
Although there is indeed an additional burden of complexity caused by a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) in a sentence containing a numerical qualification;

Nevertheless, the point is that even if one accepts a qualified injunction—which entails figurative indication (lakṣaṇā)—in the case of the Soma and other passages out of deference to established usage, it is not improper to accept a qualified injunction that does not entail such indication.

(The establishment of the final conclusion [siddhānta] based on the impossibility of prescribing both "variegated-ness" and "femininity," as well as the resulting syntactical split [vākya-bheda] in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and elsewhere, which would preclude the prescription of femininity once masculinity has been restricted.

Although it might be argued that only instrumentality (*karaṇatva*)—as conveyed by the instrumental case-ending—is being prescribed, nevertheless, since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) it is stated, "A goat (*ajaḥ*)," masculinity is established through the very same operation by which femininity functions as the instrument. Thus, because the two properties are mutually exclusive, the prescription of both is impossible. Consequently, the final conclusion is established.

Since the status of [the animal] as the instrument (karaṇatva) is already established by the force of the injunction regarding its masculinity found in such statements as "The animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," in the word *citrayā*, the single instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) merely restates that instrumentality; the feminine gender is enjoined by the suffixal portion (*pratyaya*), while the instrumentality qualified by variegatedness (*citratva*) is enjoined by that same case-ending as joined with the nominal stem (*prakṛti*). Thus, because the various things to be enjoined are not conveyed by a single denotation.

With the intention that the consequence of a syntactical split (vākyabheda) is indeed unavoidable, he states the final position (siddhānta) after having established the syntactical split in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "prāpta... and so forth.
Granted that there might somehow be a difference in the instruments [of action];
nevertheless, because masculinity is required by the archetype (prakṛti), the injunction of femininity is impossible—this is what he states with the words "in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice," etc.

In order to refute the opponent's argument regarding the absence of evidence establishing the male gender [of the sacrificial animal], the statement from another Vedic branch, "The animal for Agni and Soma is unborn" (*ajo 'gnīṣomīyaḥ*), has been cited.

This also serves as an indicator for [the refutation of] the two other points: the incoherence of the term "desiring cattle" (*paśukāma*) and the resulting contradiction with the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the sacrifices involving curd and other substances under discussion.
For this very reason, the injunction of that [male gender] even in the case of the ewe-sacrifice (*meṣī-yāga*) and the *dhānā-yāga* is also refuted.
He concludes that [the term] in the *citrā* sentence is a name by saying "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

(Establishing that the word *citrayā* refers to a name by means of conventional metaphorical indication): He dispels the objection that, under the view that it is a name, one would have to assume an independent conventional meaning—by stating, "because it consists of various substances."

We do not accept that the word *citra* has a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) here; rather, because of its abundant usage in Vedic literature in connection with the quality of having various materials, it is a case of "established metaphorical indication" (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*), as in the case of words such as *darśana*.
And in this context, "having various materials" is not intended to mean merely the state of consisting of many substances.
But it is so even by virtue of having two substances;

for this very reason, in the Taittirīya recension, after beginning with "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā; this [earth] indeed is the Citrā," the seven sacrifices to Agni, Aṣṭrā, and others—which have sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and cooked rice (caru) as their substances—are [designated] merely by the fact that they possess the substances of caru and puroḍāśa.
The establishment of the name "Citrāpadas" [is as follows]:

the sense is that even when separate sacrifices are performed—since there is an absence of a single deity common to two substances—the status of having variegated substances (citradravyakatva) is still logically consistent.
Regarding the term "feminine suffix" (strīpratyaya): it refers to a suffix that denotes the feminine gender.
Because even that [singular number] is justified by the intention of referring to the whole—as in the case of the word *rājasūya*—this [singular number] is also an indication [of the same].

(B1) Since there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in enjoining multiple qualities— such as variegatedness (*citratva*) and femaleness (*strītva*)— by way of restating an already established action (*prāptakarmānuvāda*), and since the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) residing in the animal is also already established and thus not something to be enjoined, it is impossible to enjoin a factor qualified by both [qualities]. Furthermore, because the injunction of femaleness is precluded by the masculinity (*puṃstva*) enjoined by the contextual statement "The goat is for Agni and Soma" (*ajo 'gnīṣomīyaḥ*), this is not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Therefore, the word *citrā* is a name for the very sacrifices under discussion, applied by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) because they consist of various diverse materials;
and the feminine suffix is used with the intention of referring to a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*).

Similarly, in the case of words such as *ājya* (clarified butter) and so forth, since a specific [compound] meaning is not established due to their being uninflected, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if one were to enjoin multiple qualities—such as the material and the number—by way of restating already established hymns (*stotra*).

Nor should it be argued that the injunction for the *stotra* qualified by the substance occurs only in the originative statement (*utpattivākya*), while in other places there is merely an injunction regarding the number;

for since substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) cannot function as the instrument (*karaṇa*) of a *stotra*, a qualified injunction is impossible, and furthermore, the suffix *-ḍa* in words like *pañcadaśāni*, which denotes the *stoma* consisting of the number of *ṛc*-verses within the praise, would be untenable if it were an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Therefore, in both sentences, the terms *ājya* and so forth are names of the stotras by virtue of their primary denotative power (*śakti*) alone.

Furthermore, in all the sentences prescribing qualities (*guṇavākya*), there is an injunction of the number alone, based on a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the stotras denoted by the terms *ājya* and so forth.
And in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) of the *ājya*, there are four stotras bearing that name.
For, from the plural number accompanied by the term *gamaka*, the number [of six] is understood. Thus, even in the sentence regarding the origin of the question, there are six to be performed,
though four are fixed.
Because of the scriptural injunction prescribing an option between the first two, the Bṛhat and Rathantara, and the last two, the Naudhasa and Śyaita;
and as for the refutation of those respective objections here, as well as the criticisms of other views, these are to be found in the Kaustubha. // 3 // 19 //

Thus ends the third section, titled "The Name Citrā. (B2) [In this section, it is established that the word *ājya* is a name: for in the case of the statement "there are fifteen *ājyās*," since a qualified [compound] is not etymologically derived, there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*); and in the case of "they praise with the *ājyas*," since the *ājyas* cannot be connected with the act of praising, a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*) is impossible; therefore, the status of the word *ājya* as a name is determined.]

He demonstrates that even if one accepts mutual connection between all factors (*kāraka*s) by abandoning the rule that their syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is restricted solely to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), on the grounds of conforming to the rule that in a compound (*samāsa*) such connection depends upon the capacity characterized by "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), such a qualified injunction would still be untenable; for in the absence of that [unification], mutual connection is unestablished, and thus qualification is impossible, leading to the contingency of sentence-splitting (*vākya-bheda*)—this he shows in the case of the *ājya* and other passages with the words "In this way... (*evam*).
Anticipating the objection that there is no syntactical split, he refutes it with the words "And not... (na ca).
"Of ghee and so forth."

The meaning is as follows: with respect to praise, which consists in the naming of qualities residing in a subject that can only be established through verbal testimony, it is not possible for clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and the like to function as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

For this very reason, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with *soma*," even by means of the implied indication of possession (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), there is no connection of the *ājya* (clarified butter) offerings with the hymns (*stotra*).

Nor can the status of being an instrument be established for the *ājya* offerings merely on the grounds of their being reminders due to their proximity, as in the case of the sound of a chariot and so forth.

Since in common worldly usage even the activity of the eyes, hands, and so forth is observed to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act called "giving a command," it is possible for the sound of a chariot to serve as an instrument. However, in the case of a praise (*stuti*), to assume an instrument that has not been established elsewhere would result in the contingency of an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*). Nor is it tenable that mantras related to ghee—indicated by the word *ājya*—could serve as that instrument.

Because the connection of the mantras with the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) designated as "placing" (*sthāpanā*) is not established by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and because that connection is already established through their function as illuminators (*prakāśaka*), there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting the mantras belonging to the context (*prakaraṇika-mantra*) if they were enjoined [as the instrument]. He states another objection regarding the status of the mantras connected with the clarified butter as the instrument: "pañcadaśāni" (fifteen).

The meaning is that since the word *stoma* is understood by the ritualists (*yājñika*) through its frequent usage to denote the number contained within the verses of a *stotra*, there is no evidence for assuming that it refers to a number residing merely in the means of the *stotra*.

(Conclusion of the established doctrine regarding the *ājya* passage, preceded by the objection that there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in enjoining a distinct productive operation (*bhāvanā*) qualified by number and substance while restating the productive operation of the hymn, and its refutation:

Even if, while restating the productive operation of the hymn, one were to enjoin here a distinct productive operation qualified by number and substance—just as in the case of other productive operations such as the *prayāja* offerings—it would still be possible to avoid the charge of syntactical split;

for subsequently, one could assume a relationship of qualifier and qualified between the substance and the number, just as in the case of the "red" (*aruṇā*) and the "one-year-old cow" (*ekahāyanī*). Thus, there would be no fault.

Nevertheless, since a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) cannot be enjoined without the meaning of a verbal root that serves as its delimiter, and since "existence" (*sattā*), being resident in the person for whom the action is performed (*prayojya*), cannot serve as a delimiter for the productive operation—which consists of the activity of the performer—it follows that "separating" (*pṛthakkaraṇa*) is unsuitable as an activity directed toward the clarified butter (*ājya*), because it merely effects a numerical count.

Furthermore, "placing" (*sthāpana*), whose status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*), can only be postulated after the fact; thus, it is grasped by the "context" (*prakaraṇa*) defined as the expectancy for the "manner of performance" (*katham-bhāva-ākāṅkṣā*), which seeks a specific activity.

Since grasping is impossible in that which is devoid of activity, its status as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) cannot even be understood; thus, because the notion of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) is seized by the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), it is untenable.

Considering that this [objection] cannot be avoided in any way due to the resulting split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), he concludes the established position (*siddhānta*) with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

(Since there is no possible relationship for a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in the word *ājya*, whereas it is possible in other words such as *pavamāna*, and since there is also secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), this is established after demonstrating that there is no contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārtika*:

because a qualified injunction is not possible in sentences such as those concerning the "fifteen-fold" [stotra], it is clear that the number is enjoined by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to the *ājya* and so forth;
and that is possible only when the *ājya* verses are already established.)

And that attainment is established by the word *ājya* in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) through the abandonment of its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), because of the fear of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, the meaning is that in both sentences the words *ājya* and so forth are names (*nāmadheya*).
[The phrase] "by its very power" (*śaktyaiva*) [is used].

The meaning is that, since there is no possibility of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to the absence of a possible connection with the words "clarified butter" (*ājya*) and so forth, and because there would otherwise arise the fear of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) resulting from the impossibility of coordination with the *stotra*, it is not a fault to assume a distinct conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*).
For this very reason, in the case of the term *bahiṣpavamāna*, when other *stotras* are performed within the sacrificial hall (*sadas*) near the *audumbarī* post...

Furthermore, since the external location of the *bahis-pavamāna* [laud] from the *sadas* is already established by the injunction of its specific place, there is no possibility of a conventional (nirūḍha) secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the connection with the mantras that manifest the Soma which is the substrate of the act of purifying; thus, no separate conventional meaning need be postulated there.
Even though in the Bhāṣya, Vārttika, and other works it is said: "Prajāpati, having fashioned himself as the sacrifice, gave it to the gods; those gods..."

By means of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) beginning with, “They stood ready for the *āgrayaṇa* from one another; he said to them, ‘Enter into a race in this [sacrifice]!’, and they entered the race,” and concluding with, “Because they entered the race (*āji*),

that is the reason for the *ājya* nature of the *ājyas*,” it is stated by Prajāpati to the gods— who were competing for the sake of enjoyment regarding the sacrifice— that they should go to the limit (*maryādā*) of the race (*āji*) in this sacrifice.

Those gods arrived having established these *stotras* as the limit (*kāṣṭhā*) or boundary (*maryādā*); therefore, because they deserve the clarified butter (*ājya*), the well-known meaning of the individual parts is demonstrated by the sense that they are "the *ājyas*.

Nevertheless, just like the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the etymological derivation of the word *udbhid*, since this [passage] also lacks independence regarding its own literal meaning, even if such a linguistic connection (*yoga*) exists—

Since there is no evidence for its being a primary derivative, it should be understood that this [derivation]—being merely for the purpose of grammatical justification like the rule "gamer ḍe"—is intended solely to eliminate the charge of arbitrariness regarding the abandonment of the conventional meaning.
(An exposition on the inclusion of all four [offerings] by means of the plural number in the word "ājyaiḥ" as assisted by an indicative mark):

Since the plural number is heard in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), he states—referring to the origin of the *ājya* offerings—"in the origin of the *ājyas*"—having accepted a distinction of rites based on that number.

He refutes the consequence that all three would be enjoined by means of the *kapiñjalādhikaraṇa* principle, using the principles of the subsequent successive sections (*adhikaraṇa*), with the words "gamaka" and so forth.

Just as in the case of the statement "he milks the northern [cows]," where the plural number would normally terminate in three, yet— by the force of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "Even the boys do not obtain her on this night"— it is understood to refer to a number exceeding three; so too here, in the subsequent text beginning with "O Agni, come for the feast," "O Mitra and Varuna, come to us," "Come, for we have pressed [the Soma]," and "O Indra and Agni, come to the pressed [juice]," there are those sung by means of the *gāyatra* sāman following the triad of *bahiṣpavamāna* sāmans.

The meaning is that because there exists an indicator in the form of the traditional recitation (*āmnāna*) of four triplets (*ṛcas*), and because the plural number refers to the number four—which exceeds three—it is understood that the term "many" intends the number four; thus, within those four, the number fifteen is enjoined.
And in this way, the word *ājya*, occurring in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), is the name of the four stotras.

Because [the formulas] are employed in both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*), as in the case of the four *ājya* offerings: “The *ājya* of the Hotṛ is fifteenfold, that of the Maitrāvaruṇa is seventeenfold, that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is twenty-onefold, and that of the Acchāvāka is fifteenfold.”
(The method for achieving the state of fifteen [verses] in four hymns:

Here, in the *Viṣṭuti-Brāhmaṇa*, it says: "He utters the *hiṅ* over five [verses]: three times, once, and once; he utters the *hiṅ* over five [verses]: once, three times, and once; he utters the *hiṅ* over five [verses]: once, once, and three times."

Since this number is enjoined through a *viṣṭuti*— a specific mode of chanting that effects the count of fifteen— it should be understood that, unlike the number three (*trivṛt*) in the *bahiṣpavamāna*, this number does not reside in separate entities, but is instead to be accomplished through repetition.
(The title *pavamāna* and the separate placement of the number three therein):

Thus, since the word *bahiṣpavamāna* is also the name of a *stotra* according to the manner previously stated, the number three enjoined with reference to it—as found in the subsequent text of the Sāmavedins: "Sing to him, O men," "With flashing luster," and "Of the purifying one"—[is established].
It should be understood that because three triplets beginning with "ketave" are recited, [the ritual] must indeed be performed as separate acts.

(On the fact that *pṛṣṭha* is a name, its being sixfold, and the manner of accomplishing its seventeen-fold nature): Thus, since the word *pṛṣṭha*, like the word *ājya*, would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) if it were a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), it is established as a name (*nāmadheya*) by virtue of its conventional usage in the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*). Therefore, "They praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*" (*pṛṣṭhaiḥ stuvate*) is the originative injunction; for the author of the Vārttika has written it as such. Since it is an originative injunction, he states that there are six *pṛṣṭhas*—those enjoined by that injunction—by the force of the plural number (*bahuvacana*) aided by the indicative mark (*gamaka*): "Thus... (*evam iti*).

In this context, because the six triplets beginning with "abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ," "tvām iddhi havāmahe," "kayā naścitra ā bhuvat," "taṃ vo dasma mṛtīṣaham," "abhipravassurādhasam," and "tarobhirvovidadvasuḥ" are recorded in the *Uttaragrantha*,
and because they are respectively designated by the names *rathantara*, *bṛhat*, *vāmadevya*, *naudhasa*, *śyaita*, and *kāleya*.
Regarding the six *pṛṣṭha* chants, which are designated as such, the statement "there are seventeen" is an injunction of the number seventeen as a quality (*guṇa*).

In that context as well, it is stated in the *viṣṭuti*: "He utters the *hiṅkāra* over five [verses]: three times, once, and once; he utters the *hiṅkāra* over five: once, three times, and once; he utters the *hiṅkāra* over seven: once, three times... and so forth.
The meaning is that it is to be accomplished solely through practice.
(Although the term *pṛṣṭha* is conventionally restricted to specific types of hymns, there is no contradiction with the explanatory passage [arthavāda].

Even though here too there is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to etymologically explain the word *pṛṣṭha*—beginning with, "The waters indeed approached according to their season; Vāyu moved about upon their surface; from that, desirable wealth was produced; Mitra and Varuṇa perceived it"—nevertheless, following the description of the sexual union consisting of Vāyu’s movement upon the surface of the seasonal waters, [the text continues:]

Having described the origin of the Vāmadevya and the etymology of its name, and having stated its placement within the *pṛṣṭha* stotras by the phrase "they deposited it upon the *pṛṣṭhas*," and furthermore, having explained the origin of the six *sāmans* known as Rathantara, Bṛhat, Vairūpa, Vairāja, Śākvara, and Raivata— which serve as the means for the *pṛṣṭha* stotras— by the passage beginning with "the *pṛṣṭhas* from this womb" (*etasyā yoneḥ pṛṣṭhāni*), [the text proceeds].

Because of the concluding statement, “The Vāmadevya [Sāman] is indeed the *pṛṣṭhas* for the sons,” although the word *pṛṣṭha* serves to explain the *pṛṣṭha* status within the Rathantara and other Sāmans, it does not serve to explain them as names of specific hymns (*stotra*). Therefore, there is no contradiction in assuming that the term is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*). For this very reason, the mention of the word *pṛṣṭha* in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—in the phrase “they deposited [the fires] upon the *pṛṣṭhas*”—is consistent only by taking for granted the fourfold *pṛṣṭha* status already established through conventional usage.

By this, the statement in the Vārtika—that the term *pṛṣṭha* is well-known in the case of the *Vāmadevya* and other [sāmans] because they have as their archetype the group of six sāmans beginning with the *Rathantara* called *pṛṣṭha*—is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*). Even if the application of the word *pṛṣṭha* to the *Vāmadevya* could somehow be established on the basis of its being their archetype, it is absent elsewhere; furthermore, since the application of the term *pṛṣṭha* in the phrase "they placed them upon the *pṛṣṭhas*" (*pṛṣṭheṣu nyadadhuḥ*) and the quality of being produced from the contact between water, wind, and sexual union are possible only in the *Vāmadevya* itself, it is there alone that the status of being a *pṛṣṭha* resides.

Since it is appropriate to accept [the term] primarily [in that sense], and since its application to the *rathantara* and other [sāmans] is logically explained as being secondary (*gauṇa*) due to their being produced from it;

for this very reason, even though it merely denotes placement in the second position, it is not correct to assume that its purpose is solely to explain the grounds for applying the word *pṛṣṭha* to the *vāmadevya*,

especially when the derivation of the root *spṛś* (to touch) in the *uṇādi* suffixes clearly demonstrates that the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is the state of being produced from the contact known as the union of water and wind.
When the suffix *thak* is applied, the word *pṛṣṭha* is derived as follows: by the rule "tithapṛṣṭhakuthagūthayūthaprothāḥ," the letter *s* is elided and the form is established as a *nipāta*;
then, by the rule "vraścādi," the letter *ś* is replaced by *ṣ*, and through the application of the rule regarding *ṣṭutva*, the etymological derivation of the word *pṛṣṭha* is thus explained.

Although, for fear of postulating a separate potency (*śakti*) in place of the word *pṛṣṭha*, there is indeed a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the relationship of being the means for the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* in the case of the *rathantara* and other [sāmans]; yet...
Nevertheless, because a conventional (nirūḍha) secondary sense (lakṣaṇā) is accepted on the basis of grammatical derivation (anvākhyāna), the derivation is not purposeless.

Its fruit is as follows: in the case of the statement "he stands near with the *pṛṣṭhas*," one understands that the verses have the purpose of recitation (*abhidhāna*), in accordance with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) prescribed by the rule "the middle voice is used after *upa* when a mantra is the instrument" (*upānmantrakaraṇe*). And although, with respect to this act of recitation, the verses are understood to be the instruments only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—since their primary status as the instruments of the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* is untenable—even so, this results precisely in an injunction of the *sāmans* such as the *rathantara*, by way of excluding unchanted verses from being the instruments.

Therefore, even when there is a prescription of Sāmans such as the Rathantara alone, since the Sāmans function as instruments (karaṇa) only by means of manifesting syllables— even when expressing a quality— it is not contradictory that their status as being based on [the Ṛks] is established by way of fitness. Furthermore, although the rule "yadyonyām" prescribes those [Sāmans] for the subsequent verses (uttarās) in accordance with the requirement that the Sāman used for the stotra must imitate the triplet (tṛca), there is no application of the subsequent verses here, because they lack the status of being *stotrīya* (verses forming part of a stotra).

Therefore, since the usage of the term *pṛṣṭha*— as seen in the original archetype (*prakṛti*) in passages such as “the seventeen *pṛṣṭhas*,” “they praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*,” “the twenty-one-fold *pṛṣṭha* of the Hotṛ,” “the twenty-seven-fold *pṛṣṭha* of the Maitrāvaruṇa,” “the seventeen-fold [of] the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin,” and “the fifteen-fold [of] the Acchāvāka”— is exactly like that of the *ājya* [stotras],
the word *pṛṣṭha* refers to the six stotras occurring immediately after the Mādhyandina-pavamāna.
Thus, it is established that the status of being a mere name is indeed in vain.

As for the specific use of the word *pṛṣṭha* in reference to the *hotṛ*'s *pṛṣṭha* in such passages as "the *pṛṣṭha* consists of the *Bṛhat*" and "the *Kaṇvarathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha*," which does not apply to the *Vāmadevya* and other [sāmans], this is like the use of the word "wealth" (*dravya*) for gold, or the use of the word "Pārtha" for Arjuna.
It is not a contradiction that [the object] is to be known solely through the force of habitual tendency (*nirūḍha*).
(An explanation of why only four are taken up by rule in the passage "They praise with the pṛṣṭhas"):
Now, one might ask, "If there are six pṛṣṭhas, how can there be the performance of only four?
To this he says: "They are to be performed."
Regarding the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans].
When there is an injunction of an option for the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* *sāman* *pṛṣṭha* chants by the statement, "The *pṛṣṭha* is either the *bṛhat* or the *rathantara*," then—

since the option for the final two *pṛṣṭhas* is prescribed restrictively such that the *śyaita* is the *pṛṣṭha* in the *bṛhat* alternative and the *naidhasa* is the *pṛṣṭha* in the *rathantara-pṛṣṭha* alternative— the meaning is that four [stotras] are to be performed as fixed.

Just as in this case, even though there is a difference between the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] which results in a difference in the unseen potency (*apūrva*), the ninth-book prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the confusion of the properties of the *rathantara* and *bṛhat* will be demonstrated by the venerable teacher in that very same place.
(Other objections and the manner of their refutation:

Now, [an objection may be raised]: if there were a plurality of *pṛṣṭhas* in the archetype (*prakṛti*), then the *kaṇvarathantara* and others would necessarily find a place among all the *pṛṣṭhas*, just as the *kautsa* and others do;

likewise, in the case of the statement "the *viśvajit* has all the *pṛṣṭhas*," the reference by the term "all *pṛṣṭhas*" would be justified solely through the plurality of *pṛṣṭhas* obtained from the archetype.

Since there would be the consequence of non-establishment for what will be stated in the seventh [chapter]—namely, that the *rathantara* and other *pṛṣṭha* chants belonging to the six-day period (*ṣāḍahika*) are obtained—he says: "And as here."

In the modified injunctions such as “the *kaṇvarathantara* becomes the *pṛṣṭha*,” because there is a syntactic coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word *pṛṣṭha* occurring in the original terms *rathantara* and *bṛhat*, and the word *pṛṣṭha* [in the modified injunction], it is established—by means of the tenth-book principle—that the *vairūpa* and other *sāmans* enjoined by statements such as “the *vairūpa* *sāman* [is the *pṛṣṭha*]” have the *mahendra-stotra* as their object; likewise, here too, it is appropriate that they have that same object. Therefore, [there is no contradiction].
There would be the consequence of [the term] being applied to all *pṛṣṭha* [stotras].
For this very reason—the fact that the word *pṛṣṭha* is employed in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*) by virtue of conventional usage (*nirūḍhi*)—this alone is the result.
And thus, because there is no such identical designation for the *kautsa* and others, they do not find their application in that [archetype] alone.
Moreover, since it applies everywhere, there is no inconsistency.

However, regarding the term *sarvapṛṣṭha*, if it were taken to refer to the archetypal (*prākṛta*) [sacrifices], it would result in a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) and thus be rendered purposeless; therefore, to ensure it possesses the status of an injunction (*vidheya*), the term refers to the [sacrifices] of the six-day period (*ṣāḍahika*). This is stated by the author of the Bhāṣya in his commentary on the sūtra, "Or rather, because of the injunction there from the six-day period," concerning the word *sarvapṛṣṭha*.
This has been demonstrated precisely by way of establishing its status as an injunction.
(Parthasarathi’s views and their refutations:

For this very reason—since there is no plurality of *pṛṣṭha* chants in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is logical that the conventional usage therein refers to the absence of plurality of *pṛṣṭha* not obtained through the extended application (*codaka*); thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. This being the case, out of fear of this defect, Parthasarathi, following the natural sense of the *Nemapiṅka-vārtika*, [states]: "The *bṛhat-pṛṣṭha*..."

In these two sentences, "the Rathantara becomes the *pṛṣṭha*" and "[the Bṛhat] becomes the *pṛṣṭha*," even though the words *bṛhat* and *rathantara* are primary [terms], they are accepted as having the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of signifying the means of accomplishing their own objects; since it is precisely the two stotras qualified by those [sāmans] that are enjoined under the name *māhendra*,
the word *pṛṣṭha* is primary only in that context.

In the injunction “They praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*,” the four stotras beginning with the Kaṇva-māhendra are referred to collectively by the term *pṛṣṭha* through figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*).
The purpose of this is that, in the statement “The *pṛṣṭhas* are seventeen-fold,” all of them are included by the word *pṛṣṭha*, thereby allowing that numerical measure to be applied to the four.

Furthermore, even though there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word *stotra* and the word *pṛṣṭha* in the original originative injunction, the status of *pṛṣṭha* as a name for the stotra is established.

It has been argued that otherwise, there would arise a doubt regarding the word *pṛṣṭha*—even though it is mentioned alongside the *sāman* in the originative injunction—as to whether its purpose is to denote a quality (*guṇa*).
That argument is incorrect;

for since the word *pṛṣṭha* is used everywhere by virtue of its primary denotative power (*śakti*), there is no evidence to justify assuming a secondary or figurative sense (*gauṇatva*) for it elsewhere.

Nor is there a contradiction with the assumption of figurative meaning (gauṇatva) stated in the Vārttika on the seventh book and elsewhere; for you too face an equal contradiction with the Vārttika located therein, which aims to demonstrate that the sentence "They praise with the Pṛṣṭhas" is an originative injunction (utpattividhi).

Therefore, since one of the two Vārttikas must necessarily be regarded as a mere *prauḍhivāda* (bold or tentative statement), it is more appropriate to assume that status for the one in which the defect of figurative meaning and so forth would otherwise result.

Because there is no purpose in accepting the subordinate status of the primary [meanings] in the two sentences— "the *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha*" and "the *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha*"— which would entail the fault of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication of possession) and the resulting complexity of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*),
this sentence does not aim at the origination of two distinct *pṛṣṭha* chants. Rather,

by virtue of the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the *māhendra* stotra, it aims at the injunction of two *sāmans* by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the two *pṛṣṭhas* known as *māhendra*.

Therefore, in the case of the *jaghanya* (last) *pṛṣṭha*, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) should be understood here through an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) characterized by the accomplishment of its own purpose. It is precisely for those two *pṛṣṭhas* designated as *māhendra* that an option is appropriate, based on the scriptural statement: "Either the *bṛhat* or the *rathantara* serves as the *pṛṣṭha*. Thus, an option alone is logical.
(Refutation of the Nyāyasudhākāra’s view:

By this [it is shown that] the two sentences— "They praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*" and "The *bṛhat* becomes the *pṛṣṭha* for the Mahendra [laud]"— are, as before, injunctions for two different *sāmans* within a single stotra, specifically for the single *pṛṣṭha* stotra called Mahendra.

And although these two [Sāmans] share the same purpose regarding the *pṛṣṭha* chant, since there would otherwise result an option based on the difference between their respective intermediate effects as revealed by their respective Ṛks, the option arises precisely from the scriptural statement: "The *pṛṣṭha* is either the *Bṛhat* or the *Rathantara*.

Furthermore, since in this injunction for the Sāman the word *pṛṣṭha* refers specifically to the *Māhendra-stotra*, the word *pṛṣṭha* appearing in the plural in the originative injunction is used figuratively for the collection of *pṛṣṭhas* due to the presence of that characteristic (liṅga), just as in the expression "decorate the *puroḍāśas*," the word *puroḍāśa* refers to the collection of cakes.

Furthermore, because the plural number is merely a restatement of a number already established by accumulation (*pracaya*), it lacks injunctive force and thus cannot function as a differentiator of the action, just as in the case of the injunction *samidho yajati*.
Therefore, the use of the plural *pṛṣṭhaiḥ* refers to the Āmahendra-stotra prescribed by this very sentence in conjunction with the three stotras established by other means of proof.

As for the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*’s hypothesis that even in the passage *“saptadaśāni pṛṣṭhāni”* the number is enjoined with respect to the *pṛṣṭha* in general—whether primary or secondary—that too is refuted.
Because there is no evidence for it being used in a secondary sense;

furthermore, since in the *Sāmavidhivākya* the word *pṛṣṭha* denotes only the *māhendra-stotra*, even the plural number in *pṛṣṭhaiḥ* can be justified through a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of unity according to the principle of the *pāśādhikaraṇa*. Therefore, there is no evidence for the word *pṛṣṭha* having a secondary meaning in those various instances. Thus, it is that very [primary sense]...
There would be the consequence of an association with the number seventeen.

Furthermore, there is no evidence to determine that the word *pṛṣṭha* has its primary denotation (*śakti*) only in the two *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] within the Sāma-vidhi sentence, specifically in the Māhendra-stotra.

This is because, since it lacks grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a specific action, its status as a name for a stotra is not established; consequently, its being understood as denoting the Māhendra [deity] is all the more unascertained.

For me, however, since "They praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*" is co-referential with the *stotra* (hymns of praise), it is not a defect even if it refers specifically to the *māhendra* [stotra] based on the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), provided that it serves as the name for all *stotras*.

Furthermore, since there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish the three *stotras*, and because it is impossible to refer to a number qualified by their accumulation in the absence of such a basis, it is necessary that the number itself be the thing enjoined; thus, the distinction between the *pṛṣṭha* hymns is unavoidable.
Therefore, because its capacity is not projected by anything else, "They praise with the *pṛṣṭhas*" is indeed the original injunctive statement (*utpattivākya*).
Therefore, six hymns named *pṛṣṭha* are to be enjoined, and not two *pṛṣṭhas* according to the method stated in the *Vidhirasāyana*,
nor indeed one single *pṛṣṭha* as asserted by the *Nyāyasudhā*.
The meaning is that the refutations of other views, preceded by the removal of objections arising against his own position, are to be seen in the *Kaustubha*.
(Conclusion on the status of *citrā* and other terms as names due to the consequence of sentence-splitting):

Therefore, it is established that because of the consequence of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*) in the descriptive passage (*guṇavākya*), the terms *bahiṣpavamāna*, *ājya*, and *pṛṣṭha* are names in their respective originative passages (*utpattivākya*).
As for the term *citrā*, however, because of the consequence of sentence-splitting in the passage stating the fruit (*phalavākya*), it is the name of the sacrifices dedicated to Prajāpati.
The purpose has not been stated because it is evident from the presentation of the prima facie and final positions.

Thus ends the third section concerning the designation of terms such as *citram* and others. (B1) (Section 4: "And another scriptural passage [establishes the name] because it declares that same [act]. Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.4.
That which is similar to that.

In this context, regarding words that are either conventional (*rūḍha*) or etymological (*yaugika*), and which have a possible application— as in "He offers the *agnihotra*," "He pours the *āghāra* libation," and "He sacrifices the *samidhs*"—
when there arises an inquiry as to whether words such as *agnihotra* and so forth are injunctions of accessory materials (*guṇavidhi*) or names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*),
it is more appropriate that they be injunctions of accessory materials on account of their well-known usage (*prasiddhi*).
Nor is there a syntactical split (vākyabheda) here,
because there is no multiplicity of things to be enjoined.

Therefore, in the word *agnihotra*, by the etymological derivation "that in which the offering (*hotra*) is for Agni," Agni— the subordinate member of the compound— is enjoined as the deity for the oblation (*homa*).
Nor can it be argued that this [mantra] is not enjoined because it is already obtained by the rule, "That which one offers in the evening to Agni and Prajāpati";

for since an injunction of a distinct, qualified action is necessary due to the inclusion of multiple subordinate elements (*guṇa*) therein, that [mantra] is not obtained in the rite enjoined by this particular sentence.
Therefore, in cases such as the *darvī-homa* where the *āgneya* mantra is recited, [the mantra is indeed part of the injunction].

By way of restating such *darvihoma* offerings, only the deity is enjoined by this [text]; for when that [deity] can be obtained through the direct statement, one should not assume an injunction based on the wording of a mantra.
Or it is another distinct action.
Even in the sentence regarding the *āghāra* (sprinkling), the word *āghāra* ending in the accusative case denotes a liquid substance such as clarified butter (*ājya*) that is capable of flowing;
and by the verbal root, the consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) called "flowing" is enjoined with reference to that [substance].
