Since a consecration cannot apply to that which has not been employed [in a ritual], the liquid substance is enjoined as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *upāṃśuyāja* by means of a syntactical connection (*vākya*) inferred from the context (*prakaraṇa*).

"Or rather, this [clarified butter] was taken four times, having poured the *āghāra* (libation) for it"— by this [statement], there is the presentation of a specific form consisting of the four-fold portion that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *prayāja* offerings.

In any case, since the word *āghāra* refers to the substance and is not a name, this [conclusion] is reached— provided that the deity can be obtained through an injunction inferred from the wording of the mantra itself.

Since it would result in futility for a previously existing action to be assumed as being enjoined by a new injunction, and since it is improper to enjoin the meaning of a verbal root— which is already established by a primary injunction— when a higher prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is possible, there can first of all be no injunction of a deity by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the *darvī-homa*.
Nor can there be an injunction of a distinct, qualified action (*karmāntara*).

Because the deities are obtained through the very wording of the mantras enjoined by the scriptural injunctions— “*agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā* for the evening oblation” and “*sūryo jyotir jyotir sūryaḥ svāhā* for the morning oblation”—

the passage “that which he offers in the evening to Agni and Prajāpati, and that which he offers in the morning to Sūrya and Prajāpati” merely prescribes Prajāpati alone as qualified by the conjunction of the deities of the evening and morning times, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*).

Therefore, just as the status of being a deity belongs to two deities individually by virtue of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of mantras addressed to each alone, so too does it belong to them jointly by virtue of the wording of a mantra with mixed indicative marks, namely, "Agni is light; Agni, svāhā! [at dawn].
Consequently, the words "Agni" and "Sūrya" in the sentence "That which for Agni... are indicative (*lakṣaka*) of the deities belonging to the evening and morning times respectively.

The terms *sāyam* (evening) and *prātaḥ* (morning) serve as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Furthermore, because the connection of the conjunction (*ca*)—which is brought to mind by the word *ca* itself—with Prajāpati is well-established as being the function of a particle (*nipāta*), there is no multiplicity of things to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

Consequently, since Agni is already established as the deity in the Agnihotra oblation, the term *agnihotra* is a name (*nāmadheya*) derived through the etymological analysis "the offering (*hotra*) to Agni."

Likewise, regarding the *āghāra* (libation) in the *upāṃśuyāja*, since the substance is already obtained by the very statement, "Indeed, that which is taken in the *dhruvā* vessel is for the sake of this entire sacrifice," even if one were to enjoin a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) with reference to the *prayāja* clarified butter, it would result in the application of a second type of injunction; therefore, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the word *āghāra*— derived from the verbal root in the sense of an action— is a name (*nāmadheya*).
And the oblation (*homa*) alone is that which is to be performed and is indicated by the verbal root;

for the deity Indra is obtained through the metrical description in the injunction, "He pours the *āghāra* libation with [the mantra] 'Indra, stand upright at the sacrifice,'" and the substance is obtained by the rule regarding the fourfold-drawn portion (*caturgṛhīta*).
This will be stated similarly regarding the *samidh* and other offerings as well.
In all instances, the accusative case has the sense of defining the instrument; thus, there is no contradiction. // 4 // 20 //
Thus ends the fourth section, *Tatprakhya-adhikaraṇa*.

(The analysis of the subject matter, preceded by an examination of the connection: Because the grounds for rejecting it as a subsidiary injunction (*guṇavidhi*)—namely, the occurrence of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) and syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)—which were established in the two preceding sections, are absent here.

Without explicitly stating the immediate connection (*anantara-saṅgati*) in the form of a counter-example arising from the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), as it is self-evident, [the author] shows that the specific words under consideration constitute the illustrative examples by saying: "In this [context]... (*iha*).

In this context, the inquiry concerns only derivative (*yaugika*) names, as they avoid the need for possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*); however, in the subsequent section, the inquiry concerns conventional (*sāṃvijñāyika*) names. This is established by first demonstrating the validity of the Vārttika which cites "the mention of that" (*tatprakhya*) as an example, and then determining that [the rule] applies to terms such as *amāvāsyā*.

The phrase "because of the impossibility of a split in the sentence" (*vākyabhedāsaṃbhavāt*) was stated in the *Vārttika* text to dispel the misconception that only derivative (*yaugika*) terms are examples here; therefore, it was specified as "of conventional (*rūḍha*) terms.
For this very reason, it is indicated that words such as *paurṇamāsī*, *amāvāsyā*, *samit*, and so forth, occurring in the *vidvadvākya* and other passages, are also examples.

Indeed, their status as names (*nāmadheya*) cannot be established through those arguments—the avoidance of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), the impossibility of a split in the sentence, and the designation [of the sacrifice]—which apply to them.

Therefore, since the establishment of its status as a name (nāmatā) must be accomplished right here by means of the principle of "being known from that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*), it serves as an illustrative example.

As for the passage in the Vārtika, however, it should be understood as being useful merely for demonstrating a disparity in the underlying principles, with the sole intent of avoiding the implication of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) in any way possible.
(The delineation of the fact that [the subject matter] is already established by the *tatprakhyanyāya*, through the principles of the *udbhid-citratadvyapadeśa* [and others]):
By the phrase "of those whose application is possible," it is indicated that the *citradhikaraṇa* and *tadvyapadeśādhikaraṇa* concern conventional (*rūḍha*) terms;

and by demonstrating another principle, it is shown that for etymological (*yaugika*) terms, they do not fall under the scope of the *udbhidhikaraṇa* principle, and thus there is a separate commencement of an *adhikaraṇa*.

The charge of futility has been avoided. Therefore, it is logical that here, by means of three distinct topics (*adhikaraṇa*), the status of certain words—as whether they are etymological (*yaugika*) or conventional (*rūḍha*)—as names (*nāmadheya*) is established through another principle, namely the *tatprakhya-śāstra*, after first refuting their status as injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*). This is appropriate.
The meaning is that there is a separate undertaking.
(Regarding the doubt concerning the impossibility of the *tatprakhyanyāya* being the third [topic] and its resolution:

Nor does it follow that the section on "Designation by That" (*tadvyapadeśādhikaraṇa*) should begin immediately after the section on the *citrā* sacrifice, simply because there is no difference in their status as counter-examples;
for its immediate sequence is justified by its being a counter-example to the section on "Renowned by That" (*tatprakhyādhikaraṇa*).
For there is no rule that wherever something has a connection, it must be denoted therein;
rather, whatever is denoted in a particular place [is so by virtue of that connection].
In that case, some connection must be stated for it.
Therefore, since there exists a connection with the topic under discussion—the section concerning its manifestation (*tatprakhyādhikaraṇa*)—there is no fault.
For this very reason, the objection that "because of the commonality of being etymological (*yaugikatva*), this [section] ought to begin immediately after the section on *udbhid*" is also refuted.

Since even established (rūḍha) names could be cited as examples here—given their similarity to those [etymological names] and the fact that their discussion could likewise have been commenced immediately after the section on *citras*—it follows that once both the etymological (*yaugika*) and the established (*rūḍha*) names had been examined by the two preceding sections, both types were present at hand. Since they cannot be accounted for otherwise, it is the status of these as names (*nāmadheyatā*) that is first investigated here;
thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
Because of its being well-known.
(An establishment of the *guṇavidhi* status [of the term *agnihotra*] based on its not having an equal application to both a quality and an action):
This [principle] is also an indicator for the capacity to produce a specific inclination [toward action].
Furthermore, there is no suspicion here that [the term *agnihotra*] is a name (*nāmadheya*) among derivative terms (*yaugika*), according to the logic of the *udbhid*.

Since, according to the method to be explained, the application of the etymological derivation (*avayavayoga*) consisting in the word *agni* denoting the deity for the ritual action is unestablished, and since there is likewise an absence of a common mode of occurrence (*tulyavadvṛttikatva*) with respect to both the quality and the action, there is a disparity between them; consequently, because the word *agni* within the compound *agnihotra*— which ends in a *bahuvrīhi*—
serves as the provider of the quality to be enjoined solely by its own form, there is no such etymological application even with respect to the quality.
Therefore, the meaning is that, just like the words "Soma" and so forth, this is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) on account of its well-known usage and other such factors.
(The doubt regarding the *agnihotra* being a name [of a rite] based on the *Citrā* section, and its resolution:

Since the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is obtained by resorting to the formation of a *bahuvrīhi* compound—as will be explained later—there is no need to even suspect that the term is a name (as names are easily set aside among etymological terms), because the action is merely being restated (*anuvāda*) and thus there is no possibility of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*). Therefore, having set aside that suspicion, [the author proceeds to state] the reason for rejecting the view that it is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), as presented in the immediately following section.
Anticipating the objection that this would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), he refutes it with the words "And not" (*na ca*).

(Justification for the *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound in the term *agnihotra*) Here, from the root *hu*, when the *traṇ* suffix is applied according to the *Uṇādi* rule "from *hu*, *pā*, *mā*, *śru*, *bhas*, *vas*, and *si*, [the suffix] *traṇ*," and when the *guṇa* substitution is applied by the rule "for [roots ending in] *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* [suffixes]," the word *hotra* is derived. Since the word *hotra* denotes the substance being offered (*hūyamāna-dravya*), [the compound *agni-hotra*] means "that in which fire (*agni*) is the *hotra*."
First of all, the formation of a coordinate (samānādhikaraṇa) bahuvrīhi compound is not possible for the term *agnihotra*.

Nor is it possible for a non-coordinate (vyadhikaraṇa) bahuvrīhi—such as in the case of *kaṇṭhekāla* ("black-throated")—to apply here by the force of the grammatical indicator (*jñāpaka*) stating "in a bahuvrīhi, when a locative or a qualifier [is involved]," resulting in the interpretation "that in which the offering (*hotra*) is made in the fire (*agni*).

This is because the status of the fire as the locus is already established by the rule "one offers in the *āhavanīya*," and thus such an argument fails to support the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Nor is it a genitive tatpuruṣa compound meaning "the fuel of fire," because that would result in an impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb *juhoti* (he offers),
and because the specific nature of the relationship [between the two] would remain unknown.
Since even a fourth-case (caturthī) compound is intended only when there is a relationship of material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), it is not applicable here;
furthermore, because it is not included in the *śauṇḍādi* group, a seventh-case (saptamī) tatpuruṣa compound is also impossible.

Therefore, since no other type of compound is possible, and in accordance with the requirement for coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *juhoti*, it must be explained as a bahuvrīhi compound.

Although it does not conform to the [standard] definition, that [interpretation] is accepted by both the authors of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika in their established doctrine; having somehow accepted it even in the prima facie argument on the grounds of its being archaic (chāndasa), he establishes its status as an injunction of qualities (guṇavidhi) with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).
(An examination of how, even though the term *agnihotra* refers to a qualified entity, it serves to convey only the qualifier: "It has the meaning of a subordinate element (*upasarjana*)."

Just as in the case of the statement "The priests, wearing red turbans, perform the ritual," where the red turban—a subordinate element—is enjoined upon the priests who are already established as the referents of the compound, so too here, since the substance and other factors of the *hotṛ* priest are already established, the status of Agni as the deity—which serves as a qualifying attribute—is what is enjoined; this is the meaning.

(An objection: Since there is no acquisition of the ritual action (*karman*) through the statement of the result (*phalavākya*) and so forth, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) must be formulated solely as a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*). Now, one might object: since the ritual action is not otherwise established here, it is impossible to enjoin a quality (*guṇavidhi*) by way of restating that action; therefore, just as in the case of an injunction of a quality, even in the case of a qualified injunction, the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is obtained through the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself. Consequently, just as in the sentence concerning the *citrayajña*, there is no occasion for the figurative indication of possessiveness (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) in a qualified injunction; thus, [the prima facie position] should indeed be stated as a qualified injunction.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is correct.
Furthermore, there is no injunction of a ritual action (*karmavidhāna*) by means of the sentence stating the result;
for even so, since the connection with the result would also have to be enjoined therein, it would entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) characterized by excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

For this very reason, because two points of time are mentioned, there is no injunction of a new ritual action even in the case of "that which one offers in the evening and in the morning. Nor, because of the addition of two qualities, is there an injunction of that [action] in the case of "that which [is offered] to Agni and to Prajāpati.
And it should not be argued: "In this sentence, since multiple qualities are mentioned, an injunction of a new ritual action is necessary to avoid the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)."

Since the fire (agni) is already obtained through the ritual action enjoined by this sentence, an injunction of fire is untenable; therefore, since it results in the status of being a "text that proclaims what is already known" (tatprakhya-śāstra), it follows that it must be a name (nāmadheya).

Furthermore, it is impossible to enjoin Agni as a deity by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the rite enjoined by the Sūrya-text, because the deities Sūrya and Prajāpati are already established by the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) for that rite, and because there is no possibility of inserting the deity Agni [into a rite already occupied].
[In this regard, there is also a refutation of the view of Somanātha.
Regarding the rite enjoined by the Sūrya-text, since Sūrya and Prajāpati are enjoined by the originative injunction, it is impossible to introduce the deity Agni.

As for what Somanātha [says]: since the injunction of Prajāpati conjoined with Sūrya in the Sūrya-text is obtained by the single word *ca*, the subsequent *ca* after the word *sūrya* would otherwise be rendered redundant; therefore, because it enjoins the conjunction of Agni with Sūrya as prescribed by this very sentence, Agni finds a place in the rite even though that rite is already occupied by Sūrya and Prajāpati, who are taught in the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).

For this very reason, it has been stated that since Agni is already established in the rite enjoined by the sentence "And that which for Agni," the word *ca* (and) is relied upon as having the sense of mutual conjunction (*samuccaya*). This is because it is a matter of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that a word *ca* conjoined with a particular term indicates a conjunction only with that which is conjoined with it; thus, even though conjunction with Sūrya is possible in the case of Prajāpati, [the word *ca*] indicates conjunction with Agni.
It is incorrect [to claim] that [the Sun] is impossible [to be combined],

because, as in the case of the "redness" (āruṇya) and other qualities, their combination is established through being mentioned in a single syntactical unit (ekavākya), and because even so, the second "and" (ca) would be redundant;
for the "and" could be justified even in the sentence concerning fire by taking it to mean a combination with the Sun.
Furthermore, there is no evidence for the view that these [terms] signify mutual conjunction (*parasparasamuccaya*).

For in the case of the statement, "That which one offers in the evening and in the morning," since the specific times are prescribed as part of the very origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*) of the rite enjoined by the sentence, "That which [is offered] to Agni," it would be impossible for the evening and morning times to be included through conjunction; consequently, [the injunction] would result in being devoid of a subject matter.

(This refutes the suspicion that the passage is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) by way of restating a rite already enjoined by the sentence beginning with "That which in the evening...").

Nor can there be an injunction of the quality of fire (*agni*) here by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the ritual act prescribed by the sentence "That which [is offered] in the evening," because once that act is presented by the sentence "That which [is offered] to Agni," it is impossible for this [injunction] to concern a different ritual act according to the principle of a distinct context (*prakaraṇāntara-nyāya*).
Furthermore, even if that were possible on account of the quality, two non-optional qualities (*anupādeya-guṇa*) cannot coexist.

Because it is impossible for a combination [of multiple injunctions] to be established in a single place, and because there would result the extreme complexity of having to assume two separate injunctions for two distinct actions—each producing its own unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—just as in the case of the *Āgneya* passage, this very complexity serves as the restrictive factor.

Nor can there be an injunction of deities such as Agni by means of the two sentences beginning with "That which [is offered] to Agni," based on a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the action qualified by the evening and morning times prescribed by the evening and morning sentences;
for that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), characterized by the repetition of the injunctive force due to the inclusion of multiple subordinate qualities (*guṇa*).
(Refutation of the view of the *Prakāśakāra* regarding the impossibility of an injunction for the evening-specialized oblation):

As for what was stated by the *Prakāśakāra*s here—that even if [the passage] were a restatement (*anuvāda*) qualified by the times of evening and morning, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*)—that must be disregarded, because since the words "evening" (*sāyam*) and "morning" (*prātar*) are indeclinables (*avyaya*), their meaning is already established as being construed with the meaning of the word with which they are co-occurrent (*samabhivyāhṛta*). Thus, that objection does not apply.

(Conclusion following the doubt regarding the view that the injunction prescribes an action qualified by attributes, preceded by the demonstration that sentences such as "sāyaṃ yad agnaye" are supplements to the *agnihotra* sentence, and the refutation of the *Prakāśa* school's position therein:
Therefore, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the injunction prescribing an action qualified by attributes resides in the *agnihotra* sentence itself;
in that very [sentence], the injunction for the times of evening and morning is established by the sentences concerning "evening" and "morning."

Since it is a well-established linguistic principle that the meaning of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) can be construed with the meaning of the word *ca* (and), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) even when the conjunction of the evening and morning times is enjoined by way of restating the rite prescribed in the *Agnihotra* injunction.

Furthermore, because this very rite is restated by the term *agnihotra* as the locus for the injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), the connection of the result and the occasion [with the rite] is established through the two sentences concerning the result and the occasion.

As for the other two rites enjoined by the sentence "That which [is offered] to Agni and [to Soma]," they are indeed subsidiary parts of the rite enjoined by this present sentence, because, being devoid of their own results, the context (*prakaraṇa*) remains applicable to them.

As for the claim made by the authors of the *Prakāśa* that—even if a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is accepted—the two [elements] serve the purpose of attaining heaven according to the principle of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, that is incorrect because their status as subsidiaries (*aṅgatva*) follows from the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is properly established precisely as a qualified injunction; this objection will be resolved by simply accepting it as our own position (*iṣṭāpatti*).

(The position that it is an injunction of a mere accessory according to the view of the ancients— including the doubt regarding the attainment of Agni through the sentence *yad agnaye* and the failure to avoid the resulting syntactical split,

etc.)— In this regard, following the method of the ancients, after first refuting [the opponent's view] by means of the principle of *tatprakhya-śāstra* (a scriptural statement that makes known an accessory intended to be enjoined), [the author] states "yad agnaye ca" in order to establish that it is an injunction of a mere accessory, since the attainment of the ritual act (*karman*) exists here.

By this statement, if both Agni and Prajāpati were enjoined— even though they are already combined— by way of a restatement (anuvāda) of the rite enjoined by the Agnihotra sentence, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).
Nor can this be avoided here by means of enjoining a single qualified factor (kāraka), because the factors are distinct due to the difference in their case-endings (vibhakti).

For this very reason, since factors of action (*kāraka*) are connected only with an action, and because there is no established rule for their connection with the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) expressed by the word *ca*, the objection is not resolved even by enjoining a conjunction of two factors of action. By this, the following argument is also refuted: "Since Agni is already obtained through an injunction inferred from the otherwise inexplicable application (*viniyoga*) of the mantra ‘Agnir jyotir jyotir agniḥ svāhā’, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the injunction of Prajāpati in conjunction [with Agni]."

Furthermore, since "to Agni" (*agnaye*) cannot be construed as a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) in the sense of the word "and" (*ca*), it is impossible to justify the injunction of that [Prajāpati] in conjunction with Agni.

Nor can one avoid the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) by accepting that the word "to Agni" (*agnaye*) in the sentence is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the deity Agni already obtained from the wording of the mantra, thereby enjoining Prajāpati alone;
for if that were the case, Prajāpati would already be occupied by the status of deity as conveyed by the dative-ending word in the Brāhmaṇa sentence.

Because the postulation of a deity based on the wording of a mantra is untenable— since, according to the *aindrī-nyāya*, the mantra would result in manifesting Prajāpati alone, making the mention "to Agni" an improper restatement— and because even in the solar passage, the word "Sūrya" would likewise result in being a mere restatement; furthermore, if only Prajāpati were enjoined, the attainment of Prajāpati for the oblation could be accomplished by a single sentence alone, rendering the two sentences redundant.

If Prajāpati were enjoined with reference to a homa qualified by each respective time, then—even though there would be no resulting split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) due to the aforementioned reasoning regarding a qualified reference—the injunction would be established by the mere statement "He offers to Prajāpati" (*prajāpataye juhoti*). Consequently, the words "evening" (*sāyam*) and "morning" (*prātaḥ*) would also become redundant.

Therefore, since the two sentences beginning with "That which [is offered] to Agni... must necessarily enjoin two distinct rites qualified by two deities and two times, the deity is not obtained for the rite enjoined by those [other] sentences through this [present] one.
It is not a case of a scripture that merely describes something already known (*tatprakhya-śāstra*).
Rather, by the injunction "one offers [the oblation] in the evening and in the morning," there is a prescription for the combination (*samuccaya*) of these very two acts prescribed here;
from the two oblations combined, there is only a single result.
In this view, by the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice, both rites have heaven as their purpose.

Since it is impossible to refer back to the sentence containing the fruit by means of the term "agnihotra," the injunction regarding the substances such as curd and so forth applies to these two fruitful rites themselves.
It should be understood that in the sentence concerning the fruit, Agni, who is dependent on these oblations, is enjoined for the sake of the fruit.
(On the determination that the term *agnihotra* is not a name, due to the absence of a scripture describing it as such):

For this very reason, the view that the word *agnihotra* is the name of the very rite enjoined by the sentence "That which [is offered] to Agni..."—on the grounds that there exists a scripture describing it as such (*tatprakhya-śāstra*)—is also refuted.

This is because, under the theory that it is a name, the rite itself would not be something to be enjoined; since only the rite must be enjoined, and it is impossible to enjoin what is already established.

Furthermore, since there is no possibility of an injunction in that case due to the absence of a form consisting of substance and deity when enjoining another action, and because it would be impossible to treat "agnaye hotram" as a restatement (anuvāda) once the deity has been obtained from elsewhere, it cannot be a name; rather, the meaning is that it must be an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi).
(An examination of whether the Agnihotra sentence is an injunction of a quality by way of restating the Darvihoma:
To the question, "In which ritual action, then, is there the injunction of a quality? he says: "Therefore, wherever... and so forth.

Regarding the term *darvīhoma*, it is established in the eighth [book of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā] that this is a name for all those acts enjoined by the injunctions of *juhoti* (he offers), because some of them are connected with a ladle (*darvī*) as established by custom, just like the word *vaiśvadeva*; because the ladle is prescribed through the convergence of indicative marks (*liṅga*); and because its status as a name is proven by the principle of "being known from that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*), based on the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the action understood from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "If one were to offer with a single [ladle], he should perform a *darvīhoma*."

The meaning is as follows: just as by the statement "one offers in the Āhavanīya," which is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of distant *darvī-homas*, there is an injunction (*vidhi*) of the *āhavanīya* fire as something to be adopted, so too here there is an injunction of the deity Agni as something to be adopted.

Furthermore, among those [mantras], in cases where Agni or another deity has been enjoined by means of a *taddhita* suffix or a dative case ending, since that injunction of Agni would otherwise be untenable and thus redundant, it is stated that the mantra was recited for the purpose of avoiding such futility.
Consequently, because the injunction of the deity Agni—derived from the wording of the mantra—is operative prior [to the general rule], it constitutes an injunction of the deity.
Since it is observed elsewhere that when something is obtained through a direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*), it is improper to assume its existence based on the words of a mantra (*māntravarṇika*),
therefore, by means of the term *agnihotra*, there is an injunction of Agni as the deity with reference to the *darvī-homa* for which no deity has been prescribed.

(An exposition of the view of the author of the *Prakāśa*—who maintains that the evening oblation (*sāyaṃhoma*) is the subject of restatement (*anuvāda*), preceded by the determination that the two acts enjoined by the *darvīhoma* and *sūrya* sentences are not intended [as objects of injunction] because they would otherwise result in the non-connection of the occasion and the fruit in the *Agnihotra* sentence, and because they serve to establish the Sun as the deity;
followed by its refutation.

As for the argument: "In this view, although it is possible to restate the *Agnihotra* term since the *darvīhomas* are indicated by the terms 'fruit' and 'occasion' in their respective sentences, there is no such restatement because of the remoteness [of those sentences], which prevents them from being brought to mind (*viparivṛtti*)."
A connection between the result and the cause is thus established.

Nor can it refer to the morning *homa* rite enjoined by the sentence "And that which [is offered] to Sūrya," because since that rite has Agni as its deity, it would be impossible to refer to it by the term *agnihotra*. Therefore, it must refer specifically to the evening *homa* enjoined by the sentence "And that which [is offered] to Agni."

For this very reason, because the evening oblation (*sāyaṃhoma*) possesses a fruit, it is established by the context (*prakaraṇa*); and by the sentence "He offers in the morning and evening," the two rites enjoined according to the principle of the *Āgneya* [offering] constitute subordinate elements (*aṅga*) of the evening oblation.

Since the deity is prescribed for those two rites alone—enjoined by the two sentences beginning with "Evening and morning"—by means of the mantra "Agni is light" (*agnir jyotiḥ*), the deity there is one derived from the words of the mantra (*māntravarṇikī*);
however, this is not the case for the two rites enjoined by the two sentences beginning with "That which is for Agni" (*yad agnaye ca*).

In that regard, since the mantra would be obtained through the indicative mark (liṅga) alone, the injunction would become purposeless; therefore, the commentators have established the determination [of the application] by means of syntactical connection (vākya).

(The refutation of the opinion of the earlier commentators [Prakāśakāras] on the grounds that the *darvihoma* is presented as the substratum by virtue of being an injunction for the connection between a quality and a result:
That is incorrect;

because in this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the status of the word *agnihotra* as a name is not established anywhere, it is impossible to refer back to it by means of the word *agnihotra* as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*); consequently, it would be illogical for the evening oblation—prescribed by the sentence "That which is for Agni..."—to be connected with a result.

If the term *agnihotra* were applied there merely on the basis of having Agni as its deity, then it would follow that even the other distinct rite—prescribed by the sentence "That which [is offered] in the evening"—which has Agni alone as its deity, would also be designated as such; furthermore, the statement regarding its being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) would be irrelevant.

Therefore, just as in the final Siddhānta, since the two deities Agni and Sūrya are obtained through the wording of the mantras in the two rites prescribed by the sentences for the evening and morning, it is precisely in those two rites intended for the sake of heaven that the two rites prescribed by the two sentences beginning with "That which to Agni... [are subsumed].
The phrase "and that which [is performed] in the evening" establishes a conjunction.

Since the *darvī-homa*—though remote—is presented as the subject for the prescription of an accessory (*guṇa*) by means of the two sentences concerning the result and the occasion, it is logically possible for it to serve as the substratum (*āśraya*). Thus, there is an injunction regarding the accessory in the form of the deity Agni, conveyed by the term *agnihotra*, which is based upon that [substratum], with respect to both the result and the occasion.

Alternatively: since both of the two oblations enjoined by the two sentences, "That which [is offered] for Agni... and so forth, would—by virtue of the context—attain the status of being the substratum (*āśraya*), it is the injunction of a quality (*guṇa*) that depends precisely upon that substratum.

Nor should it be argued: "While the status of being a substratum is possible in the first evening oblation dedicated to Agni because Agni is present there and thus there is no contradiction, how could Agni be included in the oblation dedicated to Sūrya? For its inclusion is justified because, as an optional rite (*kāmya*), it does not sublate the character of having Agni as its deity. Thus, the determination of the application of these sentences, as previously indicated, is indeed logical.

Nor is the injunction for the application of the mantra redundant, given that the two rites enjoined by the two sentences beginning with "yad agnaye ca" would already obtain the mantra through their own indicative power (*liṅga*) alone; for it serves a purpose as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the exclusion established by the injunction of application containing mixed indicative marks. Precisely for this reason—since those two rites also possess this [mantra] as an auxiliary by virtue of the force of the scriptural statement of application containing mixed indicative marks—they illuminate Agni and Sūrya exclusively through a secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*), according to the principle of the *aindrī* mantra; thus, everything is well-established.
(An investigation of the alternative position consisting of a qualified injunction, along with the arguments for it:

Thus, although the prima facie view— that [the sentence] is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) by way of a restatement of the oblation (*homānuvāda*)— has been established, it remains possible that Agni is obtained through the wording of the mantra even in the case of ladle-oblations (*darvīhoma*).
Then, considering that it would be improper for there to be futility because no other result occurs even when the previously established practice is not heard,

he demonstrates— by means of another position— the very injunction of a distinct, qualified action that was previously suspected as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)— with the words "viśiṣṭa" (qualified), etc.
And in this view, the systematic arrangement of all the statements was previously demonstrated under the guise of an objection.

The word *agnihotra* occurring in the sentence concerning the result and the cause serves to define the ritual whose deity is Agni—as indicated by the compound ending in the *bahuvrīhi*—in the context of the injunction, "Having sacrificed with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, one should sacrifice with *soma*";
it is not, however, a name.

In this very ritual context, there is an injunction regarding the substance [of the offering] based on the sentences concerning curds (*dadhi*) and so forth, due to the [established] context; or rather— because of a specific expectancy and because there is no evidence for restricting the word "oblation" (*homa*) [to a single act], as in the case of the statement "the oblations are twofold"— [the injunction applies] both to this primary rite and to the two subsidiary rites enjoined by the two sentences beginning with "that which is for Agni."
The meaning is that its injunction is according to the manner stated by Kaustubha.
(Establishing that the word *āghāra* refers to the substance *ājya* through etymological derivation):
"That which is capable of flowing."

And thus, from the root *ghṛ*, listed in the Dhātupāṭha as "to flow and to shine," preceded by the prefix *āṅ* and followed by the causative suffix *ṇic* in its own sense (*svārtha-ṇij*), the term *āghāra* is derived.

Following the rule "akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām" (Pāṇini 3.3.19), with the word "not denoting the agent" (*akartari*) being carried over, the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule "erac" (Pāṇini 3.3.56).

Then, by the rule "ṇeraniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51), the suffix *ṇic* is elided. Thus, through a derivation based on the object (*karma-vyutpatti*), the word *āghāra* refers to a substance capable of flowing, in the sense that "it is poured out" (*āghāryate*).
However, it is not a name of an object derived through the sense of "existence" (bhāva);

for if that were the case, since there would be no difference in the basis for its application (pravṛttinimitta), it would differ from terms such as "udbhid," and thus [the designation] would be untenable—this is the meaning.

(Secondly, the determination that even the clarified butter (*ājya*) used for the preparatory rite (*saṃskārakarman*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *upāṃśuyāja* by means of a sentence constructed through the context (*prakaraṇa*),
as well as the determination of the meaning of the words in that contextually constructed sentence:

By the phrase "clarified butter and so forth" (*ājyādī-*) and the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is indicated that the status of [the *ājya*] as being established by a scriptural statement describing its nature (*tatprakhyaśāstra*) is refuted, because the *ājya* is already obtained from the sentence, "Or [it is] fourfold-drawn" (*caturgṛhītaṃ vā*).
The meaning is this: that liquid substance which has attained the form of clarified butter (*ājya*) by this [process] is what is intended by "that" (*tat*).

Nor does it follow that, even when *ājya* and so forth are denoted, there is an impossibility of it being a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*) because, due to its primacy expressed by the accusative case, it lacks the status of being something to be enjoined;

for when, however, due to the absence of utility either as a past or future purpose—as in the case of groats (*saktu*)—its status as something to be refined (*saṃskārya*) is untenable, then the accusative case is taken as indicating the sense of the instrumental, and thus it is so stated.
Since, in that case, the status of being a ritual act (*saṃskārakarma*) would not be possible, he says: "And [the word] 'of that which is not enjoined' (*aviniyuktasya*)."

Since the purificatory act (saṃskāra) known as "flowing" (kṣaraṇa) is untenable without a substance that has been or will be used, an injunction of application (viniyogavidhi) is postulated—just as in the case of "he chooses the Adhvaryu priest" and similar passages.

And since this act of flowing is mentioned within the context (prakaraṇa), it is postulated by virtue of its capacity to be enjoined as a purification of the substance that serves as a means to the transcendental result (apūrva) belonging to that context. By virtue of its capacity to be enjoined as a purification of the substance belonging to the context, [it is thus established].

Since it is proper to conceive [the term] as having the sense of a substance (dravya) in relation to the primary substance of the context, its status as an auxiliary to the *upāṃśuyāja* alone is possible.

Consequently, there is no inconsistency in its being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), because the referent of the word *āghāra*—which was determined to be a quality in the *āghāra* sentence—is enjoined by means of an inferred sentence that does not contradict the status of a name (*nāmatā*) intended by the Siddhāntin;
this is the meaning of the phrase "by means of a sentence inferred from the context" (*prakaraṇakalpitavākyena*).
This is because the application of the *kṣaraṇa* [act of pouring] is determined by a sentence constructed through the context of its placement within the section.
(An examination of the objection regarding the contingency of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* as indicated in the *Śāstradīpikā* concerning the application within the context, and its refutation:

Therefore, since a substance lacks the nature of being a procedure (*itikartavyatā*), there is no defect even if it cannot be grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*) defined as the expectancy for a procedure.

And the point is that, out of fear that the injunctions for the preparatory acts (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) would otherwise be rendered purposeless, that very injunction for the flowing [of ghee]—aided by the context—extends as far as the application of the substance to be prepared for the sake of the *upāṃśuyāja*.

And thus, by relying on the originative injunction itself—“He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between”—which, when supported by the context (*prakaraṇa*), prescribes a sacrifice qualified by a consecrated material substrate, the laborious effort to avoid the fault of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication of possession) pointed out in the *Śāstradīpikā* does not arise;
for the sentence is construed through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) as: “One should perform the *upāṃśuyāja* with a substance consecrated by sprinkling.”
(An examination of the disparity between the sentence concerning the flour-meal and the sentence concerning the pouring-libation:
Nor does it follow that a similar application [of the injunction] must be postulated for the flour-meal as well;

for since the flour-meal is reduced to ashes by the oblation, it is impossible for it to have any further utility toward the result to be accomplished, and thus, even without resorting to an application, here [in the case of the pouring-libation], there exists the unique [function] consisting of the act of trickling.

In the world, we observe that water for drinking and the like are prepared as objects [for consumption]; since that very thing is recognized [as such], and because it is possible for the remainder to be used for a future purpose—just as in the case of *pūtīka* plants used in the *abhiṣava* (pressing)—the application [of the remainder] can be established by the force of the accusative case. Therefore, there is a disparity [between this case and others]. For this very reason, since the *upāṃśuyāja* is satisfied by this very substance, the *ghr̥ta* clarified butter remains for use elsewhere.

Alternatively, even if by this [rule] only substances such as clarified butter and milk are enjoined, there is no harm in enjoining that the *dhruvā* vessel is the locus for the clarified butter by means of the sentence "for all," which is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the clarified butter.

(An investigation into the lack of intrinsic consistency in the views of the ancients regarding the Upāṃśuyāja being for the sake of [the sacrifice] by means of postulating an injunction of application, followed by the adoption of an alternative position:
Thus far, it has been stated according to the method of the ancients that the Upāṃśuyāja is for the sake of [the sacrifice] by means of postulating an injunction of application.
However, this is not tenable.

For one who is already enjoined, there would be fitness for the consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*), and the assumption of the injunction based on the power of the *saṃskāra*-injunction would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

However, in the case of the Adhvaryu and others, we observe their employment as agents in their respective rites through injunctions assumed from the very names (*samākhyā*) of those acts; thus, because the consecratory rite of selection (*varaṇa-saṃskāra*) is prescribed for the Adhvaryu's duty, there is a difference [between this case and that of the sacrificer].

Furthermore, since the requirement for the *upāṃśuyāja* is satisfied by the *dhruvājya* itself—which is prescribed by the general statement regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣavacana*) for the sake of all the sacrificial portions—there is no occasion to postulate a rule of application (*viniyogavidhi*) for it.
As for the claim that there is merely an injunction regarding the *dhruvā* as the locus, that is untenable:

if that were enjoined with reference to *ājya* in general, it would follow that it applies even to the *ājya* used for decoration; and if it were intended as a qualification of the sacrifice (*yajati*), it would entail the fallacy of enjoining a qualified object (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*). Thus, [the former view] is incorrect.

Therefore, since it is more appropriate to enjoin the act of taking the clarified butter (ājya) with the fixed locus as its objective for the sake of the sacrifice, rather than making it subservient to the Upāṃśuyāja, [the author], being dissatisfied, states another alternative: "Or rather, the fourfold-drawn [butter]... (caturgṛhītaṃ vā).
(Conclusion based on the other alternative being useful only for establishing the non-establishment of the Siddhānta):

This is the meaning—by the injunction "He offers the Āghāra," once the pouring is prescribed as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a portion of a substance capable of flowing, there arises a desire to know the specific nature of that substance; in response to this, the statement "fourfold-drawn" (*caturgṛhīta*) merely provides that specific detail, while the term *Āgneya* [is used for another purpose].
Just as in the expression "he makes [it] fourfold," so too it is performed [here].

And thus, when there is a requirement for the application of that which is to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), one should not assume that its purpose is the *upāṃśuyāja*, which has not been previously established;
rather, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in concluding from the very sentence, "He takes four portions in the *juhū* ladle for the *prayājas*," that its purpose is the *prayājas*.

Regarding the injunction, "One pours the libation with [the mantra] 'Indra, the sacrifice is upright, it touches the sky,'" there is no fault, because by this [injunction], the mantra alone is prescribed as a subsidiary to the act of pouring (kṣaraṇa) for the purpose of reminding [the performer], just like the sound of a chariot and so forth.

(An examination of the futility [of the term] if it were a name in the *āghāra* sentence, and the impossibility of the accusative case in the *agnihotra* sentence): Thus, even though the status of this position as a qualifier-injunction (*guṇavidhi*) is untenable, the proponent of the prima facie view concludes the *pūrvapakṣa* regarding the *āghāra* sentence with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*), indicating that the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is not established even by the mere claim that the word *āghāra* refers to a quality, since that would contradict the name-status intended by the Siddhāntin.

If [the term *āghāra*] were the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), it would be redundant because, in the case of the *āghāra*, there is no separate mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and thus no purpose for a specific mention.

Even if that possibility were somehow established by the word *agnihotra*, the impossibility of the accusative case—since the action is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in both originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*)—is indicated by the word "in every way" (*sarvathā*).
(An examination of an alternative position: the injunction of a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) with reference to the *sānnāyya* [curd and milk], preceded by a refutation of Somanātha’s view.

In reality, however, it can also be stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that since the milk used in the *sānnāyya* sacrifice itself can be referred to by the term *āghāra*, the injunction of the purificatory rite here is indeed made with reference to that very milk.

As for what was stated by Somanātha according to the natural drift of the *Nyāyasudhā*—that because the substance of the *sānnāyya* and so forth is enjoined here by the term *āghāra*, it is impossible to refer to it as such—[that is not the case].

Since it is impossible to accept that the term *āghāra* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it should be disregarded because it could be a restatement (*anuvāda*) referring not only to the butter and milk not under discussion, but also to the milk used for the *sānnāyya*.
Therefore, it is also easy to argue that its status as a name is refuted by the possibility that it refers to the *sānnāyya* while simultaneously expressing a quality.

In this way, the demonstration that even the terms *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā*, which are conventionally established within the *vidvadvākya*, can refer to qualities should be seen in the *Kaustubha*.
(An examination of the impossibility of enjoining either a quality or a distinct action qualified by a quality within the Agnihotra statement.

First, regarding the term *agnihotra*, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that it is a name (*nāmadheya*), preceded by the demonstration that it cannot be an injunction of a quality—namely, "to be inferred from the wording of the mantra" (*mantravarṇakalp-ya*).
This has been explained previously.

Nor [is it the case that the time is not established by another text]. For here, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, following what was stated in the *Ṭupṭīkā* regarding the passage "That which [is offered] to Agni," explains that in this context as well—in a sentence intended to establish the deity—the time already established by another sentence is merely restated; this is discussed in the section concerning the *Āghāra* and *Agnihotra*.

Since this will be explained later in the commentary (*bhāṣya*), where the very phrase "that which [is offered] to Agni" is presented as the means for obtaining Agni, it might be argued that the attainment of Agni is stated solely from the Brāhmaṇa passage "that which [is offered] to Agni.

To refute that, [the author] states the attainment of Agni based on the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*), as discussed in the *Vārttika* on the section concerning the Āghāra and Agnihotra offerings: "Agni is light... (*agnir jyotiḥ*).
Furthermore, the manner in which that [objection] is refuted by means of the word "eva" (only), preceded by its own adoption, should be examined in the Kaustubha.
(An examination of the attainment of the deity through the wording of the mantra, preceded by the doubt regarding the *yad agnaye* formula being a provider of the deity and its subsequent resolution:

Now, one might object: since the status of Prajāpati as the deity is directly enjoined by the two sentences beginning with *yad agnaye* through the use of the dative case, and since this leaves no further expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣye*), how can it be appropriate for Agni to be enjoined by an injunction inferred from the wording of the mantra?

Alternatively, even if [the word *agni*] were intended as an agentive (*kalpaka*), there would arise the undesirable consequence that the deity Agni would be set aside by the greater force of the dative case; in order to dispel this doubt, he says: "That which [is said] for Agni... (*yad agnaye ca*).
Although it is not possible for the particle *ca* to connect with the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) expressed by the dative case in the word *agnaye*,

nevertheless, since the word *agnaye* functions as a restatement (*anuvādaka*) by way of indicating [other deities] according to the method to be explained, one may assume that its co-occurrence serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Thus, because their conjunction is established by implication, the particle *ca* does not connect with the meaning [of the word *agni*].
This is indicated by the phrase "distinguished by the collection of deities belonging to the morning and evening times."

(Refutation of the fear regarding the displacement of Agni by Prajāpati as the deity): By this— namely, that Prajāpati, being enjoined with reference to the previously established injunction for Agni, does not receive extension (*atideśa*) because he is like a subsequent attribute (*utpannaśiṣṭa*) in a context already occupied by an originative attribute (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇa*), and thus Agni would not incur the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) to Prajāpati— the doubt raised by Varadarāja is refuted.

Just as the rule prescribing the single agency of the *homa* and the *abhiṣava*—which are obtained from elsewhere—establishes that both the *homa* and the *abhiṣava* are subordinate parts (*aṅga*) of the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*), so too here, since it is possible for the injunction to be qualified by the conjunction with Agni, which is already determined to be a subordinate part from another source, that [conjunction] does not arise [as a new requirement].
For this very reason, because the deities are enjoined as mutually conjoined, there is no mutual sublation (*bādhakatā*) between them either.
(Refutation of the objection regarding the futility of the application of mixed mantras:
"That [application] applies even to the two mixed [mantras].

Nor, in this way, does the application of those [mantras] become futile—just as Viṣṇu and others are obtained for the *upāṃśuyāja* simply from the recitation of mantras based on indicative power (*liṅga*) alone—because Agni and Sūrya would likewise be obtained [therein].
This is because they serve a purpose by establishing the application [of mantras] according to their respective times.

In the same way, it should be understood that the injunctions regarding mantras with mixed gender markers also serve a purpose by establishing order, since otherwise there would be no fixed rule for both deities due to their manifesting both.

(Regarding the justification for the injunction of Prajāpati as qualified by a combination [of deities], preceded by the justification for the rule of sequence beginning with "The first oblation is for Agni":

Now, an objection is raised that there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if both the meaning of the word *ca* ("and") and Prajāpati were enjoined; to this, he says: "established by the word *ca*... )

By this, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument—that because it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), the two statements "to Agni" and "to Prajāpati" must be injunctions for two distinct qualified rituals—is refuted.

Furthermore, if there were an injunction for a separate ritual, the two injunctions prescribing the application of the two pure mantras—which already possess the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of both deities—would be rendered redundant, as those mantras would be obtained through that very indicative mark.

Nor is it the case that this injunction of their combination is useless, on the grounds that the combination is already established by the necessity of otherwise explaining the injunction of sequence—"the first oblation is for Agni, the latter for Prajāpati"—for [that argument] is not valid.
Even if they are optional, it is possible for them to be prescribed as preceding and succeeding elements through a difference in application;
therefore, since their conjunction can be prescribed within a single performance,

and since their sequence is established by the very order of the textual recitation in the passage "That which [is offered] to Agni and [to Soma]," the sentence regarding the sequence is merely a restatement (anuvāda).
(Refutation of the view that [the mantra] reveals Agni as a deity qualified by the attribute of luminosity):

As for the claim that— here, based on a misconception regarding the intent of the *Nyāyasudhā* text, which states, "And therefore, since the status of the two deities, Agni and Sūrya, in their pure form is enjoined by the Brāhmaṇa, there is an injunction [of them] as qualified by the attribute of luminosity"— it follows that, under the view that the deity is enjoined by the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*), Agni and Sūrya are indeed deities as qualified by attributes such as luminosity.
The authors of the *Prakāśa* have stated: "That is not so;

because in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the *Upāṃśuyāja*—namely, 'Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to silently, Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to silently'—only Viṣṇu and the others in their pure form are mentioned. Therefore, even when a prescription based on the wording of a mantra (*māntravarṇika-vidhi*) is postulated, just as one does not postulate a deityhood characterized by an attribute [in those cases], the same applies here."

"Only smoke was seen of the fire by day," and "The first oblation for Agni is that which is for Agni"—since in these supplementary passages (vākyaśeṣa) only the two pure [deities] are mentioned, it is more parsimonious (lāghava) to accept them as they are, rather than postulating them as deities qualified by attributes; thus, their status as deities is established in their pure form alone.
(Conclusion on the name *agnihotra*):

Therefore, since the application of the term *agnihotra* is possible in the *agnihotra* injunction even through its connection with Agni as the deity already established by another scripture (*śāstrāntara*), and since there is no indicator for a unique [specific] referent, it is improper to abandon the possibility of enjoining the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Thus, [the injunction does not apply].

This is an injunction of an accessory (guṇavidhi) with reference to the oblation (homānuvādena). Intending that it is not proper to resort to a cumbersome qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhi) when it is possible to enjoin the mere meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), he concludes that [the term] is a name (nāmadheya): "Therefore... (ataśca).
(Regarding the term *agnihotra*, the establishment of a genitive *tatpuruṣa* by refuting the locative *bahuvrīhi* and the dative *tatpuruṣa*:
Here, the author of the Bhāṣya, by stating "that for which there is an offering (*hotra*) to Agni is the *agnihotra*," has relied upon a non-co-referential (*vyadhikaraṇa*) dative *bahuvrīhi*.
The author of the Nyāyasudhā [proposes] "that in which there is an offering of Agni" as a genitive *bahuvrīhi*.
In both cases, therefore, there is figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), but the derivation [of the meaning] is not clear;
furthermore, there is the inconsistency of the final udātta accent as recited by the Taittirīyas.

Therefore, to indicate that it is more appropriate to adopt the word *hotra* by deriving it in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) as a genitive *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound) consistent with its phonetic characteristics, the specific etymological derivation "the *hotra* of Agni" (*agner hotram*) has been presented.

In this regard, although according to Kātyāyana’s view—even in the absence of a relationship between an original form and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛtibhāva*)—a dative compound (*caturthī-samāsa*) would be more appropriate here, just as in words such as *aśvaghāsa* ("horse fodder"); yet [the genitive compound is preferred].

Nevertheless, since the author of the Mahābhāṣya, on the occasion of rejecting that view, accepted a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound even in words such as *aśvaghāsa*, there is no fault whatsoever in accepting it here as well.
Nor is there, as in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), a lack of established connection between the members;

for in the final position (*siddhānta*), since the deity Agni is already established through another source, the genitive is justified by the specific qualification consisting in the fact that the deity is established elsewhere, serving as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that which has been obtained from another source.
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, because that [suffix] is to be prescribed only now, it could not have previously been connected with specific relations; thus there is a disparity.

Although the authors of the *Prakāśa* have also mentioned the *caturthī-tatpuruṣa* compound, nevertheless, this [analysis] is preferable to resorting to that [compound], which must be accepted as having no other recourse and is established only by the inclusion of the word "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*.

Considering the appropriateness of this *tatpuruṣa* compound and accepting that even the occurrence of *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) in the first member is preferable— given its conformity with the rules for accentuation (*svarita*) compared to an alternative compound— the venerable [author] has adopted this very [interpretation].
As for the fact that a *saptamī-bahuvrīhi* was also resorted to in the *Nyāyaprakāśa*, [that is not the primary view].
The refutation of that [position], even though it follows the [discussion of] vowels, is to be seen in the Kaustubha.
(An exposition establishing that the word *hotra* refers to the act of offering, by refuting the view that it refers to a substance.

And here, if the word *hotra* were to refer to a substance—meaning that it generates a cognition characterized by the possession of a substance related to fire—even though the meaning of the name could then serve as a qualifier for the meaning of the verbal root, [this would be untenable]; whereas, if the word *hotra* refers to the action (*bhāva*), [it refers to] the oblation known as the *agnihotra*.
It is not possible for [the sacrifice] to be the delimiting factor of the root-meaning;
because, in the absence of another form, it is logically untenable for something to be its own delimiting factor.
For it is not possible [to say]: "One should effect the desired result by means of a sacrifice that is connected with fire through the sacrifice itself."
For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya, the author of the Nyāyasudhā, and others have accepted that [the word] has substance (*dravya*) as its primary referent.

Thus, in this context, since the word *hotra* refers to a substance by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it signifies that which is related to substances such as curd (*dadhi*) and so forth; therefore, the genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound proposed by the Proclaimer (*prakāśakāra*) is indeed appropriate.
Nevertheless, even in this view, there arises the contingency of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *hotra*.

Since the word *hotra*—derived from the nominalizing suffix *ghañ* (bhāva-vyutpanna)—is justified as being a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the meaning of the verbal root by virtue of generating a cognition whose qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) is a specific sacrifice characterized by the nature of being an oblation (*homatva*) having Agni as its deity, and since the word *hotra* is thus dependent on that [nominalizing derivation], there is no fault: because the word *juhoti* itself expresses the qualificandum therein, the word *agnihotra*, though referring to the qualificandum, is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*) regarding the aspect of the qualificandum.
(Justification for applying the term *agnihotra* to the morning *sūryahoma*):

Although the *āhavanīya* fire is the locus for the oblation and the *gārhapatya* and *anvāhāryapacana* fires are prohibited from receiving oblations— since the two offerings are prescribed specifically for the *āhavanīya* alone—

and because no fire is prescribed for the morning oblation, it might be argued that this status of being an oblation to the deity Agni cannot serve as the basis for the application of the term *agnihotra*.

Nevertheless, in the case of ten oblations— according to the rule, "He offers two in the Āhavanīya, four in the Gārhapatya, and four in the Anvāhāryapacana"— and in the case of six oblations— according to the rule, "Two in the Āhavanīya, two in the Gārhapatya, and two in the Anvāhāryapacana"— since there exist oblations to Agni as the deity based on the wording of the mantras, such as "Svāhā to Agni Gṛhapati, Svāhā to Agni Saṃveśapati," even during the morning offering in the Gārhapatya and Anvāhāryapacana fires, [the term] "Agni" [is applicable].
The application of the word *hotrā* is not untenable.
(Conclusion on the status of the term *agnihotra* as a name, preceded by an examination of its application to the morning oblation by way of another perspective:

In reality, however, since a single *agnihotra* oblation is enjoined to be performed twice by the sentence "He offers in the evening and in the morning," there is no difference in the ritual act (*karma*) despite the difference in time—as is the case with the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Therefore, the property of having Agni as the deity applies to that which is delimited by the nature of being a distinct type of oblation (*vijātīyahomatva*).
The application of that term [as a name] is indeed justified by its co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth.

Furthermore, it will be explained in the section on the *Vaiśvadeva* sacrifice that the status of a name is established even by a partial ground for application, according to the principle of "being observed as such" (*tatprakhyanyāya*).
The avoidance of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) should be understood in the same way as in the case of the word *udbhid*.
Therefore, it is established by the principle of "designation based on its appearance" (*tatprakhyanyāya*) that the term *agnihotra* is a name;
and because the results and the causal factors for that very rite designated as *agnihotra* are set forth in the two sentences, there is a connection with it.
(The application of the sūtra in accordance with the established doctrine):

Here, in this sūtra, by supplying "in which" from the first part of the sūtra "yasmin guṇopadeśaḥ," and "name" from the preceding sūtra "api vā nāmadheyam," [the compound] *tasya vidhitsitasya guṇasya prakhyaṃ*— meaning that other scripture (*anya-śāstram*) which makes known (*prakhyāpakam*) that quality intended to be enjoined— in that [other scripture], the word *agnihotra* and so forth [is the name].
The meaning is "name."

(Just as the substance is obtained from the sentence "fourfold-taken" and the deity from the wording of the mantra, so too is it established that the term *āghāra* is a name for the oblation by virtue of its primary etymological ground, which consists in the act of flowing.
He establishes that the term *āghāra* is also a name [for the oblation] with the words "In the same way," and with the phrase "and by the expression 'fourfold-taken'."

The meaning of this statement is as follows: having performed the pouring known by the name *āghāra*—which pertains to that *jauhava* [clarified butter] which had been prepared by the process of fourfold drawing—one offers the first three *prayāja* oblations, three each, prior to this [pouring].
And here, by means of a powerful recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), [it refers to] the very same ritual act called *āghāraṇa* which was previously enjoined in the *āghāra* injunction.

The connection with a portion of the *caturgṛhīta* (fourfold-drawn) clarified butter from the *jauhava* vessel, which serves the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings, is enjoined as being for no other purpose; everything else is merely restated (*anūdya*) as it is already established by other means.
Therefore, there is no injunction for a separate act of pouring (*āghāraṇa*).

For this very reason, since the word *āghāra* is a name (*nāmadheya*) because its connection with the *caturgṛhīta* is for another purpose, the phrase "he pours the *āghāra*" (*āghāram āghārayati*)—which possesses a power not projected by anything else—denotes the *homa* (oblation) consisting of the casting of a substance after first dedicating it to a deity.

Since the substance in the form of clarified butter (*ājya*) and the deity [Agni] are obtained through the sentence consisting of four portions (*caturgṛhīta*) and the words of the mantra respectively, their connection is established by the verb *āghārayati* through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In that context, the term *āghāra* is the name of the oblation (*homa*) because it consists of a flow (*kṣaraṇa*) due to its throwing-in aspect; thus, since the basis for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*) differs, one should not suspect redundancy by assuming identity based on that [flowing nature].
(Refutation of Somanātha’s view that the basis for the application of the term *āghāra* is the state of being a substance that is being poured out):

As for the argument that—following the natural sense of the *Śāstradīpikā*, which states, “Since clarified butter (*ājya*) is already obtained by the very word ‘fourfold-drawn’ (*caturgṛhīta*), its nature as something to be poured out is established, and thus the name [‘āghāra’] is possible on that basis”—[it is replied that] because clarified butter is a liquid substance, it possesses the nature of pouring out by its own essence; therefore, the state of being a substance that is being poured out...
Somanātha stated that the term "āghāra" (the pouring) is a name (*nāmadheya*) based on its etymological ground (*pravṛttinimitta*);

however, that is not correct. Since the nature of flowing inherent in the clarified butter (*ājya*) is itself enjoined here by the verbal root, the clarified butter is already established; therefore, it is impossible for that nature of flowing to serve as the etymological ground [for naming the act].
Furthermore, this is not a name based on a connection with a quality (*guṇa*), such as the names "Agnihotra" and so forth.
Moreover, since it is connected with the nature of flowing inherent in the meaning of the verbal root, that alone is the appropriate basis for the application [of the term].
(Refutation of the opponent's claims regarding the *sānnāyya* milk and the similarity of liquid substances):
For this very reason—precisely because it would result in the second type of injunction—the term *āghāra* cannot be intended as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the *sānnāyya* milk;
nor, because it would result in the fifth type of injunction, can there be an injunction of the *āghāra* qualified by a substance through a modification of the application (*viniyoga*).

By this very [argument], the claim that "the specific [substance] is provided by the sentence *caturgṛhītam*" is also refuted; for since the desired result is established by the word *āghārya* alone, the inclusion of the word *āghāram* there would result in its redundancy. Therefore, it is proper that it be a name (*nāmadheya*).

(An examination, supported by reasoning, of whether the Āghāra sacrifice is a directly contributing subsidiary (*sannipatyopakāraka*) or a remotely contributing subsidiary (*ārādupakāraka*), similar to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering):

This sacrifice, like the *sviṣṭakṛt*, is accepted as being a remotely contributing subsidiary by virtue of its element of renunciation (*tyāga*), yet it is also accepted as a directly contributing subsidiary because it consecrates the clarified butter (*ājya*) that serves as the means for the first three *prayāja* offerings, through its element of pouring (*prakṣepa*).
For, just as in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt*, it is improper to assume the status of a remotely contributing subsidiary when the possibility of it being a directly contributing subsidiary exists.

Therefore, although the genitive case in the expression "its substrate" (*tasyāghāram*) may refer to a general relationship, it does not intend to express subordination— as in the phrase "sacrificing with clarified butter" (*ājyasya yajan*)—
because it is impossible to employ elsewhere what has already been employed elsewhere in the three *prayāja* offerings;
rather, because it serves the purpose of the result (*bhāvya*), it intends only its primary status.

Therefore, even when the subsequent *āghāra* is performed despite the loss of the *jauhavana* ladle for the purpose of offering the *prayāja*s, the subsequent *āghāra* is performed again upon its production; however, in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*s), when there is an explicit scriptural exclusion of the *prayāja*s, the subsequent *āghāra* is also excluded.
(Regarding the purpose of the name being applied to the preparatory act [saṃskārakarman]:
Nor does the name become useless even if it is a preparatory act, because its delimitation is established precisely through its dependence on the object to be prepared (saṃskārya).

Even though there may be other delimiters, by virtue of the traditional mention of this specific name, one can assume that only what is delimited by this name possesses the quality of "having prosperity as its goal" (abhyudayaśiraskatva); thus, as in the case of the injunction "he takes the Aṃśu," the name is meaningful even for a preparatory act.
The Moonlight of Logic (Nyāyasudhākara).

(An establishment, with supporting arguments, of one's own established doctrine—that the sprinkling is merely an indirect auxiliary—preceded by the refutation of the purpose and other points of the previous view:

In reality, however, if it were a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), then even regarding its connection with the substance, it would result in the status of an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*); therefore, in accordance with the parsimony of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), one must accept that the genitive case "of that" (*tasya*) denotes mere subsidiarity (*guṇatvamātra*), and it is proper to rely on its being an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakārakatva*), just like the *prayāja* offerings and others.

For this very reason, it is also not tenable to accept that the meaning of the word *homa*—which consists of the aggregate of the dedication to a deity, the casting of the substance, and its relinquishment—involves a distinction of constituent parts for the sake of its utility toward the result (*bhāvya*).

In the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* and similar offerings, however, because they serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) by the force of the accusative hearing (*dvitīyā-śruti*), such a recourse [to constituent parts] is justified.

Here, on the other hand, even if it were a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), since the postulation of an invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*) is necessary, the acceptance of a distinction between substances would be without any basis in authority.

Therefore, just as in the case of the scattering of husks (*tuṣopavāpa*), even though it subsists upon a substance employed for another purpose, there is no accomplishment of the aforementioned result because it lacks the character of a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*).

Furthermore, in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), when there is an explicit exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the rule, even if the *āghāra* oblation is performed with any kind of clarified butter (*ājya*), there is no loss of the *jauhava* clarified butter; for, like the potsherds (*kapāla*), it is employed for another purpose.

Furthermore, the fact that [the *caturgṛhīta*] is employed for another purpose is understood from the sentence regarding the *caturgṛhīta* through the word "this" (*etac-chabdena*), due to the fear that it would otherwise be useless to restate its being the means for the three *prayāja*s; thus, nothing is inconsistent.
For this very reason, the authors of the *Prakāśa*, who follow the opinion of Pārthasārathi, clearly state in the *Bhāṣya* that it is indeed a primary ritual act (*pradhāna-karma*).
As it is said in the *Śāstradīpikā*: "And we see that even consecratory acts (*saṃskāra*) have names, such as 'he takes the *aṃśu*' and 'he takes the *antaryāma*'."
Nor is this [act] a *saṃskāra* (consecration);
for, by the rule "he pours the oblation with the mantra 'Indra, stand upright at the sacrifice,'" the sacrifice is established through the divinity of Indra indicated by the words of the mantra.

(An exposition of Somanātha’s view that the *āghāra* rite is a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), which contradicts the view of the *Śāstradīpikā*): Here, since no sacrifice (*yāga*) is explicitly mentioned, even if one were to accept the opponent's claim that the *āghāra* is a preparatory act, [Somanātha] first avoids the objection regarding the redundancy of the name; then, by refuting that very point through this passage and establishing its status as a sacrifice (*yāgatva*), he proceeds.
It is understood that the impossibility of [the action] being a name has been refuted.

This being the case, we do not understand how Somanātha’s explanation of this text— which accepts [the act of throwing the grass-bundle] as being the work of a *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) while simultaneously intending it to have a dual nature like the *prastara-praharaṇa* (the throwing of the grass-bundle)— could possibly be correct.

And here, although [the mantra] is an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) by virtue of being a portion of the oblation, the *Kaustubha*—where this very point should be examined—raises and refutes the objection that it might be a direct auxiliary (*sannipatyopakāraka*) by way of reminding one of Indra, who is a deity belonging to the *sānnāyya* offering.
