In the same manner, he states that even words such as *samit* are names (*nāmadheya*), based on the principle to be explained in the section concerning repetition (*abhyāsādhikaraṇa*): namely, that they function as names through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) based on the "occasion for application" (*pravṛttinimitta*) consisting in their having Agni as the deity, as established by the wording of the mantra itself.
"Thus" (*evam*):
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the status of being names is also included for the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), and so forth.
(The justification for the second case-ending and its plural form in "agnihotram" etc.
He refutes the objection regarding the impossibility of the second case-ending raised by the proponent of the prima facie view: "In all cases."

The meaning is that since it is impossible for something unestablished to function as an instrument (*karaṇa*), the word [denoting the instrument] is a restatement (*anuvādinī*) by taking up the fact that its status as an object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*) is implied by the sense; thus, through the relation of co-inherence in a single substratum (*dvitīyaikārthasamavāya*), it indicates the state of being an instrument.

As for the plural number in the phrase "He sacrifices the *samidhs*," there is no fault, because it is a restatement based on the understanding of the plurality of the *samidh* deities from the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*): "He sacrifices as if the *samidhs* were many."
(The purpose of the preceding and subsequent arguments, and the refutation thereof by the author of the *Prakāśa*:
The purpose has not been stated because it is already clear from the presentation of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final (*uttarapakṣa*) positions.
As for that which was [asserted] by the authors of the *Prakāśa* in the prima facie position—that the *darvīhoma* oblations have Agni as their deity—
In the final conclusion (siddhānta), the purpose [of the rule] is stated as "not so";

however, since that has already been largely refuted by the Venerable Teacher himself during the exposition of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words, "where an *āgneya* mantra is recited," it should be disregarded.
Thus ends the fourth section, "The Section on Being Named After That."

(B1) (5. The Topic on Designation: And because of that designation [Jaimini 1.4.5]. In such cases as "One practicing sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena," since there is no sublation of what was stated previously, and because of the well-known usage, the words *śyena* and so forth are indeed injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*).

A quality (guṇa) based on the original Soma sacrifice is enjoined either for the sake of a result, or as a distinct ritual act qualified by that result. Nor does this entail the logical inconsistency of something being its own metaphor, as in the explanatory passage (arthavāda): "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey], so does this [sacrifice] swoop down and seize the enemy. For such a comparison is perfectly valid.

Since the concluding explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) must be interpreted otherwise in accordance with the injunction (*vidhi*) determined by the opening section, and since the figure of speech *ananvaya* (non-parallelism) is appropriate in cases of non-difference—as in the example "those [rays] are like its own playful manifestations"—this being the case, it is argued: this is not the figure *ananvaya*;
for if it were so, all the words of the explanatory passage would result in signifying the absence of any other object of comparison.

Therefore, since it is more appropriate to grant further favor [to the Vedic text], it is proper to rely on the fact that the namehood—which brings about the second type of injunction—is established by accepting a secondary (gauṇī) function in a single word occurring at the beginning [of the passage], either by way of metaphor (rūpaka) or by way of an elliptical simile (luptopamā).

As for the explanatory passage (arthavāda), it serves to establish the similarity required for the metaphor and so forth; thus, even without figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), it is not contradictory for it to serve the purpose of praising the sacrifice to be enjoined by way of a complete simile (pūrṇopamā-alaṅkāra).
Thus it is established that, in all cases, the status of being a name (nāmatva) occurs through exactly four modes. // 5 // 21 //
Thus ends the fifth section, concerning the designation of that [Brahman].
(B2) [The presentation of the subject matter preceded by an indication of the connection, and an analysis of the grammatical correctness of the reading *tatra gavābhicaryamāṇaḥ*:

Since this constitutes a counter-objection (*pratyavasthāna*) by way of setting aside the previous principle known as "the existence of a scriptural statement describing that" (*tatprakhyaśāstratā*), the author—without explicitly showing the connection as a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) because it is obvious—states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) following the presentation of the subject matter:
"By means of the *śyena*... (*śyenena iti*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of such sentences as: "Now, one who practices sorcery (*abhicaran*) should sacrifice with this *sandaṃśa*," and "Now, one who is being practiced against (*abhicaryamāṇa*) by means of a cow should sacrifice.
The sequence beginning with "Now, this... (*athaiṣa*) should also be seen at the very outset in the sentence concerning the *Śyena* sacrifice.
In this regard, in many copies of the Bhāṣya and other texts, the sentence "one practicing sorcery with a cow should sacrifice" (*gavābhicaran yajeta*) is observed to be written.
In accordance with that [tradition], it is likewise found in new manuscripts;

nevertheless, such writing must be regarded as resulting solely from the negligence of the scribes. Otherwise, for instance, in the case of the phrase "as cows protect," the syntactic connection with the remainder of the sentence would be untenable.

Since it is impossible for one who performs a sacrifice to conceal the identity of the person against whom that malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) was directed— and thus the statement regarding the concealment of an irrelevant person by the sacrificer is untenable—

it is more appropriate to say "the one being subjected to the malevolent rite. For in that case, since the performer of the sacrifice has become the object of a malevolent rite performed by another, it is logically consistent that this sacrificer is protected from the malevolent rite performed by another, just as a cow [is protected].
For this very reason, the venerable Vidyāraṇya-guru [Mādhavācārya] adopted the reading "abhicaryamāṇaḥ" alone in the *Adhikaraṇamālā*, and likewise Somanātha in his commentary on the *Śāstradīpikā*.

(The determination of the operation of the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] by showing that the principles of *udbhid*, *citratā*, and *atatkhyāti* do not apply to the sentence concerning the Śyena sacrifice:
He demonstrates that [the present case] is not the subject matter of the *udbhid*-type and other such sections by stating "as previously mentioned."
It cannot first be the subject matter of the *udbhid*-adhikaraṇa;

for in that [section], it was established that words which function equally with respect to both a quality and an action are names when they have the purpose of denoting a quality—due to the consequence of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication of "possessing")—but not so in the case of established conventional terms such as *dadhi* and *soma*. Therefore, just as in that case, here too there is the possibility of these being injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*).
Nor does it fall under the scope of the *citrā*-nyāya because it is free from a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*);
the meaning is that it does not constitute the subject matter of the preceding section precisely because there is no other scriptural passage (*śāstra*) that would declare [the term] as such.

For this very reason, he says "because of its well-known usage" (*prasiddheḥ*), asserting that the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established because the term is extremely conventional and well-established, just like the words *dadhi*, *soma*, and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "the hawk, etc.," the inclusion of the *sandaṃśa* and *gopada* [types of inference] is intended.

[The passage] "It is an injunction of qualities for the Jyotiṣṭoma, etc. [is explained as follows]: the *Śāstradīpikā* maintains that this [text] concerns the connection between a quality and a fruit (*guṇaphalasaṃbandha*). This refutes the *Nyāyasudhā*, which claims it is merely an injunction of a quality (*kevalaguṇavidhi*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is a refutation of Somanātha, who intended to include the *Viśvajit* sacrifice—which is not under discussion—within the scope of the term. Here, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* describes the intent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) as being that it is an injunction of a quality regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma, because he employs the example "like the *Udbhid* and others" (*udbhidādīnāmiva*) to establish the prima facie position through well-known instances and other means.

Since that would result in the redundancy of the mention of the fruit, and since the mention of a qualified [action] would entail a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), [the author], indicating that such a view is untenable, supports its status as an injunction according to the principle of the *Indriyakāmādhikaraṇa*: "By this, [it is shown that] there is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma and other [sacrifices]. Regarding the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the *Śāstradīpikā*, [the author notes that] because an injunction of a distinct qualified action is necessary—due to the inclusion of multiple qualities in the passage "The Viśvajit is an Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭhas"—that [injunction applies] to that Viśvajit.
The interpretation by Somanātha—that the phrase "and so forth" (ādipadena) serves as an inclusive summary—is rejected;

for while it is possible for the action under discussion (*prakṛtakarman*) to serve as the substratum, there is no evidence for postulating such a status for an action not under discussion (*aprakṛta*). Indeed, it is quite clear that in the *Udbhid-ādhikaraṇa*, after raising the objection regarding the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) in a worldly action not under discussion, the *Viśvajit* sacrifice from the Vedic corpus—which is likewise not under discussion—was introduced precisely to provide a response to that objection.
This is understood from the *Śāstradīpikā*.
For this very reason, immediately following that, the conclusion of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument is made with the intention that the Jyotiṣṭoma alone is the substratum (*āśraya*).

Therefore, the authors of the *Prakāśa* state in their text: "Because the Śyena belongs to the Sāmaveda, and since in that [Veda] another [rite] might also be the subject matter due to the differences between the recensional branches (*śākhā*), the word ‘etcetera’ (*ādi*) [is used]"—here, they employ the word ‘etcetera’ with the intention of indicating possibility.
This has been explained in the *Śāstradīpikā*.
Therefore, it is appropriate to enjoin the quality of the hawk-wing and so forth—which is based on the *jyotiṣṭoma* under discussion—with reference to a specific result.

The intention is that because it is optional (*kāmya*), it is not even improper to set aside the permanent (*nitya*) *soma*, even though the latter is enjoined at the time of the original production (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).
(An exposition following an alternative position that there is an injunction for a distinct qualified ritual action, based on the natural sense of the Bhāṣya, Vārttika, and other texts:
However, if it were the case that "there is no basis for the application [of the word] to this ritual action;
for if one were to apply it to the ritual action by adopting the sense of the suffix -vatī, there would be an extremely remote secondary usage (gauṇatā)."
In that case, it is better to resort to *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indicative function based on possession).

For a means (*sādhana*), being well-known through its absolute inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), conveys its own action to be accomplished (*svasādhyā kriyā*) without difficulty even without the elision of the *matup* suffix; this is because the *Vārttika* states that *matvarthalakṣaṇā* is superior to secondary indication (*gauṇī*) with respect to the aim of the result.
Since that [injunction] would not apply in the case of an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi), this position is not accepted by the author of the Vārttika;
for it would involve enjoining a remote object and result in the verbal root becoming subordinate to another purpose.

Considering that [the view] would contradict the Siddhāntabhāṣya stating "there is indication (lakṣaṇā) in the case of an injunction of a quality," it is observed that there is no contradiction with the Pūrvapakṣabhāṣya— "like *udbhid* and so forth"— even though there is only a similarity in being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

Alternatively, intending that even according to the literal reading [of the Bhāṣya], there is no contradiction because a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) was proposed as the Pūrvapakṣa in the *Udbhid-ādhikaraṇa*, the injunction of a distinct qualified action (*viśiṣṭakarmāntaravidhāna*) is also in accordance with the Vārttika.
He states another alternative: "viśiṣṭa" (qualified), etc.

By this, the explanation of the *Nyāyasudhā* author— which states that the passage from the *Vārttika*, "For [the sacrifice] is the means" (*sādhanaṃ hi*), indicates that the *Śyena* and other rites, being enjoined with reference to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, imply their own result as the object to be accomplished (*svasādhyalakṣaka*) because they are perceived as its means— is refuted. This is because it would involve enjoining a mere accessory (*guṇa*) with reference to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, which the authors of the *Nyāyasudhā-prakāśa* have themselves criticized.

Since it has been established hundreds of times that there is no *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication of possessive meaning) in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), the entire body of the Vārtika literature—which aims to demonstrate the superiority of *matvarthalakṣaṇā*—would otherwise fall into inconsistency.

Therefore, the authors of the *Prakāśa* maintain that the intention of the Vārtika is precisely to establish the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this is an injunction for a distinct, qualified ritual action (*viśiṣṭakarmāntara*).
(The fact that the position of the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is established in the Vārttika, just like the position of the connection between quality and fruit):
In reality, however—"An object to be enjoined is always praised by means of a distinct comparison;
for it is not accepted that a thing is praised by itself in that same manner."
Regarding the statement, “And when a quality is enjoined, the substance *śyena* is enjoined,” that very [substance] is what ought to be praised.

Furthermore, based on the passage from the *Siddhāntavārtika*, “It is not proper for it to be compared to itself,” the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerns only the injunction of the quality named *śyena*, and not the injunction of a qualified [composite] entity;

for, as in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the relationship of comparison between the sacrifice and the [hawk] is logically possible, and thus the objection [based on the *Vārtika*] would be untenable.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position regarding the injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) with reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is not refuted by the impossibility of the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison; rather, it is rejected precisely because of its prolixity (gaurava).

For this very reason, intending to show that the view of a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhi)—since it involves the indication of possessive meaning (matvarthalakṣaṇā)—is also acceptable to him, the venerable author has presented both positions as being on equal footing.
It should be understood, however, that the refutation of the view of the qualified injunction in the Vārttika was not explicitly stated there because it is self-evident.
(An objection that the first position contradicts the supplementary passage "Just as a hawk," etc.)—
and it is not so.

Regarding the first position, the meaning of the objection is as follows: in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "Just as the hawk," the word *ayam* (this) in the nominative case refers back to the hawk (*śyena*) which is the object of the injunction;

since there can be no difference within a single entity, the relationship of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) consisting of that [hawk] is impossible. Therefore, by interpreting the term figuratively (*gauṇatvena*) through a secondary sense, it is more appropriate for it to be a name (*nāmadheya*).
This is the sense of the doubt.
(Resolution of the doubt regarding contradiction by means of establishing an alternative interpretation of the remainder of the sentence:
Because it can be interpreted otherwise.

The meaning is as follows: even though the status of the object of comparison and the comparison itself is established by accepting that, under the view of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the word "this" refers to the qualificand— the sacrifice having *śyena* as its material— nevertheless, this must be interpreted otherwise, either by postulating a distinction based on factors such as state (*avasthā*) and so forth— as in the case of "the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa was like [the battle] between Rāma and Rāvaṇa"— or by characterizing it through the absence of any other object of comparison.
It has been stated that the opening [of the discussion] is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that "this very thing is a defect.
Thus, there is no fault in interpreting the conclusion differently from the opening,
for here the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*) is not ambiguous such that it would require determination by means of a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*).

The meaning is that in the absence of this [qualification], you yourself must admit that it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi), just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with Soma" and similar passages.
(Justification for the absence of contradiction with the remainder of the sentence by way of the figure of speech *ananvaya*):

In reality, however, since the word *ayam* (this) refers specifically to the hawk (*śyena*), which serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), because it shares the same case-ending, the figure of speech *ananvaya*—which consists in describing the object of comparison (*upameya*) itself as the standard of comparison to indicate the absence of any other standard—is indeed established; therefore, there is no contradiction.
He states the objection: "They are like its manifestations."

The third line of this [verse] should be understood as: "Not only was that very woman of shapely hips like a woman of shapely hips possessing the most intense beauty of fearlessness, but even her graceful movements were like the abodes of the dance."

(Refutation of Somanātha’s view that the figure *ananvaya* does not apply when there is a difference in attributes, by demonstrating its validity through the superimposition of identity even between two distinct things): As for what was stated here by Somanātha—"Nor is it appropriate to suspect the figure *ananvaya* here;
for in *ananvaya*, the identity of attributes is necessary"—[that is now refuted].

In this case, however, since there is no possibility of non-correspondence (*ananvaya*) due to the difference in properties consisting of the taking of fish and the like versus the taking of enemies (*bhrātṛvya*), it would follow that even if one were to accept non-correspondence despite a difference in properties, then in such passages as "He attained equality in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and likewise maintained the same conduct toward his younger brothers," non-correspondence would result, leading to the undesirable consequence of destroying the rule based on differences in properties.
Nor should it be argued: "In this instance, let there simply be a simile based on a difference in properties. [This cannot be said.]

[Objection: "Since the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) are designated by distinct words, their possession of a single attribute (*ekadharmikatva*) is not perceived; therefore, the simile based on a single attribute—which presupposes a distinction of attributes—is not manifested in the present case.

[Response: This is not so; for even when two subjects are distinct, it is possible for them to possess a single attribute through the intended expression of their unity (*aikya*) by virtue of their similarity.

Otherwise, even according to your own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the relationship between the standard and object of comparison would be untenable due to the absence of a single common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

Regarding the phrase "in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa," since there is no absence of identity between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), the possibility of *ananvaya* (non-repetition) does not arise. Furthermore, if one were to imagine that *ananvaya* occurs when the standard and object of comparison are designated by different words because their shared property (*ekadharmika*) is not perceived, then the use of a simile based on a difference in properties—as in "in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa"—would be inappropriate. For this very reason, the *Vārttika* raises the doubt concerning the figure of speech *ananvaya* with the example: "the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa," and so forth.

Therefore, since the relationship between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison is established even in the absence of identity—by way of the figure of speech *ananvaya*—when only the *śyena* (falcon) itself is enjoined with reference to the result; and since this is even more clearly established under the view of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) as in the Siddhānta, it is not proper to abandon its conventional meaning and treat it as a name.
Furthermore, in the case of an injunction regarding a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is not itself a fault;
for it is superior to indirect indication (*gauṇī*) when compared to indicated-indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).
Indeed, it is held that "indirect indication functions toward what is invariably connected with the primary denotation."

The sense is this: according to the method stated in the *Vārttika* on the *Siddhi-sūtra*—"Metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted as a function [of a word] due to its connection with qualities perceived [in the primary meaning]"—the metaphorical indication based on qualities (*guṇalakṣaṇā*) is clearly more cumbersome because it involves an additional step. Furthermore, in the case of a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), the literal meaning of the word, such as *śyena*, is not abandoned from its connection in the sentence-meaning, just as in the case of "red turban" (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*). However, in the other case (where there is a figurative sense), when a secondary meaning is understood, the literal meaning—which is no longer intended—is not connected to the sentence-meaning; thus, there is a violation of the direct Vedic statement (*śrutipīḍā*). Therefore, the former (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) alone is superior.

(The commencement of the established conclusion that [the *śyena*] is a name, because the relationship of object of comparison and subject of comparison is untenable in the absence of difference, and because it would likewise be untenable even through a conceptualized difference:
This is not an injunction regarding the connection of a quality with a fruit; for if it were so, the comparison understood from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would be untenable.
Although this praise does not require absolute literal truth regarding its own referent,
nevertheless, because it depends upon a basis of comparison, it cannot be established without a distinction [between the two].
Nor is it reasonable to assume a figurative distinction.

If that were the case, there would arise numerous defects, such as the conceptualization of a single individual instance (*vyakti*) as the object of comparison at different times; for instance, one would have to assume that the very same hawk individual who previously descended and ate meat is now performing the act of killing the enemy—which results in the absurdity of interpreting the word *nipatyādatta* (having descended, he took) as indicating past time (*bhūtakāla-lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, there is the problem of assuming a single referent for the words *śyena* and the pronoun (*sarvanāman*), which are co-occurrent with the two verbs and are perceived as having distinct meanings.

Thus, even if one were to assume a comparison based on a difference between individuals at the same time, there would arise the undesirable consequence that the word *śyena* (hawk) and the pronoun (*sarvanāman*), which both present the hawk as delimited by the universal *śyenatva*, would have to be taken as indicating (lakṣaka) the individual to be grasped and the individual other than it.

Furthermore, there would be the absence of praise for that which is delimited by *śyenatva*—the very delimiter of its status as the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Consequently, multiple defects would ensue.

In reality, however, in the case of non-comparison (*ananvaya*), the relationship of subject and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) is not established through the assumption of a figurative (aupacārika) distinction.
Because it would result in the destruction of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), however,
through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the absence of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), there is merely the manifestation of the state of not being connected with anything else.

Therefore, even here, in the demonstration of the absence of another standard of comparison, since the occurrence of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) would apply to many words, it is preferable [to apply it] to that single word occurring at the beginning.

Intending that it is more appropriate to accept the status of this word as a name by means of conventional indication (nirūḍhalakṣaṇā) precisely upon the word "śyena," the author states the final conclusion: "Not this... and so forth.
Because it is logical.
(The description of secondary figurative application [gauṇīvṛtti] by way of metaphor [rūpaka] in the section on the hawk):

The meaning is that it is logical because it will be stated in the twelfth [book of the Mīmāṃsāsūtra] that "favor should be shown to even the subordinate elements if they are numerous, whereas favor toward the primary element applies only when they are equal in number."

And here, following the opinion of some who hold that [the metaphor] is secondary (gauṇī) by way of a metaphor (rūpaka) consisting in the imaginative construction of identity between two distinct things, he says: "by way of a metaphor."
(An establishment of the status of names in the Veda by way of an elliptical simile, since figurative usage in the form of a metaphor is impossible):
In reality, however, because there is no person who could be the author of the Veda, there is no metaphor anywhere therein.
For this very reason: "If figurative usage were established for speakers through superimposition..."

In the *Vārttika* on the *Siddhi-sūtra*, the view that "the secondary [metaphorical] sense (*gauṇī*) is that which has its nature superimposed" was refuted by the statement: "That [secondary sense] could not exist in the Veda in any way without a person who performs the superimposition.

Therefore, because the superimposition of non-difference is impossible and because there is no word expressing a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), he states another alternative—namely, that it is a "deleted simile" (*luptopamā*)—with the intention that in the word *śyena* occurring in the injunction, the simile is elided. Thus: "It is a deleted simile."
By the phrase "secondary function" (gauṇī vṛttiḥ), the objection that it would entail the postulation of a further denotative power (śakti) is refuted.
Although the secondary function is superior to the indication of possessive meaning (matvarthalakṣaṇā), nevertheless, that [latter] would result if it were applied to an injunction (vidhi).
But since my name is merely a derivative of yours, there is no fault due to this disparity.
(An exposition of the lightness resulting from resorting to the second type of injunction when *śyena* is a name:
By the phrase "the second type of injunction," the position of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is rejected because it would entail excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

Thus, once it is understood that what is denoted by the word *śyena* is a form of sacrifice—distinct from the well-known hawk (*prasiddha-śyena*), yet resembling it—which produces the fruit of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), [the conclusion follows].

Because the name *Jyotiṣṭoma* would be contradicted by another name [for this rite], it is untenable [to apply that name here]; therefore, the status of this as a distinct ritual (*karmāntara*) is established by the name itself.

However, the purpose of accepting the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) [of the word "hawk"] is simply to bring to mind the well-known Śyena sacrifice in passages such as "The rest is the same as the Śyena," and not to refer to the actual hawk bird through its conventional sense.

Nor can it be argued that the praise of the sacrifice—based on its similarity to a hawk because it is a means of seizing enemies—is for the sake of praising the prescribed Vetasa-wood raft, just as there is praise of water [in the context of the Agnicayana]; for such a praise of the sacrifice is already established.
For it is observed that praise (stuti) which pertains to that which is to be enjoined (vidheya) is transferred elsewhere;
nor is it possible for the substance (dravya) to be enjoined as a qualification even within the injunction of the sacrifice (yāga-vidhi).

(Justification for following up the beginning with the conclusion while it still possesses expectancy): By this much, when the injunction of the connection between the quality and the fruit is established, and when the difficulties of a remote injunction (*viprakṛṣṭavidhāna*) and the subordination of the verbal root (*dhātupārārthya*) arise, as well as the introduction of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in accepting a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the indication has been provided by stating that [the former position] would entail a second type of injunction. If someone were to urge the superiority of the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) in this matter, [one should respond as follows]:
He replies: "But it is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda)."

The meaning is this: here, the initial statement (upakrama) is not altered to conform to the concluding summary (upasaṃhāra); rather, since it has been determined that the injunction for a sacrifice named Śyena is established through parsimony (lāghava) to avoid the defects mentioned previously, the word "Śyena" must be accepted as the name of the sacrifice.

This is done by relying on the similarity demonstrated in the supplementary portion of the text (vākyaśeṣa), in accordance with the requirement for a ground for its application (pravṛttinimitta), just as is the case with the name Jyotiṣṭoma.
The acceptance of a secondary sense occurs precisely through following the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa) due to the requirement of the opening statement (upakrama).

For this very reason— wherever there is such a requirement of the opening statement, there one certainly does not accept a pursuit of the meaning of a concluding statement (upasaṃhāra) that contradicts it.

For example, in the case of the injunction "he draws the fire with *avakā* plants," the word *avakā* is not accepted as having a secondary figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) referring to water, following the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) which states, "Water is indeed peaceful. This is because, according to the *Guṇavāda* Sūtra, the praise of the *avakā* plants themselves occurs by way of praising water; thus, the discrepancy between the injunction and its praise (*vidhi-stuti-vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is avoided.

For one who maintains that the concluding portion alone possesses greater authority, the occurrence of a secondary figurative meaning for *avakā* as "water" in that very instance would be unavoidable.

Therefore, since there is no further expectancy in that case, there is no following after a supplementary portion of the sentence; thus, the consequence of the superiority of the concluding statement does not arise.
And this has been indicated by the venerable teacher through the word "expected" (apekṣita).

(Regarding the statement that even though the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is more consistent if the subject is the bird, the determination that "Śyena" is the name [of the rite] in the opening section leads one to interpret the concluding section in accordance with it; this is a restatement of the subject matter found in the *Upakramaparākrama* treatise.

As for what was argued there in the *Upakramaparākrama*—that the explanatory passage is consistent only if the subject is the bird and inconsistent if the subject is the sacrifice—it is as follows: in either case, the portion concerning the point of comparison means, "Just as the Śyena bird, having swooped down, seizes fish and other prey."

In that context, even if the phrase "the fish and so forth" were not included, it would still be obtained because that which is already well-known must be taken as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
As for the portion concerning the object of comparison (*upameya*), the meaning is as follows: "In this way, he kills the enemy of the sacrificer.

For in both cases—whether regarding the bird or the sacrifice—it is impossible for the enemy to perform the primary act of pouncing and seizing; likewise, in the case of the bird, it is impossible for the bird—which has been enjoined as a means either toward the fruit or toward the sacrifice—to function in the act of seizing an enemy.

Because [the term *śyena*] falls under the category of action in the context of a sacrifice, and because the acts of flying down (*nipatana*) and seizing (*ādāna*) are in every way impossible [in that context], the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) refers to the bird. Thus, the meaning is: "Just as the hawk bird, having flown down, seizes fish and other prey, so too this hawk—whether applied to the fruit or to the sacrifice—slays the enemy of the sacrificer."

In this case, the relationship of *upamāna* (standard of comparison) and *upameya* (object of comparison) is perceived between the two acts of killing an enemy—those which are well-known in the world as being performed by a hawk and those enjoined in the scriptural injunction for the consumption of fish and so forth;

it is not, however, that the hawk is compared to itself as "by means of a hawk. Thus, there is no impossibility of similarity through difference here. Even though a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) between these two is not explicitly mentioned;

Nevertheless, just as for a fish moving at will in the water, the swooping down and seizing it by a hawk occurs suddenly and unexpectedly, so too does the killing of enemies effected by that [Māra]; thus, there certainly exists a common property that is understood [by implication].

And so, just as in such cases as "his eyes were like a lotus with petals like those of a monkey," there is never any logical inconsistency in expressing the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison through a common property that is merely implied.
Furthermore, it must necessarily be admitted that this common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is understood even in the alternative case [of the injunction].

Otherwise, since the mere killing of an enemy would be contained within the primary enunciation (*vidhyuddeśa*), one would not perceive the speed [of the action] through the force of the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) derived from the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*). Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of failing to obtain a specific praise that motivates activity;
for example, when Caitra has entered his house in secret and departed in secret, another person who knows only of his secret entry into the house might say of Devadatta: [as in the following:]...

By the statement, "He entered the house; likewise he has gone out," the relationship of subject and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) is expressed between the very acts of entering and exiting residing in Devadatta, through the common attribute of being performed secretly (*pracchannakṛtatva*), which is implied;
it is not, however, a primary relationship of subject and object of comparison in the form of "Devadatta is like Devadatta."
Thus, it is appropriate here as well.
Furthermore, if the word *ayam* (this) refers to the bird denoted by the proximate nominative-termined term, straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is observed;

however, if it refers to the sacrifice, there would be the consequence of lack of straightforwardness, because *ayam*, situated in the remainder of the sentence, would refer to the sacrifice—a distant object—merely as the instrument. Moreover, the relationship of primary simile and object of comparison between the bird and the sacrifice would be non-primary.
Because of the absence of common properties that would accompany [the comparison], primary similarity is impossible;
for in the case of the bird, there is the primary act of seizing after pouncing upon fish and the like,
whereas in the sacrifice, there is the very act of slaying one's rival.

That very [act of seizing] is metaphorically designated as "primary *nipatyādāna*" (seizing by swooping down) due to its association with the quality of being "unexpectedly present" (*āśaṅkitopasthitikatva*). Therefore, the similarity between the hawk and the sacrifice is only secondary (*amukhya*), as it is based on that [primary act].

Nor should it be argued: "Even in the view that the passage is focused on the sacrifice, it is more appropriate for the seizing of fish, etc., and the killing of the enemy—which belong to the hawk-sacrifice—to serve as the object of comparison and the subject of comparison respectively.

For by that much, one would fail to obtain the similarity to a hawk (*śyenasādṛśya*) which is the ground for applying the word "hawk" (*śyena*) to the sacrifice; consequently, it would be improper to assert that the word "hawk" is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) in accordance with the concluding portion of the text.

Even though such directness is present, for the sake of establishing the *śyena* word as the name of a sacrifice— thereby fulfilling the injunction of the sacrifice alone according to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) at the outset— when there is a requirement for a basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), and since no primary basis for application is possible for that which is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) therein, one seeks a secondary basis for application. Consequently, in accordance with the requirement of the initial context, the word "this" (*ayam*) in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) refers back to the distant instrument (*karaṇa*).
Regarding the claim that "the remainder of the sentence is interpreted as referring to a secondary similarity," whereby the conclusion is led according to the beginning—

[this is stated] because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is logically consistent only with the relationship of exemplar and exemplified between the Śyena sacrifice and [the act of striking], which thus refutes the arguments concerning the beginning and the end—
that is incorrect.

Because the pronoun *ayam* (this) conveys an object other than the hawk (*śyena*), it is impossible for it to refer back to the hawk; thus, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison cannot be established between two actions residing in a single hawk.

Furthermore, if one were to take another individual bird—already enjoined as a means—as the referent of the word *ayam*, there would result a contradiction with the perceived difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by the property of being a hawk (*śyenatva*).

If, however, the text were merely "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey], so [does he seize] his enemies," then that relationship might indeed be possible between two actions residing in a single hawk.
This is not the case;

for this very reason, even in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), if the word *ayam* (this) is present, it is indeed difficult to establish a relationship of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) between the two actions residing therein.

Even though the source text (*ākara*) states that "a distinction may be conceived," it subsequently exerts effort to resolve the perceived distinction by means of such phrases as "conceiving a figurative distinction" (*aupacārikabhedakalpanā*).
Furthermore, for you as well, there is an equal lack of consistency because the connection between the two words "yathā" and "evaṃ" would result in an interrupted (vyavahita) relation.

Therefore, to account for the perceived distinction, it is only the sacrifice (*yāga*) and the hawk (*śyena*) that can logically stand in the relationship of object of comparison (*upameya*) and standard of comparison (*upamāna*).

And in this way, by providing the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), the visible purpose of the supplementary sentence expressing the suffix *-vat*—as understood from the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyavidhi*)—is attained.

But for you, even if the praise were otherwise, there would result the unwarranted assumption of a restrictive unseen merit (*niyamādṛṣṭa*), on the grounds that [the act] must be performed with the suffix *-vat* alone because it is pleasing and brings about prosperity.

And this has been indicated by the venerable teacher in the Kaustubha through the statement that there is no assumption of a single meaning for the words *śyona* and the pronoun *sarva*, which— being uttered together with the words *yathā* and *evam*— are perceived as having distinct meanings, by means of an explanation of their distinctness.

(An exposition on how the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) serves the purpose of praising the sacrifice by means of the *pūrṇopamā* (complete simile) based on the relationship between the original object and its reflection, without resorting to figurative indication [*lakṣaṇā*].
"Without resorting to figurative indication" (*vinaiva lakṣaṇām iti*).
The meaning is "without [the cognition] characterized by the absence of another object of comparison."
By way of the poetic figure of *pūrṇopamā* (complete simile).

And here, since the [comparison] is suggested by the previously mentioned manner through the presence of qualities such as being suspected [of being harmful], one must accept a complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*) by intending to express that the seizing of fish and the like, and the killing of enemies, share a single common property. For in the case of a sacrifice, praise is required to remove the lack of inclination which acts as an obstacle to its performance; however, in the case of a substance, since there is no spontaneous inclination toward it, such praise is not strictly required. Thus, the distinction is that there is a remoteness (*viprakarṣa*) consisting in the postulation of praise for the sacrifice accomplished by means of praise for the substance. Therefore, [the passage] is for the purpose of praising the sacrifice.
This is what is indicated by this [statement].
(Establishing that *sandaṃśa* and other terms are names:

In the same way, for words such as *sandaṃśa*, one should understand their status as names because they are seen to be used as metaphors for the iron tongs used as an instrument for grasping a red-hot iron ball, as stated in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "Just as one might take hold of something difficult to grasp with a pair of tongs, so does he take [the offering] with this."
(An investigation into the fourfold nature of the mode of being a name, together with its etymological derivation):

It was previously asserted that the present section begins for the purpose of "cleansing the granary" regarding where there is a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) and where there is a name (*nāmadheya*) in the discussion of "or rather, it is a name.
He concludes by indicating the dependence upon the four modes of naming: "That is established."

In this section concerning the *udbhid*, it is precisely the etymological nature (*yaugikatva*) that establishes its status as a name; however, the metaphorical indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) serves as a corroborative factor by means of refuting the alternative view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

This is because, even in the absence of such a transfer [of the quality], the prima facie argument for a quality-injunction—whether regarding the fruit or the sacrifice—is rendered untenable by the very fact that its status as a name is established through its etymological nature alone.
Furthermore, because the status of being a name is not accepted for *soma* and other such terms merely on the grounds of the occurrence of a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*),

the fourfold classification should be understood as including both the etymological (*yaugika*) and the other types. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* that [the term] is indeed etymological.
Even the statement regarding the possessive suffix (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*) in the word *kaustubha* should be understood merely as an illustration of its etymological nature.
(The determination of the fifth type of the principle of the strength of that which is taught in the originative injunction regarding names, and its refutation:

Relying on the *Nyāyasudhā* in the section concerning the *Vaiśvadeva*, some maintain that the strength of a quality taught in the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) also constitutes a mode [of application] when it concerns a name.
As they state in the *Vaiśvadeva* section: "Because it is already occupied by another quality, no other quality finds scope."
"Conceptual construction also [does not arise] due to disparity; therefore, it is only a name that is appropriate."
The particle "eva" is used precisely to indicate the refutation of that [position];
that refutation will be examined in that very same place.
(An exposition of how terms such as *vaiśvadeva*, *jyotiḥ*, and others can, as far as possible, be made the subject matter of the *udbhid* section;
and the avoidance of redundancy.
By the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*), this is what is meant:

Although in the passage "Now this is the Jyotis; now this is the Sarvajyotis," the word *jyotis* (and so on) is mentioned first, yet—since there is no co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a word denoting a ritual (*kratu*) for that substance, it cannot be enjoined as an accessory (*aṅga*) to that ritual;

and since that which is already established in form (*siddharūpa*) cannot be enjoined by the context (*prakaraṇa*)—it [is understood] by means of the word *etena* (by this) occurring in the subsequent sentence, "One should sacrifice with this [rite] involving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee."

There arises a suspicion that this passage is intended to enjoin accessory details (guṇa), because it refers back to those things previously indicated by the nominative case in the preceding sentence and thus restates the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice while being presented through the word "this" (etad). Nevertheless, since enjoining those accessories and the thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*sahasradakṣiṇā*) by way of restating that sacrifice would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), the passage does not have the purpose of enjoining accessories, just like the word *citrayā* [in the previous discussion].
Rather, it is merely a name;

for it is appropriate to assume a distinct ritual action when qualities and the like would otherwise result in a split of the sentence (vākya-bheda). With this intention, even in this section, when those [qualities] are presented with the instrumental case in other sentences—

In the *Vārttika*, it is stated that "they are deliberated upon then. Although it might appear at first glance that words such as *jyotis* and others are subjects for deliberation in that section concerning their designation (*tadvyapadeśādhikaraṇa*),

the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* has explained this with the intention that— considering such an interpretation to be improper because those words lack that specific designation— the application of words like *jyotis* will occur, as appropriate, within the sections concerning *udbhid* and other such terms.
Therefore, in that case as well, it is appropriate to regard it as a name (*nāmadheya*).
In this same way, the status of terms such as *darvīhoma* and *vaiśvadeva* as names should also be understood through the principle of "being so-called because of that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*).
However, in the section concerning the *Vaiśvadeva* sacrifice (*Vaiśvadevādhikaraṇa*), that very point regarding the term *vaiśvadeva* is raised as an objection and then resolved.

In this eighth [section], the status of being a name (*nāmadheya*) is already established; it has been mentioned incidentally for the purpose of investigating its novelty (*apūrvatā*) and so forth, and thus there is no redundancy.
As for the practical application (*prayojana*): according to the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the *jyotiṣṭoma* is performed by means of the *śyena* bird, thereby setting aside the *soma*;
according to the second view, because the substance is a living being (*prāṇidravyaka*), the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *agnīṣomīya* applies.
In the Siddhānta, however, it is not explicitly stated that [the sacrifice] has Soma as its substance and is a modification (vikṛti) of the Somayāga, because this is self-evident.
Thus ends the fifth section, concerning that designation. (B1) (Section 6:
"If it is argued that because a quality is heard within a name, there must be an injunction [of that quality]," Jaimini 1.4.6.

The objections previously raised against the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) in both cases— namely, those concerning the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) and so forth— are here challenged. For if the sacrifice were itself a factor of action (*kāraka*), then,
since other factors such as *soma* could not logically connect with it, the indication of possessive meaning would indeed be necessary.
Or [it might be argued that] there is an injunction for the cultivation of both [the agent and the object];
but this is not the case,
because it is accepted that sacrifice is of the nature of an action (*kriyā*).

And for this reason, in that [sacrifice], the connection of all the factors of action is possible—just as in the case of *bhāvanā*—without resorting to possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) and without any lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*). Furthermore, even though the sacrifice is an action (*kriyā*), its connection with *bhāvanā* through a general relation is not contradictory.
Alternatively, one does not accept *bhāvanā* as something distinct [from the action] at all, as the Grammarians do.
Therefore, since even in cases such as *udbhid* and others, there is everywhere only the status of being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*),

and since the example of *vājapeya* in the root [of the commentary] follows the rule concerning qualities (*guṇasūtra*)— this being the position reached— it is replied: because of the analysis of the word *pacati* as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) or "he effects by means of cooking" (*pākena karoti*), the verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) is connected with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) only as a factor (*kāraka*) characterized by either the state of being an object (*karman*) or the state of being an instrument (*karaṇa*).

And how *bhāvanā* is predominant will be explained later. Therefore, since it is impossible for the other factors (*kārakas*) to be construed with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), one has no choice but to accept— in the case of *soma* and so forth— the injunction of a *bhāvanā* qualified by both [the root-meaning and the substance],
or else, according to the older method, the presence of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication of the possessive sense).

Otherwise, if the sacrifice were connected to both the result and the accessory by the Vedic text itself, there would arise the fallacy of two sets of three contradictory attributes: for the sake of connecting the sacrifice with the result, the sacrifice would possess the qualities of being something to be enjoined (*upādeyatva*), something to be prescribed (*vidheyatva*), and a subordinate element (*guṇatva*); whereas for its connection with the accessory, it would possess the qualities of being something to be referred to (*uddeśyatva*), something restated (*anuvādatva*), and a principal element (*prādhānya*).
Furthermore, the definitions and explanations of "being something to be enjoined" and so forth are to be found in the *Kaustubha*.

Therefore, since a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is untenable due to the fear of [the faults of] possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) and the like, terms such as *udbhid* must be names (*nāmadheya*). // 6 // 22 //

Thus ends the sixth section, the *viśiṣṭavidhyākṣepādhikaraṇa* (also known as the *vājapeyādhikaraṇa*). (B2) [The determination of the introductory connection (*ākṣepasaṅgati*) with the four preceding sections: He demonstrates the introductory connection of this [section] with the four preceding sections by stating: "In the view that it is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*)."

This also serves as an illustration of the position that the passage is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) with reference to the sacrifice (*yāga*), because of the employment of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) and the plural number in the phrase "matvarthalakṣaṇādīni" [which occurs] later on.
Thus: "matvarthalakṣaṇādīni."
(An objection based on the connection with the Tantras, and the demonstration that all such cases within the scope of the previous principles serve as illustrations:

By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the two defects— the meaninglessness of the word denoting the fruit when there is a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that a quality is being enjoined by restating a sacrifice, and the meaninglessness of the word denoting the quality when it is enjoined with reference to the fruit— as well as the principle of "designation" (*vyapadeśanyāya*), are all included.
In this context, because both of those [arguments] are extracted within the *pūrvapakṣa* by way of connection to the *tantra*,
there is no inclusion of even the four preceding principles (*nyāya*) stated by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*;
for it is impossible for the preceding principles to be implied by way of connection to the *tantra*.

The status as a name (nāmatva), which was established through the principle of etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*) and through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), cannot be refuted by means of a common substratum (*tantra-sambandha*);
nor can the syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) mentioned in the *Citrā-adhikaraṇa* be avoided.

This is because, even if it were possible for two qualities to be shared (*tantra*) between two sacrifices, there is no evidence for their being shared in their connection with the injunction (*vidhi-anvaya-tantratva*), and thus such a sharing is impossible.
Nor are there even the manifestation or the designation of that [quality].

Therefore, in every case where there is a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) for a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the objection consisting in the implication of a figurative indication of possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is raised; and in every case where there is a prima facie argument for an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) by way of a restatement of the sacrifice (*yāgānuvāda*), the objection consisting in the futility of the word denoting the fruit (*phalapadānarthakya*) and other such defects is raised here.

Even there, in the case of the *agnihotra* sentence, although it is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) is already expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself; thus, since the fault of "possessive indication" (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) does not arise, this [sentence] is not cited as an example.
To indicate this, the repetition "wherever... wherever" (*yatra yatra*) is employed with the intention of referring to all possible cases.

For this very reason, the sentences concerning the *samit* and other offerings—which serve as examples under the principle of "being known from another scriptural passage" (*tatprakhyānyaśāstra*)—do indeed serve as examples for the purpose of refuting that [qualified injunction], because the fault of possessive indication would arise if they were treated as qualified injunctions.
(An exposition, consistent with the *Kaustubha*, of how the *Śyena* sentence also falls within the scope of this section under the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it is a qualified injunction.

Thus, when the prima facie view holds that the *Śyena* sentence is a qualified injunction, and the metaphorical indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) based on a simultaneous connection (*tantrasambandha*) has been rejected, the injunction of a qualified sacrifice becomes free from defects. Consequently, since it is logical for a sacrifice other than the *Śyena* to serve as the object of comparison, the burden of a qualified injunction [is not incurred].

Since there is no obstacle to accepting [the term] in accordance with common usage—as in the case of the passages concerning Soma and so forth—and since the previous section is also subject to objection, it is not contradictory to commence this [section] following it.

By this, the objection raised by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*— that because this [topic] would have to begin immediately after the *Udbhid-ādhikaraṇa* due to the refutation of the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), its placement [here] is inconsistent— is refuted.
As for what was stated by the venerable teachers in the *Kaustubha*— "the principle of designation (*tadvyapadeśanyāya*) cannot at all be extracted"—
that should be understood as intending that the direct connection with the system (*tantra*) is incapable of refuting it.
For this very reason, in the *Nyāyasudhā*, having accepted the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) itself, the objection regarding the logic of that designation was demonstrated.

(An exposition on the demonstration that the application of this principle [of *tadvyapadeśa*] occurs even in the case of the *vājapeya* sentence— which is the subject of the *tatprakhyanyāya*— thereby establishing that the arguments in the *Prakāśa* and the *Kaustubha* are merely bold assertions [*prauḍhivāda*].

As for the point that the authors of the *Prakāśa*, and following them the venerable author of the *Kaustubha*, maintain that although the contingency of the implied indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) cannot be avoided in the *agnihotra* sentence,
in the example of the *vājapeya*— which falls under the scope of the *tatprakhyanyāya*— one should prefer a *karmadhāraya* compound over a *bahuvrīhi* because of its brevity;
In that case, there arises the possibility of an implication (*ākṣepa*) for the occurrence of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

For this very reason, although implication is common [to other cases], the *Vājapeya* sentence is cited in the *Ākara* (the *Tantravārttika*) to demonstrate the occurrence of possessive indication even in the scope of the *tatprakhyanyāya* principle; however, that [citing] is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), because under the *karmadhāraya* analysis, the word qualifying "drink" (*peya*) would have to be placed first, which would result in a discrepancy in the accentuation.
(An argument for the illustrative example of the *vājapeya* being a critique of the *Nyāyasudhā*, by refuting its claim that the previous section is not its subject matter:

As for what was stated in the *Nyāyasudhā*— that the purposelessness of citing the *vājapeya* as a novel example is avoided because the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is obtained through the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself in "that in which *vāja* is to be drunk" (*vājaṃ peyam asmin*), and thus there is no occurrence of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)— [this is now addressed].

Furthermore, since it is logical for the word *vāja* to function as a qualifier of the sacrificial food (*anna*) denoted by *peya*, and since it is logical to enjoin a single object characterized by its fitness for drinking, there is no syntactical split (*avākyabheda*). Moreover, because the two grounds for rejecting a secondary injunction (*guṇavidhi*)—namely, "being known from another source" (*tatprakhya*) and "being designated by another name" (*tadvyapadeśa*)—are absent, the refutation of the status of a secondary injunction by the previous four principles is not established. Therefore, the example of the *vājapeya* is introduced to refute that [status] on the grounds that it would otherwise result in a contradiction (*vairūpya*). Thus [ends the argument].

That too is not correct; for if that were the case, since [the term] would not fall under the scope of the *udbhid*-rule, there would be no occasion for the assumption of a *bahuvrīhi* compound—as in the case of the word *agnihotra*—and consequently, there would be no possibility of *matvarthalakṣaṇā*. Thus, the subject matter of this section, which aims to resolve that [objection] through a simultaneous connection (*tantrasambandha*), would not even arise.

Furthermore, in the Siddhānta, since the prohibition of the injunction of qualities is established by the very principle of *tatprakhya* (being known from another source) as stated in the *Ākara* due to the injunction of taking the *surā* cups, there is no need for that specific refutation.

Therefore, the sense is that those objections—such as the objection regarding possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) and so forth—which arise apart from the principles of etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*), syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), and "being named after that" (*tatprakhya*), are here raised and resolved.

(An exposition of the prima facie view—that a qualified injunction is impossible—preceded by the determination of the connection of the verbal root-meaning with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) through a general relation, and of qualities and so forth with it as the instrument and so on;

[this is stated] because of the impossibility of such a connection. Because of the impossibility of that connection: since factors of action (*kāraka*) connect only with an action, the meaning of the verbal root—which has become another factor of action—is the referent of that word.

Since, in the *udbhid-ādhikaraṇa*, he himself established that the quality (*guṇa*) is construed as a factor (*kāraka*) within the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) itself—thereby avoiding the fault of "implication of possessive meaning" (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)—then whatever difficulty arises from resorting to an injunction of the productive operation qualified by both the quality and the sacrifice must likewise be accepted; thus he says: "ubhayeti."
"Not this," he said.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "because there is no word here in the expression *yajeta* that expresses the objecthood (*karmatva*) or instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) residing in the sacrifice.

Although a distinct *bhāvanā* (efficient force) will be established in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, nevertheless, since that *bhāvanā*—which consists of effort—is not produced by *kārakas* (factors of action), it is impossible for *kārakas* to have a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with it.
Because when one adopts the substratum as the medium for the meaning of the verbal root, it is more logical that the [agent] be construed with that very [root-meaning] in relation to it;
therefore, all *kārakas* are construed with the meaning of the verbal root itself.
Consequently, because it is not construed with a *kāraka*, it does not possess the status of a *kāraka*.

Moreover, it is precisely of the nature of action (*kriyārūpatva*). Just as in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), *bhāvanā*—when conjoined with all the factors of action (*kāraka*)—is expressed by the suffix as being of the very nature of action, so too, according to my view, the meaning expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) is likewise of the nature of action.
For this very reason, there is no disparity caused by [factors such as] objecthood (*karmatva*) or instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), as there is in the case of *bhāvanā*.

And thus, the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), as qualified by all its factors of action (kāraka), is connected [with the nominal stem] solely through a general relation (saṃbandhasāmānya). Even the grammatical rule (anuśāsana) stating that "the base and the suffix express the meaning together" intends this general relation.
For this very reason, by the force of this rule alone, the relation appears as a word-meaning (padārtha) through conventional metaphorical indication (nirūḍhalakṣaṇā).

Nor is there a rule that what is distinct from a *kāraka* cannot at all be construed with the *bhāvanā*; for in the sentence "In these very *revatī* [verses]... it is accepted that the *bhāvanā* itself is also construed with it.
Alternatively, the *kārakas* are construed with the *bhāvanā* alone, in accordance with their primary construal [with the *bhāvanā*].

Nevertheless, since the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is construed with that [denotative power] by way of a general relation (*sambandhasāmānya*), even if one accepts that there is a single sacrifice which possesses both an object-nature (*karmatva*) defined by the quality and an instrumental-nature (*karaṇatva*) defined by the fruit, there is no occurrence of "dual form" (*vairūpya*) because such a thing is not cognized in those respective forms within the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Thus, since it is not understood as having the nature of an instrument, there is no necessity for a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) or the like for the sake of its connection; intending this, he says: "of the sacrifice" (*yāgasya*).
Thinking that the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* is not established, he states an alternative position to initiate this investigation: "Or rather, it is *bhāvanā*."
(Regarding the intention behind selecting the *vājapeya* as an example while abandoning other examples,
and the refutation therein of the views of the authors of the *Nyāyasudhā* and the *Prakāśa*:

Although there is no risk of the fault of possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) if one resorts to a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the word *vājapeya*, [the author proceeds to refute the opposing views].
In a *karmadhāraya* compound, there would be the undesirable consequence of the word *peya* (drinkable) being placed first;
nevertheless, even if one resorts to a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the sacrifice is not intended as the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*) in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Therefore, it is stated that, according to the intention of the prima facie view, the contingency of implying a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)—on the grounds that the substance denoted by the term *vājapeya* is enjoined as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*)—is not possible.

However, the intention is that the very ritual action—defined as that in which *vāja* (food) and *peya* (drink) [are present], like the substance of *surā* (liquor)—is intended to be expressed as the "other referent" (*anyapadārtha*) [of the compound]. Thus, he dispels the doubt—"Why did the ancient teachers cite the *vājapeya* itself as an example of *prasajya-matvarthalakṣaṇā*, given that by means of the compound itself, with the *surā* substance as the other referent, there is the injunction of a ritual qualified by that substance?"—by stating: "The *vājapeya*... [and so on].
(The purpose of the application of the sūtras on the qualities:
"In accordance with the sūtras on the qualities."
And in this case,

because the two actions are equal, [the rule] "not so" (Jaimini 1.4.7) is a *guṇasūtra* [referring to the previous position], since the similarity of substance prevails due to the *vājapeya* having food (*anna*) as its material, [thereby superseding] the injunction of the model sacrifice (*iṣṭi*).

When the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is reached, since the characteristics of the Soma sacrifice—such as the initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*) and the *upasad* ceremonies—are not [otherwise] obtained, the example of the Vājapeya is given in order to demonstrate the impossibility of observing the indicative marks (*liṅga*) found in the restatements (*anuvāda*) of the *dīkṣā* and *upasad*, namely: “The Vājapeya has seventeen *dīkṣās*” and “The Vājapeya has seventeen *upasads*.

For that [restatement] is possible only in the Vājapeya and not elsewhere; thus, the example of the Vājapeya follows from that necessity, and not according to the manner asserted by the author of the Nyāyasudhā and the Prakāśakāra. This is the meaning.

Having first established that the connection of the root-meaning with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) cannot occur through a general relation, but rather through specific relations such as being the object (*karman*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*), it follows that in all instances such as "one should sacrifice with *soma*," there is necessarily an indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

For if the connection between the sacrifice and the productive operation were by way of a general relation, then—since neither the quality nor the fruit would be suitable for either—the connection with the sacrifice would be untenable;
this is because a productive operation connected to a sacrifice would lack any further expectancy for either a fruit or a quality.

Therefore, since it is the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) whose instrument is the sacrifice that requires a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), its connection with the various [factors] is logically appropriate precisely in those respective forms.

When, in accordance with the previously mentioned explanation, the *bhāvanā* is understood as distinct from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and the meaning of the verbal root is perceived as having the status of either an instrument (*karaṇa*) or an object (*karman*)—that is, as one of the factors of action (*kāraka*)—then its connection is all the more appropriately in that very form.

In the presence of a co-occurrence with an injunction (*vidhi*), the meaning of the verbal root, even if it is not an end of human endeavor (*apuruṣārtha*), connects with the *bhāvanā* solely by way of being the instrument.
If, in the absence of that [direct injunction], it is understood to serve a human purpose, then it must be connected solely as an *object* (*karman*) and not through a general relation;

thus, when there is a connection with the *bhāvanā* as an instrument (*karaṇa*), at the time of the subsequent connection (*pārṣṭhikānvaya*), due to its suitability, the connection would be with the fruit alone, and not with the accessory (*guṇa*). Even if a connection with the accessory were somehow admitted by accepting it as an object despite the co-occurrence with the injunction, [the primary connection remains with the fruit].
It might not be [established] by means of the result;
however, the acceptance of the cognition of both forms simultaneously is contradictory.

Intending to show that if one accepts that the very word being heard produces two successive cognitions, this constitutes a "splitting of the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) characterized by repetition, he says: "Therefore... (*ataśca*).

(An exposition on the nature of the two sets of three contradictory factors that would result if both the substance and the fruit were connected to the sacrifice without the indication of possessive meaning [matvarthalakṣaṇā]): He states the occurrence of the two sets of three contradictory factors if both were connected to the sacrifice by direct statement (*śruti*) alone, without the indication of possessive meaning—beginning with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
For when the goal to be accomplished—such as the fruit and so forth—is understood simultaneously, its primacy is established because it is the purpose;

whereas the means, being for the sake of that which is to be accomplished, is subordinate because it exists for another's sake, a state synonymous with being a "subsidiary" (śeṣa). This is well known.

Furthermore, since predominance (*prādhānya*) is untenable without being the object of a purposeful action (*kṛtyuddeśyatva*), it entails the status of being an objective (*uddeśyatva*); and since that which has not been established cannot be made an objective, it entails the status of being a restatement (*anuvāda*) consisting in the mention of what is already established. Likewise, subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*) entails the status of being something to be adopted (*upādeyatva*), characterized by the induction of dependence upon the principal (*śeṣin*).

Since being "acceptable" (upādeyatva) depends upon injunction (vidhi), it entails being "enjoined" (vidheyatva). Thus, for a single sacrifice, the triad of being a means (sādhanatva), being subordinate (guṇatva), and being acceptable (upādeyatva), as well as the triad of being an end (sādhyatva), being primary (prādhānya), and being the subject of restatement (anuvādyatva), are mutually contradictory. Furthermore, even if there were a sequential cognition, because the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) is understood through its requirement by the injunction, priority (prāthamikatva) is necessary; therefore, it is only that which has not been previously known [that is enjoined].

By effecting the connection between the sacrifice and its fruit, the sacrifice possesses *vidheyatva* (the status of being something to be enjoined) with respect to that [connection], insofar as it is the object of making known what was previously unknown.

Furthermore, when the sacrifice—already known in its state as an instrument—is subsequently restated at the time of its connection with an accessory (*guṇa*), it possesses *anuvādyatva* (the status of being a subject of restatement) with respect to that accessory, insofar as it is the object of making known what is already known.

Thus, if one accepts the sequence of the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) for both the sacrifice and the accessory, there arises a discrepancy (*vairūpya*): first the origin of the sacrifice, and immediately thereafter the origin of the accessory.

The meaning is that there arises the fault of *vairūpya* (inconsistency) if one accepts that the directly heard [text] is intended solely for the sequential rules of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*), such that the sacrifice has the status of a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*)— synonymous with being a subsidiary (*śeṣatva*)— with respect to the fruit, while it has the status of a primary factor (*prādhānya*)— synonymous with being the principal (*śeṣitva*)— with respect to the accessory; and likewise, there is the fault of *vairūpya* if one accepts the sequence of the performance-rule (*prayoga-vidhi*), such that the sacrifice is something to be undertaken (*upādeyatva*) with respect to the fruit, but something to be referred to (*uddeśyatva*) with respect to the accessory.
(Refutation of the manner of defining "the state of being the object to be grasped" as presented by the author of the *Prakāśa*):

Now, one might ask—within the triad of "the state of being the object to be grasped" (*upādeyatva*), "the state of being the predicate" (*vidheyatva*), and "the state of being a subordinate quality" (*guṇatva*), and within the triad of "the state of being the subject" (*uddeśyatva*), "the state of being the restated" (*anuvādyatva*), and "the state of being the primary" (*prādhānya*)—what is this "state of being the object to be grasped"?
And what indeed is called "the state of being the subject"?

Furthermore, the statement by the author of the *Prakāśa*— that "being pervaded by an effort" (*kṛtivyāpyatva*) constitutes "being something to be undertaken" (*upādeyatva*), while its opposite, which is synonymous with "not being something to be undertaken," is "being something intended as a goal" (*uddeśyatva*)"—

is not correct. For [in that case], the place (such as the *samā* altar), the time (such as the period following the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice), the occasion (such as the possession of the *rathantara-sāman*), and the object to be refined (such as the *vrīhi* rice) would all result in being "things to be undertaken," since they possess the quality of being pervaded by an effort.

Because the agent, as well as the oneness residing in him, lack the quality of being pervaded by the activity (*kṛti*), they cannot be objects of prescription (*upādeya*) and must instead be objects of reference (*uddeśya*); furthermore, since the sacrifice in question is indeed pervaded by the activity, it would not [otherwise] fail to be an object of reference. Therefore, he says: "because of being an object of prescription, etc. (*upādeyatvādīti*).
(An exposition justifying the promise to define only the nature of "being subsidiary" (*śeṣatva*) and so forth, which are clearly known and unconfounded):

Because the quality termed "subsidiarity," the primacy consisting in being the object of the agent's purpose—which is synonymous with being the objective of the action (*kṛtyuddeśyatva*)—and the status of being an injunction or a restatement, known as being the object of the instigation (*pravartanā*) whose essence is the operation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), can be understood in their distinct and unconfounded forms; [therefore, they are defined].
