Since the status of being "to be adopted" (*upādeyatva*)—characterized by dependence and being brought about [by another]—is possible even within the state of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*), yet it is absent in cases such as time and place; and since, for that very reason, because of its predominance, the status of being "the object of reference" (*uddeśyatva*)—which is postulated through the otherwise inexplicability of that [status of being adopted]—is universally accepted as impossible there, and because the desire to know the essential nature [of that object] arises precisely in that case, the knowledge of its essential nature alone is useful. With this intention, [the author] stated "being-to-be-adopted and so forth," setting aside "subordinate quality" (*guṇatva*) and the rest.
(The definition of being an object of reference [uddeśyatva] and being that which is to be adopted [upādeyatva] by virtue of being free from defects:
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), being an object of reference is included.
Being an object of reference consists in not being the subject of the application of the injunction under discussion; the absence of that [application] constitutes being that which is to be adopted.
And this status of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) exists in the case of results such as heaven, as well as in time, place, and so forth;

for even though places and the like—such as those beginning with "near" (*samīpa*)—are pervaded by human effort (*kṛti*), the injunction under discussion is still valid by relying on what is already established in common worldly usage.

This is because, unlike the case of cattle and other animals, there is no pervasion by another action, such as the attainment of a specific location for subsequent wandering (*uttaravihāra*) prompted by the injunction under discussion.
Because they lack the status of being objects impelled by the primary injunction (*prakṛtavidhi*), the definition is consistently applied (*lakṣaṇasamanvaya*).

For this very reason, although substances such as animals and qualities inherent in them are established in reality through worldly means, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because they are objects impelled by the primary injunction insofar as they are the objects of actions such as being brought to the place of sacrifice. Similarly, since the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth are produced by the injunction for its installation (*ādhānavidhi*), the primary injunctions such as "one offers in the *āhavanīya*" do not function as the cause of their production.

Furthermore, there is no over-extension [of the definition], because even though [the sacrificial post] is the object of application, it exists in the form of being pervaded by other actions such as driving it into the ground or making it manifest.

Likewise, it should be understood that the *puroḍāśa*-cake’s potsherd (*kapāla*), while standing in the place of sacrifice, is also subject to the application of the present injunction by virtue of being the object of actions such as being grasped by the hand.

Although the rice and other materials to be refined (*saṃskārya*) are objects of application in the sentence “One should sacrifice with rice” (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), they do not lack the status of being the objective (*uddeśyatva*), because they are not objects of application in the present injunction which teaches the refinement itself.

Even though the agent denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) and its singularity and so forth are not prompted by the primary injunction (*prakṛtavidhi*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because they connect with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) solely through a relationship constituted by inherence (*samavāya*) as defined by the action (*kṛti*).
However, where the person is to be refined (*saṃskārya*), there is no non-extension (*avyāpti*), because the connection occurs precisely through the relationship of being the object (*karmatā*).

Consequently, since "being something to be undertaken" (*upādeyatva*)—characterized by the induction of dependence—is pervaded by "subsidiariness" (*śeṣatva*), and [the opposite] is pervaded by "primacy" (*prādhānya*).

Since even the status of being an object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) is not admitted, and since there is an impossibility of both the status of being an object of reference—consisting of the presence or absence of the status of being something to be adopted (*upādeyatva*)—even when [the sacrifice] is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) in respect to time, place, and so forth;

and since, in the present case, there is a mutual contradiction between the status of being an object of reference, which consists in not being the object of the impulsion of the primary injunction, and the status of being something to be adopted, which consists in the absence thereof, a simultaneous connection (*tantrasambandha*) is not possible.
This should be seen in the *Kaustubha*.
(Conclusion on the nominal nature of words such as *udbhid* based on the contradiction of two sets of three incompatible factors and the like:

Thus, since there is the occurrence of two sets of three incompatible factors (*viruddha-trika-dvaya*) if they were understood simultaneously, and since accepting a sequential [understanding] would result in the aforementioned inconsistency (*vairūpya*), it is impossible to accept that the directly heard word itself has both meanings simultaneously or sequentially; therefore, the directly heard injunction (*vidhi*) must be intent upon one or the other.

Since another [element] is required for the sake of the meaning, and because it is required by the injunction and is [semantically] capable, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) alone is expressed verbally through the logic of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* during the initial connection with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). Therefore, even at the time of the subsequent comprehension, the connection with the result occurs in that very form [as an instrument],
and not as an object (*karman*) or as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*).
Because that [connection with the result] occurs at a time subsequent to the connection with the fruit, it is what is sought.

Therefore, when the quality (guṇa) is first connected to the bhāvanā, it becomes an instrument (karaṇa) according to the method we have stated; then, since a connection with the sacrifice is necessary at the time of the second cognition, and because the sacrifice is the instrument toward the fruit, [the quality] must connect with the quality that has become the instrument.
An indication based on possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is necessary.

However, for those earlier scholars according to whose view even at the first stage the quality does not connect with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) as an instrument, that indication is necessarily unavoidable from the very outset; intending this, he concludes with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
By the phrase "of *udbhid* and so forth," the term *vājapeya* is also included, due to its similarity in being etymological (*yaugika*).

(Regarding the term *vājapeya*, the establishment of its equal application to both the accessory (*guṇa*) and the ritual action (*karman*) by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound in order to justify its grammatical coreferentiality [*sāmānādhikaraṇya*] with the root *yaj*):

Although, under the *karmadhāraya* view, the word *vājapeya*—being etymologically derived (*yaugika*)—would result in being a mere injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), as in the case of words like *ekahāyanī* through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), and would not possess equal application to both the accessory and the ritual action as the word *udbhid* does; [nevertheless...]

Nevertheless, once the view that [the term] refers to a quality (*guṇa*) has been rejected because it would entail a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), it is not difficult to establish its status as a name (*nāmadheya*) by resorting to the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself—the subordinate member—so as to achieve grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), according to the principle of "being known from that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*). Even though resorting to the status of a name in a *bahuvrīhi* involves a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*), which itself entails figurative indication; [it remains the best option].

Nevertheless, because that [meaning] is firmly established and arises at the time of the comprehension of the word-meaning, it is superior to the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the sentence-meaning—whether by virtue of its equality with direct audition (*śruti*) or its co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with other words;
thus, there is no fault.
However, when, according to the method I have stated, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) the compound is indeed a *bahuvrīhi*, [then this follows].
But in that case, since they function equally, there is no fault whatsoever.
(Establishing that *vājapeya* is a name by means of the *tatprakhyanyāya*):
Therefore, it is logical that it is a name according to the *tatprakhyanyāya*.
And it is possible for there to be a specific scriptural injunction regarding seventeen *prājāpatya* Soma-cups, just as there is for the [other] *prājāpatyas*.
Because of the specific scriptural injunction that "one takes seventeen soma-cups," and because, while the soma-cups have a procedure performed by the Adhvaryu at the Āhavanīya fire,

the surā-cups are prescribed to have a procedure performed by the Pratiprasthātṛ and the Vājasṛt at the Mārjālīya fire, the cups of surā also constitute repetitions of the Vājapeya sacrifice; thus, the principle of "designation by that" (tatprakhyanyāya) applies.

And in that context, regarding the *mārjālīya* [rite], even though the taking of the *surā* [liquor] is performed merely as an act of compassion, there is no dispute concerning the repetition of the sacrifice, whether it be the consumption by the *vājasṛt*s or the oblation (*homa*). This being the case, although the direct connection of *surā* with the sacrifice is not well-known, nevertheless, according to the rule "he takes seventeen *surā*-cups," since the *surā* consecrated by the act of taking is intended for distribution, one ransoms the honey-cup (*madhugraha*) with it.

In the *Kaustubha* of my venerable teacher, it is stated that because of the scriptural injunction regarding the oath, "That [vessel] along with the *brahman* priest and the cup," the honey-draught (*madhugraha*) previously given by the one who accepted the *surā* is employed as a substitute for the *surā*-draught; and since that honey-draught, together with its vessel, is employed in a gift where the *brahman* priest is the recipient, the connection of the *surā* with the sacrifice is established through this indirect succession.
The effort made to establish a connection with *surā* (liquor) is entirely futile.

Even if one were to argue that—just as in the case of terms like *agnīṣoma*—the term *vājapeya* applies precisely because the sacrifice is completed by that very [rite], since the *vājapeya-stotra* is prescribed at the end of the *bṛhatsāman* chant for Viṣṇu within the *vājapeya*, and thus the application of the word *vājapeya* is possible solely on account of its being completed by the *vājapeya-stotra*; [this still does not justify the inclusion of liquor].

Nevertheless, it should be noted that the Mīmāṃsakas follow only the etymological meaning (*yogārtha*)—namely, "that in which *vāja* (food) is to be drunk"—because the *Tāṇḍya-brāhmaṇa* provides an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating: "Prajāpati desired, 'May I obtain food (*vāja*) and the heavenly world. He saw this Vājapeya; for this is indeed the drinking of food (*vāja-peya*), the Vājapeya. By means of this, one attains the heavenly world. Thus, the term *vājapeya* is defined precisely through its connection with being the drinkable food (*vāja-rūpa-anna-peyatva*).

The purpose [of this discussion] was not stated because, although it is evident in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice applies due to the strong similarity of the substance, it is even more clearly evident in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Thus ends the sixth section, the Adhikaraṇa on the Implication of a Qualified Injunction (the Vājapeya Adhikaraṇa). (B1) (The seventh section:
"But its qualities should be enjoined, because there is no division in the purpose of the injunction."

In the case of such passages as, "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni (āgneya) is unswerving at the new moon and the full moon," there arises an inquiry whether the word *āgneya* is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or the name of a rite (*karmanāmadheya*). Since the deity Agni is already established by the wording of the mantra itself, it is argued that the term *āgneya* is a name. However, this is refuted because the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) whose object is the sacrificial cake has no requirement for a mantra, and the mantra is unsuitable for that purpose; thus, [the passage does not apply] to the *upāṃśuyāja*.
Thus, the mantra possesses the capacity to bring about the visualization of the deity;
yet, unlike the *āghāra* offering, there is no explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika-viniyoga*) for the mantra by which such a capacity might be presumed.
Furthermore, there is no evidence for the mantra being an auxiliary to the act of preparing the eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*),
since the context (*prakaraṇa*) is common to the *upāṃśuyāja* and other such offerings as well;
nor is there any evidence from sequence (*krama*).

Since it will be explained in the fifth [book] that the order of the mantra recitation is the reverse of the order of the Brāhmaṇa recitation, there is no application of the *tatprakhyanyāya* (the rule of being known by that); thus, because it cannot be a name (*nāmadheya*), there arises the cognition of an injunction for a *bhāvanā* qualified by both substance and deity. Since that [injunction] is untenable without a sacrifice, the verbal root *bhū* indicates that [sacrifice]; therefore, by means of enjoining the *bhāvanā* of the sacrifice as qualified by all its qualifiers, [the injunction is established].
Since, by implication, an injunction is also to be assumed for the qualifiers, the word *āgneya* is indeed an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: in cases such as "the milk belongs to Agni" (āgneyaṃ payaḥ), according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the ritual procedure of the Āgneya sacrifice is extended by means of name-extension (nāmātideśa);
however, in the final conclusion (siddhānta), the ritual procedure of the Sānnāyya sacrifice applies. // 7 // 23 //
Thus ends the seventh section concerning the Āgneya sacrifice.

(B2) [The determination of the connection as an exception (*apavāda*): Even though the preceding section serves the purpose of raising an objection and providing its resolution, it does not establish the name [of the sacrifice]; therefore, by means of the objection and its resolution—

Since the established conclusion (siddhānta) here provides an exception to the previously proven status of being a name, the author—without explicitly stating the connection as an exception because it is obvious—demonstrates the deliberation preceded by the presentation of the subject sentence: "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni" (*āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*).

(That this section also covers other archetypal (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛta*) sentences: By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of archetypal sentences such as "the *ekādaśakapāla* for Agni-Soma, the curd for Indra on the new moon day," as well as modified sentences such as "milk for Agni" and "the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) for Indra. (Regarding the refutation of the view of the *Nyāyasudhākāra*, who held that this section concerns all qualified injunctions by rejecting [the views] that [the terms] refer to names (*nāmadheya*) or qualities (*guṇavidhi*):)
Regarding this, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* states:

"In the fifth section [of the *Tantravārttika*], beginning with the sūtra ‘But by the mantra, there would be [application] in case of conflict’ (*mantratas tu virodhe syāt*), it will be explained that the sequence of the mantras for the *āgneya* and *agnīṣomīya* offerings is recited in a manner that reverses the sequence of the Brāhmaṇa.

Consequently, since there is no mantra enjoined by sequence, and because mantras not enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) lack the capacity to imply a connection with their own literal meaning..."

Since the postulation of a deity based on the wording of a mantra is untenable, and since it is impossible to postulate a sacrifice even through the connection of a substance and a deity, and since common usage such as "he divides the āgneya into four parts" concerns the substance and thus does not depend on the name of the ritual action, there is no possibility of suspecting that [the word] is a name because it would otherwise be purposeless; therefore, an inquiry into its being a name is not appropriate.

Therefore, since the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) was refuted in the preceding section due to the impossibility of a simultaneous syntactic connection (*tantrasambandha*), one might suspect that a qualified injunction is impossible anywhere by means of a suffix that is not repeated. Anticipating this, this present section is intended precisely to establish the theory of the qualified injunction. Furthermore, the purpose of establishing that theory is to prove the superior strength of a quality (*guṇa*) that is taught at the time of the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).
That [word] is a name (*nāmadheya*).

For when something qualified by *soma* has been produced [as the object of the injunction], a pure restatement (*anuvāda*) is impossible; therefore, since tools such as a spade are not [the objects] therein, it is established that *udbhid* and other such terms are names.

However, having enjoined a pure sacrifice (*yāga*) by means of the directly heard suffix (*pratyaya*), and desiring to avoid the meaninglessness of the secondary word (*upapada*), one might imagine another unmentioned suffix in order to enjoin its [the *soma*’s] purpose.

If one were to assume a mere repetition of what has already been heard, then since the *udbhid* and *soma* prescribed as qualifiers of the *śuddha-yāga* (pure sacrifice) would possess equal force, their optionality would be established, and thus their status as names would not be proven; therefore, in order to solidify their status as names, a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is here expounded with its specific purpose.

And thus, all qualified injunctions herein serve as examples; this was done by the Bhāṣya and Vārtika to state the connection [of the present discussion] as a rebuttal (*apavāda*) to the preceding consideration of whether [terms like *udbhid*] are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or names (*nāmadheya*).
Alternatively—since it remains that a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*) is impossible, the status of being a name was stated merely as a possibility in order to avoid redundancy.
However, it has been said that this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended solely to establish the doctrine of the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*);

to indicate that this [previous view] is incorrect, the matter has been placed within the inquiry concerning whether there is a subordinate injunction or a name for the ritual action, in accordance with the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*.

The underlying intention is as follows: first of all, the exposition of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is not relevant here in the investigation into whether [the *udbhid*] is a name (*nāmadheya*).

Even if the investigation into a qualified injunction were purposeful by virtue of establishing the superior strength of a quality (*guṇa*) taught in the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), it would still be impossible to refute its status as a quality-injunction (*guṇavidhi*), because—due to that superior strength—the sentences concerning the *udbhid* and other [terms] would result in a distinct ritual action qualified by a quality, just like the *vājina* sacrifice.
Because it does not establish [the word as a name];

for if it were argued that even by virtue of the strength of the quality prescribed at the origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa-guṇa*)—due to the predominance of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in the sentence concerning the *vājina*—the word *vājina* is not a name, then since words such as *udbhid* lack conventional usage, their status as names would be established simply through their having an equal mode of application (*tulyavadvṛttikatayā*). What, then, would be the use of the strength of the quality prescribed at the origin?
Furthermore, even in the absence of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), an option regarding the spade is not possible;
for in sentences such as those concerning the *udbhid* sacrifice, the restatement of a sacrifice (*yāgānuvāda*) is not established.

Even if the sentence "one should sacrifice with soma" (*somena yajeta*) were to enjoin a pure sacrifice by relying on its prior application, at that very moment, in order to avoid the redundancy of the co-occurring qualifier (*upapada*), [the spade cannot be treated as optional].

Since the soma is enjoined by that very same injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*)— either through a mentally supplied application or by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the sacrifice presented in its own sentence—

and since the sacrifice is thereby rendered free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣīkṛta*), it is possible to enjoin the spade and other implements mentioned in another sentence precisely through that sacrifice; thus, in that case, there follows the injunction of a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*), and not an option (*vikalpa*).
For when the quality enjoined by the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) possesses superior force, there is no other means of establishing syntactic independence (*nirākāṅkṣatā*) than this;
and that [establishment] is easily accomplished even in the absence of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*).

Therefore, having rejected the qualified injunction in that case due to the resulting necessity of figurative indication (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*), the authoritativeness of the *Nighaṇṭu* establishes its status as a name (*nāmatva*) precisely through its etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*) and so forth.

The demonstration of qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is therefore inconsistent. Furthermore, since the simultaneous injunction of both the qualifier and the qualified—which are remote [from the verbal suffix]—is based on the impossibility [of such a thing] occurring in the case of a proximate injunction, one would have to admit that its possibility exists for the sake of a proximate injunction, while its impossibility exists for the sake of a remote injunction. Consequently, because it is impossible for both possibility and impossibility to coexist simultaneously, there can never be a qualified injunction by means of a single-uttered suffix.

As for the claim that [the objection] "is possible," since it is possible even in the *āgneya* and other sentences— just as in the case of the sentence "one should sacrifice with Soma"— the statement of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) based on the contingency of splitting the sentence (vākyabheda) caused by the assumption of multiple subordinate qualities (guṇa) would merely result in portraying the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) as being of "empty heart" regarding those *āgneya* sentences.
Therefore, because it is consistent, the investigation into whether [the term] is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) or a name (nāmadheya) alone is appropriate.

(Establishing that *Āgneya* is a name according to the principle of "being perceived as such"): How, then, can the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding its status as a name be established while the collection of refutations stated in the *Nyāyasudhā* remains? To this, he says: "Of Agni... (*agner iti*).

The meaning is as follows: although in the sentence concerning the *āgneya* offering, the verbal root *bhū* (to be) expresses mere existence (*sattā*) and thus does not express either the injunction (*vidhi*), which is the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), or a suitable verbal root-meaning that could delimit that urge;

nevertheless, because the matter is not otherwise established, an injunction must be postulated. Furthermore, since the root *bhū* is logically untenable without a productive urge (*bhāvanā*), it implies such an urge, or rather, it denotes that very urge itself. And since the substance mentioned by the nominative-terminated word *aṣṭākapāla* cannot syntactically connect with that [injunction] in the same way as the flour (*saktu*) does, [the nominative case-ending] functions [as an agentive].

Because of the definition of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*), in that *bhāvanā* which has the eight-pot-sherd cake as its instrument, fire (*agni*) would also function as a qualifier; this would result in the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) due to multiple injunctions serving as the cause [for the name].
Therefore, by the principle of "that which is already known" (*tatprakhyanyāya*), the word *āgneya* is a name (*nāmadheya*).
Furthermore, in this case, the principle of *tatprakhyanyāya* applies because there exists a mantra-text that establishes Agni as the deity.

(Justification for the attainment of a deity through the wording of the mantra, by means of the application of mantras such as *agnirmūrdhā* etc., due to the proximity of performance, even though there is no difference between the readings of the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa, or even if there were a difference: Since it is understood— either through the context known as *adhikāra* or through position— that the *puronuvākyā* "Agnirmūrdhā" and the *yājyā* "Bhuvo yajñasya" are auxiliary to the *bhāvanā* of the eight-potsherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*), it is logical that they serve to determine the deity, even in the absence of a direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*), just like the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Therefore— since the status of *Āgneya* as a name is established by logic even though it is in grammatical apposition with a substance (*dravya*), its being a name is not untenable through the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of instrumentality, just like the words *agnihotra* and *āghāra*, which are in grammatical disjunction with the action and end in the accusative case. Nor is there any lack of distinction regarding the context (*adhikāra*) in the case of the *Upāṃśuyāja* and other such offerings, nor regarding the sequence (*krama*) of the mantras in relation to the Brāhmaṇa text.

The objection that the mantras cannot be subsidiary elements according to the order of recitation— on the grounds that such an order is impossible due to its contrariety— is refuted because, in the Vājasaneyi Śākhā, the Brāhmaṇa text prescribes the Āgneya sacrifice first and the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice afterwards,

thereby establishing the validity of the mantras' order of recitation; furthermore, since the author of the Tantravārtika was learned in all the Śākhās, it is impossible even to infer that the order of the mantras is not prescribed in other Śākhās.

Regarding the statement, "But by means of the mantra, there would be [the result] in case of conflict," it has been established that even where there is a recitation in reverse order, the desired result is still achieved;
however, this does not mean that there is a recitation in reverse order in every single instance.

Furthermore, although the *āgneya* [offering] is recited immediately after the *agnīṣomīya*, its status as an injunction is established because its purpose is not already obtained through the statement: "The *āgneya* is indeed the head of the sacrifice, the *upāṃśuyāja* is the heart, and the *agnīṣomīya* is the two feet. Consequently, by being drawn away from its own position—just like the performance of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice—it is understood that the pair of *yājyā-anuvākyā* verses functions as its subsidiary (*aṅga*) based on the order of position defined by performance (*anuṣṭhāna-lakṣaṇa-sthāna-krama*), just as the ritual properties of the animal sacrifice are understood to be subsidiaries of the *agnīṣomīya*.
And because the status of being an auxiliary (aṅgatva) is easily established through the manner shown by the Kaustubha.
(Regarding the doubt that the secondary derivative suffix [taddhita] indicates the deity in the term *āgneya*, and its refutation:

Nor can it be argued that—since the secondary derivative suffix is stronger than any other authority indicating all possible deities—it is improper to postulate a deity based on the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*) because the deity has already been enjoined by that very suffix; for even if the suffix is stronger in case of conflict, in the absence of conflict, it cannot be the postulator of the deity because it would entail the fault of enjoining multiple things.

Because the suffix *ḍhak* is prescribed by the rule "the suffix *ḍhak* should be stated after the words *agni* and *kali* in all cases," and because this suffix is remembered in numerous specific and general relationships— such as "this belongs to him," "this is his offspring," "this is its deity," "this is a collection of that," or "originating therein"— within the domain of *prāgdīvyatīya* derivatives, the word *āgneya* has an ambiguous meaning; consequently, it is impossible for it to function as a restrictive injunction of a deity.
Since, in the case of a name, the determination that it is a deity-designating suffix (taddhita) is established by the force of other means of knowledge alone,
it is therefore logical that the deity is obtained from the wording of the mantra itself.
(An explanation of how a specific verbal root-meaning, though not initially determined, can serve as a delimiter for the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) when it is subsequently determined:

When the productive operation requires a verbal root-meaning to delimit it, even if no suitable verbal root-meaning capable of delimiting it is heard [in the text], it is accepted that the sacrifice itself—conceived through its connection with a deity and understood only later—can serve as that delimiter.

Furthermore, in the case of the *abhyuditeṣṭi* injunction, under the view that it prescribes a distinct productive operation, it is maintained that the verbal root-meaning, which is understood only later in the sentences concerning the connection with the accessory (*guṇa*), serves as the delimiter of the productive operation.

Therefore, in cases such as "Jyotiḥ, Gauḥ, Āyuḥ," it is accepted that once it is determined that the names "Jyotis" and so forth belong specifically to the unascertained root-meaning— which is itself projected by the bhāvanā established through the otherwise inexplicable nature of an injunction postulating a result not [otherwise] obtained— thereafter the specific form of the sacrifice is determined through its connection with the substance and deity extended [from other rites] by way of similarity, such as being "unmanifest" (avyakta).

And therefore, just as in the established doctrine (siddhānta), since it is logical for the verbal root √bhū to indirectly indicate (lakṣaṇā) the injunction of the productive operation (bhāvanā) of the sacrifice understood only subsequently, it is correct that the word *āgneya* functions as a name (nāmadheya).

(Refutation of the position that the purpose of the section consists in the fourfold repetition of the sacrifice as intended by the *Prakāśakāra*, and the indication of another purpose for the prima facie view.
Just as the name [of the sacrifice] in this context is not without purpose, so too it will be demonstrated under the guise of stating the purpose of the section (*adhikaraṇa*).

As for what was stated by the *Prakāśakāra*s—that even though the fourfold division of the action of the Āgneya [offering] is impossible in the case of the injunction "one divides the Āgneya fourfold," the purpose is nevertheless its fourfold repetition—[that is now to be refuted].

This [position] was refuted in the *Kaustubha* on the grounds that, by reconciling it with the statement from another recension—"He divides the *puroḍāśa* into four parts"—it is understood that the word *āgneya* refers to the *puroḍāśa* characterized by Agni as its deity; thus, since the injunction for the division in the form of a fourfold division is perceived to apply to the *puroḍāśa* alone, [the alternative view] is untenable.

Therefore, intending to conclude that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the status of the name is very firm—having avoided all the objections raised by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*—he concludes: "The word *āgneya*..."
The term "āgneyapada" (the word for the Āgneya) is also an elliptical designation for the words for the Agniṣomīya and other [offerings].

This is not a name, because there is no scriptural injunction for its application, and because—as in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja* or the *āghāra* offerings—it is impossible for it to be connected with a mantra, and thus impossible for a deity to be obtained through the wording of a mantra; therefore, the impossibility of the term *āgneya* being a name is established.
Furthermore, it is not a name because there is no other scriptural passage (*tatprakhya-śāstra*) that would confirm it as such.

For if the cultivation (bhāvanā) having the eight-pot-sherd cake as its instrument were enjoined here, then, because a deity would be obtained through the wording of the mantra according to the method you described, it would indeed be a name;
but this is not the case.

Since the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is implied by the act of making the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*), the *bhāvanā* of the eight-potherd cake must be enjoined precisely as the operation that produces the arising of that cake, because the eight-potherd cake is syntactically connected [to the injunction] solely as its object (*karman*). It is not, however, the *bhāvanā* of a sacrifice (*yāga*) or similar acts, which would have the established eight-potherd cake as its instrument (*karaṇa*) and be delimited by a specific verbal root-meaning already determined. Therefore, it is impossible for the pair of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses—which reveal Agni and other deities—to be connected in any way with that [*bhāvanā*]. Consequently, by means of the indicative power (*liṅga*) assisted by the name (*samākhyā*) "Yājyā-Anuvākyā," [the verses] belong elsewhere.

Intending that, because there is no authority for the *bhāvanā* of the eight-pot-sherd cake being a subordinate element due to the application (*viniyoga*) and the sublation of the position characterized by performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), the attainment of a deity through the words of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*) is impossible, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "having the sacrificial cake as its object."

However, because the *upāṃśuyāja* is explicitly heard as having a direct sacrifice (*yajati*), it is logical to assume a deity based on the wording of the mantra, since the connection of the mantra with that [sacrifice] is established through its suitability and position; intending to show this distinction, the author employs a negative example (vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta) by saying "not as in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja*. Now, one might object: even for the acts of pouring (*āghāra*) which consist of dripping, the mantra "Indra, upward! cannot be connected due to the absence of both expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and suitability (*yogyatā*).

Anticipating the objection as to how the ritual of sacrifice can be postulated through the attainment of a deity by means of that [lineage], he states the distinction while dispelling the doubt: "And not... (na ca).

The meaning is that there is a disparity [between this case and others]: although there is no connection with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) there, the application of both the deity and the sacrifice is postulated by the very scriptural statement (*śruti*) through the instrumental case in "he pours the *āghāra*," because such application would otherwise be impossible; and since a contradiction arises from the postulation of the act of pouring (*homatva*) for the instrument, the status of being a name (*nāmadheya*) is established.
This is the point of difference.
(Conclusion of the Siddhānta by removing all the defects urged by the Pūrvapakṣin):

Even though the order of the recitation of the mantras is established by the method previously stated, [the author], intending that the status of being a mantra is untenable precisely because of its lack of fitness, concludes the Siddhānta by removing the multiplicity of causes for injunctions urged by the Pūrvapakṣin, stating: "Therefore... (ataḥ).
"Substance and deity."

Because the secondary derivative *āgneya* denotes a substance qualified by divinity, and because the term *aṣṭākapāla*—in accordance with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "They saw the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) as a tortoise crawling away"—denotes a sacrificial cake substance prepared on eight potsherds, its meaning is not already established [by other means]. Furthermore, due to its co-occurrence with the explanatory passage, it is determined that the suffix *laṭ* (present indicative) has the sense of the injunctive (*liṅ*). Thus, when both the injunction and the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) are perceived, within that productive energy—which consists of human activity—[the relationship between the means and the end is established].

Since it is impossible for the *aṣṭākapāla* (the cake on eight potsherds) to function as the agent, when it is construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*) through the first case-ending (*prathamā*) which indicates instrumentality, and when the divinity of Agni is also construed as a factor of action (*kāraka*), there arises the cognition that the general form of the desired end (*iṣṭasāmānya*) has as its instrument some unspecified meaning of a verbal root implied by all the qualified factors. Subsequently, because the divinity mentioned in proximity to the oblation (*havis*) cannot be realized without a sacrifice, [it is understood] as being required by the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

Even though the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is determined to be "sacrifice" (*yāga*), there is no contingency of repeating the suffix heard in the text for the purpose of establishing its verbal status; this is because, through the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the root *bhū* as "sacrifice," a single efficient force of action (*bhāvanā*) qualified by all the qualifiers presented in the sentence is enjoined.

Furthermore, the complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the postulation of injunctions for the qualifiers does not constitute a fault, as it is incurred because those qualifiers are not otherwise established.

Nor is the sequence of the recitation of the mantra redundant on the grounds that, if the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) were to enjoin the deity, the mantra would be obtained through the indicative power (*liṅga*) alone;
for it serves a purpose in securing the acquisition of a specific mantra, such as "Agni is the head" (*agnirmūrdhā*).

For this very reason, where the location of the baking vessels (*kapāla*) and the specific purificatory rite called "baking" (*śrapaṇa*) are already established by other means of knowledge—as in the injunction "he bakes [the cake] on the baking vessels"—[the mantra is still required].
In that case, even in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is no heaviness [of the sentence] caused by that, because one does not assume an injunction for its specific details.

Nor is it the case that, since the number eight is not obtained through any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the syntactical unity (*samāsa*) would be broken, making it impossible for the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) to be qualified by the sacrifice; nor is there a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) in the event of enjoining both the number eight and the sacrifice by way of restating the potsherds (*kapāla*).

This is because, although the potsherds are already established, their injunction as a qualified entity—which effects the assumption of an injunction for a previously unestablished qualification—is logically possible, as this does not entail a breach of the "single impulse" (*ekaprasaratā*).
Therefore, since that [element] is already established in that context, there is no assumption of a separate injunction for the qualifier.

Consequently, because the injunction of the qualified sacrificial production (*yāga-bhāvanā*) is thus rendered possible, the displacement (*apakarṣa*) of the mantras is also established by that very sequence; hence, it does not follow that the phrase "The head indeed" is an injunction for displacement. The underlying sense is that the word *āgneya* is merely an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).
"By means of the extension of the name."

The meaning is that even though the similarity of substance is powerful, because it takes the form of a similarity based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the injunction, it is superseded by the transfer of application (*atideśa*) through name (*nāman*), which is more powerful than that.
Thus ends the seventh section concerning the quality of being related to Agni.
(B1) (Topic 8:

Because the words *barhis* and *ājya* are employed [by those established in the scriptures] for consecrated *kuśa* grass and the like, despite there being no actual consecration [inherent in the objects themselves], these words do not denote that [consecration].

Jaimini 1.4.10: Since words such as *barhis*, *ājya*, and *puroḍāśa* are used by those following the scriptures for consecrated *kuśa* grass and so forth, they would—like the word *yūpa* and others—denote only the consecration itself.

Even though it might initially appear that [the words *kuśa*, etc. denote things distinguished by their ritual consecration (*saṃskāra*), this is not the case; because they are never used by anyone apart from the genus (*jāti*), and because they are used even without the consecration in common worldly usage—as in "The cows have gone taking the *barhis* grass," "Ghee is for sale," or "My mother gave me a riddle with a *puroḍāśa* cake"—and because this [denotation of the genus] is non-deviant and simpler, they denote only the genus such as *kuśa*-ness (*kuśatva*).

The purpose, however, is that according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there should be a performance of consecratory rites for the sacrificial grass (barhis) intended for strewing in the pit of the sacrificial post (yūpāvaṭa) and so forth; whereas according to the final conclusion (siddhānta), there is not. // 8 // 24 //

Thus ends the eighth section concerning *barhis* (sacrificial grass). (B2) [This section begins by defining the two types of connection with the preceding section, followed by the determination of the three subjects of this section.

Having established in the preceding sections that names of rituals possess both primary and secondary meanings (*sāpavāda*), this section proceeds incidentally (*prasaṅgāt*) to investigate the denotations of names pertaining to substances.

The discussion on the injunction of specific qualities (*guṇaviśe�ṣavidhivicāra*) constitutes the incidental contextual connection (*prāsaṅgikī prakaraṇasaṅgati*). Furthermore, having stated that words such as *āgneya* denote a substance qualified by a deity—based on the etymological connection (*kriyāgarbhasambandha*) with the sacrifice consisting of the relinquishment of a substance intended for a deity—and thus have the sacrifice as their cause, there arises the immediate connection (*anantarasangati*) residing in the intellect, which consists of the inquiry: "Do words such as *barhis* have the performance of a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) as their cause, or not?"

And because [the literal meaning] is clear and has not been explicitly stated, and because the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—namely, the superiority of the refined form (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth—and the reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—namely, the occurrence of prolixity (*gaurava*) if the word were based on refinement (*saṃskāra*)—are equal, and with the intention that the words *barhis* and *ājya* in the Sūtra are intended as mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), he states the prima facie view after first demonstrating the three objects of application: "barhirājya... and so on.
(The demonstration that words such as *barhis* and others, well-known among ritualists, refer to consecrated objects):

By the phrase "by those established in the scriptures" (*śāstrasthaiḥ*), the usage of those established in the scriptures with respect to unconsecrated objects is set aside according to the principle of the *pīlu* and *adhikaraṇa* sections.

Furthermore, in some cases, even the usage by those established in the scriptures with respect to unconsecrated objects is set aside by the usage among ritualists (*yājñika-prasiddhi*) according to the principle of the *aśvabāla* section; thus, the term "established in the scriptures" refers to what is well-known among ritualists.
This has been indicated.

And thus, because the usage of the unrefined language is limited in scope and resides among the uncultivated, it is weak; consequently, similarity [to the refined language] is possible, and therefore the usage of the ritualists lacks the capacity to establish that [the word] is not subject to censure. (The meaning is that, as in the case of words such as *yūpa*, there is no basis for asserting that they denote only the refined [Sanskrit] form.)

[The objection regarding] the justification for words such as *barhis*: But surely, in prescriptive injunctions concerning consecrations (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) such as "he cuts the *barhis* grass," "he purifies the clarified butter (*ājya*)," and "he spreads the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*"), since the consecration is enjoined with reference to the *barhis* and so forth, there would be a redundancy of the injunction of consecration if the *kuśa* grass and other items— already previously understood as the objects of reference (*uddeśya*) to be consecrated by cutting and so on— were already known.

But since it is impossible for something that is not understood to be the object of an injunction, the prescription of that [word] is all the more untenable; therefore, it is only logical that it denotes a genus (jāti). To this he says: "like the words 'sacrificial post' (yūpa) and so forth."

Just as in the case of the scriptural statement "he hews the palāśa," where— by resorting to an inverted mode of expression— the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) is determined to be the name for the palāśa wood consecrated by the act of hewing (based on the understanding that "that which he hews is the yūpa"), so too here, because the word *darbha* (which denotes kuśa grass) is seen in the mantra intended for the spreading of the *barhis*, the word *barhis* is determined to be the name for the kuśa grass consecrated by acts such as cutting (based on resorting to the mode of expression: "that which one cuts is the *barhis*").

The meaning is as follows: because of the scriptural statements, “He mixes the flour” and “He makes a lump,” it is determined that the word *puroḍāśa* denotes a lump of flour prepared by such processes as spreading; and since the acts of purifying (*utpavana*) and so forth can somehow be considered to have flour as their object, it is determined that the word *ājya* (clarified butter) denotes ghee that has been purified and otherwise processed. Thus, just as in the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), one would have to resort to an inversion of the verbal expression, which would render the injunctions for these preparatory rites (*saṃskāra-vidhi*) purposeless.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the term *āhavanīya* is included.

In that case as well, according to the maxim "that which has not grasped its qualifier [cannot grasp the qualified]," the words *yūpa* (sacrificial post) and so forth have their denotative power (*śakti*) only in the consecrations (*saṃskāra*). Alternatively, since there are many consecrations, it would follow that one must assume multiple denotative powers; therefore, the view is that the power resides in the wood itself as qualified by those consecrations. The word "or" (*vā*) is used to indicate this difference of opinion, just as it is here as well.
(The established conclusion is that, since they are not employed [synonymously] after abandoning the genus, words such as *barhis* denote the genus itself:

There is no denotative power (*śakti*) of words like *barhis* with respect to a substance possessing a genus qualified by a refinement (*saṃskāra*), because that would entail the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*).

For this very reason, it does not apply even to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, because there is no usage [of the term] for that which is conditioned but lacks that specific genus (*tajjāti*),

even though such is the case, if there were no usage for that which is devoid of conditioning, then one would have to accept its denotation of that [conditioned state], even by accepting the [grammatical] complexity (*gaurava*).
And there is indeed an application [of the word] even in that case;

for this very reason, since such an application does not exist in the case of sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and the like, its denotation of a *saṃskāra* (consecration) is certainly accepted. Furthermore, because there is no contradiction with those established in the scriptures due to its being employed while setting aside the universal (*jāti*), it is not [established] by the authority of those established in the scriptures either.

Intending that it is not proper to resort to a reversal of the verbal formulation because of the contradiction [with perception], he states the final position (siddhānta): "Leaving aside the genus... and so forth.
By the phrase "by whomsoever," the contradiction is shown;
as for the purpose, it is as follows.
(An examination of the prima facie and final positions regarding the external locus, along with their purpose:

The meaning is that, because words denoting consecratory acts (*saṃskāra*) bring about those acts through the extension of the name (*nāmātideśa*), just as the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) does in the case of the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*), one must perform the consecrations.
This applies likewise to the clarified butter intended for the anointing of the sacrificial post.

Likewise, regarding the two oblations pertaining to the deities of day and night— prescribed by the passage beginning, "By means of the two Rohiṇas, the gods went to the heavenly world"— which are to be performed before and after the *pravargya* oblation that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the Siddhāntin maintains that although the act of placing [the offering] upon the Gārhapatya fire by the Agnīdhra priest is performed, the other purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) are not to be performed, because the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) named Rohiṇa are prescribed as the material substance (*dravya*) for those two oblations.
It should also be understood that its performance occurs during the *pūrvapakṣa* (the first half of the month).

Furthermore, here—as with the purpose of the subsequent section—one should observe another purpose for *ūha* (modification) and *anūha* (non-modification) in the mantra "strew with darbhas," similar to the case of the word *puṇḍarīka* in the *mudga-caru*.

Having accepted this established fact that [the word] denotes a genus (*jāti*), one might raise the objection that since the properties of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) apply to both the subsidiary and the primary rites, those properties would consequently apply to the grass used for covering the sacrificial post-pit (*yūpāvaṭa*). Anticipating this, [the author proceeds as follows]:
It will be refuted later; thus, there is no tautology.
Thus ends the eighth section concerning the sacrificial grass (barhis).
(B1) (Section 9 / ) [The term *prokṣaṇī* refers to] water because of its connection with a purpose. Jaimini 1.4.11:

Even though the word *prokṣaṇī* denotes a consecrated substance (*saṃskāra*), as in the previous case, it is used in common worldly usage to denote the consecration itself, as in the expression, "We are distressed by the *prokṣaṇīs*."

Since the word is seen to be used even when devoid of its birth (i.e., its etymological origin), and since it might be argued that it denotes the universal *jalatva* (water-ness) by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there is no evidence for postulating such a convention when its meaning can be established through the application of its already established etymological parts (*avayavayoga*).
For this very reason, in the case of words such as *aśvakarṇa*, the assumption of a conventional meaning is made only when the etymological meaning is sublated.
Nor is there an absence of the connection consisting in being an excellent means for sprinkling (*ukṣaṇa*) in the state of neutrality;
for even though the actual production of the result is impossible [in that state], the capacity for the essential nature of the act of sprinkling is possible.

Nor does this lead to the untenability of postulating a denotative power (*śakti*) for a specific caste in the word *rathakāra*, since a connection consisting in being a chariot-maker is possible there as well.

This is because such a construction would be based on the force of an injunction; furthermore, since the capacity for the nature of agency is not excluded [from others], it would result in the redundancy of the rule "for the chariot-maker in the rainy season.
However, regarding the word *prokṣaṇī*, since there is no evidence for assuming a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), it must be etymological (*yaugika*) in nature.

The purpose [of this discussion] regarding the modification (*vikṛti*) in cases such as "ghee is for sprinkling" (*ghṛtaṃ prokṣaṇam*) is as follows: it should be understood that the unmodified application, "bring the sprinkling-water" (*prokṣaṇīr āsādaya*), applies when the word denotes a preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*); "bring the ghee" (*ghṛtam āsādaya*) applies when it denotes a genus (*jāti*); and "bring the sprinkling" (*prokṣaṇam āsādaya*) applies when it is used etymologically (*yaugika*). // 9 // 25 //
Thus ends the ninth section concerning the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī).

(B2) (The commencement of the prima facie argument, preceded by an examination of the connection, regarding the two positions that [the word] denotes both the *saṃskāra* and the genus, and the establishment of those two positions:
"As before."
By this, both the thematic connection (*prakaraṇasaṅgati*) and the immediate sequential connection (*ānantarasaṅgati*) are indicated as exceptions.

Regarding the passage "Bring the *prokṣaṇī* waters," he states the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the word refers to the genus because it is used for water characterized by purificatory rites such as sprinkling (*utpavana*) and consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), and the second prima facie view because it is used even without those rites. [The Siddhāntin begins with: "By purificatory rites... (In response to the need to postulate a conventional meaning, the established etymological sense is more powerful; thus, the Siddhānta begins by asserting that the word *prokṣaṇī* refers to being the instrument for excellent sprinkling.)

Since the primary meaning of the word [prokṣaṇī] is not established— given that water in its state of neutrality lacks the quality of being an excellent instrument for sprinkling— and since the term *prokṣaṇī* is not applied to oil and the like even though the primary meaning exists there, and since fitness (like the ritual consecration) is shown by both positive and negative concomitance to be non-deviant [from the application of the term], it is impossible for it to be the ground for the word's application; therefore, as in the case of words such as *aśvakarṇa*, it is necessary to postulate a distinct power (*śakti*) in the water.
Since it will be explained in the *Rathakārādhikaraṇa* that the well-established conventional meaning of a whole sublates the meaning derived from its constituent parts,
the sense here is that, just like that case, the word denotes the genus *aptva* (the state of being a water-carrier) by virtue of the well-established conventional meaning of the whole.

(Since the conventional meaning of the whole [word] is not established, and because the word *prokṣaṇa* is seen to be used even for ghee and other substances, it is established that only the etymological meaning—consisting in the fitness to be a means of excellent sprinkling—is to be accepted; this is the beginning of the final conclusion.
True, the conventional meaning of the whole is more powerful, provided that such a convention were established.

Even in the state of neutrality (*audāsīnya*), since the understanding of the qualified meaning is possible through the power of the individual components alone—by virtue of the mere fitness (*yogyatā*) to be an instrument for excellent sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)—there is no evidence for postulating an additional power for the aggregate (*samudāya-śakti*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the total elimination of all derivative (*yaugika*) words; thus, the word *prokṣaṇa* does not denote the universal (*jāti*) of "being fit.

Even though oil and other substances possess the quality of being instruments for excellent sprinkling and could therefore be denoted by the word *prokṣaṇa*, the feminine suffix and the plural number simply cannot be construed [with them].

Intending to show that the non-employment of the word *prokṣaṇī* is logically consistent—and because the mere use of the nominal stem devoid of that suffix is observed in such cases as "the ghee becomes the sprinkling" (*ghṛtaṃ prokṣaṇaṃ bhavati*)—he states the final conclusion: "Because [the meaning] is already established... (*kḷpteti*).

Regarding the case where the cognition of the etymological meaning is entirely impossible, and the case where there is an established conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), he explains that the aforementioned governing principle (*adhikaraṇa*) does not apply;

for where the cognition of the meaning of the parts is by no means possible, it is indeed accepted that the well-established conventional meaning of the whole subverts the established meaning of the parts. Thus he says: "For this very reason."

Now, one might raise the following objection: "Since it is possible for the quality of being engaged in the construction of chariots to exist even in a particular caste by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatā*), and moreover, since their engagement in the construction of chariots is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, ‘The *Ṛbhus* lead the rim [of the wheel],' the word *rathakāra* would also necessarily be etymological (*yaugika*). Given this lack of distinction in being etymological, it follows—on the grounds of parsimony—that the term *rathakāra* should refer only to a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). Having thus restated this doubt:
He refutes this, saying: "And it is not thus."
"Instruction."

The meaning is that, by the force of the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*) in the form of the mantra-text "ṛbhūṇāṃ tve," the word *rathakāra* is understood to refer to a specific caste (*jāti-viśeṣa*), and thus its general applicability based on mere capability (*yogyatā*) is sublated.

If one were to accept the etymological application (*yoga*) based merely on general capability, then since a member of any of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) could always potentially be a chariot-maker, the status of being a "chariot-maker" would fail to function as a limiting occasion (*nimitta*). This would further result in the redundancy of the term *rathakāra* occurring within the injunction for the rainy-season rites (*varṣā-vidhi*).
This is what is meant by the phrase "kartṛtva... [in the original commentary].

Therefore, in the injunction regarding the ritual of the rains (varṣā-vidhi), the connection must be stated precisely as the agency of constructing the chariot as qualified by the fruit [of the rite]; and since such a connection is impossible in the case of a specific caste—namely, those called Saudhanvanas—who are in a state of indifference, there arises the necessity of postulating a distinct conventional meaning (rūḍhi).
This is the sense in which there is a disparity [between the two cases].
(An examination of the purpose of the alternative views regarding the preceding and following sections on the *prokṣaṇī* vessel): "In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)."
The meaning is: "in the case of the *caru* oblation dedicated to Soma-Rudra, which is unmodified (*avikṛta*).
Regarding "unmodified": [it refers to that which has not undergone modification].
The meaning is that [the word remains] unmodified because, prior to the consecration (*saṃskāra*), the nominal stem alone of *prokṣaṇa* is never employed even in the context of any consecration;

because it is accepted that the word *prokṣaṇī* itself denotes the consecrated substance; and because, even when the feminine suffix *-ī* and the plural ending are employed, there is no exclusion of ghee (*ghṛta*) and so forth, and thus an adaptation (*ūha*) such as "bring the sprinkling" (*prokṣaṇam āsādaya*) is impossible.

As for the usage "clarified butter is the sprinkling" (*ghṛtaṃ prokṣaṇam*), it does not intend to refer to purificatory rites such as straining (*utpavana*); for if that were the case, in order to achieve grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "clarified butter," one would have to resort to a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word "sprinkling" to mean the action of sprinkling that serves as the instrument for the effects of straining and so forth.

Therefore, in that context, having accepted the word *prokṣaṇa* as etymological (*yaugika*)—meaning it denotes merely the act of sprinkling by virtue of being formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an abstract action—the injunction of ghee as its instrument is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Consequently, because this is based on a direct scriptural statement (*aupadeśikatva*), it sets aside the water; thus, the point is that the nominal stem *prokṣaṇa* does not, in any case, have the purpose of denoting a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*).
[This is expressed in the phrase: "one should set down the ghee."

The meaning is that, because clarified butter (*ghṛta*) has taken on the status of the original pre-archetypal effect—just like the sun and other [substances]—the word *prokṣaṇī* (sprinkling water), which is no longer expressive [of that function], is set aside; thus, the modification (*ūha*) consisting in the insertion of the word *ghṛta* is appropriate.
[The resulting formula is: "Place the *prokṣaṇīs*."

If the term is used in its etymological sense (*yaugika*), then because the plural ending and the suffix *-ka*—which are employed in grammatical coordination with the word *āpaḥ* (water) following the nominal stem *prokṣaṇa*—are withdrawn due to the disappearance of their meaning (*arthalopa*), there is no elision of the nominal stem *prokṣaṇa* as it is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*). Therefore, that very stem must be understood as ending in the neuter singular, by virtue of the subordinate gender.
Furthermore, there is no restriction regarding the specific wording found in the injunction (*vidhi*) when it comes to the substance (*dravya*) in a recitation (*nigada*).

The meaning is that by this [principle], the use of the word *ghṛta* itself, as it occurs within the injunction, would be possible; for in the tenth [book], a restriction regarding that very term will be stated specifically with respect to the deity.
Thus ends the ninth section concerning the *prokṣaṇī* water.
(B1). (Section 10:
Likewise regarding the *nirmanthya* fire. Jaimini 1.4.12:

Regarding the statement, "They bake the bricks with the *nirmanthya* fire," if the word *nirmanthya*—as in the previous case—denotes a consecrated object (*saṃskāra*), then [the injunction] is "Bring the *nirmanthya* fire."

When [the opponent's view] is rejected by the common usage "we shall cook," it follows that the term [‘agni’] must denote a sub-class of fire produced by the *araṇi* (fire-drills), because the status of being the object of churning is absent in the fire that serves as the means for cooking, whereas the state of being brought about by churning exists even in the case of cooking or butter (*navanīta*), which would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). However, since this is already accounted for simply by its connection with the state of being brought about by churning, there is no evidence for postulating the aforementioned conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*); thus, the charge of over-extension remains.

Furthermore, since in cases such as cooking, the lack of expressive power (*abodhakatva*) can be established simply by the absence of prior usage, and since it is possible to argue that "butter" (*navanīta*) is indeed the denotation [of the term *nirmanthya*], the word *nirmanthya* is purely etymological (*yaugika*).

Consequently, in the injunction "one should [use] bricks with the *nirmanthya* fire," since the fire is already obtained through its very capacity for cooking, the injunction merely prescribes the act of churning; thus, its performance during the ritual procedure is the practical application of this established conclusion (*siddhāntaprayojana*).
Thus ends the tenth section concerning the fire produced by friction.
(B2) [The connection of the present section with the preceding one on *nirmanthya*, and the presentation of the two prima facie views along with their supporting arguments:

Just as before, since the contextual connection indicated by the word "likewise" (*tathā*) in the Sūtra, as well as the extension (*atideśa*) indicated by that same term and the immediate sequence of the discussion, are clear, they are not explicitly stated; rather, a passage from the context of the fire-altar construction (*agnicayana*) is cited.
Just as in the previous section, he presents the first two positions as the prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*), stating: "By means of the fire produced by friction... (*nirmanthya*).

The meaning of the first position is as follows: since, in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the production of fire by friction is prescribed as a subsidiary act, and since the consecrations such as manifestation are prescribed for the fire produced by that friction—by means of the injunction “Recite for the one born” (*jātāyānubrūhi*) and the mantra “Dhanañjaya in battle” (*dhanañjayaṃ raṇe*)—the word *nirmanthya* is used by those who stand upon the authority of the scriptures to denote the fire thus consecrated; therefore, it signifies a consecration (*saṃskāra*). This is the first view.

By this, the following are refuted: the statement by Prakāśakāra that "the *nirmanthya* [fire] alone is enjoined because it has the character of a consecration (*saṃskāra*)," as well as the statement by Somanātha that "since consecrations are also prescribed for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and because there is no determining factor—as in the case of the consecrations belonging to the archetype of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*)—the consecrations pertaining to the animal sacrifice must also be expressed.
This is because nowhere do ritualists ever employ the word *nirmanthya* with reference to a fire qualified by consecrations performed at the time of the fire-installation.
For this very reason, the use of the term *nirmanthya* (to be produced by friction) like that used for an animal is shown in the context of the *Cāturmāsya*, the *Atithyā*, and other rites.
To refute the first position and establish the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says: "by the one being produced by friction" (*nirmanthyamānayā*).
(Regarding the doubt that the matter is already settled by the previous section and its resolution:

An objection is raised: "Since the application of the word [‘cow’] can be accounted for simply through its connection with the status of being the object of the act of churning, in accordance with the logic of the preceding section—and since there is no evidence for postulating an additional power—how can the position that it denotes a genus (jāti) even be proposed? Furthermore, because the matter would already be established by that very [previous] section, the commencement of a new section is redundant. To dispel these two doubts, he says: "Because of the status of being the object of churning... etc.

Because the word *nirmanthya*— being formed with the suffix *ṇyat*, which according to the rule *ṛhalorṇyat* denotes the object of the action— possesses a primary etymological connection (*yoga*) consisting in being pervaded by the act of churning (which is synonymous with being the object of churning), this connection is non-existent in the fire that has not been produced by churning but serves as a means for the sacrifice; therefore, like a consecration (*saṃskāra*), it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāritva*).
Furthermore, because there is a difference in size and luminosity due to the accumulation and depletion of substances in contact with fire and other elements at every moment,

and because the recognition "this is that same fire" can be accounted for as being produced by a homogeneous continuum rather than proving identity, it is impossible for the fire serving as the means of cooking to be pervaded by friction even in its prior state; thus, once destroyed, the fire— just like something merely capable of destruction— is no longer pervaded by friction when it has been struck.

The commencement of a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*) is due to the suspicion of a distinction: that while the capacity for sprinkling exists even in neutral things, there is a lack of such capacity in the case of *yoga* (conjunction), which would render it fallacious;
thus, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the word] denotes a genus (*jāti*) is established. This is the meaning.

(The statement "due to over-extension" [atiprasaṅgāt] is a restatement of Bhavadeva’s view that the definition of *yoga* as "being employed for churning" would over-extend to butter; it is also the refutation of that view.)
And this demonstration of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is to be understood by relying on the statement of Bhavadeva.

For he has shown there a specific objection: that even in the case of *navanīta* (fresh butter), because the application of the etymological derivation (*yoga*) as "the object of the act of churning" would lead to an over-extension—wherein the word lacks usage in certain instances—the constituent meaning would be absent;

thus, due to the impossibility [of such a restriction], there is a deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), and consequently, the possibility of being etymologically derived (*yaugikatva*) cannot exist. Having thus presented this specific doubt:
It is established by means of *yogarūḍhi* (etymological-conventional derivation).

However, in reality, in the sentence under discussion, the word *nirmanthya* is not derived from the root *math*, meaning "to churn" or "to agitate"— which is synonymous with the whirling of a staff and so forth—
because that [root] refers to liquid substances and is therefore impossible in relation to fire.

Furthermore, [the word *nirmantha*] is derived from the root *manth*, listed in the *trayādi-gaṇa* as *mantha* and *manthana*, which signifies the act of churning—a synonym for the whirling and turning of the churning-stick (*daṇḍa*) and other implements used as the means of churning.

For this very reason, the distinction in meaning between the two instructional forms *mantha* (in the sense of "stirring") and *manthana* (in the sense of "churning") is justified; thus, it is not correct to urge an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the word *nirmantha* to substances such as butter (*navanīta*), because—as stated in the *Nyāyasudhā* in its refutation of that [objection]—the etymological meaning (*yogārtha*) is impossible [in such cases], as there would be no application [of the term] to fire produced by lightning and the like.

As for the specific objection raised by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, who argued that since the manifestation of fire from lightning and so forth lacks the capacity to be produced by friction, it does not conform to the previous reasoning: that objection is addressed in the *Vārttika* on the *Bhāṣya*'s challenge regarding the causal efficiency [of the rule], which asks: "Since [the fire] arising from lightning, the striking of stones, sun-crystals, and so forth has already fulfilled its purpose upon ceasing, how could the fire produced by friction be considered new?"

Since it has been stated that lightning and the like are not denotable by the word *nirmanthya*, and since the objection regarding the etymological meaning (*avayavārtha*)— based on the non-application of the word *nirmanthya* to them—
is improper due to its contradiction with the *Vārttika*, this [objection] was refuted by the authors of the *Prakāśa* and thus ignored by the venerable [author].

(Refutation of the author of the *Prakāśa*’s view—that the term "araṇiprayojyāgnitva" refers to a subordinate genus within the universal of fire—on the grounds of its contradiction with the *Vārttika*):
He concludes the second prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) with the words: "araṇiprayojyeti."

Since the specific sub-genus "fire-ness" (agnitva) does not depart from the consecrated fire produced by the prescribed churning, nor from the ordinary cooking fire produced by un-prescribed churning—because that very genus persists in both—the term *nirmanthya* denotes that [sub-genus] itself; thus, there is no deviation [in the application of the term] anywhere.

As for what was stated by the authors of the *Prakāśa*: "Since the application of the term 'fire' to lightning and the like is established through the persistence of the universal *agnitva* (fire-ness), the usage 'to that which is being churned' (*nirmanthyamāne*) regarding them is not defective, as it is accepted as occurring through the primary sense (*mukhya-vṛtti*) itself, even without resorting to a secondary sense (*gauṇī*)."

The inclusion of the two subordinate terms "araṇi" and "vāntara" is intended to indicate that [the opponent's position] is incorrect; for it was previously shown that there is a contradiction with the Vārttika, and since the word *nirmanthya* is not used there, it would follow that even in that case one would have to establish the view that the word denotes a genus by taking the general genus of "fire-ness" common to all fires—which is improper. This is done in order to refute the specific doubts raised by the author of the Nyāyasudhā himself.

And thus, the intention is that the usage "we shall cook it by means of what is being churned" applies only to that which is produced specifically by the act of churning, and not to fire in its general sense.

(The commencement of the final conclusion, following an examination—by means of the phrase "in reality" (*vastutastu*) and so forth—of both the accepted view that *navanīta* (butter) is the denotation [of the word] due to its connection with being produced by churning, and the non-accepted view of that same matter.
This suffix *-tavya* is not used here in the sense of an object (*karman*), as that would result in the faults previously mentioned;

rather, accepting it in the sense of "fitness" (*arha*) according to the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*, when there arises an expectation for a specific relation regarding the fitness for churning, [the following applies].

Intending that since the state of being produced by churning itself is accepted as the basis for the application of the word *nirmanthya* (produced by churning) with respect to the series of fires produced by churning— and that consequently,

because the usage is established everywhere through connection with its parts alone, excluding fires such as lightning, it is not proper to postulate an additional power (*śakti*)— the author states the final conclusion: "by way of being produced by churning."
The same applies to the state of being expressible as well.
Nor is it logical to claim that *navanīta* (fresh butter) is not denotable [by a certain word] simply because of a lack of usage;

for there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for the restrictive rule that "whatever word denotes a certain object must be used by everyone for that object. Thus, even in the absence of prior usage, once the word is employed, since the hearer immediately understands the meaning through the connection with the meanings of its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*), there is no obstacle to postulating that it is indeed denotative of that meaning.

In reality, however, it has already been indicated that it is not appropriate for *navanīta* (fresh butter) to be denoted by the word *nirmanthya*, which signifies fire, because its usage in that sense can also be justified as being derived from the root *manth*, meaning "to churn. Indeed,
in no authoritative treatises (*ākaragrantha*) is the use of the word *nirmanthya* as a designation for fire ever stated to apply to fresh butter.
On the contrary, it should be understood that Bhavadeva himself employed the practice of *yogarūḍhi* precisely for the purpose of refuting that [opponent's] view.

(Regarding the sentence *nirmanthyena*, the determination that the injunction for churning is directed toward fire—which has already attained the capacity for cooking—in order to give meaning to the word *nirmanthya*; and from that, the establishment of the performance of churning even within the ritual procedure, etc.

Now, an objection: whether one assumes that the word *nirmanthya* denotes even things like fresh butter (*navanīta*) or whether it denotes fire alone, how is the necessity of performing churning directed toward fire established?
Nor can it be argued that the necessity of performing the churning is established simply because the term *nirmanthya* would otherwise be rendered meaningless.
To resolve the objection that [the term] is purposeful because it serves to exclude [entities] such as lightning, he says: "And thus... (evañca).

The meaning is as follows: since here the cooking of a substance produced by friction (nirmanthya) is enjoined with reference to the bricks (iṣṭakā), a specific substance in the form of fire is obtained through the very power of that enjoined cooking. Just as in the case of "red turbans" (lohitoṣṇīṣa), an injunction of a qualification is postulated regarding the aspect of mere friction which was not previously established;
