and since the exclusion of lightning and other such sources is thereby accomplished, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

Therefore, in this view, since the subsidiary (aṅga) and primary (pradhāna) acts—namely, churning and the sacrifice—attain the same place, time, and agent, and because they attain the state of occurring within the same performance, one performs the churning alone, devoid of such ritual details as placing the fire-drill pieces (*adhimanthana-śakala*) and so forth, and then performs the sacrifice with the fire produced thereby. Thus, he states that the purpose mentioned in the Bhāṣya—"not in the case of a recently churned [fire] when it is etymologically derived" (*yaugike 'ciramathite na*)—is obtained: "of that too," etc.

By the employment of the term *siddhānta* (conclusion), it is indicated that there is a difference in purpose through contrast: under the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the word denotes a consecrated object (*saṃskāra*), the churning together with all the consecrations prescribed in the context of the animal sacrifice would not fall within the scope of the ritual performance; however, under the view that it denotes a genus (*jāti*), the cooking could be performed by any fire whatsoever, even one external to the performance.
Therefore, it is established that the word *nirmanthya* is purely etymological (*yaugika*), just like the word *prokṣaṇī*.

(The exposition of his own view: [the possibility of achieving consistency with the Vārttika regarding the purpose intended by the author of the root-text only if the word *nirmanthya* is etymologically derived from fire produced directly by churning])—
In this context, since it is impossible to define a single, inclusive relationship that applies equally to the fire produced directly by churning and the fire produced by that [first] fire,
and because one must accept "being produced" (*janyatva*) itself as the relationship, the word *nirmanthya* is etymologically applicable only to that which is produced directly.

The assumption of denotability is appropriate; however, the usage [of the term] with respect to its continuum is by way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) through the relationship of being "that which is produced. Since, in the present case, it is improper to adopt a figurative sense when the primary meaning is possible, one must accept that very primary meaning; thus, because the cause of churning is established within the usage, [the term] applies everywhere to fire by virtue of its etymological derivation (yogikatva).
The status of being the expressed meaning (vācyatva) need not be resorted to.
Furthermore, if the injunction of cooking already obtained is accepted according to the method stated by Kaustubha, then,

because there is no redundancy in an injunction regarding a qualified object through the injunction of cooking qualified by the substance of fire produced by friction (nirmanthya), [the injunction remains purposeful].

Since the term *nirmanthya* (produced by churning) serves a purpose by excluding lightning and other such sources, why resort to the cumbersome assumption of a prescription for a qualification (*viśeṣaṇavidhi*) and thereby accept its injunction even with respect to the act of churning itself?
If, however, it is argued that it functions as the objective (*uddeśya*) based on the fact that cooking is obtained from another source, [then...]
Since that [fire] is already obtained at that time, the injunction (vidhi) culminates in its qualifying portion;

yet, because the fire—the substantive—is also obtained through the capacity for cooking, it culminates here in the action alone which serves as the qualifier of the substance, just like the "red turban" (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*). Thus, its performance is secured during the course of the ritual application, because the fire has been acquired by means of cooking, and the scriptural statement is intent upon the qualifier.
"And that [rite] shall be performed in that same place and so forth, because it is an auxiliary part of the cooking."

The Vārttika verse intended to establish that [the milk] has not been churned for long should also be interpreted in this very same way. In that regard, how is the attainment of cooking [of the curd] possible?
Or even if it were attained, why would there not be a specific mention [of the curd as the object]?

It appears to me that this [objection] must be refuted because, through the attainment of what is desired via intermediate sections and so forth arising from such a doubt, the state of being a brick is necessarily concomitant with baking, and thus the act of baking is obtained by implication.
Thus ends the tenth section concerning the fire produced by friction.
(B1) (Section 11: If it is argued that there is an option regarding the Vaiśvadeva [offering], [the reply is:

In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, having prescribed eight sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya at the first section, the Vaiśvadeva, the scripture states: "One should sacrifice to the Vaiśvadevas. Jaimini 1.4.13.

In this regard, when considering whether the two terms *vaiśvadeva* [in the sentences "vaiśvadevyāmikṣā" and "vaiśvadevena yajeta"] constitute an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or a name for the ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*), since it would follow that the entire sentence would be purposeless if they were names, there is no other recourse but to accept them as an injunction of deities for the seven [offerings] beginning with the *āgneya*; for the Viśvedevas are already established in the case of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice.
Alternatively, there is the injunction of another distinct rite characterized by a specific deity, because of the mention of a quality;
or else, within this very same rite, there is the injunction of the substance alone by means of the sentence concerning *āmikṣā*.

In this way, the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "there are eight oblations"—is also rendered consistent. Such being the position reached, [the reply is: it is not an injunction of a quality in the case of the *Āgneya* and other offerings.
Because it is sublated by the deity prescribed for the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa-devatā*),
nor is it an injunction for a different ritual action;

for since the means of knowledge that indicate difference can be explained as being merely names, it is untenable for them to indicate difference in a way that would entail the complexity of a new injunction.

Therefore, even in the sentence concerning the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), there is only the injunction of a substance; for otherwise, there would arise a discrepancy (*vairūpya*) in that the word *nirvapet*—which, in sentences such as "one should offer the eight-potherd cake to Agni" (*āgneyam aṣṭākapālam nirvapet*), functions as an injunction of a qualified [action]—is applied by ellipsis (*anuṣakta*) to the *āmikṣā* sentence and would thereby function merely as an injunction of a substance.
Consequently, the word *vaiśvadeva* is the name of all eight sacrifices, beginning with the one to Agni.
This is due to the principle of "being named after that" (*tatprakhya-nyāya*), which is assisted by the fact that the deity is already prescribed by the originative injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).
Furthermore, the basis for the application [of the name] consists in being the locus of a collection composed of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice whose deity is the Viśvedevas.
And the sentence is a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of the constituent parts for the sake of establishing the collection.

The purpose of this [discussion] regarding all eight sacrifices is that, by means of their connection with spring and so forth—as in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva in spring"—they acquire the designation *Cāturmāsya* (Four-Monthly Rites), which thereby establishes their connection with the fruit [of the ritual]. Otherwise, since only the Āmikṣā sacrifice has Viśvedevas as its deity, it would alone acquire the designation *Cāturmāsya* through its connection with spring and so forth, and consequently, its connection with the fruit; this would result in the other [seven] sacrifices becoming merely subsidiary (*aṅga*) rites.
This is clear in the Kaustubha. // 11 // 27 //
Thus ends the eleventh section concerning the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.

(B2) (Demonstrating that the *vaiśvadeva* section has an apavāda connection with both the preceding section and the *āgneya* section): Following the discussion regarding whether [the term *vaiśvadevam*] is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*), there is a topical connection (*prakaraṇasaṅgati*). Furthermore, since it was established in the *āgneya* section that [the term *vaiśvadeva*] is an injunction of an accessory because the principle of "being known from elsewhere" (*tatprakhyanyāya*) is inapplicable, and once the discussion concerning the injunction of specific accessories had been undertaken as a consequence, that which arose as a further consequence [is now addressed].

By the principle that "at the conclusion of that [topic], the same [point] is presented again," since the status of this as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*)— as stated in the *Āgneyādhikaraṇa*— is here also challenged by the application of the *tatprakhya*-principle, an immediate connection (*anantara-saṅgati*) is established on the basis of an exception (*āpavādika*).
Alternatively, in the preceding case, although the word *nirmanthya* primarily denoted a substance (*dravyapradhāna*), the object to be qualified was already obtained from another source.

Since it has been established that [the term] has the purpose of enjoining only a qualification, the opponent objects—relying on the utility of the previous section—that the word *vaiśvadeva* should likewise refer to the deities who constitute that qualification. Without explicitly stating the immediate connection (*anantara-saṅgati*) as an exception (*āpavādikī*), because it is clear, the author shows the subject of the inquiry: "In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices... and so forth.

[This section] establishes that, according to the final Siddhānta, the inclusion of the phrases "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva," "during the Cāturmāsya sacrifices," and "having prescribed eight sacrifices" as qualifiers of the specific subject-sentence serves the purpose of indicating that each [sacrifice] would otherwise result in a separate performance, and thus necessitates the understanding of the purpose of the collective restatement (*samudāyānuvāda*).
If the fruit of the eight sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya were heaven, according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice (*viśvajinnyāya*), then...

In that case, just as in the sentence "one who desires [such-and-such]," because the connection with time, place, and so forth enjoined by sentences such as "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva in spring" occurs individually with each [deity], there would follow— despite the determination in the Siddhānta that the eight [deities] constitute the name in the sentence "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva"— the consequence that each must be performed separately; therefore, the term *cāturmāsya* (the four-month sacrifice) is employed.

And thus, by the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Cāturmāsya [rites]," all the sacrifices—which must be performed simultaneously as means to a single result according to the principle of the *ekādaśādi*—are understood to share a single time because they are all named "Vaiśvadeva.

Consequently, through that [commonality], there is obtained both the unity of the intermediate performance (*avāntara-prayoga*) and the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) "I shall sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva. This is the meaning.
The rite known as the Cāturmāsya has three other sections called Varuṇapraghāsa, Sākamedha, and Sunāsīrīya; with reference to those, it is called "the first.

Furthermore, the purpose of introducing this [term] in the Siddhānta is precisely to make known that the conventional designation "four sections" (catvāri parvāṇi) functions as a collective restatement (samudāyānuvāda).
For if only the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice were the subject under discussion here, then since the deity Viśvedevas would already be established there, [there would be no need for such a designation].

The phrase "the Āgneya and others" is stated in order to prevent the impossibility of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), which holds that the purpose is a reference to a collective (*samudāyānuvāda*), because there would otherwise be an absence of many constituent parts for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding a prescription of qualities (*guṇavidhi*).
These [offerings] are: "He offers the eight-potherd cake to Agni; the pap to Soma; the twelve-potherd cake to Savitṛ; [the cake] to Sarasvatī..."

The meaning is that [the injunction] is established by the sentence: "A *caru* for Pūṣan, a *caru* for the Maruts, a cake on seven potsherds for the Viśvedevas, *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth."
(Justifying that the word *vaiśvadeva* has the purpose of enjoining a deity, because otherwise the entire sentence would result in meaninglessness): "The entire... and so forth.

If, in the final position (*siddhānta*), it is intended that the name [of the sacrifice] applies to the entire sacrifice including the *āmikṣā* by the principle of "having that as its characteristic" (*tatprakhyanyāya*),

then even in the absence of that [specific material], its inclusion in the sentence prescribing the spring and other seasons would be redundant, since its inclusion is already justified by its having Vaiśvadeva as its deity.
However, if [the name applies] to all seven [materials],...

However, in that case, since the deity is not mentioned there, the rule of "designation by scripture" (*tatprakhya-śāstra*) does not apply, and thus its status as a name is impossible. Furthermore, because the suffix denoting a deity (*taddhita*) is restricted to hymns (*sūkta*) and oblations (*havis*), it is untenable for it to refer to a sacrifice; moreover, this would necessitate a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a sacrifice characterized by an oblation having that deity, so its being a name is not logical.

For this very reason, even if the term *agnihotra* were the name for the two repeated performances in the evening and morning by accepting a partial basis for its application, it is not equal to the present case, as no such figurative indication or other defects arise.
Nor is it appropriate to resort to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) on the grounds that the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) has the general relation as its meaning;

for even in the case of a secondary suffix denoting a deity (*devatātaddhita*), since it is possible for it to reach its final signification by taking the general relation and then settling upon the specific relation consisting of the status of being a deity, the rule "that which is his deity" (*sāsya devatā*) would become redundant. This is because, if one accepts that very rule as teaching the primary (literal) meaning and accepts another as teaching a metaphorical meaning, the redundancy cannot be avoided.

Therefore, since there is no other thing to be enjoined and since a name itself cannot be enjoined, and because it would otherwise follow that the entire sentence is purposeless, the meaning is that this is indeed an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
[The opponent says: "It is an injunction of a deity (*devatāvidhi*)."

(There is no syntactical split [avākyabheda] because, although the word *vaiśvadeva* refers to both substance and deity, the operation of the injunction applies only to the qualifying portion consisting of the deity.

Nor does there arise a syntactical split from enjoining both the deity and the substance by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the sacrifice; for if it is argued that such a split would not occur because the connection of the primary meaning [the Viśvedevas] as the deity with the substance is already established through linguistic usage (*vyutpannatvāt*), [we reply: *(Note: This sentence fragment represents the opponent's objection to the previous point.)*

In that case, even if the absence of a "form" (*arūpatva*) is avoided by prescribing the substance and deity through the word *āgneya* in the *āgneya*-passage—which merely restates the action enjoined by the words of the learned—the resulting syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would still not be established in the final Siddhānta position.

Therefore, one must argue as follows: since in such instances the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is accepted as a factor (*kāraka*) and thus construed with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) itself—rather than being construed with the substance—the possibility of that [syntactical split] is established. Consequently, the same consequence would apply to the present case as well.
This is what must be stated.

The meaning is this: since the pronoun *asya* (of this) refers back to what has been previously mentioned, and because no specific substance is obtained within its own sentence, it is logical for it to refer to the substances previously mentioned, such as the "eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapāla*).
And since those substances are already established by their own originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*), it is possible for [the subsequent sentence] to enjoin the deities who serve as qualifiers.

(Regarding the two-fold resolution of the contradiction with the *utpattiśiṣṭa* principle when the term *vaiśvadeva* serves as a qualifier for the sacrifices enjoined by the sentences concerning the Āgneya and others:

To dispel the doubt that the introduction of a deity enjoined at the time of origin (*utpannaśiṣṭa*) is impossible because it is obstructed by other deities such as Agni who are enjoined at the time of origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*), the word "without any alternative" (*agatyā*) was used with the intention that the previously established principle is inapplicable.
Furthermore, this indicates that the strength of a quality enjoined at the time of origin—which will be discussed in the *guṇādhikaraṇa*—is also addressed here by way of implication.

Alternatively, because of the direct mention of the generic term (*sarvanāman*), the injunction regarding the deities for the substances such as the *aṣṭākapāla* is unavoidable; thus, it is not improper that this injunction prescribes a deity even though one has already been established by the original injunction (*utpannaśiṣṭa*).

For if one had heard, "The *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas, and the *vājina* to the Vājins," then one might somehow have accepted the superiority of what is established by the original injunction in that case.

For this very reason, in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the section on qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*), the suspicion regarding the superiority of a quality enjoined in the originative injunction was set aside by accepting the meaning: "The *vājina* [offering] is for those *Viśvedevas* who have food consisting of *vāja* (barley-gruel) and *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture); therefore, it is the *vājina* for them.
However, in the present case, since the etymological nature of the word *vaiśvadeva* is beyond doubt, the reference to the eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth is logically established.

In that case as well, since we observe that a pronoun refers to a pure substance in instances such as "There is a jar on the carrying-pole; bring it," and because it is improper for the connection with another deity to occur through the repetition of the principal [action]—thereby abandoning the prior connection with the deity—the formation of a conjunction (samuccaya) is untenable; therefore, its inclusion is properly established only by way of option (vikalpa).

And it is not the case that— just as in the case of the *savanīya* oblations, where although Harivat and others are deities for the offerings prescribed by such injunctions as "one should offer parched grains (*dhānā*) to Indra Harivat," there is no option because one relies on the connection of these offerings with the deity Indra who is enjoined by another scriptural statement, namely "they sacrifice to Indra alone"— so too here, since this is logically consistent, why resort to that [alternative]?

Thus it should not be said [that there is no distinction]; for while the connection with a deity is possible in that case (the *dhānā* offering) during the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*), here, if one were to accept it in the same way, the words "eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth would result in a lack of syntactic connection. Since there is no other recourse, one must necessarily accept the injunction as enjoining a sacrifice through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which constitutes a difference from the former case.

In that case, however, because the pouring out of roasted grains (*dhānā*) and so forth is possible, their connection with the act of pouring out is logical, and thus their connection with the pouring out is appropriate.
However, there is a distinction regarding the *aṣṭākapāla* and other offerings because they are unfit for that connection [with the singular number].

Although, if referring to the substances under discussion, the use of the plural would result due to their multiplicity; nevertheless, the meaning is that the use of the singular is justified by the intention to express the unity of the attribute of being the *havis* (sacrificial oblation) as it occurs in the context.
(An exposition on the statement "in seven [sacrifices]" regarding the impossibility of restating the *vājina* sacrifice and the *āmikṣā* sacrifice as the objects of reference.

Because the *vājina* sacrifice is a disposal (*pratipatti*) and thus a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice, there is no possibility of a context (*prakaraṇa*); therefore, with the intention that a restatement by means of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is impossible, it was stated: "in seven.

Even though a context for the *āmikṣā* sacrifice is possible, it was stated "in seven" so that, according to the maxim "an injunction is purposeful when its object is not already established," there would be no contingency of heterogeneity (*vairūpya*) in the application of the root *yaj*.
He clarifies that very point with the words: "not repeatedly."

(Resolution of the contradiction with the principle of the "injunction of the origin" by accepting a qualified injunction, like the *vājinavākya*, and the justification for observing the indicative mark of the accomplishment of thirty oblations therein):
Even though the strength of that which is enjoined at the origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*) is more powerful;

Nevertheless, just as in the case of the Vājina sacrifice, he strengthens the position of it being an injunction for a distinct qualified action (guṇavidhi) by means of an alternative view, stating: "qualified by the deity."

The meaning is that when a specific substance has been understood but not yet determined by means of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), and there arises a requirement for such determination, the specific substances such as the *puroḍāśa* cake are established through extension (*atideśa*) based on the similarity of having multiple deities.

Furthermore, there is no occurrence of the flaw mentioned by the author of the *Prakāśa*— namely, that if it were a separate ritual (*karmāntara*), the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) showing the accomplishment of thirty oblations would be untenable because it would result in thirty-one oblations.

Since the *puroḍāśa* and the *āmikṣā* have a single deity, they are understood to constitute a single sacrifice together, just like the *sānnāyya*; thus, it is logically consistent to say, "There are thirteen [offerings] at the new moon."

In order to avoid contradicting the indicative mark (*liṅga*) seen in the text, "There are eight oblations" (*aṣṭau havīṃṣi*), and so forth, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is presented by another method; furthermore, this method avoids the other difficulties raised by the author of the *Prakāśa* against the prima facie argument regarding the qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

By demonstrating, through another perspective, that the specific substances are obtained, he resolves the inconsistency of the indicative mark "There are eight oblations" by means of the following passage: "In this very [context]," etc. (*etasminneva vā iti*).
By the word "api" (also/and), my own resolution of the inconsistency regarding the inferential mark (*liṅga*) presented by the author of the *Prakāśa* is indicated.

By this [it is shown that]—even if the term *vaiśvadeva* refers to the substance (*dravya*), since there are many substances under discussion and because the singular number, as an attribute of the thing to be enjoined (*upādeya-viśeṣaṇa*), is intended to be significant—the specific substance cannot be determined; therefore, [the sacrifice would have to be performed] alternatively.

Furthermore, because the fault lies precisely in the figurative application (*paryāyavṛtti*) [of the term] when grasping everything else, and because it would lead to the contingency of an alternative view (*vikalpa*), the position of the *Prakāśakāra*— that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) for a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) is not tenable by resorting to a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*)— is refuted; for there is no rule that pronouns (*sarvanāman*) must refer only to what has been previously mentioned, since, as in the word *tat* in the sūtra *tadguṇās tu* (JS 1.4.9), they can refer to whatever is present in the mind.

In this context, since the determination of the specific [object] is established by the previously stated method, it is not accepted that the term refers to all [offerings] such as the eight-pot-sherd (aṣṭākapāla) and others; otherwise, the aforementioned defect would follow.

Or, even if such a restriction were granted, there is still no evidence for abandoning the quality of referring to the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) in favor of referring to what is immediately contiguous (*avyavahita*); furthermore, since the determination of the specific [object] and so forth is possible through the reference to the single pot-sherd alone, [the view of the opponent is untenable].
The word "vā" (or) is employed at the beginning [of the verse] to indicate another undesirable consequence that has not been previously stated.

(The demonstration that the prima facie view of combination— which holds that both being a quality-injunction and being a name, as accepted by the author of the Vārttika, may coexist— is merely a bold assertion. As for what is stated in the Vārttika—
that since the word *nirmanthya*, though etymological, is seen to function as a quality-injunction even while being a name,
and since the word *vaiśvadeva* is likewise etymological, it too may function as a quality-injunction even while being a name— this is intended as a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was presented by way of a combination [of various arguments], while the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) was shown through the alternative position that it is merely a name; however, since it has already been stated that being a name is untenable due to the absence of *matvarthalakṣaṇā*, syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), *tatprakhyatva*, and *tadvyapadeśa*, a combination with an unestablished status as a name is impossible, especially since a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is in every case untenable.

Furthermore, because the status of being a name (*nāmatva*) is untenable—since the word *vaiśvadeva*, when uttered once, would result in the contradiction of having two mutually exclusive forms, and since there can be no namehood in the absence of a counter-correlative that is a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*)—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding their combination (*samuccaya*) is impossible; thus, [the Nyāyasudhā] has declared this to be a mere bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), and for this reason it was disregarded by the Venerable Teacher.

(The conclusion that the word *vaiśvadeva*—ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) expressing a general relationship—is indeed the name of a sacrifice is established because it results in a parsimony of injunctions. He states the final conclusion: "In the case of the Āgneya and other sacrifices... As for what was said—that because a pronoun refers back to a substance under discussion, the deity is enjoined therein according to the method of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section on Qualities (*guṇādhikaraṇa*)—[that is not so].

That is not so; for although a pronoun may not be capable of referring to a substance (dravya) not mentioned in its own sentence, it is possible for it to refer to a sacrifice (yajña) mentioned in its own sentence.
Indeed, there is no restrictive rule that a devatā-taddhita suffix occurs only in the co-occurrence with a hymn (sūkta) or an oblation (havir);
for we observe the devatā-taddhita even in the absence of such co-occurrence, as in the passage: "The Āgneya is indeed the head of the sacrifice, while the Upāṃśuyāja is the heart," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: because the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix has been frequently employed, its capacity to denote even a general relationship is understood; since the specific relationship consisting of the status of a deity can be established through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no occasion for resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, since this [denotation] is possible here as well, the statement serves a purpose by way of being a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the whole, and therefore lacks no utility.
The term "vidhigaurava" (redundancy of the injunction) is also an elliptical expression for the occurrence of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication of the possessive sense).

(Refutation of the view that the word *vaiśvadeva* refers to a subordinate accessory, based on the necessity of the term *nirvapet*— which intends an injunction of a qualified entity in the *āgneya* passage— to likewise apply when it is supplied by ellipsis to the *āmikṣā* passage; and based on the necessity of enjoining the connection between the material and the deity in the *āmikṣā* passage for the purpose of postulating a sacrifice therein.)
And because it would result in a loss of uniformity (*vairūpya*).

For just as in the case of the statement, "One dedicates seventeen three-year-old heifers to the Maruts and as many bulls," even though there is no extended application (*atideśa*) of the group of eleven cuttings (*avadāna*) produced from a single animal— which would otherwise cause a division of the ritual action (*karmabheda*)— in the case of the bulls whose fire-circumambulation has been performed, [the same applies] to that which resides in the sentence concerning the Marutīs.

Since it would result in a syntactical inconsistency (*vairūpya*) here for the verb that prescribes seventeen actions—which is connected from the preceding context—to prescribe those same actions again, distinct actions are indeed enjoined;

likewise, here too, because it would result in a syntactical inconsistency for the word *nirvapati* (he offers) which is connected from the preceding context, it is proper that it should enjoin an action.
Furthermore, if the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) were not supplied in the sentence concerning the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*), with reference to what would the *āmikṣā* be enjoined?
It cannot first be by way of restating the Viśvedevas;

for if that were the case, the substance would become a subordinate element of the deity rather than a subordinate element of the sacrifice, since the word *āmikṣā* is taken up as the very object [of the injunction] through the *āmikṣā*-term acting as a restrictor of the intention (*tātparya*) of the *taddhita* suffix in the word *vaiśvadevī*; furthermore, if the substance were enjoined by the word *vaiśvadevī* alone, it would result in a violation of the principle of "single thrust" (*ekaprasaratā*).

Therefore, since it is necessary to postulate a *yajati* (sacrificial act) for the purpose of enjoining a substance by way of restating (*anuvāda*) a sacrifice, it is likewise necessary to enjoin therein the relationship between the substance and the deity, which serves as the basis for that postulation. Consequently, because the *āmikṣā* lacks the expectancy for connection with another action qualified by those [deity and substance], it does not apply to the action enjoined by this sentence; this is the meaning.

As for the objection raised in the *Nyāyaprakāśa*: "If 'vaiśvadevena yajeta' were an injunction of a sacrifice, then, like the *āmikṣā*, the *vājina* would also result in being an accessory (*aṅga*) of this same sacrifice, leading to the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*) [between the two]."

The objection raised is not valid; for in the sentence concerning the whey (*vājina*), since there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of a sacrifice having the Viśvedevas as its deity, this sacrifice would require a specific substance.

Consequently, because the requirement is satisfied by enjoining the *āmikṣā*—which is enjoined by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to this very sacrifice and is presented immediately by the word "vaiśvadeva"—it is impossible for the whey to be introduced into it.
Therefore, the previously stated objection alone is correct.

Consequently, since a secondary injunction (*guṇavidhi*) is impossible regarding the sacrifices under discussion, he concludes that the word *vaiśvadeva* is the name of all sacrifices referred to by the root *yaj* through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*): "Therefore" (the logic of *tatprakhya*—assisted by the logic of the *utpattiśiṣṭa* [injunction of the origin]—is the authority for the name *vaiśvadeva*).
And here, it is not merely by the principle of "being known from that" (*tatprakhya-nyāya*) that [the word *vaiśvadeva*] functions as a name;

for while it serves to establish the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) by way of precluding a quality-injunction (*guṇavidhi*) in the case of the *āmikṣā* sacrifice, it is impossible to effect such a preclusion in the case of the *āgneya* and other sacrifices, since the grounds for application cannot be established there. Therefore, there is also the superior force of a quality specified in the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*).
Intending to express their state of cooperation, he says: "In [the case of] origination," and so forth.

(An exposition establishing that the basis for the application [of the term] is the state of being the locus of a collection constituted by sacrifices performed by the Viśvedevas, preceded by the refutation of other possible bases for its application:

As for what was stated by the ancients— that the basis for the application is the status of being a sacrifice performed by the Viśvedevas, as understood from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "that which the Viśvedevas sacrifice together"—
that is incorrect, because it is impossible for something unreal to serve as a basis for application.

Furthermore, although some have demonstrated that the word *viśva* denotes all [deities] by intending it to signify "all," and thus [the sacrifice] has all deities such as Agni and others as its recipients— that too is improper because it abandons conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). With this in mind, when investigating that matter, even if the *āmikṣā* sacrifice alone is established as the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) according to the principle of "being well-known from that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*), nevertheless, since there is no distinction in their being the subject under discussion (*prakṛtatva*) by the term "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), and for the sake of the meaningfulness of what is to be stated hereafter, [the name applies] to all sacrifices indeed.

Because there is a restatement for the purpose of forming a collective, and because the status of having the Viśvedevas as the deity exists in that collective by way of the relation of being composed of its own constituent parts,
he says "and the ground for application" with the intention of explaining how the ground for application is successfully established in the eight individual members through that medium.

And thus, although the members of the collection are expressed by the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), once their general relationship is understood through the direct hearing of the word (*pada-śruti*), there arises an expectation for a specific relationship.

Then, by virtue of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*), a specific relationship is understood—namely, that the collection has as its basis a sacrifice of curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) whose deity is the Viśvedevas.

Since this is grasped by the single term *vaiśvadeva*, even though there is no mention in a single word within the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*) as there is with the *prājāpatya* offerings, a single collection is nonetheless established for those [offerings] produced by various separate sentences.

The sense is that, by the "umbrella-logic" (*chatrinyāya*), there would also be the hardship of resorting to a definition established by the ancients for the term *vaiśvadeva*, which would apply to the entire collection of both *vaiśvadeva* and non-*vaiśvadeva* offerings.

(The purpose of the Vaiśvadeva term being a collective reference [samudāyānuvāda] is established as its connection with all fruits by excluding [the application of] the Āmikṣā sacrifice alone; this is the determination. And as for that purpose: "Otherwise" [means]:

in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that there is an injunction of deities for the seven [sacrifices], there is indeed the possibility that those [other sacrifices] would also be included by the term *vaiśvadeva*; therefore, the particle *eva* ("only") is employed to rule out such a doubt, [indicating] that it applies to the Āmikṣā sacrifice alone.

The meaning is that, since even Agni and the others would only optionally be deities according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there would arise a contradiction regarding the connection between the permanent and the non-permanent in the injunctions concerning spring and so forth; therefore, they are not included.

In reality, however, under the prima facie view that this is a separate ritual (*karmāntara*), because the words have identical gender endings, it is impossible to restrict the word *vaiśvadeva* in the sentence concerning spring and so forth to being the name of this [specific sacrifice] alone; thus, the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "only the *āmikṣā* sacrifice" should be understood as serving as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), and the particle *eva* is intended to exclude the seven sacrifices beginning with the *āgneya*. This is how it should be understood.

(An exposition establishing that the purpose of the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices is the attainment of a connection with the fruit— preceded by a refutation of the ancient view that the connection of the *Āgneya* and others with the spring season and so forth is established simply by the term "vaiśvadeva" referring to the *āmikṣā* sacrifice.)

And here, in the treatises of the ancients, it is stated that the purpose of the collective reference (*samudāyānuvāda*) is to establish the connection of the [offerings] beginning with the Āgneya with the spring season and the eastern-sloping region;
however, this is not the sole purpose,
since that [connection] could be established in other ways as well.
For instance, in the absence of this [principle], even though in the sentence concerning the spring season (*vasanta*) and so forth, the *āmikṣā* sacrifice alone would directly connect with the time,

it would follow that in the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Cāturmāsyas," only the *āmikṣā* sacrifice— being associated with other seasonal festivals such as the Varuṇapraghāsa— would be connected to the result; consequently, the Āgneya and other sacrifices would, by virtue of the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the Vaiśvadeva, become subordinate members (*aṅga*) of that [single sacrifice].

For the term *cāturmāsya*—in accordance with another scriptural statement, "One should sacrifice with one festival every fourth month"—denotes the four festivals by virtue of its etymological basis (*pravṛttinimitta*), which consists in their occurring before and after a period of four months.

This is because, when the scripturally expressed state of being "four months later" applies to the three subsequent festivals, there arises an expectancy for a prior limit; and it is understood by implication that the first festival occurs four months prior [to the others].
Thus, the name is applied based on the relationship of being both before and after a four-month interval.

Furthermore, when the specific sequence of priority and posteriority is required, since time is prescribed by the sentences concerning spring (*vasanta*) and so forth, it is understood that only those [sacrifices] connected with spring and the other seasons—which constitute the sequence of priority and posteriority—are linked to the result by means of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) as delimited by the name "Cāturmāsya. Once it is understood that the Āmikṣā sacrifice alone is connected to the result, the other sacrifices—just like the Vājina sacrifice—would necessarily become its subsidiaries. Consequently, through the established rule that subsidiaries and the primary rite share the same place, time, and agent, the requirement for the spring season and the eastern-sloping ground is obtained.
The pursuit [of the inquiry] until the establishment of the connection with the fruit is intended to indicate that its purpose does not consist merely in that much.
Since the observation of the mark of thirty oblations is also consistent only with the status of *vaiśvadeva* as a name,
the conclusion that it is a name is clear in the Kaustubha.
This has been established.

Likewise, there is the constant scriptural mention of the oblations in the Āhavanīya fire during the Vaiśvadeva parvan: "nine fore-offerings," "nine after-offerings," "two āghāra-libations," "two ājyabhāga-portions," "eight sacrificial offerings," and "thirty oblations are offered."
The observation of thirty deities is thus established.

Otherwise, under the view that the term *vaiśvadeva* prescribes seven deities, there would be a contradiction because the seven [offerings] beginning with the *āgneya*—having a single common deity—would have to be performed together like the *sānnāyya*, resulting in only a single oblation. Therefore, it is proven that the word *vaiśvadeva* is a name (*nāmadheya*).

The purpose [of this discussion] has not been stated explicitly because it is easily understood through the presentation of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and final (uttarapakṣa) views, and because it was already stated directly by the sūtra itself: "In the Vaiśvadeva, there is an option" (sūtra 3.1.22).
Thus ends the eleventh section concerning the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.

(B1) (Section 12: Those [mantras] which possess a prior [basis] are not for the purpose of injunction; their capacity [for such] exists in the sacred collection (samāmnāya). Jaimini 1.4.17: Those which possess a prior [basis] are not for the purpose of injunction; their capacity [for such] exists in the sacred collection.

Having enjoined the sacrifice with the words, "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," [the text] subsequently restates the results of the cakes on eight, nine, ten, eleven, and twelve potsherds through such passages as, "In that there is a cake on eight potsherds, by means of the Gāyatrī he purifies him with spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa)," and so forth; and finally concludes: "He upon whose birth one performs this offering is indeed purified, radiant, an eater of food, and possessed of sensory power."
It is heard in the scripture: "He becomes possessed of cattle.

In that context, since the number twelve already includes [the numbers] eight and so forth, the first position is that words such as "eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapāla*) are names of the Vaiśvānara sacrifice.
However, even though they are established by their own form, because they have not been established as qualifiers, they are indeed injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*).
Either the number eight or the substance consisting of eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) is enjoined in the preceding sacrifice;
for, since the unity of the sentence is perceived through the identity of its opening and conclusion, the twelve potsherds do not possess the status of being an original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).
Alternatively, let there be a plurality of sentences.
Nevertheless, there are three possible views: first, that the injunction for that [offering] is established by the very statement "that which consists of twelve potsherds";
second, that in the Vaiśvānara sentence, the mention of that [twelve-potsherd offering] is merely a restatement (anuvāda);
and third, that the eight-potsherd and other offerings are enjoined as qualities based on the previously mentioned sacrifice, with a view toward results such as spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that since it is improper to split a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) when a unified meaning is possible, this entire passage is a praise of the sacrifice under discussion itself.

The point is: if even a portion of the twelve-potsherd cake (*dvādaśakapāla*) which serves as a subsidiary (*aṅga*)—such as the eight-potsherd portion—is a means to achieve each individual fruit, then what doubt can there be regarding the twelve-potsherd cake in its entirety, endowed with all its parts, being the producer of all fruits? Thus, it is a praise of the sacrifice.

The term *aṣṭākapāla* (eight-potherd) is capable of applying to the *āgneya-aṣṭākapāla* through a figurative function (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), being figurative with respect to a portion of the twelve-potherd cake by virtue of its similarity—namely, being baked on eight potsherds which are the substratum of the number eight. By means of that portion, the whole—the twelve-potherd cake—is indicated (*lakṣyate*). Thus, through this indication (*lakṣaṇayā*), there is a praise of the sacrifice.
And it should be understood that this section, although its meaning is already established by the logic of the Audumbara-section, has been stated here for the benefit of the students. // 12 // 28 //
Thus ends the twelfth section, the Vaiśvānara-Adhikaraṇa.
(The summary of the subject matter of the passage and the connection of the Vaiśvānara-Adhikaraṇa as a counter-example to the preceding section:

By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādinā*)—the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes [passages such as]: "In that it is offered on nine potsherds, by means of the threefold [stoma], he bestows brilliance upon him; in that it is offered on ten potsherds... [and so on].

This is a summary of the passage ending with: "By means of the Virāj he bestows food upon him; because it is on eleven potsherds, by means of the Triṣṭubh he bestows power upon him; because it is on twelve potsherds, by means of the Jagatī he bestows cattle upon him.
The word "at the end" (*ante*) is used to indicate that this forms a single syntactical unit.

"Since it has been stated in the introductory commentary to the second chapter— up until the section on *aktāḥ* (the 'anointed' offering)— that 'it has been determined whether [a term] is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*), and that the determination of doubtful meanings is made through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) and from the sense (*artha*'),

it follows that the discussion of names is directly perceived there; therefore, having raised here the doubt that terms such as *aṣṭākapāla* are names just as they were suspected there of being injunctions of qualities, this [section] serves as an exception (*apavāda*)."

Having thus established the topical connection (*prakaraṇasaṃgati*) by way of an objection based on the instrument (*karaṇa*), [the author proceeds as follows]: In the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the passage] enjoins a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) was refuted on the grounds that it would be purposeless (*ānarthakya*) since it could be rendered meaningful as a restatement of the whole (*samudāyānuvāda*). However, in the present case, such meaningfulness is impossible; furthermore, if the word *dvādaśakapāla* ("twelve-potherd") occurring at the beginning were intended to be significant, then the words *aṣṭākapāla* ("eight-potherd") and so forth would result in being purposeless. Therefore, by departing from the logic of the previous section, [the conclusion is reached that this is indeed] an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhitva*).
Without explicitly stating the immediate connection— which takes the form of a counter-example due to the rebuttal— and the doubt, because they are clear,
he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

Up to the words "when a son is born," [the text] refers to the oblation (*nirvāpa*) obtained through extension (*atideśa*), by way of restating that oblation according to the logic stated in the *Āgneya-adhikaraṇa*.

Since the word *vaiśvānara* ending in the accusative case and the phrase *dvādaśakapāla* (twelve-potherd) are intended as objects of sacrifice (*yāga-lakṣyatvāt*), and since the accusative case is accepted as indicating instrumentality (*karaṇatva-lakṣaṇā*)—

thereby accepting that they provide the instrumental factor— the meaning "one should sacrifice with Vaiśvānara and twelve potsherds on the occasion of the birth of a son" is beyond doubt; thus, because it lacks the status of being a subject for deliberation, the nature of the subject of deliberation must be extracted [from this].
To indicate this, the word "there" (tatra) was stated.

(Regarding the status of terms such as *aṣṭākapāla* as names [of sacrifices] according to the principle of "being known from that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*), and the purpose of accepting distinct names for what is in fact one [sacrifice]):

although in the term *aṣṭākapāla* only the number eight, the potsherds, the consecration having those as its substratum, and the substance are understood— and not the sacrifice— nevertheless, since all these [details] are already obtained through the term *dvādaśakapāla* itself, the words *aṣṭākapāla* and so forth are names by means of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) according to the principle of "being known from that," just like the words *samit* and others.

Just as when it is said, "One hundred Brahmins consume the Soma," and then a distributive statement is made, "Twelve [consume] each one," the rule of distribution applies because the twelve are included within the hundred; so too, the status of eight is obtained within the twelve.
Nor is there a lack of grammatical coreferentiality with the sacrifice, since those words ending in the nominative case are construed with the verb *nirvapet* (he should offer).

Even in the absence of that [separate sacrifice], since it is possible to enjoin the sacrifice under discussion by means of the words "eight-potherd" (*aṣṭākapāla*), the designation "the eight-potherd sacrifice comes into being" is logically consistent.
Nor does the use of a name necessarily entail a difference in the ritual action (*karmabheda*);

for there is no evidence to accept such a difference when a single, previously mentioned sacrifice can be justified even without it—just as in the case of terms like "cook" or "butcher," which do not imply a different person from the one previously mentioned.

Nor is there an absence of purpose in its being a name; for, by applying the *rātrisatra* principle here, the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—namely, "by means of the *gāyatrī* itself"—is postulated.
Thus, although the names are meaningful when used as options in the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), the respective fruits are nonetheless accomplished through resolves delimited by those specific names.
The meaning is that [the word "dharma"] acquires the status of being the purpose.

(Regarding the pursuit of an alternative view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*)— due to the absence of the attainment of the number eight by way of delimitation, which results in the non-application of the rule *tatprakhyaśāstra*—

and the demonstration of the purposefulness of the re-injunction of the *aṣṭākapāla*, even though it is already obtained through extension [*atideśa*]: From the word *aṣṭākapāla* etc., when the term *tatra* is carried over from the sūtra "In that case, [the name applies] to what is prepared in vessels from which [the offering] has been drawn out," [it is understood that] "that which is prepared..."
By the rule "bhakṣāḥ," a secondary derivative (taddhita) form is prescribed in the sense of "prepared in eight potsherds" (*aṣṭasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtam*).

According to the rule "dvigor lug-anapatye," since this is a compound preceded by a numeral, it receives the designation *dvigu*; consequently, when following the nominal stem *aṣṭākapāla* and so forth, the suffix is subject to elision.

Once it is understood that the word ends in a secondary derivative, the number eight contained therein is established. However, because this depends upon other numbers such as four and so on, there is a lack of semantic independence (*asāmarthya*).

Refuting the first position—that there is no possibility of [the term] being a name because the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is impossible, and since it is impossible for it to attain the number eight by way of delimiting twelve [days], the principle of "being known from that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*) does not apply—the author states the second position: "In its own form" (*svarūpeṇa*).
Therefore, in the case of the twelve potsherds, there is an injunction of qualities such as "eight" and so forth, because otherwise it would be impossible to praise what has not been enjoined.
Even though the number eight is obtained through the injunctive passage concerning the Āgneya sacrifice;
Nevertheless, the injunction is meaningful once again so that there may be no sublation by the non-scriptural [number] twelve, which is already established.

However, if it were argued that—due to the syntactic connection (*pada-śruti*) with the number twelve in the phrase "on twelve potsherds"—the number eight cannot be introduced because it is already occupied by the number twelve, and furthermore, that in the case of an injunction of the number eight with reference to the potsherds, there would arise a violation of the principle of single semantic thrust (*ekaprasaratā-bhaṅga*); [to this we reply:]...

In that case, just as with the three qualities, by conceiving of a distinct class (*vaijātya*) in the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), it was stated that "the substance is the eight-potherd [cake] and so forth," with the intention of prescribing a different substance such as the eight-potherd for the very same prior sacrifice.

(Regarding the determination of the distinction between sacrifices involving a single substance, based on the fact that the twelve-potherd [offering] is taught as an original injunction, according to the principle of the Prājāpatya sacrifice): "Being taught as an original injunction."

And thus, having accepted that "bhavati" (becomes) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), and having accepted its connection with "nirvapet" (one should offer) through the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the accusative case as having the meaning of the instrumental,

and by accepting the connection of "vaiśvānaram dvādaśakapālam aṣṭākapālam" and so forth, all [the materials] indeed possess the status of being prescribed at the origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*). And therein, because the substances such as the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) and others are connected to the deity only while remaining mutually unconnected, according to the principle of the Prājāpatya sacrifice—

The meaning is that because there is a distinction between sacrifices due to the difference in the relationship between substance and deity, there can be no occurrence of combination (samuccaya) within a single sacrifice— unlike the case of "redness" (*āruṇya*) and other qualities— since they are all presented by a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*).
As for the statement in the *Kaustubha* regarding the view that the substance is an injunction (*dravyavidhi*), which accepts combination as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*),

that should be interpreted somehow with the intention that the singular ending in the word *iṣṭi* used in the concluding summary (*upasaṃhāra*)— "this [sacrifice]" (*etām*)— indicates that it refers to a single sacrifice.
But it is not ultimately real;

for even on the view that the sacrifices such as the curd-offering and others are multiple, the use of the singular number here is justifiable—just as the singular "in the Citrā" is justified—by intending the five sacrifices as a single sacrifice. This is because, given the resulting distinction between sacrifices according to the previously stated method, there is no evidence for the unity of the sacrifice.

(Due to dissatisfaction with the previous [view], and by adopting the position that there are multiple sentences— since all [the terms] are taught as having already arisen [in usage]— one follows the second alternative, which consists in their being injunctions of accessories through option: Since it is untenable for many [words] in "bhavati" and so forth to be mere restatements (*anuvāda*), and since if the nominative case were taken as indicating the accusative meaning, there would result a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the word "bhavati," and because accepting repetition (*āvṛtti*) would itself be a fault, one becomes dissatisfied and, while accepting the multiplicity of sentences, [admits this] even within a single sacrifice.

By establishing that all [of them] are *śiṣṭa* (cultured/learned), he supports the position of an injunction regarding the substance (*dravyavidhi*) through an alternative view, stating: "Or rather... (*athavā*).

In the concluding sentences such as “it consists of eight potsherds” and “it consists of twelve potsherds,” since the word *bhavati* (is/exists) refers to an unestablished matter, it is accepted as an injunction (*vidhi*). This injunction concerns the substance alone. Furthermore, the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) required by that injunction—which has sacrifice as its object—is restated through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the verb *bhavati*, as it is already established by the Vaiśvānara sentence. However, because the Vaiśvānara sentence merely restates a substance already established by another means of knowledge, the term “twelve potsherds” is accepted as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all [the potsherds]; thus, it pertains exclusively to the sacrifice qualified by the deity Vaiśvānara alone.
The injunction is [established] due to parsimony (*lāghava*).
However, the passage beginning with "by means of the *gāyatrī* itself" is a praise of the substance—the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*)—which is the object of the injunction.

And by attaching the phrase "this sacrifice" (*etām iṣṭim*) to each [of the subsequent clauses], it follows that he who, upon the birth of a son, performs this sacrifice characterized by the eight-potherd cake, becomes purified.

The meaning is as follows: because of the connection made for each individual case—such as "one who performs this sacrifice characterized by nine potsherds (navakapāla) becomes possessed of splendor"—the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passage (arthavāda), such as purity and so forth, is attributed to the sacrifice itself, and not to the substance consisting of the eight potsherds (aṣṭākapāla) and the rest.

Since all the potsherds from twelve onwards are prescribed as established options (utpannaśiṣṭa), it is logical that they all find a place within the archetype sacrifice (prakṛtayāga); and since they function as independent means of accomplishment, there is an option (vikalpa) among these substances, just as there is between rice (vrīhi) and barley (yava).

(Third position: establishing the view by accepting that the twelve-potsherd [offering] is taught as the primary injunction and that the eight-potsherd and other sentences are injunctions of accessory qualities and results;

therein, the avoidance of contradiction with the Vārtika. Even while accepting the status of separate sentences—since otherwise the fault of necessitating an option would arise—the author states the third prima facie position: "By means of spiritual luster... (*brahmavarcasena*).

In passages such as "when there is an offering on eight potsherds," since [the result] has not been previously established, an injunction is first postulated. Then, for the offerings on eight potsherds and so forth thus enjoined, a result—namely, purification—is postulated based on the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "By means of the Gāyatrī alone he purifies him with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

When there arises a requirement for a substratum (*āśraya*) for that very [purification], it is logical that the Vaiśvānara sacrifice under discussion serves as that substratum; this is because, precisely due to its being optional (*kāmya*), it can serve as a substratum even though it is already prescribed by the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).

The meaning is that since the sublation of the permanent twelve-potsherd offering is logically established, and since the twelve-potsherd offering— being directly mentioned by its own word— is rendered self-sufficient by its own praise, namely, "by means of the Jagatī meter alone he wins cattle for him," it is not proper to accept that the words "eight-potsherd" and so forth function as praises of the twelve-potsherd offering through a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) preceded by a secondary sense (*gauṇī*).

As for what is stated in the Vārttika: "But surely—'If it is intended as having results such as the attainment of Brahman-splendor and so forth, by what [means] could there be an injunction for those [passages] that employ the present tense, given the absence of praise?'"

Having thus raised the objection that [the passage] serves the purpose of establishing *brahmavarcasa* as the fruit, [the author replies that] through the words "by means of the Gāyatrī alone" and so forth, only a glorification (*stuti*) is performed, not a connection with a fruit. However, by the manifestation of an injunction (*vidhi*) consisting of what was previously unestablished, there is a connection with fruits— such as "he is indeed purified"— for each of the offerings prescribed individually by the sentences beginning with "that which is on eight potsherds," together with their respective explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), according to their respective order.
It has been stated: "it is performed.
Since that [statement] is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it lacks the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*);

and since the status of being an explanatory passage depends on that [lack of injunction], the assumption of an injunction based on an explanatory passage is beset by the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Therefore, in that case...

By the phrase "born," since the connection with results such as purity (*pūtatva*) and so forth belongs to the sacrifice itself, the inclusion of those qualities [in the agent] is untenable; thus, the expression "brahmic luster and so forth" (*brahmavarcasādi*) is stated merely to indicate that [the previous argument] is a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*).

Consequently, because only an unestablished matter that pervades everything can determine the *leṭ* suffix and thereby constitute an injunction, the result—namely, purity and so forth caused by brahmic luster—is derived from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), just as in the case of the *Rātrisatra*.

This is correct. And thus, since the statement "when [he] is born" would otherwise be an unintelligible description of something as already established, one must assume an injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*). Consequently, the connection of the desired result with the sacrifice—which is intended to be the substratum—is also established. The sense is that the results, such as being purified (*pūtatva*), belong to the sacrifice itself.

In the original [text], by the phrase "the fruit in the form of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and so forth," it should be understood that the meaning is the fruit as presented in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) containing the term *brahmavarcasa*.

As for the statement in the *Kaustubha* that purity (*pūtatva*) and so forth constitute the fruit [of the rite], that should be understood in some way either by relying on the statement of the *Vārttika*, or else—so as to avoid contradicting the statement of the root text—with the intention that purity is caused by spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). This is the general direction.

(An exposition establishing that the sentences concerning the eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) and others have as their purport the praise of the twelve-pot-sherd cake itself—by avoiding the resulting syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) through [the following means]: by the distinction of verbal roots; by the distinction of the intended objects in the form of causes and results; by the intention toward another result in the form of the destruction of sin (*pratyavāya*); and by the connection with multiple results such as purification (*pūtatva*), all while maintaining the unity of the sentence as understood from the beginning and the conclusion.)

Indicating that the refutation of the second and third positions—which were firmly established by accepting a split in the sentence (vākyabheda)—is accomplished by the same reason, he states the final conclusion (siddhānta): "The conclusion, however... and so forth.
By the statement, "When a single syntactical unity is possible," the alternative view beginning with "or rather" (*athavāstu*) has been refuted.
The view that this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) for the sake of a result should likewise be refuted.

For if the injunction enjoining the substratum (*āśraya*), having enjoined the substratum in its entirety, were to become free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), then, by obtaining the substratum enjoined by that [injunction], there could be an injunction of a subordinate quality for the sake of a result.

For a single sentence, as understood through a consideration of its opening and conclusion, cannot have its expectancy for syntactic connection satisfied by the phrase "one should perform this sacrifice" (*etām iṣṭim nirvartayet*);
otherwise, the unity of the sentence itself would be destroyed.

Therefore, since the Vaiśvānara passage lacks completion and there is no injunction for a sacrifice, there is no basis (āśraya) provided; consequently, the sentences concerning the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth, which fall within that [passage], [cannot be independent injunctions].

Since it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to a difference in meaning if [the word] were an independent injunction, there is no injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) here.
By this, the claim that "there is no fault in a syntactical split when there is a difference in verbal roots" is also refuted;

for even when there is a difference in verbal roots—as in the case of "He whose both... and so forth, where unity of sentence is achieved solely by the force of the word *yat*—here too, in the phrase "In which... [the same principle applies].

Since the concluding statement "when [a son] is born" is connected with the relative pronouns *yat* and *tat*, and since this leads to the understanding that the opening statement refers to the *jāteṣṭi* (the sacrifice on birth), the two are perceived as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).

Furthermore, because the word expressing a desire (*kāma*) is absent, there is no perception of Brahman-splendor (*brahmavarcasa*) and so forth as the fruit; or even if such a perception were to occur, since the phrase "this sacrifice" (*etām iṣṭim*) and so forth indicates that the fruit belongs specifically to the sacrifice itself, there is no connection between a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and a fruit.

Moreover, even in our own system (*siddhānta*), syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is not necessarily required due to the mention of both the occasion (*nimitta*) and the fruit (*phala*) as intended objects (*uddeśya*); for although the occasion possesses the status of being an intended object in the sense of being that which necessitates performance, it lacks the status of being an intended object in the sense of being the most desired (*ripsitatama*), and thus only the fruit connects with that [status]. This is because even when two heterogeneous things are connected by one [word], there remains no cessation of the expectancy regarding the other object.
For in that case as well, since the connection [of the fruit] is logically possible, there is no risk of sentence-split (*vākya-bheda*).

Nor should it be argued that—even though there is no multiplicity of things to be enjoined (*uddeśya*) due to the connection with the cause (*nimitta*)—there remains the same problem of sentence-split because the destruction of sin (*pāpa-kṣaya*), which is postulated through the impossibility of its otherwise being connected, must connect with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) solely as something to be enjoined, just like "being purified" (*pūtatva*). This is because... [the text continues].

Even if one were to assume that the destruction of sin (*pāpakṣaya*) is what is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), since that assumption here depends upon the presentation of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), it is more reasonable to assume that qualities such as purity (*pūtatva*), which are presented more rapidly, are what is to be brought about.

For this very reason, the view that there is no need to assume a fruit mentioned in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—since the destruction of the transgression (*pratyavāya*) understood through the force of the occasion (*nimitta*) itself can logically serve as the fruit—is also refuted.
Furthermore, even if multiple fruits such as purity and so forth are assumed, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in their connection with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

One who desires the fruit mentioned in the *arthavāda* should perform the sacrifice; thus, by conceiving purity (*pūtatva*) and other such results as having a collective function (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), they are not conceived as individual objects of reference (*uddeśya*).

For this very reason, through the attainment of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the qualification for the performance (*adhikāra*) is established as a combined whole; consequently, unlike the injunctions for the *agnihotra* and other rites, there is no implication of a separate performance.

And so, since the status of being a "condition" (*nimitta*) is untenable, even if one were to conceive of mere sin (*pratyavāya*) arising from non-performance, the destruction of that sin is not conceived as the result [of the rite].
Even when the birth of a son exists, the occasion of that birth is not the motivator for the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice;
because the qualification [for the rite] is based on a combination [of factors],
therefore, when the birth of a son is the occasion, the *jāteṣṭi* must be performed for the sake of the son’s purity and other such qualities.

From the understanding of the meaning as "otherwise one incurs sin," it should also be known that there is no sin incurred by the father in the non-performance [of the rite]. As for those who—under the view that the opening statement (*upakrama*) is more authoritative—argue that since the *jāteṣṭi* (the sacrifice on the birth of a son) has its eligibility determined by the incidental occasion (*naimittika-adhikāra*) combined with the opening words "when a son is born," it cannot have an eligibility conjoined with results such as the son’s purity (*pūtatva*) based on the subsequent restatement (*vākyaśeṣa*); therefore, they maintain that the restatement is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
"An undesirable consequence follows," they say, regarding the section [of the scripture] conjoined with the force of the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*).
Their refutation should also be understood from this very point:
for no sublation of anything in the introduction (*upakrama*) has been made here in accordance with the conclusion.

Because the injunctive force (*vidhi*) reaches its conclusion as an impeller precisely by not abandoning the fact that the birth of a son is understood from the introductory context (*upakrama*), the result such as "being purified" (*pūtatva*) is postulated through the very requirement of the injunction, according to the principle of the *Rātrisatra*.

For this very reason, where the injunctive force reaches its conclusion as an impeller solely as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to something else and thus lacks such a requirement, there is no postulation of results for things like "hearing the verse of non-sin" (*apāpaśloka-śravaṇa*) on the basis of the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*).
However, he states that it is more appropriate for this to be an *arthavāda*, intended solely as praise: "of the very sacrifice under discussion."
(The removal of the doubt regarding the lack of expectancy [of the injunction] through the praise of the twelve-potsherd [offering] by the very sentence "jagatyaivāsmin..."):

As for what was said— that because the twelve-potsherd [offering] has its lack of expectancy satisfied by the praise alone, "jagatyaivāsmin...", there is no purpose for a further praise by way of the eight-potsherd [offering]—
the word "sarvāḥ" is stated in order to refute that.

For this very reason it is stated in the *Vārttika*: "Because praise is immeasurable, the injunctive statement accepts in its entirety whatever praise is perceived, maintaining a single uniform character throughout. Indeed, in all cases, praises are seen to consist of either few or many syllables."
Furthermore, because there is a multiplicity of types of listeners, in some cases certain [words] become meaningful.
Just as for some people, when an activity is accomplished by the mere statement of an injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*), praise (*stuti*) is resorted to for another purpose;
likewise, even when a task is established by a brief praise, recourse may be taken to an extensive praise.

And therefore, since the preceding praises are grasped simultaneously as being the means for establishing the commendation expressed in such passages as, "He who, upon [the son's] birth, performs this sacrifice, becomes indeed purified," there is no lack of expectancy through any single one alone; thus, because even a large praise is required,
the meaning is that the entire praise is not redundant.

(Refutation of the First Prima Facie View) As for the prima facie argument that, having accepted syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the number eight or the substance consisting of eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) is being enjoined—

that is improper, as has already been indicated; for it would entail the violation of the principle of single thrust (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*), since enjoining multiple distinct meanings in the middle of a sentence results in the breakdown of syntactic unity.

(First establishing that the term *aṣṭākapāla* refers to a part of the *dvādaśakapāla*, and then explaining how the sentences concerning the *aṣṭākapāla* and so forth function as praise for the *dvādaśakapāla*:

Now, one might ask: "Since the *aṣṭākapāla* and other such offerings have not been prescribed, how can there be praise of the prescribed *dvādaśakapāla* by means of the words *aṣṭākapāla* and so forth? To this, he states the manner of the praise: "When, my dear... (*yadaṅga*).

Even though there is no injunction regarding the eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth, nevertheless, the praise— which is perceived as producing Brahman-splendor and other results through the number eight residing in the potsherds (due to the similarity of the number eight with the eight syllables of the *gāyatrī* and other meters that are the causes of purity and so forth)— is stated figuratively and transferred to the constituent part of the "eight-potsherd" offering.

Therefore, since that [the twelvefold nature] is also not directly enjoined, the meaning is that the praise of the composite whole—the twelve potsherds—characterized by the relationship between part and whole, is in fact a praise of the sacrifice.

Now, one might object: since the term *aṣṭākapāla* refers to that which is consecrated on eight potsherds (*kapāla*) as delimited by the number eight, it does not include a part of a twelve-potsherd [cake] by that [term]. To this, he says: "And the term *aṣṭākapāla* [is used] figuratively."

The meaning is that since only the Vedic mode of cooking is denoted by the term "preparation" (saṃskāra), here, even though that [Vedic mode] is absent, the term is used in a figurative sense (gauṇī) due to its connection with the genus and quality of the cooking produced from the eight-potsherd offering (aṣṭākapāla).
[The phrase] "for the benefit of the students" [is added].
The phrase "under the guise of removing specific doubts" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
The purpose has not been stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the twelfth section, the Vaiśvānara Adhikaraṇa.

(B1) (Section 13: The Establishment of That) / Its establishment [is as follows]: Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.23 states: “In cases such as ‘The sacrificer is the prastara-grass-bundle,’ because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), one is the name of the other.”

Therefore, since that [meaning] is impossible due to its being a conventional term (*rūḍha*), or because it is subordinate, the sacrificer is enjoined as the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) with respect to the act of holding the *sruva*-ladle—the function of the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) indicated by the word "prastara. This being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), we reply: because no direct injunction (*pratyakṣa-vidhi*) is heard, and because it forms a single syntactical unit with another injunction—"He places the *prastara* above the *barhis*"—its status as an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) is established by the logic of the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*.
The word "sacrificer," however, praises the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) by means of a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*).
Now, it is well known in common usage that figurativeness consists in the application of a term to an object onto which a different quality has been superimposed,
as in the case of [the word] "lion."
