If it is argued that [the secondary application] occurs in the case of Devadatta due to an imposed attribution (*āhāryyāropa*), and that this is not possible in the Veda because of the absence of a person to perform the imposition—[we reply: even without such an imposition, we observe the use of the word "lion" for Devadatta in both poetry and common parlance with the intention of expressing mere similarity; thus, *gauṇatva* (secondary application) consists in being based on a connection with qualities of the same class as the qualities constituting its own primary denotation.

Furthermore, because the word "lion" (*siṃha*) is applied to Devadatta due to his possession of a cruelty that belongs to the same class as the cruelty of a lion's roar, the definition [of metaphorical application] is consistent in the case of "Devadatta is a lion.

As for the expression "the sky-flower is not your tenet," there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*); for, by accepting the referent of the word "sky-flower" as something superimposed through the attribution of its own relatedness to flowers and so forth, and because qualities such as non-existence (*asattva*) residing in that [superimposed object] are established in your own system, the definition applies.
Therefore, such a secondary (gauṇa) usage is indeed possible even in the Veda.
And although a secondary function is observed even through superimposition (āropa) in instances of metaphor (rūpaka) such as "the river of beauty," nevertheless,
that [secondary function] experienced in the case of the figure of speech simile (upamā), which occurs by mere similarity alone, cannot be denied.

Therefore, the secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*) consists in possessing that which is inherent (*samaveta*) in what is denotable by the word itself, common to both [the primary and secondary senses].

And the distinction is that "possessing that which is inherent" occurs in some cases through the relation of superimposition (*āropitatva*), and in others through the relation of possessing qualities of the same genus as itself (*svasamānajātīyaguṇavattā*).
Regarding this, the ancients hold that after the lion is presented by the word "lion" through primary denotation (*śakti*), cruelty is subsequently presented through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In reality, however, the presentation of that [secondary meaning] occurs precisely through the mechanism of recollection—namely, the recollection of one related entity upon the perception of another related entity.

Alternatively, the delimitor of the causal efficacy (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the cognition of a secondary sense (*gauṇī*) is "the state of being a verbal cognition (*śābdatva*) having Devadatta as its qualificandum and a property inherent in its own primary denotation (*svaśakyasamavetadharma*) as its qualifier, by way of either of the two aforementioned types of relations.
Thus, there is no risk of qualities such as cruelty (*krūratva*) not being part of the verbal content (*aśābdatva*).

Nor is there no difference between secondary indication (gauṇī) and metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā); for metaphorical indication occurs where there is a cognition of the qualities residing in the primary sense itself as being related [to another], whereas secondary indication occurs when there is a cognition by way of [abstract] properties such as "cruelty-ness" (krūratvatva), and thus the two are distinct.
And those qualities are of six kinds:
(1) establishment in a certain place, which is the performance of its function, as in the case of the term "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*);
[for example], the sacrificer is one who performs his own specific function.
"Likewise, so too is the prastara [the grass-bundle].
Thus, there is praise of the prastara by means of a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) containing a metaphorical sense (*gauṇī*).
In this way, the other five qualities should also be understood from the subsequent sūtras. // 13 // 29 //
Thus ends the investigation into the examples for establishing that [point] in the *Tatsiddhipeṭikā*.
Regarding the birth [of the Brahmin]:
in the passage "Agni indeed is the Brahmin," the word *agni* is used figuratively for the Brahmin, just as in the previous case,
because both Agni and the Brahmin originate from a single source.
In this case, the quality is precisely that which produces something of the same genus as the production of fire. // 13 // 29 //
Because of similarity;
[the word] "sārūpya" means similarity.
In cases such as "The sacrificial post is the sun," however, similarity (*sārūpya*) is the basis for the secondary (*gauṇī*) usage.
One might ask: "Is that alone the basis in all instances? What is the distinction here?
The ancients [hold] that in this case, the quality of being luminous and so forth, which is perceptible by the eye, is the basis.

In reality, however, it is only a quality whose perfection is possible elsewhere that serves as the cause [of the metaphorical application], by virtue of being a qualifier through the relation of possessing a quality of the same class as itself;
it is not similarity (sārūpya) that is the cause, because that functions merely as the relation.

In this case, however, the distinction is that similarity (*sārūpya*)—consisting in the possession of qualities of the same genus as the qualities whose perfection is possible—is itself the cause, because it serves as the qualifier through relations such as inherence (*samavāya*). // 13 // 29 //

Praise (praśaṃsā). Jaimini 1.4.26: Regarding the passage, “Other animals are indeed non-animals; cows and horses are the [true] animals,” since goats and other such creatures are prescribed for various purposes elsewhere, a prohibition or an exclusion (paryudāsa) regarding their role as sacrificial animals is untenable. Therefore, this is an explanatory praise (arthavāda).

For the word *apaśu* (non-animal) is used in its primary sense with respect to jars and the like; however, being applied figuratively (*gauṇa*) to goats and others by virtue of their lack of the excellence found in cows and horses, it functions through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to serve as a praise of cows and horses.

In the view of the Easterners (Prācām), however, the distinction is that the word *paśu* within the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) indicates excellence (*prāśastya*) residing in cows and horses, and the negative particle (*nañ*) then presents the quality consisting in the absence of that [excellence].
In every respect, it is established that praise is the constituent factor for the basis of secondary usage (*gauṇī*). // 13 // 29 //
*Bhūmā* (Jaimini 1.4.27):
In the passage "He lays down the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks," because there is no syntactic unity with another injunction and because an explicit injunction is heard, it possesses the character of an injunction.
And therein, the act of laying down (*upadhāna*) itself is enjoined for the purpose of consecrating the bricks.
Although the laying down of the bricks would be established by the very fact that their status as subsidiaries to the piling (cayana) could not otherwise be accounted for,
nevertheless, it is enjoined even prior to that by an explicit injunction (pratyakṣavidhi).
And the results of this are the accomplishment of the laying down of each individual brick and the establishment of the common agency (samānakartṛkatva) with the piling.
Otherwise, one might occasionally encounter even the simultaneous placement [of bricks];
furthermore, because it serves a purpose, there would also be the possibility of different agents for the piling (*cayana*).

However, when this injunction exists—which makes known that the piling has the bricks as its subordinate element (*aṅga*) by way of being a consecration (*saṃskāra*)—the accomplishment of both results follows from the principle of repetition according to each primary (*pratipradhānāvṛtti*) and from the rule that the agent of the subordinate and the primary must be the same.

The Commentator [Bhāṣyakāra] maintains that the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) is a figurative restatement (*anuvāda*) of only those mantras pertaining to creation and non-creation, which are already established by the context of the *liṅga*.
However, the Vārtikakāra argues that this is not merely an injunction regarding the placing [of the bricks].
For if it were so, there would result the redundancy of numerous other injunctions for placing, such as "one places the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks."

Therefore, either the mantra alone is enjoined as a qualification for the act of laying down (upadhāna) by way of restatement, or the laying down qualified by the mantra is enjoined for the purpose of consecrating the bricks.
In that case, the result of the injunction regarding the laying down is as previously stated;
however, the result of the injunction regarding the mantra is the restriction of its use to that specific act of laying down.
For the mantras merely illuminate the bricks; since they could apply to their grasping and so forth as well, they do not necessarily apply to the act of laying them down (*upadhāna*).

Therefore, the restriction [of the mantras to the laying down] has as its result either an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of their application to grasping and other acts, or else their connection with the middle layer (*madhyamaciti*).

By the statement, “Whatever brick one recognizes as being accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa passage, that one should place in the middle layer,” there is a connection of those bricks accompanied by direct Brāhmaṇa texts with the middle layer;

otherwise, for those mantras lacking inclusion within the specific sub-contexts (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of each respective layer, they would—by virtue of the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) of the piling (*cayana*)—either apply to all layers or, at most, be restricted to the final layer.
Therefore, this is an injunction of mantras for the purpose of connecting them with the middle layer.
The state of having a direct Brāhmaṇa text for the bricks consists in having mantras prescribed by words recited in a direct Brāhmaṇa text that denote the bricks.
For the term "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) refers to those bricks upon which mantras manifesting creation are placed.
And since the mantra, as the qualifying element therein, is what is to be prescribed, the state of those bricks having a direct Brāhmaṇa text is established.

Since the word *lokaṃ-pṛṇā*—even when the particle *iti* is attached to it—would otherwise apply to the middle layer alone, the term *iṣṭakā-vācinī* (denoting bricks) is used as a qualifier for the word.

Consequently, what is enjoined here is the act of placing (*upadhāna*) characterized by the mantra. The word *sṛṣṭi*, however, refers by way of secondary figurative usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) to the seventeen mantras consisting of both the *sṛṣṭi* and *asṛṣṭi* types.
“Because he lays down seventeen bricks,” according to the explanatory passage (arthavāda).

In that context, there are fourteen creation-mantras (*sṛṣṭi-mantra*) and three non-creation-mantras; thus, the abundance of creation-mantras is the quality (*guṇa*) that serves as the basis for the secondary application (*gauṇīvṛtti*). // 17 // 33 //
Thus ends the consideration of the illustration regarding the stages [of practice] in the *Tatsiddhipeṭikā*.
Because of the presence of the indicative mark (liṅga). Regarding [the injunction] "he places the prāṇabhṛt bricks," etc., the small number is the cause [for the application of the name];
the rest is as before.
Thus, there are six types of secondary (gauṇī) function. // 18 // 34 //
Thus ends the thirteenth section, the Section on the Basket of Accomplishments.
(Section 14:
[The rule applies] to doubtful cases because of the sequence of the sentences.

Regarding the statement, "He places the smeared pebbles," since the word "smeared" (aktāḥ) does not specify [the substance], any substance whatsoever that serves as a means for smearing is determined by the injunction; therefore, because a restriction by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) located in the conclusion—namely, "Clarified butter is indeed brilliance"—is untenable, it follows that the *arthavāda* has no authority in determining a doubtful meaning. To this, [the reply is: precisely because the injunction functions without specification...

Since the requirement is fulfilled even by taking "clarified butter" (ghṛta) alone, there is no evidence that it implies other substances; furthermore, since the introductory statement can be explained without contradiction, there is no evidence that the explanatory passage (arthavāda) located in the conclusion is intended as a mere illustration. Moreover, because the injunction and the explanatory passage form a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatva), they must necessarily share the same subject matter.

Therefore, it is logical that the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa) possesses authority in determining a doubtful meaning; thus, the anointing is to be done with clarified butter alone. 14 // 35 //
Thus ends the fourteenth section concerning anger.
(Section 15:
Or rather, [the whole is inferred] from the object, because it is a part of that conceptual construction.

In such cases as "he cuts with a struvā ladle," "he cuts with a knife," or "he cuts with his hand," the determination of the substance to be cut— which is subject to doubt regarding the injunction— is made through the force of contextual capacity (*sāmarthya*).

According to Struve, liquid substances such as clarified butter (*ājya*) are offered with a *struva* ladle, meat and the like with a *svadhiti* (knife), and solid offerings such as the *puroḍāśa* cake with the hand.

Therefore, since the act of offering (*avadyati*)—aided by the inherent capacity [of the substances]—indicates through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) that the offering of liquids and so forth is the intended object, there is no contradiction whatsoever in prescribing the *struva* and other implements as correlative to that [act of offering].
Likewise, in cases such as "one offers groats (*saktu*) with joined palms (*añjali*)," the *añjali* does not consist of the hands formed into a hollow cup.
Rather, it is by its very nature expanded, due to its inherent capacity.

Thus, these eight means of knowledge—consisting of injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), mantras, traditional law (smṛti), custom (ācāra), etymological names (nāmadheya), supplementary statements (vākyaśeṣa), and inherent capacity (sāmarthya)—have been defined as the authorities for determining dharma and adharma.
Hereafter, their specific nature will be defined through categories such as their distinctions and so forth. // 15 // 36 //
Thus ends the fifteenth section, concerning the capacity of the meaning.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the Bhāṭṭadīpikā composed by the venerable Khaṇḍadeva.
Thus ends the first chapter.
(B2) [The commencement of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), preceded by the determination of the connection (*saṅgati*) starting from the previous section:

And here, by means of the single reading: “‘Success (*tatsiddhi*), genus (*jāti*), similarity (*sārūpya*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), location (*bhūma*), and indicative mark (*liṅga*)—these are the grounds for figurative application (*guṇāśrayāḥ*).”*
Although the *sūtra* exists [in its entirety], it has been read in fragments for the sake of ease of exposition, much like the *pūrvapakṣa-sūtra* of the section on Mantras (*Mantrādhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the connection with the context (*prakaraṇasaṃgati*) arising from the investigation into whether [the terms] are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or names (*nāmadheya*), and the immediate connection (*anantara-saṃgati*) based on an objection and its resolution— namely, that since the possibility of a basis for the metaphorical application (*gauṇī*) mentioned in the preceding section (that the words "eight-potsherd" and so forth function through a metaphorical sense as a part of the "twelve-potsherd") is untenable— [the discussion proceeds].

Since the doubt is evident, it is not explicitly stated; however, although this sūtra serves the purpose of objecting to and resolving [the application of] figurative usage (*guṇavṛtti*), the Commentator has cited a specific example in order to indicate that its purpose is to resolve figurative usage in all cases.
By demonstrating that example, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "The sacrificer... (*yajamāna*).
(Refutation of the objection that the point has already been established by the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*):

For this very reason—even the status of being intended as praise, which was established in the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*, must be maintained through figurative application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) in the same manner as before; for, just as it was impossible [to establish praise] with the word "eight-potherd" (*aṣṭākapāla*) because it denotes a different object, so too it is impossible [to establish praise] with the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) in the case of the praise of the grass-bundle (*prastara*).
And that [independent injunction] is not possible, because the definition of it as accepted by the opponent is untenable;

therefore, in order to establish its validity, one must supply the word "should be made" (*kartavya*) and accept that it is indeed an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*). Having raised this objection, the conclusion is reached that it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), which is established through the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*.
It should also be understood that this refers to the state of having the meaning already conveyed.

(An exposition of the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] that the word *yajamāna* is a name for the sacrificial grass-bundle [prastara], in order to establish grammatical coreferentiality [sāmānādhikaraṇya] due to the impossibility of [the word] having either a basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) or a purpose.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), examples such as "the sacrificer is the cake on one potsherd" (*yajamāna ekakapāla*) are included.

Although the Bhāṣya presents two alternatives by way of being either an injunction (*vidhi*) or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the Vārttika, in order to indicate the connection [of the topic], states the prima facie view regarding its being a name: "Because of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyāt*).
For grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) among words—consisting in their expression of a single meaning—is not possible without that single meaning;
therefore, it follows that [the word] is a name (*nāmadheya*).
Nor is there any pointlessness of the sentence, given that a name cannot be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and thus there would be no other thing to be enjoined delimited by it.
It should not be argued that, because it possesses the names of two distinct things, this [passage] is intended as praise and thus does not differ from the position that it is an *arthavāda*;

for, given the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement, "The *barhis* is indeed offspring, the *prastara* is the sacrificer," once the word *prajā* (offspring) is established as a name for the *barhis* and the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) as a name for the *prastara*, then by placing the *prastara*— which bears the name of the sacrificer— above the *barhis*— which bears the name of offspring— [the purpose is achieved].

Just as for one who is a well-known sacrificer, there is a superiority over one who is not a sacrificer, so too, because the praise of the state of being above— which takes the form of the injunction, "He places the *prastara* above the *barhis*"— is obtained through that [injunction], there is no pointlessness;
whereas if it were merely an *arthavāda*, its purpose would consist solely in direct praise.
The only difference, however, is that in the case of being a name (*nāmadheya*), it occurs through a traditional lineage (*paramparayā*).
Nor is there an absence of a basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) even when it is a name;

for since the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) denotes the agency of performing a sacrifice, and since the grass-bundle (*prastara*) and the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) are insentient, they cannot possibly possess the status of being the agent of a sacrifice.

Since it is possible for [the sacrificer] to possess the status of an agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to his own activity included within that performance—just as a cooking pot is an agent with respect to its own function—it is likewise possible for that very [activity] to be the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the term.

For this very reason, although it was stated in the *Mūla* under the general heading (*saṃmugdhādhikāra*) that "the word *prastara* is a name for that which is measured as one," because such a connection is impossible in the case of the sacrificer, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) should be understood as being precisely this: that the word *yajamāna* itself is the name for the *prastara*.
And this has been established in the *Kaustubha* as well:

because the term *yajamāna* possesses both etymological and conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhi*), it cannot be a name like *soma* and the like; therefore, there is an investigation into another mode of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), namely that it is an injunction of the quality of the agent in the form of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) with respect to the function of the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*).
For this very reason, it is not the name of the sacrificer.
The word *yajamāna* does not denote merely the performer of a sacrifice;

rather, because it ends in the suffix *śānac*, which is a substitute for an ātmanepada affix denoting the locus of the fruit produced by an action residing in the agent, it is etymologically and conventionally (*yogarūḍha*) expressive of the locus of the fruit produced by the action. Since that meaning is impossible in the case of the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), [the term *yajamāna*] applies [to the bundle] merely through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), just as in the case of words such as *soma*.

He states the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) that it is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi), on the grounds that its status as a name (nāmadheya) is untenable: "Because it is [already] conventional" (rūḍhatvena).
Now, even so, in response to the expectation—"Where and what quality is prescribed?"—he says: "By means of the term *prastara* [used] in its secondary sense."

In the section on the Kauṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice, regarding the scriptural statement “He who is the Hotṛ is the Adhvaryu,” it is stated in the third book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] under the heading “In case of conflict, the instrument [prevails], due to a specific connection,” that because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would otherwise be untenable, one must accept the primary sense of the words *hotṛ* and so forth, while the words *adhvaryava* and so forth are taken in their secondary (metaphorical) sense.

Similarly here as well, having accepted that the word *prastara* (the sacrificial grass-bundle) has the sense of indicating a function (*kāryalakṣaṇārthatva*), the meaning is that the quality consisting of the sacrificer (*yajamānarūpaguṇa*) is enjoined as the agent.
(This means either the injunction of the *prastara* with reference to the sacrificer, or the injunction of the sacrificer with reference to the *prastara*.

In that regard, if someone [objects] that there is an injunction of even the insentient *prastara* for the sake of the sacrificer’s function because of its suitability in some respect, or due to the absence of a specific determinant (*vinigamakābhāva*), or because of the existence of priority—which is a regulator of the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatā*) as stated in the rule "priority belongs to the connection with the object of reference"—[we reply: *Note: The text provided is a fragment of a commentary on Mīmāṃsā principles regarding the interpretation of Vedic injunctions.*

To refute that [objection], it is stated "jaghanya" (secondary). This indicates the principle of favoring the primary (*mukhyānugraha-nyāya*)—as taught in the twelfth *adhikaraṇa* by the rule "or the primary, because of the prior injunction, as in common worldly usage"—which holds that that which occurs at the beginning (*mukhe*), being free from contradiction, deserves to be favored by its own inherent property (*svadharmatva*), whereas the secondary does not.

Consequently, since it is improper to resort to a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the "function" (*kārya*) there in order to conform to the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) functioning in its primary sense, there is no resulting contingency of enjoining the ritual grass-bundle (*prastara*) for the function of the sacrificer. This is the meaning.

The inclusion of the term "kārye" (in the sense of "when their functions are [to be performed]") is intended to dispel the apprehension that the entire ritual system (*sarvatantra*) might be lost due to the destruction of the sacrificer, which would follow if the rules regarding the sacrificer were applied to the *prastara* grass-bundle and the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*)— just as those rules apply to them— thereby necessitating their disposal (*praharaṇa*) and complete offering (*sarvahoma*).

This is because the two functions consisting of holding the *sruva*-ladle and the sacrifice themselves are to be accomplished through the disposal and offering of the *prastara* and *ekakapāla*, which have already been assigned to those specific roles.

Since those two [acts] are not the effects of that [main sacrifice], even though the *yajamāna*— who serves another purpose— is enjoined for acts such as holding the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) performed by a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*), there is no occurrence of a disposal (*pratipatti*), because the act does not fulfill its purpose through the completion of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) and thus is unfit for disposal; consequently, there is no contingency of the entire ritual procedure being lost.

The meaning is that there is no contingency of the injunction regarding the sacrificial grass (*prastara*) becoming purposeless, because one does not accept [the sacrificer] as being subject to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

For, when the sacrificer is enjoined to perform the function of the sacrificial grass, this serves to specify the particular task— namely, to avoid the inconsistency of the general injunction that "standing to the south occurs while the ritual action is being performed," which would otherwise preclude the sacrificer's standing to the south as its performer.
The term "holding the ladle" (strugdhāraṇa) is employed [as a qualification].
And thus, since that [person] is established both before and after the holding of the ladle, there is no contradiction; this is the meaning.

(The justification for the *yajamāna* term being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) on the grounds that its being a figurative expression (*gauṇatva*) is untenable, similar to the case of the *aṣṭākapāla* term): Nor should it be argued that, since this [passage] is justified as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), it is not proper to assume a separate injunction (*vidhi*) to establish it as an injunction of a quality— just as in the case of the *aṣṭākapāla* and so forth— because in that case, by the inclusion of phrases such as "by the *gāyatrī* itself," there is the perception of a praise of the *aṣṭākapāla* etc., which are constituent parts, through the relationship of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*).

Even though the twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*) are supported by praise, here— in the case of the statement "Vāyu is the swiftest"— just as there is no praise due to the absence of a quality that bestows excellence, so too here, despite the possibility of supporting the praise for the twelve potsherds through the relationship of part and whole based on the word "single sacrificer" (*ekayajamāna*), there is no such relationship of part and whole here; furthermore, since praise for the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is untenable even by means of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it cannot be an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) because it differs from the previous case.
Nor can that be established through figurative usage (gauṇī), because the definitions and essential natures of figurative usage are difficult to determine.

(An exposition that [the following] is not figurative usage (*gauṇīvṛtti*): abandoning a well-known meaning to express an unknown one; expressing a part when a whole is denoted; or having as its object a meaning superimposed through the power of one's own imagination.

For instance: if, first of all, its definition were "abandoning a well-known meaning to express qualities (*guṇa*) that are not [otherwise] well-known," then—having abandoned the well-known meaning [of the word *siṃha*, "lion"]—[one would have to admit it applies] to qualities residing in Devadatta, such as his being prone to rashness, on account of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *devadatta*.

If it were argued that the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established through the assumption of another potency (*śaktyantara*) and through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) because of their connection, then—while such an indication might be possible in common worldly usage in accordance with the speaker’s indirect intention—it cannot be so in the Veda, as that [intention] is absent. Consequently, since abandoning the well-known meaning would result in a loss of authority (*aprāmāṇya*), praise cannot be established by means of such figurative usage (*gauṇatva*).
As for the definition that figurative usage consists in the application of a word denoting a whole to a single part through indication (*lakṣaṇā*)...
For all words such as "lion" and so forth do not denote the genus alone;
for if that were the case, it would be impossible for them to stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting qualities, such as "white.

Rather, they denote a collection (*samudāya*) consisting of genus, substance, quality, action, and so on. Since such a collection cannot exist in Devadatta, [the word "lion"] cannot stand in coreferentiality with the word "Devadatta" and so forth.

The construction [of the compound] is achieved by some through the following reasoning: since the performance of the action is impossible for the whole, the word "lion" (*siṃha*) applies to a part of that whole by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established, and the syntactic connection is maintained. However, even this is untenable, because since a collection (*samudāya*) is non-eternal, it would be conjoined with a non-eternal object, resulting in a loss of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) in the Veda; for without a universal (*jāti*), individual entities, qualities, and actions [cannot be denoted].

It is incorrect [to claim that figurative usage is distinct from indication], because since it is impossible to distinguish [the object] otherwise, the cognition of the individual is established simply by the word necessarily denoting the genus (*jāti*), as it is impossible to distinguish individuals, qualities, or actions [without it]; furthermore, there is no evidence for accepting a separate category of figurative usage (*gauṇī*).

As for the definition of figurative usage—that it consists in residing in an object that has become the locus of a superimposition produced by the power of one's own imagination—[that too is untenable].

Furthermore, one might argue that the application of the word "lion" to Devadatta is possible because the listener infers that it was used by the speaker through the superimposition (*āropa*) of lionhood, since its use otherwise would be inexplicable; thus, there is a consistent connection (*samanvaya*).

However, that too is incorrect because in the Veda there is no person who could perform such a superimposition. Therefore, even by means of this definition of secondary indication (*gauṇī-lakṣaṇa*), the justification for praise (*stuti*) via secondary indication is not established here. Consequently, in no way can the status of being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) be maintained on the grounds of providing praise; thus, out of necessity—
The sense is that, even by abandoning the unity of the sentence, this is simply an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi).

(An exposition of the final conclusion by means of the *audumbara-adhikaraṇa* logic, through the refutation of its being an injunction of a subordinate quality [guṇavidhi], because that would entail the performance of the throwing [of the sacrificial grass-bundle] and other acts, and because it would result in the nullification of the subsequent ritual procedure.

If there were an explicit injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*) here, then— in accordance with this which is enjoined by an explicit injunction— one would have to assume a restriction of the placement in the southern region for the injunction regarding the *prastara*, as well as its optional character and the disruption of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).
In this case, however, there is no direct injunction (pratyakṣo vidhiḥ).

Therefore, since it is improper to accept that [the word] as part of an injunction that must be inferred, it cannot be an injunction of a subordinate element (guṇavidhiḥ). With this intention, he states the final conclusion (siddhānta): "pratyakṣa... etc.
Furthermore, by virtue of the sacrificer occupying the position of the *prastara* (grass-bundle), he undergoes the acts of throwing (*praharaṇa*) and the final oblation (*sarvahoma*).
Although those two acts do not have the same functional purpose as the *prastara* or the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*),

nevertheless, with respect to the disposal acts of throwing and the oblation, they serve as means by way of their own functions— namely, the holding of the *sruva*-ladle and the performance of the sacrifice.

Because the *prastara* (grass-bundle) and the *ekakapāla* (single-plate offering) are the objects of consecration (*saṃskārya*) by virtue of their form (*rūpa*), and because that same form exists in the sacrificer as well, it is logical that the act of placing (*sthāpanā*) would apply to him too. Nor is there a lack of purposeful efficacy (*akṛtārthatva*).

The sense is that even if the sequence is set aside in accordance with the primary requirement (*pradhāna*), the resulting consequence is unavoidable after all the *yājamāna* (officiant’s) acts have been performed; and if such a consequence were accepted, it would lead to the loss of the subsequent ritual framework (*uttaratantra*) for the *Somayāga* and other rites bound by that sequence. Having resolved the objection raised in the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*, he states that its status as an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) alone is logical: "Therefore, it is an *arthavāda*."
He dispels the impossibility of the praise mentioned previously with the words: "But the word 'yajamāna'..."

(An examination of the nature of figurative indication (*gauṇī-lakṣaṇā*) which does not entail the invalidity of the Vedas, and the demonstration that this [definition] is common to the claim "the sky-flower is your established doctrine" [i.e., your doctrine is as non-existent as a sky-flower].

Since the first two definitions are unestablished, they are set aside; instead, an objection is raised regarding the impossibility of the previously mentioned well-known final definition of figurative function—beginning with "But surely... (*nanu*).)
"Therefore" means:

The word "ataḥ" (hence) is used here with the ablative case (*pañcamī*) by eliding the suffix *-lyap* (as in *lyablope*). Therefore, the meaning is that [the definition] is not based on the observation of usage (*prayogadarśanāt*), because one abandons the previously stated definition and adopts the definition to be stated later—beginning with "its own capacity" (*svaśakya*)—on account of such observation. Thus, there is no logical inconsistency in the construction of the ablative ending in "prayogadarśanāt. Now, an objection might be raised: just as, by taking some particular form, a certain definition is constituted by the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) characterized by the conceptualization of that form upon another form; [is this not the case here?]

In such cases as "The sky-flower is your tenet," there is an over-narrowness (avyāpti) [in your definition], because since sky-flowers and the like have never been experienced, they cannot be determined as being "like this," and thus superimposition (āropa) is impossible; consequently, the term cannot be secondary (gauṇa).

Likewise, since the primary meaning (śakyārtha) itself is unestablished in that case, there can be no connection with qualities residing therein; therefore, because it is impossible for the word "sky-flower" to be secondary in relation to the tenet, your stated definition also suffers from over-narrowness.
To dispel such a doubt, he says: "In the case of flowers and so forth."

Even if there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*)— since the definition of that [secondary usage] as "functioning with a superimposed object" can be established by demonstrating the nature of a non-entity by taking a "sky-flower" in the manner we have described—

the definition would still result in the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). This is because the word "sky-flower" itself would incur the status of being secondary (*gauṇa*), as it functions with a superimposed object when applied to a flower on a creeper.
For no one in the world asserts that the word "sky-flower" (khapuṣpa) is used figuratively (gauṇa), such that one could claim this as an accepted consequence (iṣṭāpatti).

By this, the following [argument] is refuted: "Since figurative usage is not established for the superimposed qualities such as 'lionhood' (siṃhatva) themselves, but rather for Devadatta and others who are the substrates of those superimpositions, figurative usage consists precisely in having a superimposed object as its substrate."

Since it is impossible for a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*), which is itself unestablished, to be superimposed, one must accept that what is superimposed is a flower already established in something well-known, such as the sky or a creeper; and since the establishment [of the object] occurs through its dependence on something well-known, the quality of being based on a superimposed object exists in the sky.
Therefore, because the word "sky-flower" is not excluded from being figurative (*gauṇa*) with respect to the sky-flower itself, the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) remains unavoidable.
Therefore, in your view, there is the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

In my view, however, because the term "capable" (*śakya*) is intended to denote only the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*), and since a superimposed (*āropita*) thing does not forfeit its status as a primary meaning, there is no fault whatsoever.
For primariness is not caused by being non-superimposed.
However, the intended meaning is that [the application of the word] is produced by the usage of the term itself, without depending on any other function.

Nor should it be argued: "Even so, since the Buddhist who says 'your doctrine is like a sky-flower' does not admit the existence of the doctrine which serves as the object of comparison (*upameya*), how can there be an absence of connection with qualities when that [doctrine] is in fact non-existent?

This should not be said; for although the certainty denoted by the word "doctrine" is an error due to its lack of an existent form, it is established as an object of comparison because it exists in its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*).

In this very way, although the sky is unreal in its nature as a flower-modification, it possesses the status of being the counter-correlate of similarity because it is real in its own essential form; thus, there is no invalidity of the simile.
And this has been stated according to the view of Pārthasārathi and others, by means of the superimposition of the creeper-flower upon the sky itself.

However, when the intention of the Venerable Teacher (Pūjyapāda) is that the superimposition consists in attributing the state of having the sky as its locus to the creeper-flower, [the same conclusion follows].

In that case, although the sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*) is unreal insofar as it has the sky as its locus when taken as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), its status as a standard of comparison is easily established because it possesses reality in the form of a creeper-flower, serving as the correlate of similarity (*sādṛśya-pratiyogin*).
For this very reason, it should be understood that in this view, the perception of the sky-flower itself as the standard of comparison is not at all sublated.

As for what was stated in the *Vārttika*—that the word "sky-flower" denotes the absence delimited by a flower located in the sky, even without a superimposed flower—[this refers to a different context].
That [objection] should be seen as already refuted by what was established regarding the Kaustubha.
Therefore, because the definition stated by himself does not entail the invalidity of the Veda, he concludes with the intention that it is indeed logical: "And therefore, such... and so forth.

Such a word-meaning is established through the intentionality of similarity, which serves to justify the designation by means of secondary (gauṇa) words whose application to the object arises from a connection with a function based on qualities.

Although superimposition is indeed observed even in the Veda—as in passages such as "Man, O Gautama, is indeed fire"—nevertheless, while it is possible there for a practitioner to perform a rite of superimposition in the form of meditation for the sake of unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*), here that is not the case. Since there is no such [unseen result] and since the Veda lacks a speaker, a superimposition created by one cannot be established. Furthermore, because ordinary worldly usage can be accounted for otherwise, there is no grounds for postulating superimposition.
The word "proper" (yuktam) indicates that the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is possible within the Veda.
(The application of the definition of secondary indication [gauṇa-lakṣaṇa]: "inhering in what is denotable by itself," etc.

Since secondary indication is observed through the superimposition of "lion-ness" upon Devadatta just as one superimposes "cruelty" and so forth, the author provides the definition—accepting that the word *guṇa* (quality) in the definition refers to that which is inherent (*samaveta*) for the sake of commonality between both types—stating: "inhering in what is denotable by itself" and "in some cases through superimposition."

In cases such as poetic metaphor (*rūpaka*), where, despite the perception of difference, the word "lion" is applied to Devadatta by superimposing qualities such as lionhood and ferocity based on mere similarity—

and where the listener likewise understands it so— there is no evidence to deny the superimposition established by experience; therefore, through the superimposition of lionhood and so forth, the definition [of lakṣaṇā] applies directly to Devadatta itself, because of the actual existence of lionhood and other qualities inherent in the lion within him by virtue of his own power (*svaśakti*).
This is the meaning;
[it occurs] only in certain cases.

The meaning is that even when the word "lion" is applied to Devadatta— desiring to express a mere similarity based on the presence in Devadatta of qualities of the same genus as those existing in the lion, such as its natural capacity for forceful action and so forth— the definition is fully applicable.

(The justification for the understanding of qualities through secondary indication [lakṣaṇā] according to the opinion of the ancients, by reconciling the Vārttika’s statement that "it is due to the connection with the qualities of the indicated object" with the definition beginning with "inhering in what is capable of its own [denotation]"):
And in this regard, it is said: "The operation of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) is held to occur toward that which is invariably connected with the primary denotation;
however, the operation is considered figurative (gauṇī) when it arises from a connection with the qualities of the indicated object."

Thus, it has been stated in the *Vārttika* concerning the determination of the non-difference of characteristics that the definition of secondary indication (*gauṇī*) as being based on the connection with qualities inherent in the indicated meaning is not tenable;
for if that were the case, it would result in the abandonment of the primary meaning (*jahatsvārthatā*).
To avoid this, if [the word] were restricted solely to its own primary meaning, there would be the consequence that the qualities would not be conveyed by the word (*aśābdatva*).

Therefore, having first denoted the primary meaning (the referent) by the word "lion" according to its primary power (*śakti*), the qualities (*guṇa*) are also indicated through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Thus, in the *Nyāyasudhā*, it is explained that the statement in the *Vārttika*—"therefore, by means of the qualities being indicated"—accepts a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*) and asserts that secondary indication regarding the qualities is preceded by the denotation of the word's own primary meaning; this is said with reference to the definition of qualities as intended by the ancients.
He establishes that view with the words: "In this regard."

[The author] states "In reality, however... out of dissatisfaction with the following: that when qualities (*guṇa*) are presented through secondary indication (*gauṇī*), one can first establish the lack of contradiction between his own view and the *Vārttika* on "qualities indicated by the power [of the word]" (*svaśaktyādi-lakṣyamāṇa-guṇa-vārttika*); then, having refuted the *Nyāyasudhā* and other works therein; and finally, because the occurrence of two simultaneous functions (*vṛtti-dvaya*) would lead to a logical contradiction, the verbal cognition of the qualifying quality—which serves to present the primary meaning as possessing those qualities—is established by the secondary indication itself relied upon for that purpose. Thus, since there is no possibility of the quality not being conveyed verbally (*aśābdatva-prasaṅga*), the acceptance of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the qualities is purposeless. Therefore, he says: "In reality, however... (*vastutastu*).

Since even in the case of indication (lakṣaṇā), the presence of the object itself is accepted for the sake of establishing its status as being conveyed by words, [the author] establishes that the presence of the quality is also necessary in the case of secondary indication (gauṇī) with the words: "one related to the same... (ekasaṃbandhī).
And thus, in the Vārttika "by means of the qualities indicated," there is no connection with a *karmadhāraya* compound;

rather, it is precisely a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*: "by means of the qualities residing in that individual (*vyakti*) which is indicated by the words denoting the universals (*jāti*) of 'lion-ness' and 'fire-ness.'"

For this very reason, the Vārttika states: "Just as in the first half [of the verse], attention is shown toward a relationship inseparably connected with the primary meaning through indication (lakṣaṇā), so too in the second half, there is merely an attention toward a similarity to the primary meaning; there is no indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding the qualities.
For this same reason: "That which is understood from the yellowness and so forth, which are indicated by the property of fire-ness (vahnitva)..."
Therefore, the cognition of "boy" arises with respect to that [elephant] due to similarity."

Thus, in the subsequent statement, it is understood that [the word] "is understood" has been stated. Likewise, in the *Vārttika*, regarding the secondary (gauṇī) usage, it is stated that the cause is precisely the prior capacity (*pūrvaśakti*), as follows: "And here, because there arises from the cognition of various properties such as 'acting with violence'—which are presented by the individual entity understood through the sense of 'lion'—a cognition of Devadatta, the prior capacity alone is the cause."

The sense is that the explanation by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* as being intended for "indication based on a quality" (*guṇalakṣaṇā*) is indeed improper. Now, one might raise the objection: "Since words such as 'lion' can be construed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word 'Devadatta' simply through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of something related to a lion, why accept an additional function called 'secondary indication' (*gauṇīvṛtti*)? This doubt is addressed by establishing a distinction [between the two] through the refutation of the doubt regarding their non-difference.
He refutes this with the words "and not."

In the previously cited *vārttika*, "in that which is inseparably connected with the denoted meaning," the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is not established as the cause for secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*);
for that [indication] is possible through mere relation by virtue of the word's intended purport (*tātparya*).
Nor is it stated here that there is an inseparable connection between the denoted meaning—the indicator—and the indicated meaning, as there is between fire and smoke.
This is because it is stated that the signifier (*lakṣaka*) is inseparably connected (*avinābhāva*) with the signified (*abhidheya*), which is itself the object to be characterized (*lakṣya*);
however, the mention of that [inseparable connection] is merely for the purpose of demonstrating respect [for the signified] by way of its relationship to the signified.

For this very reason, in cases such as "Bring in the staffs" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), although the staffs and so forth are inseparably connected with the persons [carrying them], the words "staff" and so forth—

Since it is stated that [the word] functions by way of an inseparable connection with the denoted object—due to the absence of its function upon the nature of the person (puruṣa) when disregarding the relationship with the staff and so forth which constitute the denotation—and since the mere relationship exists as the cause for indication (lakṣaṇā), it is indeed correct that its function occurs through indication; thus, indication is described with regard to the connection with the denoted object.

However, in the case of secondary metaphorical usage (gauṇī), although the relationship that serves as the cause for indication exists, it does not possess the form of a connection with the denoted object, because it proceeds from a disregard for similarity based on shared attributes such as cruelty.

Intending to show the disparity by pointing out that [the opponent's view] would result in the fallacy of *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indication based on what is indicated), he provides the following resolution: "By its own power... (*svaśakyeti*).

Precisely because there is a distinction between indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and secondary usage (*gauṇī*), Akṣapāda and others stated in the sūtra—"On account of association, location, purpose, activity, measure, support, proximity, connection, instrumentality, and sovereignty, there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) to a Brāhmaṇa, a bed, a mat, a king, groats, sandalwood, the Gaṅgā, a cloth, food, and a person, even when those [qualities] are not present"—the causes of indication. Jaimini, however, stated the qualities that are the causes of secondary usage separately in the section beginning with *tatsiddhi*. Thus he says: "And those... (*te ca*).

Since the word *siddhi* (accomplishment) denotes the "effect" (*kārya*) in such passages as "he attains supreme accomplishment," the author intends to convey that the term *tatsiddhi* found in the aphorism—by means of a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that [text] in which the primary accomplishment resides"—expresses the capacity to produce the primary object; with this in mind, he says: "its accomplishment."

Since there is no distinction in the status of being an agent between the grass-bundle (*prastara*) and the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) and the sacrificer, they are both defined by the same action called "sacrifice" (*yajña*).

Because their respective instrumentalities (*karaṇatva*) residing in the grass-bundle and the sacrificer share this common property, and because the grass-bundle and the single potsherd possess a quality consisting of an agency in an action that is of the same genus as the agency in the action residing in the sacrificer,

it is possible for the subordinate sentence-meaning to be established through figurative indication (*gauṇī-lakṣaṇā*), whereby the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the terms "grass-bundle" and "single potsherd" with [the term "sacrificer"] is justified.
Subsequently, he states that praise is its defining characteristic: "Just as the sacrificer... and so forth.
The purpose has not been stated because it is obvious.
Thus concludes the consideration of examples for establishing that [point] in the section on the "Basket of Proofs" (Tatsiddhipetikā).
(An examination of the reason for setting aside the passage cited by the author of the Bhāṣya, *āgneyo brāhmaṇaḥ*, and instead citing *agnir vai brāhmaṇaḥ* as the example.

Here, the author of the Bhāṣya [cites] the remainder of the injunction: “A Brāhmaṇa desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni (*āgneyamaṣṭākapālaṃ nirvapet brāhmaṇo brahmavarcasakāmaḥ*); in that context, it is heard: “The Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni (*āgneyo vai brāhmaṇaḥ*), the Rājanya to Indra, and the Vaiśya to the Viśvedevas.”

Having thus cited [the passage], [he explains] the words "Āgneya" and so forth: "Prajāpati desired, 'May I create offspring. From his mouth he fashioned the Trivṛt-stoma; Agni was released as its deity, the Gāyatrī as its metre, the Rathantara as its Sāman, the Brāhmaṇa among men, and the goat among animals. From his chest and arms he fashioned the Pañcadaśa-stoma; Indra was released as its deity, and the Triṣṭubh [as its metre]."
"The *gāyatrī* is the metre, the *bṛhat* the *sāman*, the Kṣatriya among men, and the sheep among animals; therefore they are powerful, for they were created from power.

From the thighs and the middle he fashioned the seventeen-fold [stoma]; after him the Viśvedevas were created: the *jagatī* is the metre, the *vairūpa* the *sāman*, the Vaiśya among men, and the cows among animals. Thus, from the mouth of Prajāpati as proclaimed in these injunctions and explanatory passages (*vidhi* and *arthavāda*)—
Having established its figurative nature through the similarity of having a single origin, it was concluded that [the passage] is an *arthavāda*.

Even though the application of the *taddhita* suffix denoting a deity (*devatā-taddhita*) would be untenable for the word *āgneya* in the absence of its co-occurrence with a hymn (*sūkta*) or an oblation (*havis*), it is nevertheless tenable as a *taddhita* suffix expressing a general relationship, based on the traditional rule (*smṛti*) under the heading "this belongs to that" (*tasyedaṃ*): "The suffix *ḍhak* must always be stated after the roots *agni* and *kali*. Thus, its status as a *taddhita* suffix expressing a general connection is established.

This is because it is most appropriately established through the specific relationship consisting in having a single origin from the mouth of Prajāpati, as proclaimed by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the "enemy" (*bhrātṛvya*); furthermore, even if a relationship characterized by being a deity were required, a relationship of Agni with the Brāhmaṇa— as the sacrificer—
with the status of a deity is observed in such passages as "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed of Agni as his deity," and this is likewise appropriate here.

Having refuted [the opponent's view] by stating that there is no evidence for its being secondary (gauṇatva), the author of the Vārttika cites another example, which he himself here illustrates with the words: "Agni, indeed... (agnir vai).
(Regarding the passage "Agni indeed," this section establishes the figurative nature of the word *agni* by first refuting its status as a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) and so forth.

Here too, as before, having raised the possibility that it is either a name (*nāmadheya*) or a prescription of a quality, and having refuted those views on the grounds that it forms a single syntactical unit with another injunction and because it is impossible to enjoin an insentient fire for the duties of a Brāhmaṇa such as renunciation (*tyāga*), the figurative nature of the word *agni* is established through its being an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*).
The phrase "it is certain" is indicated by the expression "as before.

To dispel the doubt as to why a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) was established based on a portion of the Sūtra, he states another reason—thereby indicating its purposefulness—and provides that other reason: "of both," by connecting it with the word *tat* from the preceding Sūtra; and by the etymology "that from which [something] is born," the term *jāti* refers to the material cause (*upādāna*) of birth.

Intending to express this, he says "one" (ekā), having in mind that the term *jāti* in the Sūtra refers to the state of being of one kind (*ekajātīyatā*) as a secondary cause (*gauṇanimitta*), by means of a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound: namely, that the very *jāti* which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of fire—the primary referent (*mukhyārtha*)—is itself the *jāti* of that Brāhmaṇa.
The use of the word *janana* (birth) is intended to indicate that the term *jāti* (caste/lineage) does not denote a generic property (*sāmānya*).

Although, in cases such as the *śrāddha* rite or the *pāṇi-homa*, the Brāhmaṇa’s status as the performer of the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) could serve as a basis [for the application of the term], since this is established by his being a performer of a ritual action of the same class as those residing in the fire; nevertheless, because that [fire-based status] is not intended to be expressed, when the term is used with the intention of expressing birth from a single source, its application occurs solely for the purpose of making known another basis [of caste].
And although having a single source is unreal— both because there is a lack of evidence and because the *arthavāda* is intent upon another purpose—
nevertheless, even though it is unreal, it will be understood here as the basis for the word "that" (*tat*), since it has been mentioned in another *arthavāda*.
Thus ends the examination of examples regarding genus (*jāti*) in the *Tatsiddhipeṭikā*.
—(The demonstration that similarity (*sārūpya*) is the basis for secondary figurative application [*gauṇīvṛtti*] in the case of "The sacrificial post is the sun" [Ādityo yūpaḥ]):

In passages such as "The sacrificial post is the sun," the refutation of the doubt regarding whether they are names (*nāmadheya*) or injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) can certainly be understood just as clearly as before; therefore, having set that aside, only another basis for secondary figurative application that establishes their status as explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) is presented here.
Intending to say "it is stated," he says: "The sacrificial post is the sun."
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), examples such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial post" (yajamāno yūpaḥ) and so forth are included.
(The demonstration, according to the opinion of the ancients, that [passages] such as "The sacrificer is the prastara" cannot serve as examples of similarity. Thus say the ancients.

Now, if the cognition of similarity [is established] by means of a property such as "being light perceptible to the eye," then in cases such as "The sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)," the cognition of that [identity] would likewise be the same on the basis of performing its function (*tatkāryakaratva*) and so forth; thus, there would be no distinction [between these two cases] based on "being light perceptible to the eye. Therefore, the statement of the ancients as heard [in their texts], which provides the distinguishing factor, [remains valid].
Intending to show that it does not exist, he clarifies its underlying intention with the words: "But in reality..."

The meaning is this: although similarity between the *prastara* (the grass-bundle) and so forth is possible on the basis of common properties such as performing that same function, nevertheless, because the word’s purport is restricted merely to the performance of that function and so on, that [similarity] lacks the status of being the object of verbal cognition; and since that which is not an object cannot serve as the ground for the operation of a word whose nature is to convey meaning, it does not constitute the ground for the operation of the word.
Therefore, in that case (the simile), it is precisely the performance of that function which, being understood from the word, becomes the qualifying attribute (*prakāra*).

Here, however, because similarity— having been first perceived through direct perception— is determined by the word to be its primary intended meaning (*tātparya*), and because the speaker’s intention known as *tātparya* is immediately determined regarding similarity since it is swiftly perceived as the object of verbal cognition, [the word] functions to denote the specific ground for the application of the word (*śabdavṛttinimitta*) consisting in being an object of cognition.
Because it is based on reasons such as its performing that function, it is mentioned here separately and uniquely from those secondary grounds which consist merely in existence.
For this very reason— namely, that in this context the fact of being perceptible by the eye (*cakṣurgrāhyatva*) alone is not the cause for separate mention,
since in cases such as "the umbrella-bearers are going," it would be illogical to separately mention plurality (*bahutva*) and so forth because they too are perceptible by the eye—

it is indicated, through the supplied ablative case-ending, that the distinct cause is the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) of the similarity consisting of the nature of verticality (*ūrdhvatva*) and luminosity (*tejastva*), which are perceptible by the eye.
In the Bhāṣya and other works, the portion of the sūtra beginning with "sārūpyāt" has been cited.

(An exposition of the author’s view that "the sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*) is not an example of *sārūpya* [similarity], because it lacks the quality of producing a cognition whose mode is the property of being perceivable by the eye. However, the Venerable Teacher (Pūjyapāda), observing the nominative plural ending in the compound *liṅgasamavāyāḥ* as a *dvandva* compound, and intending the analysis (*vigraha*) to be "its establishment (*tatsiddhi*), its genus (*jāti*), and its similarity (*sārūpya*"), has employed the word *sārūpya* as a nominative singular.

Therefore, it should be understood that in the Sūtra, by the term *sārūpya* (similarity), not merely the possession of common properties is intended; rather, with the intention of referring to the object of the word "form" (*rūpa*) as perceivable by the eye exactly as it exists, the term conveys the state of being perceivable by the eye—thus, it refers specifically to such a property alone.
Thus ends the examination of examples of similarity in the *Tatsiddhipeṭikā*.
—(Summary of the subject sentence; the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] that, even though the word *apaśu* cannot be a name, it serves to provide a quality for the purpose of prohibition:

Regarding the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), in connection with the laying down of fifteen heads, it is heard: "He lays down the horse's head facing west in the front, and the bull's head facing east in the back. This is cited as an example of a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the injunction for laying down the heads of cows and horses.
"Non-animals," they say.

And this [statement]—“That which is without *sāman* is indeed no sacrifice,” and “That which is without *chandoma* is indeed no *sattra*”—is also an elliptical reference (*upalakṣaṇa*) to other supplementary injunctions.

In that context, since goats and the like, distinct from cows and horses, are denoted by the word "animal" (*paśu*), it is untenable for them to be designated as "non-animals" (*apaśu*). Therefore, regarding the word "non-animal" (*apaśu*) heard in the Taittirīya [Brāhmaṇa] in grammatical coordination with the word "animal" in the passage, “Others than cows and horses are indeed non-animals; [cows and horses] are animals,”...

Since even the status of "name" (nāmatva) for words such as *ghaṭa* is untenable— because it is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) alone, which would render the act of naming redundant— and since there is no possibility of suspecting such a status, one must set that aside; otherwise, due to the impossibility of any other explanation, one might, by way of supposition, entertain the doubt that in the word *paśu*, having accepted a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the function of cattle,
there is either an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) or a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) of goats and others distinct from cows and horses.
Rejecting even that [objection], he recalls its status as an explanatory statement (arthavāda) with the words "of goats and so forth."

By this—namely, by the investigation into whether it is possible for [the word] to be an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) even though its status as a name (nāmatva) is impossible—the connection [of the present discussion] has been indicated.
For there is no royal decree that only a quality that is itself enjoined can be the subject of such an investigation;

rather, the sense is that since the word "injunction" (vidhi) serves as an indicator for "prohibition" (niṣedha), the explanation holds even when [the passage] provides a quality that is to be prohibited.
(The demonstration that the word *apaśu* is an explanatory eulogy [arthavāda].
"In that case, in that case" refers to this.

The meaning is that, in passages such as "the goat is for Agni-Soma" and "a ewe for Sarasvatī," a prohibition is impossible because [the animal] is already enjoined; and since a prohibition cannot apply to what is not enjoined—because there would be no possibility of its occurrence—it is improper to resort to an option (vikalpa) by assuming that established injunctions are merely optional in order to accommodate a hypothetical prohibition.
Therefore, it is more appropriate that these are indeed explanatory passages (arthavāda) intended to praise cows and horses.

In response to the inquiry as to what the status would be for those things other than cows and horses—whether they are non-animals, or whether they could possibly serve the functions of animals, or whether there is a prohibition against them—he says: "For the word 'non-animal' (apaśu)... and so forth.

(The demonstration that the word *apaśu* indicates the absence of excellence found in cows, horses, and so forth, such that praise can be established as a result [of the injunction] just as by being in syntactic unity with the injunction;
and the determination that praise serves as the basis for secondary figurative usage (*gauṇī*) by way of constituting the absence of praise.

The word *apaśu*, ending in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), while denoting objects such as jars and the like, [is understood] in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in accordance with its syntactic unity with the injunction regarding cows and horses.

Furthermore, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "animals, [namely] cows and horses," the absence of excellence residing in the literal meaning (*śakyārtha*) as it pertains to cows and horses is presented by way of the recollection of one related member through the cognition of another related member. Consequently, since this is established through the secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*) based on the connection with the quality of the absence of excellence in cows and horses— as found in the case of goats and so forth— it follows that, by the principle of "praise by means of censure" (*nahinindānyāya*), the understanding of the excellence pertaining to the horse, which is the subject of the injunction, becomes easily accessible.

Although the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) can be justified even by its indication of the excellence residing in cows and horses, and thus there would be no utility in stating the absence of such excellence therein; nevertheless, its utility in producing an excellence of the praise that results from the glorification of the enjoined act through the disparagement of others is not untenable. For this very reason, since the praise residing in cows and horses—which was accepted as the ground [for the application of the term *paśu*] due to the impossibility of any other ground—is accepted as the result [of the injunction] through syntactic unity with the injunction itself, there is not even the slightest suspicion of futility.

However, in the case of the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*), since the qualifying attribute (*guṇa*) is precisely the performance of the ritual action, that [action] itself constitutes the result; this is the distinction.

And thus, since praise is included within the quality that consists in the absence of praise (as something being excluded), it should be understood that in the Sūtra, praise is mentioned as a separate ground [of inference] precisely by taking its inclusion therein.

For if taken literally, it would be impossible for the praise inherent in cows and horses to constitute a quality of jars and the like—which are the literal meanings of the words—or a quality of goats and the like;

on the contrary, for the purpose of praising the enjoined cows and horses, one must rather expect the lack of excellence (aprāśastya) in other animals such as goats, and thus their status as a "quality" (guṇatā) would be untenable.
Therefore, in this context, the word *apaśu* is indeed a specific figurative expression.
(Regarding the view of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* that the word *paśu* indicates excellence, and the examination of its lack of cogency as suggested by the word *tu*:
As for [the statement]— "Having first taken up the excellence residing in cows, horses, and so forth..."

In accordance with the natural sense of the Vārttika, "The absence of that [excellence] is expressed by the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) in the case of other animals and so forth," the author of the Nyāyasudhā and others have established that the word *paśu* (animal), as a constituent of the negative compound, indicates excellence (*praśastatā*), and that the absence of that [excellence] in other animals is then expressed by the negative compound.

In that case, since the application of the word *apaśu* (non-animal) to goats and other [animals] would be established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone—just as it is applied to jars and the like—the attempt to establish a figurative usage (*gauṇīvṛtti*) is untenable; this has been demonstrated in the Kaustubha.

Even though, in the statement "cattle and horses are animals" (*paśavo go-aśvāḥ*), the mention of "animal-ness" (*paśutva*) is useless unless animal-ness already exists, and thus the word *apaśu* would be understood from the exclusion of the meaning of the word *paśu* as used through the secondary indication of "excellence," namely as the absence of excellence; [nevertheless...]

Nevertheless, for the sake of establishing a figurative (gauṇī) function, that cognition occurs precisely through the principle of the recollection of one related member [of a relation], and not by means of indication (lakṣaṇā).

Thus, first, the word *apaśu*, ending in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), denotes its meaning as "that which is different from a beast" by primary power (*śakti*) alone; subsequently, its figurative nature is to be established through its connection with qualities residing in that [referred object].

Therefore, the statement in the *Śāstradīpikā* that the word "apaśu" denotes objects such as jars and the like is consistent [with this view]. Indicating this very lack of satisfaction with the word "tu," [the author] presents the meaning shown by the authors of the *Nyāyasudhā* and others as being the opinion of the ancients, stating: "But in the opinion of the ancients..."
(Conclusion following the demonstration that figurative indication (*gauṇī*) is the cause for praise in other examples such as "non-sacrifice" and "non-food"):

Thus, in passages such as "That which is without *sāman* is indeed no sacrifice," although there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the sacrifice— unlike the case of the *sāman*— by which the excellence inherent in it would be brought to mind, [the same principle applies].

Nevertheless, in order to avoid this inconsistency, and because the term "yajña" is enjoined as a whole within the explanatory passages (arthavāda) of the injunctions such as "āgneyāhi," it is stated that one "makes it possessed of a *sāman*. Thus, by connecting the quality of being devoid of excellence— which pertains to the sacrifice— located in things like jars denoted by the word "ayajña" (non-sacrifice),
with the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites which are themselves sacrifices by nature, the term "ayajña" should be understood figuratively (*gauṇa*) even in reference to those very sacrifices.
As for what was stated in the *Kaustubha*— that its presentation [in the context] occurs because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunctions for the *Sāman*-based sacrifices—

that should be understood as referring to other examples, since this [text], being recited within the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* section, lacks a single syntactical connection with other sacrifices. The meaning of the passage, “That which is without the *Chandomas* is indeed not a *Sattra*,” is as follows:

By the injunction "it becomes twenty-fourfold," the first *chandoma* day is established as an *ukthya* sacrifice characterized by the *rathantara* *sāman* and having the twenty-fourfold *stoma*. By the injunction "it becomes forty-fourfold," the second *chandoma* day is established as an *ukthya* sacrifice characterized by the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* *sāmans* and having the forty-fourfold *stoma*.
By the injunction "it becomes forty-eightfold," the third *chandoma* day is established as an *ukthya* sacrifice characterized by the *bṛhat* *sāman* and having the forty-eightfold *stoma*.

Then, because the stomas are measured and defined by the *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *jagatī* meters through the equality of their numerical counts, they are designated as "metrical" (*chandoma*) based on this etymological derivation; thus, the sacrificial session (*satra*) consisting of these three *chandomas*— such as the fifteen-night rite (*pañcadaśarātra*) and others— is highly praised.

However, in the case of the fourteen-night sacrifice (*caturdaśarātra*), where the first day is the *prāyaṇīya*, the middle consists of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* and twelve days in direct and reverse order, and the final day is the *udayanīya*— thus, in this arrangement of days, because the *chandomas* are absent in the middle, the fourteen-night sacrifice, although it is a *satra*, is not a *satra* in the sense of possessing the excellence produced by the *chandomas* belonging to a *satra*; therefore, it is called a "satra" only figuratively.

Therefore, it should be understood that by means of this censure of the absence of meters and the praise of the constituent parts consisting of meters, there is a praise of the whole—the fifteen-night sacrifice—which is enjoined in the passage: "Those who, knowing thus, perform the fifteen-night sacrifice.

Thus, whether according to his own view or the view of the ancients, although there is a difference in the manner of communicating the excellence residing in the cow and the horse, there is no dispute whatsoever regarding the fact that the praise, which enters as the counter-correlative (pratiyogin), serves as the ground for the secondary sense (gauṇī); with this intention, he concludes with the words "sarvathā" (in every way).
Thus ends the investigation of examples of praise in the *Tatsiddhipeṭikā*.

— (Demonstrating the author of the *Bhāṣya*’s position that there is an injunction regarding the specific placement [of bricks] characterized by creation, preceded by an examination of the connection and an examination of the meaning of the term "creation" [in the preceding example]):

Having established in the previous case that [the passage] is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) due to its syntactic unity with another injunction and so forth, [the author] indicates the connection in the form of a counter-example— that where that [unity] does not exist, the status of being an injunction itself must be accepted in order to avoid purposelessness— and thus, even in the case of an injunction...
He provides an example to show that the purpose of the subsequent section is to state another ground for the secondary application [of a term]: "the *sṛṣṭis*," he says.

Although— since an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is impossible here and a prescriptive function is necessary, and since the piling (*cayana*) cannot be performed with bricks that are not laid down, the laying down (*upadhāna*) is established by the very fact that the injunction "one piles the fire-altar with bricks" would otherwise be inexplicable, both in its own form and as connected to the bricks— it is proper to enjoin the very substance of the *sṛṣṭi* (creation) formulas by way of restating the laying down, because the injunctive power has been transferred to the subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
Moreover, that [word "creation"] does not have the form of bricks themselves,
because it is not understood as having the nature of being the creation of bricks;

rather, by accepting that the word "creation"— which refers to the mantras of creation— is used metaphorically (lakṣaṇā) for the bricks which serve as the substrata for those very creations, [the mantra applies] to the bricks.
Even though they are denoted by the term "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*), since no specific distinction is understood as to which bricks among them are to be laid down with the *sṛṣṭi*-mantras—

and because the laying down of bricks in general is already established by the injunction for the bricks themselves, making it even more certain that this specific subset is connected to the laying down, such that a further injunction would be redundant— it follows by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that these mantras consist precisely of those characterized by the root *sṛj* (to create), such as "With three [bricks] he created the earth; Brahmā was created," and so forth.
