As for the argument by the ancients that— based on the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating "the *mantra* containing that [word] is the *upadhāna-mantra* for these" and "there is elision of the *matup* suffix in the case of bricks"— the bricks to be laid down with mantras denoting creation (*sṛṣṭi*) are [to be understood through] the elision of the *matup* suffix, that is incorrect; because if that were the case, there would result the simultaneous application (*prāpti*) of the elision of the *matup* suffix together with the suffix [itself], which is enjoined as being invariably connected (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*), as in the injunction "one lays down the *ṛtavyā* bricks."
Nor should it be argued that, even in your own view, the suffix *matup* would be unavoidable when there is an intention to express "mantra-hood";

for, while the elision of *matup* could be established through its inclusion in the section on *matup* by treating the elision of the *yat* suffix as merely Vedic (*chāndasa*), it is more appropriate—on account of parsimony—to assume the non-universality (*anityatā*) of the rule for *matup* itself, based on the statement of Pāṇini that "in the Veda, one follows the observed usage" (*dṛṣṭānuvidhiśchandasī*). Therefore...

It has been stated in the Kaustubha that, precisely because of the feminine gender [of the word *iṣṭakā*], the word *sṛṣṭi* refers to the bricks upon which the *sṛṣṭi-mantras* are to be placed, solely by way of secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

As for the objection that—since this mantra is already obtained here through both indicative power (*liṅga*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) just like other mantras—an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) of what is already obtained would result in the threefold defect (*traidoṣya*) and the futility of the recitation of the other mantras—that is not correct; for since this injunction operates even prior to the scriptural text (*śruti*) inferred from indicative power and context, it results effectively in an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*).

Since there is no possibility of the three defects [of over-extension, under-extension, and futility], and since the injunction can be justified as a restrictive rule (*parisaṅkhyā*) regarding the remaining items such as the "taking up" (*grahaṇa*), and since the other mantras can achieve their purpose by having the "taking up of bricks" (*iṣṭakā-grahaṇa*) as their subject— given that they lack any exclusive indicative mark (*liṅga*) for insertion—

the injunction is justified as being an injunction of the *sṛṣṭi*-mantras. Therefore, one need not resort to the view that the injunction refers to non-*sṛṣṭi* mantras, which would entail a secondary or figurative indication (*gauṇī-lakṣaṇā*).

Nevertheless, since both the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and the meaning of the subordinate word (*upapadārtha*) can potentially be established, the author of the *Bhāṣya* states his own final position (*siddhānta*)— namely, that "in that case" (*tatra ca*)— with the intention that, according to the principle of the section on the meaning of the verbal suffix (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇanyāya*), it is more appropriate to enjoin the meaning of the verbal root itself first for the sake of another purpose through implication (*ākṣepataḥ*).
(An examination of the purpose of the rule for laying down [the bricks]):
The word "eva" (only/just) indicates the refutation of the prima facie view regarding the previously mentioned rule of mantras.

He states—"by way of being a refinement of the bricks"—to show that although the laying down is already established by implication, it is prescribed again for this specific purpose because it cannot be considered a refinement of the bricks since the bricks are themselves the means to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Now, one might object: "Even if there is a difference in the primary acts, for the sake of fulfilling the requirement of simultaneity understood from the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*), it is more appropriate that the placing [of the bricks] be done collectively, just as the touching of the vessels is done according to one's capacity.
Anticipating this objection and in order to refute it, he states another purpose by pointing out an undesirable consequence: "And because it is implied by the sense (*ārthikatvāt*)."
He states that very point: "satitviti" (because it exists).

Since the act of placing [the bricks] in a specific arrangement (*vyūha*) is required for the purpose of the *upadhāna* (the act of laying down), and since it lacks the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) by virtue of being prescribed—unlike the case of plowing and so forth—and since there is no identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*) with the *cayanam* (the piling) because the latter has the *adhvaryu* as its agent; just as Devadatta’s status as the agent of cooking is established even when the kindling and such are performed by another, here too, even if the intermediate operation in the form of the *upadhāna* is performed by another, the *adhvaryu*’s agency in the *cayanam* remains logically possible. Therefore, because the *adhvaryu*’s agency is not necessarily obtained, it is necessary to enjoin it as an auxiliary (*aṅga*).

Consequently, because the subsidiary (aṅga) and the principal (pradhāna) share a single agent, that [agent] is established. For this very reason, it is not at all the purpose [of the injunction] to establish that the Adhvaryu is the agent by means of establishing his status as the subject of the designation "Adhvaryava"— as is the case with the injunction for spreading [the altar] and so forth—
since that is obtained simply from the fact that the piling (cayana) has the same agent.
Therefore, the meaning is that the purpose [of the statement] is precisely to establish the identity of the agent with that of the *cayana* (the piling of the altar).
(An exposition on the manner of grasping the *sṛṣṭi* and *asṛṣṭi* mantras by means of the term *sṛṣṭi*:

Although the term *sṛṣṭi* serves as the indicator of the subject (*uddeśya*) through its substantive portion and functions as a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the portion consisting of the *sṛṣṭi* mantras, those mantras are recited as seventeen, beginning with the introductory statement, "He lays down the *sṛṣṭis*," and continuing with, "With one [verse] they praised; progeny are produced," and so forth.

In this regard, just as there is a restatement (anuvāda) of the fourteen mantras recited in connection with the root *sṛj* (to create)—beginning with "They praised with three; Brahman was created"—because their status as subsidiaries is understood through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of creation supported by proximity (*sannidhāna*), so too [is there a restatement] of [the mantras]:
"Prajāpati was the overlord; they praised with twenty-seven; heaven and earth were obtained; the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas..."
He says:

"The phrase 'the word *sṛṣṭi* (creation),' etc., is a restatement of what is already established as an auxiliary element through proximity and other criteria, because the concluding statement—'When he lays down seventeen bricks'—applies to the first seventeen mantras of the three [sections], and thus even those mantras within the seventeen that bear the mark of creation (*sṛṣṭi*) are included. [Anuvyāyan was their overlord; they praised with thirty-three [verses]; the beings became pacified; Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin was the overlord. Thus, since the conclusion "when he lays down seventeen bricks" applies to the first seventeen mantras of the three [sections], it is a restatement of the fact that even those mantras among the seventeen containing the indicative marks of creation (*sṛṣṭi*) have attained the status of auxiliaries through proximity and so forth. This is what he says: "But the word *sṛṣṭi*... and so on.

By the word *mātra* (only), there is the exclusion of the bricks which serve as the qualificands (*viśeṣya*). Alternatively, it may be taken as referring to the entirety (*kārtsnya*) residing in the mantra. As for the question of how that term [“mantra”] can apply to something characterized by non-creation (*asṛṣṭi*), it is stated that this occurs through figurative usage (*gauṇī*).
The specific manner of this, however, will be demonstrated when taking up the introductory citations from other sections.
(The purpose of including the word "creation" [sṛṣṭi] in the mantra-selection):

This is a restatement (anuvāda); its purpose is for the sake of praise, namely that this laying down (upadhāna) is praiseworthy because it is performed with mantras characterized by creation (sṛṣṭivat), according to how they were created.

The expansion [of the sacrificial ground] is not inappropriate, as it serves as the basis for the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "He obtains everything exactly as it was created. This passage means that the sacrificer attains all those fruits proclaimed in the *anuvāka* as created by Brahmā, having cast aside obstacles caused by transgressions.
Thus, the mantra "O wide one, expand" (*uru pratha*), which cites the opening words of a mantra, is justified.
(An exposition of the Vārttikakāra’s position, preceded by an examination of the lack of internal consistency in the Bhāṣyakāra’s view, regarding the injunction of the mantra alone:

Having thus established the Bhāṣyakāra’s position, [the author] notes that according to this view, since only the act of placing (*upadhāna*) is enjoined in all the sentences, a distinction [between the acts] would result from repetition; furthermore, even though the act has been enjoined once, since it is an auxiliary to each brick, its repetition would be established for every individual brick. Therefore, [the opponent argues] the injunction must be repeated more than once.

Being dissatisfied because it would result in the [mantra] being purposeless, and considering the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the previously established rule for mantras to be the more logical one, he states another alternative view as expressed by the author of the *Vārttika*: "But the author of the *Vārttika*... and so forth.

(An examination of the intended meaning of the Vārttika regarding the injunction of the mantra alone, as maintained by the author of the Nyāyasudhā, which [actually] intends an injunction for the placing [of the bricks] qualified by the mantra): Here, the author of the Nyāyasudhā has described the intention of the Vārttika as being merely an injunction of the mantra alone—by way of a restatement of the placing [of the bricks] implied by the sense—in accordance with the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
That is incorrect.

Since it is understood from the accusative case that the bricks themselves are the objects [of the action], it is understood that the act of placing (*upadhāna*) is what is to be enjoined as the instrument; furthermore, since its result is obtained as before, there is no reason to deviate from that injunction.

For the fact that the mantra belongs to the Adhvaryu does not establish that the act of placing—which is implied by the purpose—must have the Adhvaryu as its agent, because it is possible for it to have a different agent, just like the *yājyā* verse.

Therefore, intending that it is appropriate for the Vārttika’s purport to lie precisely in the injunction regarding the placing [of the stone] as qualified by the mantra, he states another position: "mantraviśiṣṭa" (qualified by the mantra).

(An exposition of the position that there is an injunction for the insertion [upadhāna] qualified by the mantra, because other injunctions would otherwise be rendered meaningless and because it does not entail a violation of the principle of single-scope [ekaprasaratā]): "Therefore, that is the restriction."
By the word "niyama" (restriction), the three types of *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification)—namely, of the subsidiary (*śeṣa*), the principal (*śeṣin*), or both—is intended.

This is because, in the case of injunctions such as those for the *citriṇī* and *vajriṇī* bricks taught outside of a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), there is no possibility of enjoining the mantra alone by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the placement (*upadhāna*) implied by the distant injunction for piling (*cayana*).

Since this would involve connecting the mantra with the quality of the form of the consecrated bricks—which would result in it being a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*)—and since that is untenable due to the obstruction of the mantras already present within the context, one must resort to this [specification] as the only remaining alternative.
Since a rule for placing [the bricks] qualified by a mantra is necessary, it is likewise appropriate here as well to have a qualified injunction.

Nor should it be argued that—even so—the injunction for the other [mantras] remains useless because the purpose is accomplished by the single injunction for placing with a mantra alone; for while that consequence would follow if there were an injunction for mere placing, when the injunction is for placing qualified by a mantra, a distinction among the placings is established through the specific quality (the mantra), and thus there is no contingency of futility since distinct acts of placing are enjoined as qualified by their respective mantras.

Nor can it be argued that if the laying down of bricks to be laid with certain mantras is enjoined by a single sentence, the injunction for the laying down of bricks to be laid with other mantras would be rendered useless;
for such an injunction is necessary to establish that the act of laying is performed by the Adhvaryu priest in those other instances.

Therefore, although upon careful consideration of this natural implication one understands that all the bricks are to be consecrated by individual sentences, nevertheless, due to the force of the specific laying down qualified by each respective mantra to be enjoined, the determination of the particulars occurs within each individual sentence.
This is not untenable;

however, according to the view of the author of the Bhāṣya, since it would be impossible for the enjoined act of placing (*upadhāna*) to indicate a specific type of brick, it would follow that it applies to all bricks, making other injunctions redundant—a difficulty difficult to avoid. Therefore, it is more appropriate to regard this as an injunction for the act of placing qualified by its respective mantra.

The sense is that there is no risk of violating the principle of "single-directionality" (*ekaprasaratā*) in the injunction for laying down [the bricks] with mantras while aiming at the bricks, because although the bricks are the objects aimed at as defined by the act of laying down (*upadhāna*), they are not the objects aimed at as defined by the mantras; thus, that [violation] does not apply.

Furthermore, this statement regarding the contingency of other injunctions becoming redundant—made according to the view of the Bhāṣyakāra when the injunction pertains to the mere act of laying down—is stated relying on what was said by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*.

(An exposition of the author of the *Prakāśa*’s view— that there is an injunction for the rite of laying down (*upadhāna*) with reference to the bricks upon which the mantras are to be placed— demonstrated as being consistent with the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vārttika*, and other works, and as not rendering other injunctions redundant: In reality, since the status of the bricks as the objects of reference must be expressed by the very use of the word *sṛṣṭi*, it is difficult to establish the connection of the mantras— which are linked to the bricks by the force of being within a single compound— as qualifiers of the bricks, with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of laying them down.

Therefore, since there is no risk of a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) even when the mantras serve as qualifiers for the bricks which constitute the subject matter by virtue of being mentioned in a single word,

it is indeed possible for the other injunctions to function as sanctifications (saṃskāraka) of those [specific] bricks; for even if only the act of laying down (upadhāna) is enjoined as a sanctification for the bricks to be laid with the *sṛṣṭi*-mantras, the exclusion of bricks to be laid with other mantras is automatically established.

Therefore, it is observed that the authors of the Bhāṣya, the Vārttika, and others have raised the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—that all bricks would be affected—only against the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the mantra is enjoined with reference to the brick in general, because no specific brick is perceived therein;
this, however, does not apply even to the injunction for placing (*upadhāna*).
Nor can it be asked: "Why should not all bricks be those upon which the *sṛṣṭi*-mantras are to be placed?"

This should not be said; for, according to the principle stated in *Jaiminīya-sūtra* 1.4.29— "In cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) by means of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that begins with 'He lays down the creation-bricks' and concludes with 'Because he lays down seventeen bricks'"—
it is logical that this refers to the seventeen bricks to be laid down by the seventeen mantras.

Furthermore, although this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) was disregarded by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) because he accepted the injunctions for the primary signs of creation alone, it must necessarily be respected by the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*), who maintains that the injunction applies to the mantras themselves.
Otherwise, due to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*), it would be impossible to justify the employment of exactly seventeen bricks.

Likewise, even in the case of an injunction for placing [the bricks] qualified by the mantras, since there would otherwise follow the consequence of placing all the bricks, this explanatory passage must necessarily be accepted in order to establish the restriction that "only seventeen are to be placed with these other mantras."
It is to be worshipped.

And thus, because there is a connection between the seventeen sets of eight [bricks] and the creation-mantras, it is logical that the act of placing (*upadhāna*), though already enjoined by a single injunction through the mention of those same seventeen sets of eight, is prescribed again as a further rite for another purpose; therefore, there is no risk of redundancy.
What the author of the commentary has stated is indeed correct.

(An exposition of the intended meaning of the phrase "rendering other injunctions redundant" according to the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, and of the "justification for the injunction of mantras" according to the view of the Vārttikakāra, as maintained in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*: However, the venerable [author] states that, according to the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, prior to this injunction for laying down [the bricks], it is not established that the bricks are to be laid down with the *sṛṣṭi*-mantras; therefore, since they cannot be designated in that form, the word *sṛṣṭi* does not serve to designate the objects of the injunction by denoting the bricks.

Otherwise, how could the Commentator state that the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) serves as the indicator of the object to be enjoined (*uddeśya*), while simultaneously asserting that this word is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)?

Rather, it is precisely that laying down (*upadhāna*)—which is implied by the injunction for the piling of bricks (*iṣṭakā-karaṇaka-cayana-vidhi*) and is thus subject to being enjoined because it has already been previously established—that becomes the object to be enjoined (*uddeśyatva*).
This is because, once that laying down is understood as connected with the bricks, it is accepted as the basis for the injunction since it serves to sanctify the bricks already present.
Furthermore, since that form (rūpa) recurs even in all the bricks, the laying down of all of them is established; thus, the others would be redundant.

For this very reason, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) also results in being merely for the purpose of praising the seventeen bricks that constitute a part of that aggregate of bricks, because an injunction does not apply there when there is no ambiguity regarding its meaning.
Therefore, even the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) refers only to the mantras, just like the term "red turban" (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*).

When there is doubt as to how many "creation-mantras" there are, the concluding summary (*upasaṃhāra*) serves as the deciding factor; it does not, however, decide the nature of the bricks themselves when they are already free from doubt.

This is because, although an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) may determine the nature of the thing enjoined (*vidheya*) through its syntactic unity with the injunction (*vidhi*) in accordance with the praise, the determination of the nature of the subject (*uddeśya*) has never been observed to occur in such a manner.
Even though in the injunction for the carrying forward of the fire— “They carry it forward for two”— it is understood that it is by means of two alone,

and even though in the explanatory passage (arthavāda)— “The Varuṇapraghāsas and the Sākamedhas are the thighs of the sacrifice”— the two middle sections, which are praised as being the thighs, are perceived to be the instruments of movement,
a determination of the two intended objects is thus seen in the arthavāda.
Nevertheless, since there is no determination as to which two among the four [are intended], their status as determinants is appropriate;
however, because there is no doubt in the present case, they are simply non-determinant.

For this very reason, just as by the force of the placement accompanied by mantras being enjoined, in our view it is established that [the number] refers to seventeen bricks in the final conclusion (siddhānta).

Intending to show that since [the result] is established, the meditative worship (*upāsana*) mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not necessary therein, the author of the *Vārttika* has demonstrated—according to the view of the *Bhāṣyakāra*—both the resulting futility of other injunctions and the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of the mantras with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of laying down the bricks.

This very point is stated in the *Kaustubha*: "But in the view of the *Bhāṣyakāra*, because the laying down (*upadhāna*) which is to be enjoined lacks the capacity to indicate specific bricks, [there would be no need for the mantras]."

"Because it is untenable for [the injunction] to be a qualifier of the bricks, and because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) stating 'he lays down seventeen bricks'—once it is determined that the injunction refers to all bricks—is incapable of providing a definitive conclusion due to the absence of doubt, the other sentence would be purposeless; this is the distinction."

(An examination of another purpose for the injunction regarding mantras, namely their connection with the middle layer): In the fifth [chapter], in the section beginning with “But in the middle [layer], because of the scriptural statement, it is accompanied by the Brāhmaṇa,” there is the statement: “Whatever brick one recognizes as being accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa description, that one should place in the middle layer. This is because the verb *jānāti* preceded by the prefix *abhi-* denotes direct perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*).

Since it will be stated later that the bricks prescribed by direct Vedic injunction (pratyakṣabrāhmaṇa) have the middle layer (madhyamaciti) as their locus, he says "the middle" (madhyamā), indicating that this too may serve as another purpose here.
Since it will be stated in the fifth [section] that even the final placement of the *āgantus* occurs at the end, it is said [here] that it is "only in the last one.

Anticipating the objection—"In the absence of a prescription for the bricks in the Brāhmaṇa, how can there be the quality of being 'according to the Brāhmaṇa'?"—he refutes it by establishing the definition of "being according to the Brāhmaṇa" with the words: "perceptible... and so forth.
The passage beginning with "In that regard" has already been explained previously.

(An exposition of the contradiction with the ritual tradition regarding the connection of the *mantravidhāna* section with the middle layer, and the difficulty of avoiding it according to the Vārttikakāra’s view:
However, in the opinion of the Vārttikakāra, the contradiction arising from the performance of the *sṛṣṭi* bricks by the ritualists (*yājñika*) during the fourth layer is indeed difficult to avoid;

for, since this [section] would result in the connection of all *prāṇabhṛt* bricks with the middle layer alone, there would also be a contradiction with the performance of the first and subsequent layers.

If it is argued that in that case the general statement "whichever [vessel] it may be" is set aside by the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), then one should also consider that this is equally applicable to the *sṛṣṭi*-offerings as well.
(Conclusion of the Vārtika’s doctrine) He concludes the Vārtika’s doctrine with the words: "Therefore, etc."

Since the attainment of the fruit of the injunction occurs either in the portion consisting of the mantra or in the ritual application (upadhāna), therefore that very form is the reason; this is the meaning of the word "ataḥ" (therefore).

(Refutation of the view of the author of the *Prakāśa* following the *Śāstradīpikā*—that the secondary meaning (*gauṇārtha*) is the aggregate itself which is the locus of plurality—and the determination that the secondary meaning consists of the individual members of the aggregate themselves, by virtue of their connection with the quality of being based on an aggregate that is co-locus with the plurality of created things: And here [the question arises]: "What, then, is the quality (*guṇa*) in this case?"
"Bhūman" [means abundance]; for indeed, there is an abundance of creation within the collection of creations.

Even in the collection of both creation and non-creation, there is an abundance of creation in the section beginning with "They praised with one," and by virtue of this similarity, the word "creation" [is applied].

Thus, following the natural sense of the word "collection" (*samudāya*) found in the *Śāstradīpikā* text, and relying on the fact that abundance is a quality, just as abundance exists among the creations—

Likewise, regarding the claim by the authors of the *Prakāśa* that the secondary (gauṇī) meaning resides in the collection (*samudāya*) of "creation" and "non-creation" because such a collection is somehow connected to the object, and thus the secondary meaning belongs to the collection itself—

that is incorrect. This is because, at that time, the collection lacks a single unified meaning, and therefore its capacity to signify [the object] is untenable, except perhaps through the medium of its individual members (*samudāyin*).

Furthermore, even if that [substitution] were possible, since the entire collection as a whole would be enjoined as the instrument by virtue of its verbal nature, it would follow that the placing [of the bricks] should occur only once after the recitation of all the mantras.
Moreover, does the quality of "plurality" belong to the collection of *sṛṣṭi*-mantras themselves, or does it belong to the plurality residing in the substratum of that collection of *sṛṣṭi*-mantras?

In the first case, a plurality [of members] within the aggregate is impossible; in the second case, since the plurality residing in the aggregate exists only in the individual members, it is absent from the aggregate of both created and uncreated things, and thus the figurative nature of the aggregate's meaning is not established.
Now, if it is argued that the plurality residing in the created things alone constitutes some kind of connection there [to the aggregate], [the response follows].

In that case, there would be a contradiction with the fundamental text (mūlagrantha), which aims to establish that "plurality" (bhūman) resides in the aggregate of created things by stating, "for plurality exists in the aggregate of creation.

Therefore, in order to justify the status of being the instrument belonging to the individual members of that aggregate, it is appropriate to adopt the view stated by the author of the Nyāyasudhā: that the term [bhūman] applies figuratively to the individual members of both the created and uncreated aggregates by virtue of their connection to the quality of residing in an aggregate that is co-extensive with the plurality inherent in creation.

Nor should it be argued: "Since multiplicity exists even in the three mantras that do not involve creation—just as it does in those that do—let that [multiplicity] itself be the qualifying attribute; what is the point of further introducing the collection [of all three]? For [the rule applies] where, in the midst of many, there is the mention of two or one.
In that case, since that [individual] is impossible, it is necessary for [the individual] to enter into the whole (*bhūman*) in order to establish its status as a quality (*guṇatva*).
Nor is a single aggregate (*samudāya*) without proof;
for it is perceived through the employment of a single word within a single section (*anuvāka*) in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), namely: "that which consists of seventeen bricks."
Nor should it be argued: "Let the quality (guṇa) be simply the state of being based on a collection formed by creation;
what is the use of including multiplicity? For multiplicity, as perceived from the word "creation" itself, must necessarily be considered the quality.

And it is stated in the *Nyāyasudhā*: “Just as in other cases [the word ‘cow’ applies] due to similarity consisting in performing that function, here, because of the cognition of a multiplicity of creations arising from the word ‘creation,’ that [multiplicity] alone is the basis for its application.”

Therefore, since there is no contradiction in taking the word *gaṇa* (group) mentioned by the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) in the subsequent section— namely, in the statement “one should observe the group of mantras from the word ‘creation’”—

as referring merely to a collection; and since the word *samudāya* (aggregate) found in the *Śāstradīpikā* is justified as being intended merely to indicate those things alone that are capable of being construed with plurality, given that each individual [mantra] is incapable of being construed with plurality [if taken as a single unit].

Intending to show that the secondary (gauṇī) usage is appropriate only in those mantras where there is both the creation and non-creation of the constituent parts, he says: "The word 'creation' is supreme."

(The description of secondary figurative function [gauṇīvṛtti] even in the case of an injunction, as if it were an explanatory passage [arthavāda]): Since only explanatory passages were cited previously, and since the statement of the grounds for secondary figurative function was introduced in that very context, the objection might arise that it is inappropriate to state those grounds here regarding the word *sṛṣṭi*, which denotes the object of an injunction. To dispel this doubt, the term *para* is employed.

The meaning is that there is no inconsistency, because the Sūtra—without depending on the status of being an *arthavāda*—aims merely to state the grounds for its secondary (figurative) application (*gauṇīvṛtti*), and since those grounds are possible even with respect to what is enjoined here, they are not abandoned.

In cases such as *tatsiddhi* ("accomplishing that"), although there is an abandonment of the primary meaning due to the cognition of performing that function and so forth, the secondary (*gauṇī*) sense remains merely as a means because it is not defective; thus, there is no intended focus on the primary meaning. This is established by refuting the strength of the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) based on the principle that the secondary sense prevails when it exists in abundance (*bhūman*), rather than abandoning its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*).

In this case, however, since it is the collection of both the expressible and the inexpressible that constitutes the quality (*guṇa*), and since that [quality] exists as a distributed whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), it cannot acquire its own nature by abandoning one member of the collection; therefore, because there is no disparity—just as with the non-created verses (*asṛṣṭi*) included within that collection by virtue of being its constituent parts—there is also such [absence of disparity] regarding the created verses (*sṛṣṭi*).

Thus, in order to show the secondary (*gauṇī*) figurative sense which does not abandon its primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*), the word "created" (*sṛṣṭi*) is employed to indicate that the mantra pertains to both the created and the non-created.
Nor does this constitute a counter-argument for one who maintains the superiority of the concluding passage (upasaṃhāra);

for if the single word "creation" (sṛṣṭi) were taken in its primary sense, the other words praising non-creation would become redundant. Thus, by the principle of "the rejection of what is purposeless" (ānarthakyapratihata-nyāya), figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is accepted here, and since there is no sublation caused by the conclusion, it serves as the basis for the secondary (gauṇī) mode of operation.
The meaning is that it is a constituent of the secondary (gauṇī) function.
The purpose has not been stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the investigation into the illustration of the stages [of practice] within the *Tatsiddhipeṭikā*.

By demonstrating that the examples of sentences found in the three *prastāras* involve the inclusion of non-breathing beings (*aprāṇabhṛt*) and others based on the reason of "smallness" (*alpatva*) in words such as "breathing beings" (*prāṇabhṛt*), [the author] indicates a distinction between the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) by means of the word "but" (*tu*)—since they aim at different grounds for secondary figurative application (*gauṇīvṛtti*)—and shows the subject sentence: "The breathing beings... (*prāṇabhṛtaḥ*).
In this treatise, the three statements found in the first, second, and third *prastāra*s are also taken up collectively (*tantra*).
Among them, regarding the first *prastāra*:
"This one here is Bhuvah; his breath is the descendant of Bhuvah"; "Spring is the source of breath"; "I take hold of the breath for the sake of progeny."

Having enumerated these three [verses] containing the word *prāṇa*, there follows the placement of forty-seven other mantras not containing the word *prāṇa* according to the sequence of the ten directions. This is because they are enjoined through five successive cycles by injunctions such as, "He places one in front with the words 'This one is the earth in front'; verily, by these he establishes the breath (*prāṇa*)," and because of the concluding summary at the end: "He places them ten by ten."
The injunction for the laying down [of bricks] is: “He lays down the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks,” which refers to fifty bricks upon which mantras are placed.
Among the second and third layers, in the second layer, there is one mantra containing the word “breath” (*prāṇa*), namely, “Protect my breath.

Together with that, because of the application of the other four *prāṇabhṛt* bricks as they are recited, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) states: “He places the vital breaths in four [bricks] alone.”

Because of the hearing of the number five—due to the similarity with the number five residing in the seasons mentioned within another explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "five seasons"—there is an injunction for the laying down (*upadhāna*) of the bricks to be laid with five mantras, namely:

"He lays down the *prāṇabhṛts*. This is in contrast to the nine other mantras recited that do not contain the word *prāṇa*, which are taught alongside the single mantra containing the word *prāṇa*, namely "Protect my breath" (*prāṇaṃ me pāhi*), as found in the third [section].

In the sentence, “He places ten *prāṇabhṛt* bricks in front,” because of the application (*viniyoga*), the injunction for placement is “He places the *prāṇabhṛts*,” which refers to the ten bricks to be placed by means of the ten mantras.

By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), there is included the injunction “He places the *ajyānis*” (*ajyānīrupadadhāti*), which is the injunction for placing the bricks to be laid with four other mantras, together with the single mantra containing the term *ajyāni*: “The four paths that...”.

Therefore: although, because the word *prāṇabhṛt* does not occur in the mantras, its usage as a form ending in the suffix *matup*—by means of the elision of that suffix as prescribed by the sūtra "tadvānāsām" (Pāṇini 5.2.94)—is not possible in the same way as it is for the word *sṛṣṭi*; nevertheless, its application to the mantras and the bricks superposed with those mantras should be understood through the etymological derivation (*yoga*) "that which bears (*bibhrati*) the breath (*prāṇam*), i.e., the word 'breath' (*prāṇaśabdam*)," since they bear the word "breath" by means of the mantras. He shows another ground for its distinction from the earth: "smallness" (*alpatvam*).

In that case, by virtue of the quality of being the substratum of a collection that is co-extensive with the smallness of living beings, the term is used figuratively (*gauṇī*) with respect to all mantras that serve as the substratum for the collection of both living and non-living beings;
the meaning is that "smallness" is the cause [of the figurative usage] because it is included within that quality.
(An exposition on the quality of even a small degree of similarity:

Furthermore, although it has been accepted that the term *liṅgasamudāya* refers to a smallness of the denoted meaning in view of its secondary sense (*gauṇārtha*), where there is equality between both [the primary and secondary meanings],
as in the case of "only one umbrella-bearer," [it applies].

In that context, since there is no absence of the indication of a secondary sense, it should be explained that even similarity—which is distinct from "abundance" (bhūman)—serves as an indicator for establishing the coexistence of the characteristic marks.

(An exposition of the author’s own established doctrine following the *Nyāyasudhā*, concerning the fact that the word *liṅgasamavāya* refers to the connection with a mark rather than the connection with smallness):

In reality, however, because the word *liṅga* in the Sūtra signifies a "mark," and because it is stated that the mere connection with that [mark] is the cause [of the application of the name], smallness (*alpatva*) is not the cause.
For this very reason, just as "abundance" (*bhūman*) was the cause in the preceding case, here smallness is neither mentioned by the author of the Sūtras nor is it the object of that cognition.

Therefore, in the *Nyāyasudhā*, having explained the word *liṅga* as meaning "mark" (*cihna*), it is stated: "But because from the word *prāṇabhṛt* there arises only the cognition of the presence of the marks of a living being (*prāṇabhṛt-liṅga-samavāya*), and that alone is the ground for its application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), it is mentioned separately";
thus, the word *alpa* found in the Vārttika is explained as being intended to demonstrate the cognition [of the class] without regard for numerical plurality (*bhūyastva*).
But not by way of referring to the cause [of the name].

Therefore, since the connection with the mark itself is the object of cognition, it is logical that the quality consists precisely in its being based on the whole, like the word "prāṇa" which is based on the connection with the mark.
As before.

The meaning is that the application here also of the various views stated in the passage concerning creation, as well as the demonstration of the figurative sense (gauna-artha) in which the constituent parts do not abandon their own primary meanings, should be understood.

(Regarding the futility of the objection concerning figurative usage and its refutation: It should not be argued that—“In the case of the mantras concerning creation and the sustainers of life (*prāṇabhṛt*), since figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) itself is appropriate through the relation of being the locus of the group in which they are included—just as in the common worldly expression ‘the umbrella-bearers are going’—why resort to figurative usage (*gauṇī*)?

This is because it has already been shown that such [figurative usage] is necessary for the purpose of producing a cognition characterized by those specific qualities, based on the connection with qualities rather than the literal meaning, and motivated by similarity.

(An investigation into the inclusion of concealment (*pracchannatva*) and other factors within similarity (*sārūpya*) and so forth, thereby establishing the sixfold nature of the grounds for figurative usage (*gauṇī*), as well as the fact that the establishment of that [figurative usage] and other such factors serve as its indicators.

Since the status of figurative usage based on concealment and the like is accepted in the *Ākara* (the *Mahābhāṣya*) in passages such as "The mind is a thief" (*stenaṃ manaḥ*), and because that [concealment] is perceptible (*pratyakṣagrāhya*).
Intending to include [the term] within some form of similarity (*sārūpya*), he concludes the manner of figurative application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) with the words "Thus" (*evam*).

Although the *Tatsiddhipeṭikā* is devoted solely to explaining the manner of figurative application (*gauṇīvṛtti*) for the purpose of establishing that [the passage] is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*)—by virtue of its consisting of a name, a quality-injunction (*guṇavidhi*), and an explanatory statement—it does not aim to determine the specific types of grounds for figurative usage. Therefore, even if "being hidden" (*pracchannatva*) and so forth are not included here, there is no deficiency;
this is the intention behind not employing the particle *eva* immediately after the six terms.
Thus ends the example of the co-inherence of marks (*liṅgasamavāya*) in the *Tatsiddhipeṭikā*.
Thus concludes the section on the basket of established tenets.

— (The indication of the subject matter preceded by an examination of the connection with the *Pādādhyāya*): Having established that even words such as *udbhid*, which are included within an injunction, possess authority by way of being names (*nāmadheya*) that delimit the meaning of the verbal root— distinct from the injunction itself— the opportunity now arises to establish the authority of words contained within explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), which function as glorifiers (*stāvaka*).

Since the inquiry into the existence or non-existence of validity occurs even without reference to a specific ritual injunction (*vidhi*), the connection to the [specific] chapter and section (*pādādhyāyasaṅgati*) remains intact due to its status as a distinct topic (*prakaraṇāntaratva*); thus, although there is no immediate sequential connection (*anantara-saṅgati*), there is no deficiency.

Without explicitly stating the doubt (*saṃśaya*)—as it is obvious—the author cites a sentence found in the context of the *kāṭhaka-cayana* ritual and states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) as follows: "The [objects] are smeared" (*aktāḥ*).
Small stones mixed with earth are the meaning of the term "śarkarā."
(The demonstration that, because the accomplishment of understanding is finalized by the injunction itself, there is no dependence upon an explanatory passage [arthavāda]:

Although it would have been appropriate to introduce only the arthavāda as the subject matter for determining the authority regarding a doubtful meaning, the injunction was also introduced in order to make known that it is the subject matter of that [determination].
For, by the mere statement "anointed" (*aktā*), the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*) determines all objects implied in a general sense, and thus there is no contradiction with the arthavādas.

Intending to show that when there is a connection [of the words] through mutual expectancy alone, as in the case of a modified subsidiary (vaikṛtāṅga), it is proper to assume that [the meaning] in accordance with the injunction itself, he says:
"by the word 'aktāḥ' (smeared)."

(It is not in the section on *arthavādas* that it is understood that an injunction is incomplete without an *arthavāda*, but rather here; thus follows the presentation of the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa]: "The application of collyrium is to be done with any one of [substances] such as ghee").

Although the prima facie view does not arise here based on the completion of the injunction [without an *arthavāda*], because in the section on *arthavādas* the possibility of an injunction being complete without the *arthavāda* put forward by the opponent was already refuted.

Nevertheless, since the established conclusion (siddhānta) regarding that [Arthavāda section] is reached through its connection with another [injunction] via mutual expectancy— by merely excluding the possibility of it ending as a mere Arthavāda even in the absence of an injunction—

there is no purpose in refuting the conclusion that it ends as an injunction. Thus, there is no fault, because by refuting the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) based on its ending as an injunction right here, one establishes the conclusion that it does not so end.

In this context, since only the rule for the pillow (*upadhāna*) is understood through the mention of sugar (*śarkarā*), there might arise a doubt that there is no injunction regarding the substance to be used as the means for the collyrium (*añjana*). To dispel this, [the author] says "by the word *aktā* (smeared). Since the general [substance] mentioned by that term cannot be performed as it stands, the injunction—which requires a specific [substance]—cannot reach completion without depending on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that provides the necessary incentive (*prarocanā*). Therefore, because its connection with that [explanatory passage] is indispensable, the specific [substance] is appropriately supplied by that very passage; thus, the general [term] does not [require a separate injunction].

The phrase "because it has been determined" (*nirṇītatvāt*) is stated to dispel the doubt that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding ointment might be established by any one of several specific substances such as ghee, since it is possible for a general term to imply a specific instance.

The meaning is that because the injunction itself implies the incitement to action (*prarocanā*), it is logically possible for the general term to imply the specific; thus, since the conclusion is reached without depending on an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the matter is "determined."

(Refutation of the requirement for an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) even for a rule already determined, by means of the principle of the section on the beginning [*upakramādhikaraṇa*]): Now, one might object: "Even for a rule that has been determined, it is possible to interpret it otherwise in accordance with an explanatory passage, following the principle of the section on the beginning of the Veda. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By that which stands in the conclusion. The meaning is that while there is a discrepancy here because the situation is reversed—namely, that in that [other] case the rule standing in the conclusion is interpreted otherwise in accordance with the explanatory passage standing in the beginning—the two cases are not identical.

(An examination of the superiority of injunctions based on primacy, etc. By way of illustration, because it is stated that the *arthavāda* occurs in the concluding portion [of the passage], the superiority of the injunction is established through its contrast [with the *arthavāda*]: [the injunction possesses] primacy because it functions according to its own literal meaning; non-contradiction with what has already arisen because it is heard first; and the quality of referring to an unestablished object because it conveys a meaning not yet known.

Having thus indicated the three reasons for the weakness of the *arthavāda*— namely, its non-literal nature due to being merely laudatory (*stāvakatva*), its status as a subsequent element due to being heard last (*caramaśrutatva*), and its character as a restatement of what is already established (*prāptārthānuvāditva*) because its meaning has already arisen— it is shown that this constitutes a triad of reasons for its inferiority. Furthermore, although there is a restriction (*saṃkoca*) of the injunction "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*), which prescribes animals in general, in accordance with the wording of the mantra "recite for the omentum and fat of the goat" (*chāgasya vapāyā medaso 'nubrūhi*), this does not constitute an illustration of that [rule].

In this context, the term "by means of the explanatory passage" (*arthavādena*) is stated to indicate that there would otherwise result the fault of redundancy, since it has been established in the final section of the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭhāntye*) that injunctions (*vidhi*) and mantras share a single objective through syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*).
Thus, the meaning is that it is not proper to accept a restriction of the injunction based on an explanatory passage that is here connected with it only through word-unity (*padaikavākyatā*).
(Refutation of the superiority of arthavādas by means of the "Kāṃsyabhojinī" maxim):

Now, one might object that, according to the "Kāṃsyabhojinī" maxim, the injunction itself should conform to the subordinate arthavādas; to dispel this doubt, the term "restriction" (saṅkoca) is employed.
This applies where the principal [injunction] is not in the least degree contradicted by the subordinate injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).

In that very case, the analogy of the one who eats from a bronze vessel applies; however, in the present context, because it would result in a sublation consisting of the contraction of the primary [rule], that analogy does not apply.

(Just as the Agnihotra and other rites, being accomplished through the knowledge of the sacred fires (*agni-vidyā*), are restricted to the three higher castes in accordance with that requirement, so too, since the injunction is established by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), any attempt to interpret the injunction otherwise in conformity with it is refuted. By this, [the following objection] is also rejected: "Just as the Agnihotra and other rites—which are accomplished through the knowledge of the sacred fires—are restricted to the three higher castes in accordance with that requirement, so here too, because the injunction is established by the *arthavāda*, there should likewise be a restriction of its scope in accordance with it."

In cases where a primary element cannot be accomplished without a certain subsidiary, and that subsidiary is itself implied by the context, one may indeed accept a restriction of the primary element to conform to it; however, in this instance, even without an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the injunctive power of the injunction itself can be established by assuming an inherent capacity for inducement (*prarocanā*). Therefore, there is no dependence on such an explanatory passage.
(An exposition on how, in accordance with the subsidiary mantra, there is no restriction of the injunction following the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), just as in the case of the Soma-draught):

Therefore, just as in the case of the Soma-draught performed with the mantra "I take thee for Indra accompanied by the Vasus," even though the draught is accomplished by that Aindra-mantra, its performance is possible through recollection by means of meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth in the absence of the mantra; thus, the primary act is not [restricted] in accordance with the subsidiary mantra.

The restriction of the mention of "Soma" to the scope of only those sacrifices where Indra is the principal deity will be explained in the third book, in the section titled "On account of the specification of a particular gender.
Similarly, the meaning here is that it is not proper to restrict the primary injunction in accordance with a subordinate explanatory passage (arthavāda).
(An examination of how the grasping of an unsettled meaning occurs due to an ambiguous word within a sūtra):
"The determination of a doubtful meaning."

Although, since the doubt is impossible— given that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) there is certainty regarding the general form, and in the final view (*siddhānta*) there is certainty regarding the fixed form due to syntactic unity—
it would not be appropriate to conclude with the denial of non-authoritativeness for a doubtful meaning (as intended by the proponent of the final view) because the meaning is not actually doubtful;
nevertheless, the word "doubtful" (*sandigdha*) used in the Sūtra intends merely the perception of an unsettled meaning, as it refers solely to the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*).

The meaning is this: that cognition which arises is refuted by the proponent through a systematic rule established by the remainder of the sentence, and it is by means of that [refutation] that the authoritative status of the *arthavāda* is sought to be proven;
however, it is precisely the cognition of an unsettled meaning that is logical.

(Regarding the justification for the word *ghṛta* [clarified butter] occurring in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—whether as being figurative (*gauṇa*), indicative (*lāk�aṇika*), or suggestive (*upalakṣaṇa*)—in the prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa]: The word *ghṛta*, however, is figurative because it possesses the quality of being a means for anointing (*añjana-sādhanatva*) with respect to the general substance understood from the injunction; or else, it is simply indicative by virtue of its connection to the status of being a means for anointing.
Alternatively, since ghee is also obtained by way of a general rule, [the statement] refers exclusively to ghee alone through a partial restatement (avayutyānuvāda).

Even if the commendatory character of the injunction is assumed regarding the general portion, it is purely commendatory because such a character is not assumed regarding the specific portion consisting of ghee.

(The conclusion of the prima facie view that "there is indication by the word *ghṛta* due to the presence of the indicative mark," following the refutation of the views of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* and others: "one may apply any [substance] whatsoever as the ointment.
As for the explanation provided here by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* and others—that there is figurative usage (*gauṇatva*) because of the presence of the indicative mark—that is to be disregarded;

for since there is no evidence for the existence of a single collective group of substances used as means for the ointment, it is impossible for any one of them to be the means, and thus a connection with the mark of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) cannot be established.
By this, the claim that even "smallness" (*alpatva*) serves as a cause in this context is refuted.

And thus, since a general term cannot serve as a defining characteristic because it is subject to deviation from the particular, whereas a particular term that does not deviate from the general can properly define the general, it is established by implication (through *ākṣepa*)—even prior to the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—that "one applies collyrium with whatever [substance]," for the explanatory passage connects clarified butter (*ghṛta*) specifically as the means of applying collyrium. (The introduction of the final conclusion is that it is not the case that "one applies collyrium with whatever [substance] at random"). Since practical usage is impossible through a mere generality, the injunction must imply all the particulars in order to fulfill its function as an instigator of performance.

First, since the requirement for a specific object is satisfied by the arthavāda itself— which, being necessary as a provider of encouragement (*prarocanā*), forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunction— it is not proper to establish that the injunction has as its purport only the specific object provided by that arthavāda; for such a restriction is accepted in common practice and is required precisely for the sake of its own meaning.

Therefore, in this case, there is no sublation of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) found in the conclusion by means of the opening statement through the characteristic of annulment (*upamarda-lakṣaṇa-bādha*), nor is there a sublation of the opening statement by means of the conclusion through the characteristic of restriction (*saṅkoca-lakṣaṇa-bādha*).
And thus, the power of the injunction to provide incentive (*prarocanā-śakti*) is not even postulated.

Intending to show that once the sentence has been completed by the recommendation of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), there is no risk of the fault of "splitting the sentence" (*vākya-bheda*)—which would result from either an imaginary recommendation of oil (*taila*) and so forth, or from the consequence of the sentence acquiring the meaning of another sentence—the author states the final conclusion: "Because the injunction is non-distinct. (*vidher aviśeṣāt*).

Since the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is justified by its very requirement for an introductory application (*upakrama*), the word "clarified butter" (*ghṛta*) does not imply [the inclusion of] oil and the like.

Just as in cases such as "one praises with a *ṛc*," where the censure of the *ṛc* serves as a means to reach the subject matter of the injunction "one should praise with a *sāman*," so too here there is a commonality of subject matter;
it is precisely for this reason that the injunction "one should sacrifice with *soma*" is rendered free from further expectancy.
In this case, there is no restriction [of the injunction] to the mere offering to Indra on account of following the subordinate mantras.

And thus, since the connection of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is established by the very requirement of the introductory section (*upakrama*), the acceptance of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word "clarified butter" (*ghṛta*) therein is both purposeless and without proof; so he says: "of that which stands in the conclusion," [meaning] "because of having a single subject matter."

For example, regarding the passage in an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), "When they praise with the Ṛg-veda, the Asuras follow after; when they praise with the Sāman, the Asuras do not follow after," a doubt arises as to whether the Ṛg-veda is here censured as being the cause for the arrival of the Asuras, or whether it is praised as the means for bringing even those Asuras—who cannot otherwise be subdued—under control. This doubt is resolved by the injunction immediately following concerning the Sāman, "He who, knowing thus, praises with the Sāman," which indicates that the Ṛg-veda is mentioned solely for the purpose of praising the Sāman intended to be enjoined.

It is determined that [the passage] is censured, because its status as a single syntactical unit is only possible if it is intent upon that censure; this will be stated in the ninth book, in the section beginning with "due to the unity of purpose" (*arthakatvāt*).
Likewise, here too, in accordance with the requirement of a single subject matter, even an injunction whose meaning is doubtful is established by means of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
And it has been said in the *Vārttika* on that very point: "The operation of an injunction and a praise is always held to have a common object."
Therefore, that which is doubtful in one instance is determined by the other.
By the term *saṃdigdha* (ambiguous), both that which is unsettled and that which concerns a doubtful object are intended.
For this very reason, there is the determination [of the deity] as Aditi in cases such as "The *āditya* [offering] is the *prāyaṇīya*; that which belongs to Agni... and so forth.
And in this Sūtra, by the word *saṃdigdha*, both that doubt which is well-known and that cognition of an unsettled meaning are intended as being of the nature of doubt.

Because there is no difference in their nature as being non-determinative, it has been stated in the *Vyavahārādhikaraṇa-vārtika*: "In all cases where there is doubt, the determination will indeed be made by means of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*); therefore, no separate investigation need be undertaken here."

Therefore, even in cases where there is doubt regarding the base (prakṛti) or the suffix (pratyaya) prior to the cognition of the established meaning, the determination is made by means of the explanatory passage (arthavāda).
For example, in the case of "ādityaḥ prāyaṇīyaḥ," is the word *aditi* the base for the secondary derivative (taddhita), or is it *āditya*?

In the case of doubt— where there is no difference in form due to the suffix *ṇya* prescribed by the rule "dityadityādityapatyuttarapadāṇṇya," and where both are equally established as deities in passages such as "He digs with Aditi herself" and "He approaches that very Āditya with his own portion"— nevertheless, on account of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "They enclosed themselves within Aditi," it is [the word] *Aditi* alone [that is intended].
It is the determination according to reality.
For example, as in the case of "the eight-potherd [cake] for Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*) and "for Agni Kṛttikā" (*agnaye kṛttikābhyaḥ*), where the word *agni* is used in the singular;

and in such passages as "may those Agnis grant us wealth" (*te asmā agnayo draviṇaṃ dadata*), where it is used in the plural. Thus, there is a distinction between the singular and plural endings regarding the designation of the deity by the word *agni*.

In a case of doubt, by means of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "O Agni, be firm," it is determined that the singular form is the original (*prakṛti*); the same should be inferred in other cases as well.
And thus, where in an injunction the very form of the word cannot be determined from its base (*prakṛti*) or its suffix (*pratyaya*), [the *arthavāda* serves to establish it].
Even when there are multiple possible meanings, the intended meaning in the context at hand is not determined;

in such cases, the determination of the specific meaning is to be established by this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*) through an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) capable of determining the distinction,
and not by the strength of the concluding summary (*upasaṃhāra*).
Furthermore, conducting an investigation again in that very tantra for the purpose of dispelling excessive doubt is not contradictory.

For this very reason, regarding the injunction "he puts on a garment," the Commentator has stated here that when there is uncertainty due to the perception of an unsettled meaning, the specific determination is made by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "This linen cloth, indeed, belongs to all the deities."

However, if it were argued that even in cases such as "the deerskin or the garment" (*ajinaṃ vāso vā*), because no one perceives an indefinite meaning from the word "garment" (*vāsas*), the term is here also considered doubtful due to the perception of an indefinite meaning by the word "garment," even then there is no fault; for since the perception of an indefinite meaning is possible precisely through its denoting a general category (*sāmānya*), doubtfulness indeed remains possible.
(The body of this section consists precisely in the fact that injunction (*vidhi*) and praise (*stuti*) have a single object;
nevertheless, the conclusion is reached by demonstrating that the body of the *vedopakrama* section is also necessary, and so forth.

For this very reason, here, because a specific injunction (*viśeṣapravṛttavidhi*) requires a specific detail in order to fulfill its capacity to motivate performance (*anuṣṭhāpakatva*), there is a requirement for a specific detail.
Since in the world one does not observe a dependence on that [specific detail] in the case of rules for giving clothing and so forth,
it is nevertheless not untenable to determine a specific [detail] through an implied expectancy even of the injunction, in order to establish that the injunction and the eulogy have the same object.
For this very reason:
"Or [it is so] because of being a part of the conceptualization, by implication" (Jaimini 1.4.30).

Here, by the ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) of the words "part of the conceptualization" (*kalpanaikadeśa*) found in the subsequent sūtra, there is a restriction of the conceptualization due to the completion of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). Why is this so?
Because they share a single locus (*ekadeśatvāt*):
those two, namely the injunction (*vidhi*) and the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), by which a single object (*eka-artha*) is indicated or established, are the "two parts" (*ekadeśau*);
their state (*bhāva*), that is, their essence (*tattva*), is the fact of having a single object (*ekaviṣayatva*).

Therefore, intending that the author of the Sūtras has presented "having the same object" (*ekaviṣayatva*) as the primary reason, the Venerable Teacher (Pūjyapāda) stated, "and because having the same object is necessary due to its pervasiveness over all cases.

This is so even in the case of the statement, "The *Ṛg* [Veda] is recited loudly," where the subject matter of this section applies because the Vedas are intended, precisely on the basis of the necessity of having the same object.

Nevertheless, because the words such as *ṛk* and so forth have their meanings determined therein, there is no ambiguity; and since they belong to the injunctive portion [of the text], it is improper to interpret them otherwise. Thus, the removal of this further objection will be demonstrated by the superior force of the opening statement (*upakrama*), and therefore there is no redundancy.

Nor is there a problem even if an injunction that has already reached its completion requires a supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*)—provided it lacks syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*)—but in the case of one that has indeed reached completion...

The sense is that even the sixth chapter's first section (adhikaraṇa), which was undertaken to dispel the further doubt that a restriction of the injunction itself would be appropriate, would likewise be rendered useless.
He concludes the established doctrine (siddhānta) with the word "yuktam" (it is proper).

By the word "api" (also/even), the connection with what was previously stated is indicated. Therefore, by postulating a word denoting clarified butter (*ghṛta*) which is brought to mind through an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and intending that this very [butter] is the means for the application of collyrium, he says: "The application of collyrium is indeed with clarified butter."
Thus ends the fourteenth section concerning anger.
—(Since the connection between the chapter, section, and topic is clear and the prima facie view is easily refuted, the author begins with the established conclusion.
He cites the scriptural passage concerning the subject matter: "With the *sruc*... and so forth.

The connection with the chapter (*adhyāya-saṅgati*) is established because, just as in the previous case, here too an injunction—whose authority has been demonstrated by its capacity to be supported by the power of the injunction itself—is used to determine a doubtful meaning; the connection with the section (*pāda-saṅgati*) is established because, like the word *udbhid* and others, there is an inquiry into the validity or invalidity of the word *dravya* and so forth which is inferred through that capacity;

and the connection by way of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa-saṅgati*) is established because the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises due to the absence of a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), which was stated in the preceding section as the cause for determination.

Alternatively, since [the topic] has been introduced as having a doubtful scope, and because the immediate connection in the form of a *prasaṅga* (reductio) is clear and thus need not be explicitly stated,

[the author proceeds as follows]: likewise, in the case of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), since no specific liquid substance to be offered is heard of in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), and because the Veda would fall into the state of being non-authoritative due to its dependence on the capacity of things known through other means of knowledge, [it follows that] in the case of the *sruc* (ladle), which has a sharp-pointed tip, for the purpose of offering a solid substance...
Furthermore, since capacity is possible even when cutting pieces of flesh from the *stru* and *hastau* by means of the support of iron,

and since the capacity for cutting liquid substances with a hollow-edged *svadhiti* is also possible, and because the requirement for auxiliary aids does not undermine the status of the instrument as being independent, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) remains unsettled; moreover, it is impossible for an injunction to prescribe the performance of what is impossible to carry out.
The capacity of all injunctions is established because otherwise their function as motivators would be contradicted.

Furthermore, although the capacity of that which is to be depended upon—such as the determination of words and word-meanings—is cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the authority of the Veda is nonetheless justified because its subject matter is not known from any other source. This is because it is impossible to cut a piece of meat with a *struva* ladle, even if its tip is sharp.
Even when a mere wooden sword (*svadhiti*) is sufficient for the extraction of the sacrificial portion from a liquid substance, there is no evidence to assume that iron serves as an auxiliary;

furthermore, to assume such a thing would be difficult to reconcile with the contradiction of [iron] being an independent means of accomplishment. Moreover, in the case of the *svadhiti* and other implements, it is logical to accept only those things established by worldly usage, according to the principle of the section on the "antelope skin and garment" (*ajinavāsodhikaraṇanyāya*). Since the creation of a hollow cavity is otherwise impossible, a fixed restriction (*vyavasthā*) alone is appropriate—thus should this [objection] be easily refuted.
And having considered this, he states the established conclusion itself: "of the injunction," etc.
(An exposition on how the application of the stated principles occurs because an injunction is free from doubt):

It has been stated that the authority for determining a doubtful matter—specifically the determination of the relationship between the subsidiary and the principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*)—resides solely in the injunction itself, assisted by the capacity [of the words].

Therefore, in cases such as the injunctions for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, where there is no doubt because it is certain—by means of the eleven-fold principle already mentioned—that the injunction refers to an action qualified by all its subsidiaries, [the aforementioned rule applies].

In this regard, it has been indicated by way of contrast that, in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, there is no assumption of a restriction [of the rule] to only those things that can be performed, according to one's capacity.
This is expressed by the word "saṃhatam" (in combination).
The meaning is "hard."
(Description of the sentence-meaning by refuting the view of the ancient masters who advocate the mental supply [adhyāhāra] of words such as "liquid" [drava]):

In this context, it is the injunction (*vidhi*) itself, aided by semantic competency (*sāmarthya*), that conveys that the *sruc* and other implements are the means for the act of offering (*avadāna*). Since this would otherwise be inexplicable, there arises the postulation of a specific object such as "liquid. However, because such a postulated meaning is not directly expressed by the words (*aśabda*), its connection with the verbal meaning is untenable; therefore, one must supply words such as "liquid" [into the sentence].

Having explained the word *ekadeśa* (part) in the Sūtra as referring to being a "remainder of a sentence" (*vākyaśeṣa*) in the sense of being a portion of the Veda, the ancient commentators stated that the words "liquid" (*drava*) and so forth must be supplied.

However, [the author] shows the meaning of the sentence without such a supply, intending that there is no purpose for it, since the status of the liquid and other substances as the objects of the act of cutting (*avadāna*) is established by the word *avadyati* itself, which is supported by the force of the context (*sāmarthya*).
This is indicated by the phrase *ataśca*.
(An exposition of one's own established doctrine due to the necessity of supplying words such as "liquid" [drava]):
In reality, however, because a collection of words that conveys a single unified meaning— characterized by its constituent parts being syntactically expectant when analyzed—

is what constitutes a sentence, and because such a sentence, being incomplete due to its expectancy in the absence of words expressing the implied word-meanings that serve as the means for understanding the sentence-meaning, remains deficient.

It should be understood that because it is impossible for [the root] *ava-dā* to convey a specific meaning, and because the verb *ava-dā*, which requires an object, remains incomplete without a word denoting an object, the necessary supply (*adhyāhāra*) of a word signifying a liquid or similar substance is indeed mandatory.
(Through implication, there is a determination of the specific thing enjoined just as there is of the specific thing intended; for this purpose, another example is presented:

Just as in the injunction "they lead forth two [fires]," there is a determination regarding the specific object intended by virtue of the principle stated in the preceding section, so too, having explained the determination of the specific object intended through implication, one should likewise explain here the determination of the specific thing enjoined through implication.
To demonstrate this further, he provides another example, beginning with "In this way."

(An Analysis of the Meaning of *Añjali*) Here too, since the meaning of the word *añjali* is observed in contexts such as addressing a deity or making a request to be granted a boon when the two hands are joined with their fingers completely interlaced; and since in expressions such as "one should drink with the *añjali*" (*añjalinā pibet*), its meaning is seen to consist in being open enough to be capable of holding water; [this applies] in the case of the homa-mantra as well.

The meaning is that, in case of doubt, the determination [of the ritual] arises from the force of the injunction for the *añjali* (handful-offering) which has the *saktu* (groats) and the *homa* (oblation) as its intended objects;
otherwise, the taking up of the groats would be untenable.

As for the term "having the nature of being opened" (*vyākośātmaka*), since the prefix *vi-* signifies "expanded" and the prefix *ā-* signifies "slight," the meaning is "having the form of a bud, which is a slightly opened calyx."

(An examination of how the axe is obtained through the cutting of the sacrificial cake, based on the fact that capacity alone, when accompanied by "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), is the determinative factor):
In this case, the determination is not made by capacity alone;
for if it were so, since the axe also possesses the capacity for the cutting of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), the restriction to the cutting of meat would remain unestablished.

However, it should be understood that because [the requirement] is satisfied by that [injunction] together with the impossibility of any other explanation (*anyathānupapatti*), and since the cutting of the *puroḍāśa* can also be accomplished by hand, the assumption that the axe is the motivator (*prayojaka*) must not be made, as the logical necessity (*arthāpatti*) is exhausted.

(An interpretation of the section containing the word *vā* as constituting a separate topical discussion: Although, by the force of employing the word *vā* in the sūtra *arthād vā*, it appears that there is indeed a single topical discussion (*aikādhikaraṇya*) due to its forming a single syntactical unit with the preceding sūtra;

nevertheless, because it is impossible for a single word occurring within one sentence to have two distinct meanings, and considering that there is no obstacle to the application of the recurring term to a different meaning in another sentence, [the author] treats it as a separate topical discussion.
The explanations of the Bhāṣyakāra and others should be consulted.

Furthermore, in this sentence, the word *pradātavye* is also cited in the Kaustubha; its meaning should be understood as the Vaiśvānara fire that arises from the burning of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) spread upon the Great Altar (*mahāvedi*) by the brand of the Āhavanīya fire.
He concludes the subject matter of the chapter with the words: "Thus, therefore."

Although the name (*nāmadheya*) occurs in proximity to injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras, it is mentioned first in the sequence of exposition by taking into account its treatment in the *Smṛti* and traditional practice (*ācāra*).

Since the establishment of the object of knowledge (*meyasiddhi*) depends upon the means of knowledge (*māna*), he declares the subject matter of the forthcoming chapters—by way of indicating that the necessary determination of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇanirūpaṇa*) serves as the cause for what follows—in order to prevent the students from becoming despondent:
"Henceforth... (*ataḥparam*).

Since the knowledge of the essential nature [of the Veda] is established by the two aforementioned definitions of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the phrase "by way of difference, etc. (*bhedādinā*) is stated in order to avoid the charge that the subsequent investigation is redundant.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), other forms such as being the object of the rules of application (*viniyoga*) and performance (*prayoga*) are also included.
Whatever commentary I have composed upon this chapter of profound meaning,
its accomplishment is due to the grace of my teacher and not to the power of my own intellect.
Thus it is said.
Thus ends the fifteenth section, concerning the capacity of the meaning.

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikāprabhāvalī*, composed by Śambhubhaṭṭa, the ornament of the scholarly world and disciple of the venerable Khaṇḍadeva, who was preeminent among those who have crossed the vast ocean of the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā.
Thus ends the first chapter.
